units.la: Si quando mecum ipse considero, Ecclesiae originem & progressum, qualem B. Lucas in altero Euangeliorum libro, qui De Actis Apostolorum inscribitur, accurate descripsit: considero autem saepius, vti par est: videre mihi videor, beata illa tempora patrum nostrorum, quibus in medio Antichristi regno Regnum sibi asseruit CHRISTVS, & operaⅴsus obscurorum quorundam hominum, qui καθάρματα mundi habebantur, vt in prima Ecclesiae aetate Hierosolymitanorum, ita in eius senatu Romanensium Pontificum indomitam potentiam subiugauit.
units.tr: When I sometimes consider with myself the origin and progress of the Church, which St Luke described accurately in the second book of the Gospels, the one entitled The Acts of the Apostles, and I consider it often, as is fitting, I seem to see those blessed times of our fathers, when Christ claimed his kingdom in the midst of the kingdom of Antichrist. Through the work of certain obscure men, who were regarded as the scum of the world, he subdued the untamed power of the Roman pontiffs in the Church's senate, just as in the first age of the Church he had subdued that of the Jerusalemites.

units.la: Rursum autem si quando in memoriam mihi revoco tot florentissimarum Asiae Ecclesiarum, Hierosolymitanae, Antiochenae, Ephesinae, Corinthiacae, & aliarum, quas ipsi Apostoli plantarunt, viri Apostolici exco-luerunt, et constantissimi Martyres suo sanguine irrigârunt, horrendam τὸ προσ‑‑ολα‑ρίαν, non possum non male omittari etiam no‑stræ; non quidem propter fatalem quamdam ut Imperij ita & Ecclesiæ periodum, ut Sa‑pientibus quibusdam placet; sed propter fa‑tualem nostram ingratitudinem.
units.tr: Again, when I call to mind so many most flourishing churches of Asia, Jerusalem, Antioch, Ephesus, Corinth and others, which the Apostles themselves planted, apostolic men tended, and most constant martyrs watered with their blood, I cannot help dreading the horrible apostasy for our own churches as well. I do not mean this because of some fated period for Empire and Church, as certain wise men think, but because of our own fated ingratitude.

units.la: Itaque ut prior illa Contemplatio, ex re‑cordatione prisca tum pietatis, tum inde e‑natæ beatitatis, animum meum suaviter adfi‑cit, & diuino quodam gaudio perfundit: ita altera hæc, ex metu venturæ abominationis & desolationis in Israel, eundem mœrorem & tristitiam fere non conficit, & miserè confundit.
units.tr: So, as that earlier contemplation, drawing on the old memory of piety and the blessedness that grew from it, sweetly stirs my mind and fills it with a certain divine joy, so this other one, from fear of the coming abomination and desolation in Israel, almost wears down the same grief and sadness and wretchedly overwhelms me.

units.la: Unum me recreat, in his angustijs consti‑tutum, quòd clementissimum Deum, promis‑sionum suarum nunquam non memorem, sic‑cut primitiuæ Ecclesiæ per Apostolos, mox secuturam abominationem maturè prædixit, & ut sibi caveant, ac quomodo præmonuit electos: ita nos quoque nostræ Ecclesiæ ruinam ab exemplo prioris, (cuius ideleam, sine incunabula utriusq; respicias, sive e quæ utrique à Satana obiecta fuerunt obstaculala, piè semper est æmulata) prænosse & præcavere revelle firmiter confido.
units.tr: One thing refreshes me in these straits: that the most merciful God, never unmindful of his promises, just as he foretold through the Apostles the abomination soon to follow in the primitive Church, and how they should guard themselves, and how he forewarned the elect, so I firmly trust we too can foreknow and guard against the ruin of our Church from the example of the former one. Its beginnings, or the obstacles Satan threw against both, have always been piously imitated.

units.la: Unde nec à præsentis Operis argumen‑to, quod Primitiuæ Ecclesiæ fatum continet,
units.tr: Hence I have not judged this foreign to the subject of the present work, which contains the fate of the primitive Church,

units.la: nec a pio vestro in propaganda propugnanda, que veritate studio, immo nec a studijs meis Iatro-Theologicis alienum iudicaui, si quod imminnenti nobis malo remedium ⟨Greek⟩ λαxτικον maturè adferre conarer. Si enim patriæ, in qua ad mortem nati sumus, prima debemus pietatis officia, vtique Ecclesiæ, in qua ad vitam renati, omnia atque adeò nos ipsos mœs debere fatebimur.
units.tr: nor to your pious zeal in spreading and defending the truth, nor even to my iatro-theological studies, if I try to bring an early remedy against the impending evil. For if we owe the first duties of piety to the fatherland in which we were born to die, we must surely confess that we owe everything, and indeed ourselves, to the Church, in which we were reborn to life.

units.la: At quia non ea in me est vel dicendi vis & facultas, vel etiam authoritas tanta, qua quemquam permouere possim, ne dum communem causam multum promouere, plaa cet ab aliis Apostolorum hæc documenta re- peterre. In his verò B. Lucas duo præcipua Ecclesiæ conseruandæ præsidia & fulcra no- bis proponit: Vnum Commune, Concordiam & vnitatem, quam propter primitiuam Ec- clesiam omnibus terrori & admirationi su- isse scribit: alterum Proprium, Episcopo- rum & præsidum vigilantiam.
units.tr: But since I have neither such power and facility in speaking, nor such authority that I could move anyone, much less greatly advance the common cause, it is good to seek these teachings from the writings of other Apostles. In these, St Luke sets before us two chief supports and buttresses for preserving the Church. One is common: concord and unity, which he writes made the primitive Church a terror and wonder to all. The other is proper: the vigilance of bishops and presidents.

units.la: Ac de Concordia quidem & pace Ecclesiastica alias copiosè diximus; & sub finem huius Operis repetemus: De Episcoporum & Præsidum vigilantia audiamus electum illud Dei organon, Gentium adeoque no- strum Apostolum (cuius Oratio, vt de Periele scripsit Eupolis, cum delectatione aculeos relinquit in animis auditorum) ad Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ presbyteros graviter differentem: Attendite vos ipsos & totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus constituit Episcopos, ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam proprio illo sanguine acquisiuit. Ego enim hoc noui post discessum meum lupos graues, non parcentes gregi ingressuros esse in Vos: & ex vobis ipsis exoritu ros qui loquantur perversa, vt discipulos post se abstrahant.
units.tr: We have spoken at length elsewhere about concord and ecclesiastical peace, and will return to it at the end of this work. Let us hear about the vigilance of bishops and presidents from that chosen instrument of God, the apostle of the Gentiles and therefore of us. His speech, as Eupolis wrote of Pericles, leaves stings in the minds of its hearers with delight. He addresses the elders of the Ephesian Church gravely: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood. For I know this, that after my departure grievous wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among yourselves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw disciples away after them."

units.la: Est quidem hæc exigua pars præstantissimæ Orationis, quam ad Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ presbyteros, postremò ab illa discessurus, habuit Apostolus: sed qua graphice admodum & pathetice, Cygnæa tanquam voce, & futuram unitatis Ecclesiæ distractionem, & aduersus hanc unicè profuturum remedium nobis demonstrat. Quæ vt me ... ius intelligantur singula, tum ... huius hortationis, tum etiam argumenta, quibus suum propositum Apostolus confirmat & vt singula nostris temporibus & moribus inseruiant, ordine considerabimus.
units.tr: This is indeed a small part of the most excellent speech which the Apostle gave to the elders of the Ephesian Church when he was at last about to leave them. Yet in it, vividly and movingly, with a voice like a swan's, he shows us both the future division of the Church and the one remedy that will profit us against it. So that each point may be properly understood, we shall consider in order both the parts of this exhortation and the arguments by which the Apostle confirms his purpose, and how each may serve our own times and manners.

units.la: Oratio tota est παραινετικη, qua Apostolus cum suo exemplo proposito, tum multis rationibus hortatur presbyteros, vt magna cum fide, studio & vigilantia suo munere nere fungantur. Attendite,inquit, Vos & vniuersum gregem. Attendere iubet, vel vt Graece dicam σχέσιν, id est, animum mentemq; adhibere, & mtente cauere, ne in eo quod tui est Officij aberres & decipiaris. Et hoc σωθῆναι in omnibus functionibus & actionibus huius vitae requiritur, quas qui dem cum laude obire velis. Sic aeger medicorum praecepta attendit, ne quid contra illa agat: Sic viator, ne a via aberret: sic athleta pro corona decertaturus, summopere cauet, ne quid eorum vel omittat vel committat, quae agonotheta praescripsit aut prohibuit. Ita agricolae, pastores, milites, architecti & caeteri artifices attendunt, ne quid temere contra artis suae praescripta faciant. Parinunc ratione Paulus, Presbyteros hortatur, & ab eis postulat, vt suum munus attente, rite ac legitime obeant; & ad hoc perficiendum hortatur, vt Attendant primum seipsos, deinde, vniuersum gregem.
units.tr: The whole speech is paraenetic, in which the Apostle, setting forth his own example and offering many reasons, exhorts the elders to discharge their office with great faith, zeal and vigilance. "Take heed," he says, "to yourselves and to the whole flock." He bids them attend, or, to speak in Greek, [προσοχήν], that is, to apply mind and attention, and to take care with a watchful mind that you do not stray from, or be deceived in, what belongs to your office. This attentiveness is required in all the functions and actions of this life, for anyone who wishes to perform them with credit. So a sick man heeds the physician's instructions, lest he act against them; a traveller, lest he wander from the road; an athlete about to contend for the crown takes great care neither to omit nor to commit anything the president of the games has prescribed or forbidden. Likewise farmers, shepherds, soldiers, architects and other craftsmen take heed, lest they rashly do anything against the rules of their art. So now Paul, by reasoning, exhorts the elders and asks of them that they discharge their office attentively, properly and lawfully. To bring this about, he urges them to attend first to themselves, and then to the whole flock.

units.la: Etsi vero omnium fidelium munus est, vt quisque seipsum attendat, quia vnicuique vitae suae ratio erit reddenda in magno illo & catholico iudicio: & CHRISTVS ipse filu-tarum & prudentium virginum parabola, aliorum fidem & pietatem nobis nihil profuturam, si ipsi fide & pietate destituti simus,
units.tr: Although it is the duty of all believers that each should attend to himself, since each will have to render an account of his life at that great and universal judgment, and Christ himself clearly teaches in the parable of the foolish and wise virgins that the faith and piety of others will profit us nothing if we ourselves lack faith and piety,

units.la: Matt. 25. 1. luculenter doceat; attamen præter communem illam attentionem aliquid amplius ab Episcopis requirit Apostolus, ut nimirum non ipsi solùm probè instructi sint & confirmati in fide; verùm & alios tum doctrina tum vitæ exemplo ad pietatem erudiant.
units.tr: Matt. 25. 1. Yet beyond that common attentiveness the Apostle requires something more of bishops: that they themselves should not only be well instructed and confirmed in the faith, but also train others to piety, both by their teaching and by the example of their lives.

units.la: Itaque Attentio illa duo præcipit Episcopis, ad pascendum gregem adprimè necessaria, Doctrinæ puritatem, & in ea tum proponenda tum etiam propugnanda, indefessum studium: & Vitæ integritatem. Ex quibus illa, absolutè necessaria est ad pascendum gregem; quia est unicum illud pabulum quo ad vitam æternam nutriuntur omnes CHRISTI: hæc, propter exemplum. Illa, pura erit & sana, si ex scripturis confirmetur: hæc, integra & sancta, si secundùm easdem conformetur, ita ut nihil agant in omni vita, cuius ratione ex ijs reddere non possint. Nihil est enim quod minus ferendum sit, ut Ciceronis verbis utar, quàm rationem ab altero vitæ reposcere eum, qui non possit reddere suæ. Quid quòd Episcopus ignavus et degener, non sibi solum, sed & universo gregi exitio est. Neq; enim adeò facilè naphta ignem, aër fœtores concipit, quàm Superiorum vitiis animi plebis inficiuntur. Huiusmodi enim magistri Pastores
units.tr: So this attentiveness enjoins on bishops two things most necessary for feeding the flock: purity of doctrine, with tireless zeal both in setting it forth and in defending it; and integrity of life. The former is absolutely necessary for feeding the flock, because it is the sole food by which all of Christ's people are nourished to eternal life; the latter is needed for the sake of example. The former will be pure and sound if it is confirmed from Scripture; the latter will be whole and holy if it is conformed to the same, so that they do nothing in their whole life for which they cannot render an account from it. For, to use Cicero's words, nothing is less bearable than to demand an account of life from one who cannot give an account of his own. Moreover, an idle and degenerate bishop is a ruin not only to himself but to the whole flock. Fire does not catch so easily from naphtha, nor air from a stench, as the minds of the common people are infected by the vices of their superiors. For such teachers, ministers...

units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Pastores multis quidem prosunt dicendo quae non faciunt, (vt Augustinus monet) sed longè pluribus prodesse ent faciendo quae dicunt. Abundant enim, qui malae vitae defensionem ex ipsis suis Praepositis & Doctoribus quaerunt, respondentes cordeo suo, atque dicentes, Quod mihi praecipis, cur ipse non facis? Ita fit ut eum non obedienter audiant qui se ipse non audit, & Dei Verbum, quod eis praedicatur, simul cum ipso praedicatore contemnant. Ideo Nazianzenus, magnus ille Theologus graviter admodum alloquitur Episcopum, [illegible, ~1 letters] Μὴ διδάσκειν, ἢ διδάσκειν τῷ τρόπῳ Μὴ τῇ μὲν γλώσσῃ, τῇ δ' ἀπωθεῖσθαι χείροιν Ἡ τῷ δὲ σιωπῇ λέγειν, πρότερον ἂ δεῖ Γεαφέως διδάσκει τὸ πλεῖον τοῖς ἐκ τῶν ποιῶν.
units.tr: Pastors indeed benefit many by saying what they do not do (as Augustine warns), but they benefit far more by doing what they say. For there are many who seek a defence of a bad life from their own superiors and teachers, answering in their own hearts and saying, "Why do you not do yourself what you order me to do?" Thus it happens that they do not obediently hear the one who does not listen to himself, and they despise the Word of God that is preached to them together with the preacher himself. Hence Nazianzen, that great theologian, addresses a bishop very seriously: "Either do not teach, or teach by your conduct: not with your tongue while you push away with your hands, nor by keeping silent while your deeds speak more than your words." [Μὴ διδάσκειν, ἢ διδάσκειν τῷ τρόπῳ. Μὴ τῇ μὲν γλώσσῃ, τῇ δ' ἀπωθεῖσθαι χείροιν. Ἡ τῷ δὲ σιωπῇ λέγειν, πρότερον ἂ δεῖ.]

units.la: Vel non doceto, vel doceto moribus: Hac ne trahens manu repellas altera. Verbis egebit, sanctius viuens, minus Pictor tabellis comprobatur editis.
units.tr: Either do not teach, or teach by your conduct: lest, while holding the one hand, you push away the other with the hand. A man who lives more holily will need fewer words; a painter is judged less by the pictures he has put on display.

units.la: Sed grauius adhuc & vehementius D. Ambrosius, seuerus adeo & sincerus morum uitaeque Censor, vt ne Imperatori quidem Theodosio, Thessalonicensis imusie persequuto, pepercerit in huiusmodi atactus , muehitur: Vides, inquit, dimissiones? Nihil in
units.tr: But even more severely and vehemently did Saint Ambrose, so strict and sincere a censor of morals and of life, that he spared not even the emperor Theodosius, though he had massacred the Thessalonians, in such faults, he exclaims: "Do you see the laxity? Nothing in

units.la: {*}sacerdotibus plebeium requiri, nihil popula-re, nihil commune cum studio atque vsu in-conditae multitudinis? Sobriam a turbis gra-uitatem, seriam vitam, singulare pondus di-gnitas sibi vendicat Sacerdotalis. Quomodo enim potest obseruari a populo, qui nihil ha-bet secretum a populo, nihil dispar a multitu-dine? Quid in te miretur si sua in te recogno-scat, si nihil in te aspiciat quod ultra se mue-niat, si quae in se erubescit, in te quem reueren-du arbitratur inueniat? Quod Ethnicus Poe-ta animaduertentes valde Ethice pronuntiat, Quis ruleri t Grachos de seditione quaerentes? Quis coelum terrae non miscebat, & mare coelo, Si fur displiceat Verri, si homicida Miloni, Clodius accusat moechos, Catilina Cethegum, In tabulam Syllae si dicanr discipuli tres?
units.tr: ...of the priests should be plebeian, nothing popular, nothing in common with the pursuits and practices of the unrestrained multitude? Sober gravity set apart from the crowd, a serious life, and a singular weight of dignity belong to the priestly office. For how can he be observed by the people who has nothing hidden from the people, nothing different from the multitude? What will they admire in you, if they recognise their own faults in you, if they see nothing in you that rises above themselves, if they find in you, whom they think they should revere, the things of which they are ashamed in themselves? The heathen poet, noticing this, rightly says in his moral way: "Who could endure the Gracchi complaining about sedition? Who would not have mixed heaven with earth and sea with heaven, if the thief displeased Verres, the murderer Milo, Clodius accuses adulterers, Catiline Cethegus, if three pupils were to speak against the tablet of Sulla?"

units.la: Nec vero se duntaxat vitamq; suam attendet Minister, sed, quod Paulus alibi praecipit, familiae suae curam habebit, sedulo cauens, ne quod a domesticis scandalum oriatur, & propter ipsos vniuersum ministerium & doctrina vilescat, quod tempore Heli fa-ctum fuisse legimus; & hodierno die hinc in, de fieri dolemus. Nam si quis propriae domui praeesse nescit, quomodo Ecclesiam Dei cura-bit? Cogitet igitur quisq;, se non modo Chri-stianum, sed Christianorum pastorem in ex-cellentiori loco constitutum esse, vt aliis prae-luceat. Est.
units.tr: Nor shall the minister look only to his own life and conduct; rather, as Paul elsewhere instructs, he shall take care of his household, carefully guarding lest a scandal arise from his own people, and because of them the whole ministry and doctrine be held in contempt, as we read was done in the time of Eli, and as we grieve is still happening today. For if anyone does not know how to rule his own house, how will he care for the Church of God? Let each one therefore consider that he is set not only as a Christian, but as the pastor of Christians, in a more prominent place, so that he may shine before others. It is.
Titus 1. ... 1 Sam. 2. ... 2 Tim. 3.

units.la: PRAEFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Est autem elegans allegoria in oratione Apostoli, qua gregem ποίμνιον, attendere in bet Episcopos. Hoc enim verbo exponit, qualem attentionem in Episcopo requirat. Vt enim pastor bonus in laeta pascua deducit gregem, & die noctu salutem eius & incolumitatem procurat, atque adeo vitam ipsam ponit pro ouibus: ita pastores ouium Christi at tentos & vigiles esse oportet in procuranda incolumitate gregis sui. Neque in deserta traditionum humanarum post se abducere oues; sed in laeta pascua Verbi Diuini, ad exortum Solis iustitiae, eas deducere; perdi tas quaerere; propulsatas vi & tyrannide, reducere; contritas obligare; infirmas, roborare; pingues & ferocientes, pedo cohercere. Denique non vnius aut alterius rationem habe re; sed attendere vniuersum gregem. Neque enim bonum pastorem dixero, qui plenas lacte oues mulget ac tondet, macilentas vero & aegras luporum praedam esse finit: Neque bonum Episcopum, qui diuites atque potentes studiose sectatur; pauperum vero & afflictorum nullam rationem habet. Nam in CHRISTO IESV non est Iudaeus aut Graecus, non mas aut foemina, non seruus aut liber, non diues aut pauper. Qui noua creatura est, hic est ouis CHRISTI, in numero gregis. gis sanctli, cuiuscunque aetatis aut artis, nationis aut conditionis fuerit. Hic grex ministris commissus est, hunc attendere iubet Apostolus.
units.tr: There is an elegant allegory in the Apostle's words, where he calls the flock ποίμνιον [poimnion] and bids the bishops to attend to it. By this word he sets out the kind of care he requires in a bishop. A good shepherd leads his flock into rich pastures, watches over their safety and well-being by day and by night, and even lays down his life for the sheep. So the shepherds of Christ's sheep must be attentive and watchful in securing the safety of their flock. They must not lead the sheep away after them into the barren wilderness of human traditions, but lead them into the rich pastures of the divine Word, toward the rising of the Sun of righteousness. They must seek out the lost, bring back those driven off by violence and tyranny, bind up the broken, strengthen the weak, and restrain the fat and the wild. In short, they must not consider the interests of one or two sheep only, but must attend to the whole flock. I would not call a shepherd good if he milks and shears the full-fed sheep but lets the thin and sick become the prey of wolves. Nor is a bishop good if he eagerly courts the rich and powerful and takes no account of the poor and afflicted. For in Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither male nor female, neither slave nor free, neither rich nor poor. Whoever is a new creature is a sheep of Christ, in the number of the holy flock, whatever his age, craft, nation or condition. This flock has been entrusted to the ministers, and the Apostle orders them to attend to it.

units.la: VERVM ne quis Hierarchiam Romanam hic somniet, & omne pascendi gregis ius & officium solis ministris Verbi, Magistratibus Christianis exclusis, superciliose adscribat, quae de illis modo diximus, eadem de his cum ratione intelligenda esse vel magnus ille Pastor ovium docet, qui iam ante per Prophetam Reges Ecclesiae nutricios fore & populi sui pastores praedixit; & Paulus ipse, qui Presbyteros ante vocavit, quos hic Episcopos vocat, innuens illud ἐπισκοπεῖν non solum de Verbi ministris, sed & reliquis presbyteris, quibus Ecclesiae gubernacula (ut pote sub Magistratu gentili) tum temporis erant commissa, ac proinde vel imprimis de Magistratu Christiano accipiendum esse. Nam ut ministrorum est non nisi veram & sanam doctrinam proponere, & erroribus ac erroribus sese opponere; ita magistratuum est officium, non nisi fidos & bonos pastores praeponere gregi; & fures ac mercenarios mature deponere. Ut ministrorum est utraque manu, doctrina nimirum & vita aedificare Ecclesiam sibi commissam; ita & magistratuum, non solum
units.tr: But lest anyone dream here of a Roman hierarchy, and haughtily claim for the ministers of the Word alone, with the Christian magistrates excluded, the whole right and duty of feeding the flock, we must understand with judgment that what we have just said of the ministers must be understood in the same way of the magistrates as well. That great Shepherd of the sheep teaches this, who already through the Prophet foretold that kings would be nursing fathers of the Church and shepherds of his people. And Paul himself, who calls them elders, and whom here he calls bishops, shows that the word ἐπισκοπεῖν [episkopein] is to be taken not only of the ministers of the Word but also of the other elders, to whom the governance of the Church was then committed (since they lived under a pagan magistracy), and therefore especially of the Christian magistrate. For just as it is the duty of the ministers to set forth only true and sound doctrine, and to oppose themselves to errors and errors, so it is the duty of magistrates to set over the flock only faithful and good shepherds, and to remove thieves and hirelings promptly. As it is the duty of the ministers to build up the Church committed to them with both hands, namely by doctrine and by life, so it is also the duty of magistrates, not only by the fairness of their rule but also by readiness to obey, to go before the people of God. Finally, to say it in one word: as it is the duty of ministers to attend to themselves and to the flock, so it is the duty of magistrates to attend to themselves and to the Law.

units.la: Heb. 13.10. Isa. 49. solum imperij æquitate, sed & obedientiæ promptitudine præire populo Dei. Denique vt vno verbo dicam, vt minstrorum est, Attendere seipsos & gregem; ita & magistratuum, seipsos & Legem.
units.tr: Heb. 13.10. Isa. 49. But this is the sense, this the aim of the Apostolic address. Because neither the ministers always attend closely enough to doctrine, nor the magistrates with them to discipline, he directs and sharpens his exhortation with arguments drawn from their office, from the dignity of the Church, and from the necessity of avoiding great dangers.

units.la: Atque hic statu est, hic scopus Orationis Apostolicæ. Hunc quia nec ministri semper in doctrina, nec cum iis magistratus in discipli na, satis attendunt, Exhortationem suam intendit et acuit rationibus, ab ipsorum officio, ab Ecclesiæ dignitate, & a necessario, sine periculorum magnitudine, petitis.
units.tr: This is the main point, the aim of the Apostle's address. Since ministers do not always attend to it in teaching, nor magistrates along with them in discipline, he sharpens and presses his exhortation with arguments drawn from their office, from the dignity of the Church, and from necessity and the great dangers involved.

units.la: PRIMAM ita proponit Apostolus, vt & authorem vocationis ipsorum, & finem exponat: Spiritus sanctus, inquit, posuit vos Episcopos ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei.
units.tr: FIRST, the Apostle sets out the matter so as to explain both the author of their calling and its purpose: "The Holy Spirit, he says, has made you bishops to feed the Church of God."

units.la: Vocatio ad ministerium & Magistratum (li benter enim conjungo, quæ Deus, distincta li cet, in veteri populo & legibus & exemplo conjunctissima esse voluit) non est hominum sed Dei, licet in electione utriusque horum opera utatur Deus. Nam in Ecclesia alios quidem constituit Episcopos, alios prophetas, alios potestates: Et omnis potestas est a Suprema illa Potestate. Itaque cum et illi dispensatores sint mysteriorum Dei & hi, ministeriorum: Illi, Cooperarij Dei, hi, Vicarij, requiritur vt fidus quisque reperiatur, a singulis enim
units.tr: The call to the ministry and to the magistracy (for I gladly join them, since God wished them to be most closely joined in the ancient people, both in laws and in example, though they are distinct) is not of men but of God, although God uses human work in the choosing of both. For in the Church he appoints some as bishops, others as prophets, others as powers; and every power is from that supreme Power. Therefore, since the former are stewards of the mysteries of God and the latter of his ministries, the former as fellow workers with God and the latter as his vicars, it is required that each one be found faithful; for from each

units.la: Ioh. 19. 11. Rom. 13. 1. 1. Cor. 4. rationem reposcet is, cuius nec iudicium falle-re quisquam potest, nec effugere sententiam Qui rerumpub. rationes administrant, si quid interuerterint, peculatus reisunt, sed tamen amicorum opeet opera, opibus item suis non raro immunes euadunt, at in Ecclesiastica ad ministratione, iustissimo iudici ratio est red-denda, qui neque donis, ut αὐταρκείας, neque fauore & gratia, ut ἀπροσωπολήπτως, ne-que eloquentiae vi, ut χαριδλιογνώστης, a in-sto abducipotest. Omnino ergo attentos esse oportet; qui huic rationem reddituri sunt.
units.tr: he will demand an account, whom no one can deceive in judgment or escape from his sentence. Those who administer the affairs of the commonwealth, if they embezzle anything, are liable for theft, yet they often escape through the efforts and help of friends, and are often immune through their own wealth. But in ecclesiastical administration an account must be rendered to the most just Judge, who cannot be drawn aside from what is right by gifts, as [αὐταρκείας], nor by favour and partiality, as [ἀπροσωπολήπτως], nor by the power of eloquence, as [χαριδλιογνώστης]. It is altogether necessary, therefore, for those who are going to render an account for this to be attentive. 1. Cor. 4.

units.la: Neq; vero vel ministri sibi persuadeant, se conspe-ctu periculi magnitudine, posse silere; vel Magistratus, in gratiam mundi a cæpta Ecclesiarum reformatione aut suscepto patrocinio resilere. Qui enim manum aratro admo-litur, & in tergum respicit, indignus est qui Christi minister vocetur. Ionas Dominum fugit Tharsis, sed non effugit: quum in mare abiectus, & à Cete immanißima Bellua inte-ger deglutitus, Diuinæ vocationi sero quidem, at serio, obedire discit & desiderat. Pla-to turpe dicit esse militistationem, in qua ab Imperatore sit collocatus deserere; et iure Ca-strensi in desertores Capitis pœna aut saltem diminutio iuste decernitur; qua igitur ignomi-nia, aut quibus supplicijs dignus iudicabitur, quæ qui stationem suam in qua à summo Imperatore locatus est, vel segnitie vel metu deserit? Est quidem prudentiæ signum, in periculis viribus suis non nimium sidere, sed earum propter imbecillitatē diffidere Deo, incredulitatu. Quin potius cogitet quisque, se à Deo in hoc munere constitutū, ipsius auxilio nunquam destitutum iri. Ieremias Vates vaticinandi munus ob pueritiam cum detrectaret, audit à Iehoua: Ne dicito, puer sum: sed ad quæcunq; misero te, ito: & quæcunq; præcepero tibi, loquitor. Ne timeto ab istis, nam adsum tibi ad eripiendum te. Et Apostoli rudes quidē & idiotæ vocati sunt à Domino, sed non emissi nisi instructissimi. Sic Salomon puer quidē Rex constituitur, sed mox Sapientia cœlitus instruitur.
units.tr: Nor let the ministers persuade themselves that they may keep silent because of the magnitude of the danger, or the magistrates draw back, for the sake of the world, from the reformation of the Churches once begun or from the patronage once undertaken. For whoever puts his hand to the plough and looks back is unworthy to be called a minister of Christ. Jonah fled from the Lord to Tarshish, but did not escape; cast into the sea and swallowed whole by a huge whale, he learns and desires to obey the divine call, late indeed, but earnestly. Plato says it is a shameful thing to desert a military post in which a commander has placed one; and by camp law, capital punishment, or at least loss of rank, is justly decreed against deserters. What disgrace, then, or what punishments will he be judged worthy of, who deserts his post, in which the supreme Commander has placed him, through sloth or fear? It is indeed a sign of prudence not to trust too much in one's own strength in dangers, but it is unbelief to distrust God on account of one's weakness. Rather, let each consider that he has been placed in this office by God, and will never be left without his help. When the prophet Jeremiah shrank from the office of prophesying because of his youth, he hears from Jehovah: "Do not say, I am a boy; but go wherever I send you, and speak whatever I command you. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to rescue you." And the Apostles, indeed rude and unlearned, were called by the Lord, but were not sent out until they were thoroughly equipped. So Solomon, a boy, was made king, but soon wisdom was given him from heaven.

units.la: Etsi autem hodie, quando Euangelium in vniuersum orbem propagatum est, & Ecclesiæ constitutæ, Credentes non repentino Spiritus S. afflatu extraordinariis donis illustrantur, illis tamen non omnino destituuntur. Nam eadem nobis laborantibus & orantibus consfert Deus, qui vel Ethnico teste, laborib. omnia vendit. Siue enim linguarum peritiam, siue Scripturarum interpretationem, siue alia dona ad conseruationē Ecclesiæ necessaria de sideres, omnia habentur, sed diuersa ratione. Tunc enim repente infundebantur, quia siĉ opus erat, nunc studio & diligentia impensâ conceduntur; cum & otium & facultas ad illa paranda non desint. Neque propterea minus dona Dei sunt, vel minoris pretij aut vsus, quàm antiquitus. Filij Israel in deserto ab omnibus deserti cum non esset unde victum quærerent, Man pro pane cœlitus acce-perunt: Ai vbi ad terram promissionis ventum esset, & commeatus laboribus inuentus, cessauit esca cœlestis. Sic in primitiua Eccle-sia Apostoli, sic in ipsa nostrarum Eccle-siarum reformatione maiores nostri, extra-ordinarijs donis ad miraculum instructi regnum Diaboli destruxerunt; nostrum nunc est ipsorum labores excolere nostris, & gre-gem in quo ipsis succesßimus, atque adeo nos ipsos diligenter attendere: Et quemadmo-dum Aharon, ad mandatum Iehouæ, Gomer Man plenum in Sanctuario atque adeo in ar-ca testimonij repositum, cœlestis beneficij æter-num testimonium reliquit prosperis, sic et nos dona Dei in maiorum nostrorum monimen-tis admirari, & quantum studio aßequi pos-sumus, imitari decet. Sed ô tempora! A Neo-phytis fere lacerantur, quorum fide Fides no-bis illuxit, plerisque vel conniuentibus, vel etiam applaudentibus. Vnde periculum, ne quod Israelitis ingratis per Prophetam mina-turtur Dominus, se ablaturum eis esse panem suum, vinum suum, oleum suum, daturumq; ipsis cælum æreum & terram ferream; nos quo que fame verbi miserè plectat miseros. Quamobrem euigilate quicunq; populo Dei prædicatoris Ministri & Magistratus, & gregem Christi diu noctuque attendite; dona gratiæ in vobis excolite, & si quæ desunt necessaria ab authore omnis boni impetrari precibus ea efflagitate. Vocavit enim vos (inquit Apostolus) Episcopos non ad deglubendum sed pascendum gregem suum. Vigilate igitur, & quod Episcopi proprium, diligenter circumspicite, ne quid Relig. Christiana patiatur. Inuigilate, in quam, non opibus acquirendis, sed quibus miserè sparsis, inquirendis. Homericum præceptum est & verè Heroicum,
units.tr: And although today, when the Gospel has been spread throughout the whole world and Churches established, believers are not illumined with extraordinary gifts by a sudden breath of the Holy Spirit, they are nonetheless not wholly deprived of them. For God bestows the same things on us as we labour and pray, he who, as even a heathen witness says, sells all things for labours. For whether we seek skill in languages, or the interpretation of Scriptures, or other gifts necessary for the preservation of the Church, all are to be had, but in a different way. For then they were poured in suddenly, because it was so necessary; now they are granted through study and diligent effort, since leisure and opportunity to acquire them are not lacking. Nor for that reason are they any less gifts of God, or of less worth or use than of old. When the children of Israel in the desert, deserted by everyone, had no means of seeking food, they received manna from heaven in place of bread; but when they came to the land of promise, and provision was found by labour, the heavenly food ceased. So in the primitive Church the Apostles, and in the very reformation of our Churches our forefathers, equipped with extraordinary gifts for miracles, destroyed the kingdom of the devil. It is now ours to cultivate their labours with our own, and to attend diligently to the flock in which we have succeeded them, and indeed to ourselves. And just as Aaron, at Jehovah's command, placed a full omer of manna in the sanctuary, indeed before the ark of the testimony, as an everlasting witness to the heavenly benefit for posterity, so it is fitting for us to admire the gifts of God in the monuments of our forefathers, and to imitate them as far as we can with zeal. But oh, the times! They are almost torn apart by neophytes, by whose faith our faith has shone upon us, while most people either look the other way or even applaud. Hence the danger that the Lord, who threatens the ungrateful Israelites through the Prophet that he will take away their bread, their wine, and their oil, and will give them a brazen sky and an iron earth, may also wretchedly punish us with a famine of the word. Wherefore, awake, all you ministers and magistrates of the preachers of God's people, and attend night and day to the flock of Christ. Cultivate the gifts of grace in yourselves, and if anything necessary is lacking, earnestly seek it by prayer from the author of every good. For he has called you (the Apostle says) bishops, not to shear but to feed his flock. Watch, therefore, and carefully look about you for what belongs to bishops, lest the Christian religion suffer anything. Keep watch, not to acquire riches, but to search out what has been wretchedly scattered. It is a Homeric precept, and truly heroic:

units.la: οὐ χρὴ πανυχίον ἐυδλεὶν βουλυφόρον ἀνδρὸς.
units.tr: It is not right for a counsellor of men to sleep through the whole night. [οὐ χρὴ πανυχίον ἐυδλεὶν βουλυφόρον ἀνδρὸς.]

units.la: Ὢ λαοῖτ' ἐπιτιτράφαται, ὣ τόσα μέα μνλε.
units.tr: Oh, to whom the peoples are entrusted, and on whom so many cares rest. [Ὢ λαοῖτ' ἐπιτιτράφαται, ὣ τόσα μέα μνλε.]

units.la: Stertere perpetua non dignu est principe nocte Cui populique salus, & tanta negotia Curæ.
units.tr: It is not fitting for a prince, on whose safety the safety of the people depends, and who bears so great a burden of affairs, to snore through the endless night.

units.la: Quin igitur vel Episcopi nomen & Pastoris vox vigiles, circumspectos et fidos esse doceat, in pascenda Ecclesia, non vestra, non hominum, sed Dei, quam proprio illo sanguine acquisivit. Hac enim secunda ratione, Apostolus, tanquam stimulo acerrimo ad
units.tr: Why then does the very name of bishop, and the word pastor, not teach them to be watchful, circumspect and faithful in feeding the Church, which is not yours, nor men's, but God's, whom he acquired with his own blood? For by this second reason the Apostle, as with a very sharp goad, ...

units.la: b
units.tr: b

units.la: maiorem vigilantiam excitat Presbyteros. Est quidem Ecclesiae exiguus coetus hominum pauperculorum, si opibus & potentia hostilium suorum conferantur, unde & Christiani Belgae ab Anti Christianis, Iberis Gös tanquam mendicantes ipsorum lingua infignifuntur; sed apud Deum preciosus est sanguis iusti, & vel ipsa pupilla oculi carior Iehovae omnis qui in vijs eius ambulat. Adeo enim nos dilexit coelestis pater, ut pretiosō sanguinē filij sui nos redemerit. Nominat autē Sanguinem Dei Apostolus, non quod Deum corporeum imaginari nos oporteat cum Anthropomorphitis, sed vsitata phrasi scripturarum, qua per Communicationem Idiomatum (vt in Scholis loquuntur) vni naturae tribuntur, quae alterius sunt propria, propter vnionem duarum naturarum hypostaticam. Pretio ergo pretiosissimo sanguinis CHRISTI cum redempti sint Christiani, si quos negligat Episcopi, & ipsorum et suum sanguine ab ipsis requiret in extremo illo iudicio Supremus index. Videmus olim gentes sacra & Ceremonias mysłagogis suis non aliter commisse, nisi accepta prius Satisdatione, si quid eorum vitio culpae periret. At refert Plinius fuisse Romae in Capitolio, in Cella Iunonis, priusquam
units.tr: Lest anyone, persuaded by a false opinion about the glory of Christ's kingdom, and about earthly and gospel peace, should indulge himself with the disciples, the Apostle now shows in the third place that this exhortation is necessary, since, besides the external enemies who were already raging then, ravening wolves were to arise within the flock itself: "I know that after my departure grievous wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among yourselves will arise men speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them." The Church in Paul's time was indeed in grave dangers, but it was then being shaken chiefly by external enemies, while the domestic wolves were still restrained by apostolic authority. But after the departure of the Apostles these too arose, and assailed the flock of Christ on every side. For the death of great men is usually, for the most part, a presage of evils.

units.la: Zach.4.
units.tr: Zach. 4.

units.la: Nat.hist. lib.34.cap.7. quàm id à Vitellianis incensum conflagrarit, Canem ex ære, vulnus suum lambentem, tantæ artis vt Tutelarij capite pro eo satis dárent, quòd nullo digno pretio tantam artem compensare posse populus Romanus iudicaret. Nostra ætate videmus Diuorum reliquias immensis thesauris præferri, ac in munitissimis atq; tutissimis templorum adytis abditas religiosè seruari & obseruari. Quòd sitanto studio ea homines custodiunt, quæ vel propter artem magni æstimant, vel ficta quadam & falsa persuasione sanctá putant, quo quæsto studio pascenda erit Ecclesia Dei, quæ mfenito pretio, sanguine CHRISTI, Jesu demta & sanctificata est?
units.tr: Nat. hist. lib. 34, cap. 7. ...when it was burned by the Vitellians, they gave surety, on the head of the guardian, for a bronze dog licking its wound, of such skill that the Roman people judged that no worthy price could compensate for so great an art. In our age we see the relics of the saints valued above immense treasures, and kept and observed with reverence, hidden in the most fortified and secure shrines of temples. If men guard with such great zeal those things they value greatly for their art, or hold sacred through some fictitious and false persuasion, with what zeal ought the Church of God to be fed, which was redeemed and sanctified by the blood of Christ Jesus at an infinite price?

units.la: At ne quis falsa opinione de gloria regni Christi terrena & Euangelica pace, cum dis-cipulis persuasus sibi ipsi delicias faciat, ostendit nunc tertio loco Apostolus, necessariam esse hanc Exhortationem, cum præter externos hostes, qui iam tum grassabantur, in ipso grege exorituri sint Lupi rapaces: Noui (inquit) post discessum meum lupos graues, non parcentes gregi, ingressuros esse in vos: & ex vobis ipsis exorituros, qui loquantur peruersa, vt discipulos post se ab stratant. Versabatur quidem Ecclesia Pauli tempore gravibus in periculis, sed quae ab ex-ternis fere hostibus concutiebantur, domesticis lupis Apostolica authoritate adhuc detentis: At post discessum Apostolorum, etiam hi exorti sunt, et gregem Christi vndiquaque adorti. Solet enim Magnorum virorum obitus, ut plurimum malorum esse praesagium.
units.tr: But lest anyone, persuaded by a false opinion about the glory of Christ's kingdom and the earthly and gospel peace, should indulge himself with the disciples, the Apostle now shows in the third place that this exhortation is necessary, since, besides the external enemies who were already raging at that time, savage wolves were to arise within the flock itself: "I know," he says, "that after my departure grievous wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among yourselves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them." The Church in Paul's time was indeed in grave dangers, but those that assailed it were mostly external enemies, while the domestic wolves were still held in check by apostolic authority. But after the departure of the Apostles these also arose and attacked the flock of Christ on every side. For the death of great men is usually a presage of evils.

units.la: Sunt autem duo genera Luporum, Vnum eorum, qui Marte et vi aperta; Alterum, qui arte, fraude et dolis Euangelium oppugant. De primis CHRISTVS inquit, Se mittere suos tanquam in medium luporum. Et hi Pauli aetate primùm in Iudaea saeuiebant, armati ciuili et Ecclesiastica potestate, Scribae, Pharisaei, Pontifices, Herodes: Postea rabies haec Iudaeae fines egressa, Romanos Imperatores, Luporum progeniem, minafit, qui totum orbem aduersus Christianos commouerunt, Nero, Domitianus, Traianus, Seuerus, Decius, Valerianus, Diocletianus cum Maximianis, Maximino et Licinio. Hodie huiusmodi lupis plena sunt omnia. Grassatur Turcicus furor, et gangraena instar longe lateque serpit: reges potentissimi in gratiam Babyloniae meretricis Veritatem turpiter abnegant, plerique etiam crudeliter oppugnant. Ipsa autem Babylonia meretrix cum suis purpuratis procis, et porcis {p}orcus saginatis, qui vel vestitu ipso se sangui ne sanctorum timctos esse gloriantur, & cum omnibus suis asseclis, qui characterem Bestiae gerunt, crudelissime in omnes pios graßatur, estq; omnino lupus ille Ouidianus, Oblitus & spumis & crasso sanguine rictus Fulmineus, rubra suffusus lumina flamma. Qui quamquam saevit pariter rabieq; fameq; Acrior est rabie, neque enim iciunia curat Caede boum, diramq; famem finire, sed omne Vulnerat armentum fertilitate, hostiliter omnes.
units.tr: Now there are two kinds of wolves: one kind assails the Gospel with open war and force; the other with craft, fraud and deceit. Of the first kind CHRIST says that he sends his own "as sheep in the midst of wolves." In Paul's age these raged first in Judaea, armed with civil and ecclesiastical power: the scribes, the Pharisees, the high priests, Herod. Afterwards this madness, leaving the borders of Judaea, threatened with the Roman emperors, the offspring of wolves, who stirred up the whole world against Christians: Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Severus, Decius, Valerian, Diocletian with the Maximians, Maximin and Licinius. Today all things are full of such wolves. The Turkish fury rages, and like a gangrene it creeps far and wide; the most powerful kings, for the sake of the harlot of Babylon, shamefully deny the truth, and most of them even cruelly attack it. But the harlot Babylon herself, with her purple-clad suitors and her fat swine, who boast that they are dyed in the blood of the saints even by their very clothing, and with all her followers who bear the mark of the Beast, rages most cruelly against all the godly; and she is altogether that Ovidian wolf: "his jaws foul with foam and thick blood, fiery-eyed, his eyes suffused with a red flame. Although he rages equally with madness and hunger, he is fiercer in his madness, for he cares not to satisfy his hunger with the slaughter of oxen, but wounds the whole herd, in hostile fashion, for the sake of fertility."

units.la: Huiusmodi lupos a grege arcere iubet Scriptura, tum gladio Spirituali, Ministros; tum materiali, vt ita dicam, & Politico, Legitimos Magistratus. Prioris praeceptum habemus Pauli; posteriores, exemplum eiusdem; quando Centurionis praesidio aduersus Iudaeorum insidias sese tutatus est, & aduersus Phariseos Praesidis iniquitatem, Romanae Ciuitatis iure. Porro ministri quam felicissime resistent huiusmodi lupis, si id cui maxime inhiant, suis ouibus eripi non patiantur, fidei & religionis integritatem; Magistratus vero Christiani, si pio patrocinio adsint pastoribus & ouibus; & nec illos fraudulenter abigi a grege; nec hunc subigi facile permittant. Etsi enim regnum Christi non sit de hoc mundo, ac propterea humanis armis & artibus propagari nec velit nec posit; tamen
units.tr: Scripture commands that such wolves be kept away from the flock: ministers with the spiritual sword, and lawful magistrates with the material, as I may say, and political sword. We have Paul's precept for the former; for the latter we have his example, when with the protection of a centurion he guarded himself against the plots of the Jews, and against the injustice of the governor, by the right of Roman citizenship. Moreover, ministers will most happily resist such wolves if they do not allow what they most long for to be snatched from their sheep, namely the integrity of faith and religion; and Christian magistrates, if they stand by the pastors and sheep with pious protection, will allow neither that the sheep be driven off from the flock by fraud, nor that the flock be easily subdued. For although the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, and therefore neither wills nor is able to be propagated by human arms and arts, nevertheless

units.la: {a} Aa. 2 Christiano Magistratui permissum est imo commissum iniquis conatibus hostium obsistere, nihil in gratiam purpuratorum concedere, quod veritati, libertati et paci Ecclesiasticae praeiudicare possit. Quod si vero vel Christiani Magistratus nobis, vel ipsis Magistratibus vires desint, optimum est praesidium in armatura Christiana, quam Paulus ad Ephesios nobis describit, et qua ipse armatus in Confessione fidei constantissime perstitit, et in ipsis vinculis Verbo et Scriptis Ecclesiae in studio pietatis confirmavit, satis ostendens, Christianorum vincula non vinciri Spiritum inhabitantem in ipsis, qui flat ubi et quando vult.
units.tr: {a} Aa. 2 a Christian magistrate is permitted, indeed entrusted, to resist the wicked attempts of enemies, and to concede nothing to the favour of the purple-clad, which could prejudice the truth, the liberty and the ecclesiastical peace. But if either Christian magistrates or the magistrates themselves lack strength, the best defence is the Christian armour which Paul describes to us in his letter to the Ephesians, and with which he himself, armed, stood most firmly in the confession of faith, and even in his chains strengthened the Church by his word and writings in the pursuit of godliness, sufficiently showing that the bonds of Christians cannot bind the Spirit who dwells in them, who blows where and when he wills.

units.la: Secundum genus Luporum prima fronte non ita ferum et crudele videtur; reipsa tamen plus nocet Ecclesiis. Sunt autem hi lupi falsi doctores, de quibus Dominus ait: Venient ad vos in vestitu ovium, intus autem sunt lupi rapaces. Qui aperte se hostes fatentur, caueri possunt, ideoque minus ab illis est periculi: qui vero fratrum nomine se vestiunt, facilius imponunt simplicioribus. Irruunt autem hi lupi non aliunde, sed ex vobis, inquit, orientur. Sic et Iohannes, Anobis professi sunt, sed non erant ex nobis. Si enim ex nobis fuissent, nobiscum mansissent. fiffent. Caussa quæ eos impellit, eadem est quæ Luciferum de Luce suprema depulit, ambitio nimirum & peruersa studia quibus post fe abducere conantur discipulos.
units.tr: The second kind of wolves does not at first sight seem so savage and cruel; yet in fact it does more harm to the Churches. These are the false teachers, of whom the Lord says: "They will come to you in sheep's clothing, but inside they are ravening wolves." Those who openly confess themselves enemies can be guarded against, and so there is less danger from them; but those who clothe themselves in the name of brothers more easily deceive the simpler sort. Yet these wolves do not come from elsewhere, but, says Scripture, "they will arise from among you." So John too: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us." The cause that drives them is the same that threw Lucifer down from the highest light: ambition, and the perverse zeal by which they seek to draw disciples after themselves.

units.la: Contra huiusmodi Lupos cumprimis attentos nos & vigiles esse iubet Apostolus:Et D.Chrifoftomus in oratione prima aduersus Iudaeos: Quemadmodum, inquit, ouium pastores simul atque senserint aliunde luporum incursionem imminere, mox abiecta fistula, fundam arripiunt fustibus et faxis obarmant sese, proque vepris consistentes magno lon- goque eiulatu vociferantes ipso clamore fe- ram priusquam irrumpat, abigunt; sic bonus Ecclesiastes, cum hæreticorum turba, lupis omnibus fæuerioris hostes ingruunt, ac fi- delibus falso dogmate insidiantur, tunc ad pugnos accingitur, ne quid ei ereptum cedat in prædam luporum spiritualium.
units.tr: Against such wolves the Apostle orders us to be especially attentive and watchful. And Chrysostom, in his first homily against the Jews: "As shepherds of sheep, as soon as they perceive that an attack of wolves is threatening from somewhere, straightway put down their pipes, seize slings and arm themselves with clubs and stones, and standing before the thicket, with a great and long cry, drive away the beast before it breaks in; so the good minister, when the crowd of heretics, more savage than all wolves, assails the enemies and lies in wait for the faithful with a false doctrine, then girds himself for the fight, lest anything be snatched from him and given as prey to the spiritual wolves."

units.la: Et hactenus quidem, VIRI MAGNI- FICI, quæ fit Luporum Spiritualium in gre- gem CHRISTI rabies, & quanta Pa- ftorum aduersus eorum incursus & morsus lethiferos debeat esse diligentia, diximus, eoq; lubentius & fufius de vtroq;, quòd nec à præ- fentis Operis argumento, nec à nostri temporis fato, immò nec ab Officio vestro hæc aliena indicauerimus. Proponit enim nobis B. Luc. quibus artibus, quibus armis & conatibus Antiquus ille Serpens nascentem Ecclesiam sit aggressus; & simul exponit quanta fide, quantis laboribus & periculis Apostoli, Paulus cum primis, sese opposuerunt ipsius furijs, & sub vexillo crucis, breui annorum spacio de vniuerso terrarum orbe subacti, victores triumpharunt. Ita autem proponit singula, ut in iis praeter Primitiuae Ecclesiae historiam etiam maiorum nostrorum agones & labores varios, quos pro renascente Euangelij luce, fortiter sustinuerunt, quodammodo adum bratos, non absque iucunda quadam & pia animorum oblectatione, inspicere; & quid por rò nostrarum sit partium, discere possimus.
units.tr: And so far, most distinguished gentlemen, we have described what a rage the spiritual wolves direct against the flock of Christ, and how great the vigilance of the ministers ought to be against their attacks and deadly bites. We have spoken of both more gladly and at greater length, because we have judged these matters neither foreign to the subject of the present work, nor to the fate of our own time, and indeed not foreign to your office either. For St Luke sets before us the arts, weapons and efforts by which that ancient Serpent assailed the newborn Church, and at the same time shows with what faith, what labours and what dangers the Apostles, Paul above all, opposed his furies, and under the banner of the cross, having subdued the whole world within a short span of years, triumphed as victors. He presents these matters one by one in such a way that, besides the history of the primitive Church, we may also behold, as it were portrayed, the struggles and various labours of our forefathers, which they bravely endured for the renewed light of the gospel; and that we may learn what is our own part. This we do not without a certain pleasant and pious delight of the mind.

units.la: Vnde nec absurdum fore iudicaui, nec vobis VIRI MAGNIFICI, ingratum, si post Quatuor Euangeliorum Exegesin, quam Quatuor Euangelicarum Heluetiae Ciuitatum Principibus superiori anno dicani; nunc vestro cum primis nomini hanc Primitiuae Ecclesiae historiam, Euangelicae Complementum; ae in eam pios GVALTHERI labores, nostro labore ex infinitis eius sche-dis collectos & correctos, deuoto animo consecrarem. Nam & Maiores vestri, viri fortissimi, Tetrapolitanis Ecclesijs in restitutione sanae doctrinae proximi fuerunt, imo so-cij
units.tr: Hence I have judged that it would be neither absurd nor unwelcome to you, most distinguished gentlemen, if, after the exposition of the four Gospels, which I delivered last year to the Princes of the four Evangelical cities of Helvetia, I now dedicate with devoted mind this history of the primitive Church, as a complement to the Gospel, first of all to your name, and in it the pious labours of Gwalther, which I have gathered and corrected with my own labour from his countless notes. For your forefathers, very brave men, were also the nearest to the Tetrapolitan Churches in restoring sound doctrine; indeed they were companions...

units.la: tij, & in dubijs rebus fidi amici: Et vos ab illustri maiorum virtute nequaquam degene res, non solum antiquo Societatis, sed & sanctissimo, Religionis vinculo ijsdem coniunctissimi communem Patriae & Ecclesiae libertatem aduersus Internos Externosque lupos fortiter vindicare non veremini.
units.tr: ...and faithful friends in doubtful matters. And you, not at all degenerate from the illustrious virtue of your ancestors, bound to them by the ancient bond of fellowship and also by the most sacred bond of religion, do not hesitate to bravely defend the common liberty of country and Church against internal and external wolves.

units.la: Accipite igitur VIRI MAGNIFICI, VIRI PRVDENTES, VIRI FORTES, auditum hoc Opus eodem vultu quo auuum, D. Gualtherum p.m. vestri studiosissimum, non semel excerpistis; & Ecclesiae Christi apud vos patrocinium porro suscipite, ac stationem vestram, vtcunque fremat mundus, fortiter tueamini. Inuicta est Veritas, et Dominus est pastor Israelis sui. Cur ergo timeamus Lupos, quorum dentes attriti sunt et ossa contrita? quorum corpora breui redibunt in terram, & vbi Spiritum quem in naribus gestant, efflauerint, in nihilum rediguntur omnes cogitationes ipsorum. Consilium autem DOMINI manet in aeternum. TIGVRI Idib. Mart. Anno MDCI.
units.tr: Accept, then, this work, most distinguished sirs, prudent sirs, brave sirs, which you heard with the same good will with which you so often drew upon the late Dr. Gwalther, your most devoted scholar. Continue to extend your patronage to the Church of Christ among you, and bravely guard your post, however the world may rage. Truth is unconquered, and the Lord is the shepherd of his Israel. Why then should we fear wolves, whose teeth are worn down and whose bones are broken? Their bodies will soon return to the earth, and when they have breathed out the spirit they carry in their nostrils, all their schemes will come to nothing. But the counsel of the Lord stands forever. Zurich, 15 March 1601.

units.tr: HOMILY I.

units.la: PRimum quidem librum confeci, Theophile de omnibus quae coepit IESVS & facere, & docere.
units.tr: I wrote the first book, Theophilus, concerning all that Jesus began both to do and to teach.

units.la: 2 Ad eum vsq; diem, quo, quum mandata dedisset Apostolis per Spiritum sanctum, quos elegerat, sursum receptus est,
units.tr: 2 Up to the day on which, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up.

units.la: DIVVS Lucas duos libros scripsit. 1. Euangelium, quod historiam Filij Dei ab eius incarnatione vsq; ad Ascensionem continet. 2. Huc, qui res ab Apostolis gestas & progressum Ecclesię per 27. annos describit: nimirum ad secundum Neronis vsq;, quo Paulus Romam ductus fuit. Etsi vero omnis Scriptura θεόπνευστος (2. Tim. 3.
units.tr: St Luke wrote two books. (1) The Gospel, which contains the history of the Son of God from his incarnation to the Ascension. (2) This one, which describes the things done by the apostles and the progress of the Church over 27 years, that is, down to the second year of Nero, when Paul was taken to Rome. Although all Scripture is God-breathed [θεόπνευστος] (2 Tim. 3.

units.la: A 3.)ideoq; diligenter inspici mereatur,hoc tamen in hoc praesenti in primis fieri debet. Continet enim breuiter quaecunque ad Christi & Ecclesiae eius cognitionem faciunt,adeoq; πρᾶξιν Christianorum tradit, in qua se exerceant, qui seruari volunt.
units.tr: ...and so deserves to be examined carefully. Yet this must be done first of all in the present book. For it briefly contains everything that pertains to the knowledge of Christ and of his Church, and it sets out the practice of Christians, in which those who wish to be saved should exercise themselves.

units.la: ¶ 1. Regni Christi initium, progressus & incrementum. Vide vaticinia,Psal.2.72. Isa.2.54.60.Zach.9.Dan 9 2.Mich.4. &c. At historia Euangelij nihil huius docet. Ibi Christus proponitur humilis, pauper, ignominiosus(Luc.2.Mat.8.Luc.23.&c.) & qui inter Iudaeos solos vix discipulos inuenit pauculos, &c. At hic implentur quae olim praedicta. Ascendit enim coelos (Psalm.68.) mittit Spiritum Apostolis,hi praedicant,& ex Zion egressi omnes gentes ei adducunt. Ita exeritse eius potentia in verbo(Psal.150.)quae etiam hodie cernitur. Et ex eo debet iudicium de regno illius fieri, non ex specie externa, Iohannis 18.
units.tr: ¶ 1. The beginning, progress and increase of Christ's kingdom. See the prophecies: Ps. 2; 72. Isa. 2; 54; 60. Zech. 9. Dan. 9:2. Mic. 4, etc. But the history of the Gospel teaches nothing of this. There Christ is presented as humble, poor and ignominious (Luke 2; Matt. 8; Luke 23, etc.), and among the Jews alone he hardly finds a few disciples, etc. But here what was foretold of old is fulfilled. For he ascends into heaven (Ps. 68), sends the Spirit to the apostles, and they preach; going out from Zion, they bring all nations to him. Thus his power is displayed in the word (Ps. 150), which is seen even today. And from this a judgment about his kingdom ought to be made, not from its outward appearance (John 18).

units.la: ¶ 2. Formam Ecclesiae primitiuae & Apostolicae, quae haud dubie optima fuit & omnibus seculis esse debet reformationis regula, Ioh.17.Matth.28. Quoad doctrinam,vnum Christum tradiderunt, qui no bis a Deo datus sit poenitentiae verae & remismisfsionis peccatorum Mediator, adeoque Seruator vnicus, Act.5.4. Vbi obseruandum, quòd ne Legem quidem huic volucrunt coniungi, Act.15.&c. Quoad cere monias, contenti fuerunt simplici Baptismo, quo adoptârunt credentes cum suis in Ecclesiæ societatem, Act.2.8 10.16. Habuerunt cœtus frequentes. In his fregerunt panem Dominicum. Orârunt, fecerunt Collectas, ex quibus prospexerunt egenis, Act.4 &c. Eadem ergo etiam retineri debent, & secundùm hæc instituatur Reformatio. Si enim olim suffecit Christus, certè etiam hodie, Hebr.13. Si olim non opus fuit alijs Ceremonijs, certè ne hodie quidem opus erit. Nec audiri mec-rentur, qui Apostolorum nomine abutun tur ad superstitionem.
units.tr: ¶ 2. The form of the primitive and apostolic Church, which was undoubtedly the best, and which must always be the rule of reformation in every age (John 17; Matt. 28). As to doctrine, they taught only Christ, who was given to us by God as the Mediator of true repentance and of the remission of sins, and so the one Saviour (Acts 5.4). Here it is to be noted that they would not even have the Law joined to him (Acts 15, etc.). As to ceremonies, they were content with simple Baptism, by which they admitted believers with their households into the fellowship of the Church (Acts 2.8; 10.16). They had frequent assemblies. In these they broke the Lord's bread. They prayed and made collections, from which they provided for the needy (Acts 4, etc.). Therefore these same things ought to be retained too, and reformation should be carried out according to them. For if Christ sufficed of old, certainly he suffices today also (Heb. 13). If there was no need of other ceremonies then, certainly there will be no need of them even now. Nor should they be heard who abuse the name of the apostles to support superstition.

units.la: ¶ 3. Conditionem Ecclesiæ in terris. Prædixerat Christus, quid futurum, Matth. 10. Iohan.16. Luc 21. Habuerunt ergo vbique aduersarios. Inter Iudæos, qui doctissimi & sanctissimi, Pfalm.118. Actor. 5.6. Inter gentes item, &c. Hinc vincula, verbera, cædes, exilia, &c. Ad ista nos præparemus, nec offendamur hominum authoritate. Est enim hæc perpetua fors fidelium Christi, Matthæi 16. 2. Timoth.3. Soletur autem, quòd Christus suarum promisionum memor, illos fecit superiores: Ita nobis fiet, modo constantes in ipso per seueremus, Iohan. 16.
units.tr: ¶ 3. The condition of the Church on earth. Christ had foretold what would happen (Matt. 10; John 16; Luke 21). They therefore had adversaries everywhere: among the Jews, who were the most learned and the most holy (Ps. 118; Acts 5, 6), and likewise among the Gentiles, etc. Hence chains, beatings, slaughters, exiles, etc. Let us prepare ourselves for these things, and not be offended by the authority of men. For this is the constant lot of Christ's faithful (Matt. 16; 2 Tim. 3). It is a comfort, however, that Christ, mindful of his promises, made them superior; so it will be for us too, provided we persevere steadfast in him (John 16).

units.la: ¶ 4. Exempla omnis loci hominum. Apostoli, qui ministrant, erudiunt. Magistratus boni & mali. Diuites & pauperes, &c. Exordio connectit librum hunc cum priori. Sensus: Priori narraui quæ Dei Filius ipse in terris fecit vsque ad Ascensionem. Nunc ea exponam, quæ egit per Apostolos. Inscribit autem librum Theophilo, qui princeps fuit, &c. Ifa. 49. Ergo ad principes viros pertinet, vt norint, quales debeant instituere Ecclesias.
units.tr: ¶ 4. Examples from every station of human life: apostles who minister and teach; magistrates, good and bad; rich and poor, etc. By the opening he connects this book with the former one. The sense is this: in the former I related what the Son of God himself did on earth up to the Ascension; now I will set out what he did through the apostles. He inscribes the book to Theophilus, who was a man of rank, etc. (Isa. 49). Therefore it pertains to men in high office, so that they may know what kind of churches they ought to establish.

units.la: Obseruemus: I. Quod se de omnibus scripsisse ait. Videtur contrarium, Ioh. 21. Non omnia, sed de omnibus, quæ ad Christi cognitionem & salutem faciunt. Nec enim opus fuit omnia scribere, quando omnium finis est idem, Ioh. 20.
units.tr: We observe: I. That he says he has written about all things. This seems to contradict John 21. He did not write all things, but about all things that pertain to the knowledge and salvation of Christ. Nor was it necessary to write everything, since the end of all is the same (John 20).

units.la: NOTA. ¶ Argui eos, qui omnia scripta esse negant, vt sua commenta stabiliant sub Traditionum nomine. Atqui fides in Christum ad salutem sufficit: Illa ex Euangelio plenè discitur: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: NOTE. ¶ Those who deny that everything has been written are to be refuted, since they wish to establish their own inventions under the name of tradition. Yet faith in Christ suffices for salvation, and this is fully learned from the Gospel. Therefore, etc.

units.la: II. Totum Christi negotiu operibus & doctrinis comprehendit. Opera sunt quæcunque propter nos fecit, vt Rex & Sacerdos. His coniunxit doctrinam, quam signis gnis confirmauit. Nota. ¶In Christo debere duo ista coniungi. Quia enim opera & doctrina testantur, illorum simplex narratio non iuuat,Iohan.8.10. Errant, qui omnia quidem Christi opera fatentur, salutem vero alibi quaerunt, contra illud quod ipse clamat, Iohan.8 Matthaei 11.Isa.55.Iohan.7.4. Similes eorum, qui medicum laudant, eodem autem nolunt uti.
units.tr: II. He comprehended the whole work of Christ in his deeds and his teachings. The deeds are whatever he did for us as King and Priest. To these he joined the doctrine, which he confirmed by signs. NOTE. ¶ In Christ these two must be joined together. For since both deeds and doctrine bear witness, a simple narration of the deeds does not help (John 8, 10). Those err who acknowledge all of Christ's works but seek salvation elsewhere, against what he himself cries out (John 8; Matt. 11; Isa. 55; John 7). They are like those who praise a physician but refuse to use him.

units.la: III. Ascensionem fuisse terminum omnium quae Christus fecit.Ea ergo imple uitnoftram redemptionem, & proinde non opus est porro corporali praesentia, Ioh.16.
units.tr: III. The Ascension was the end of all that Christ did. Having accomplished our redemption, he therefore no longer needs bodily presence (John 16).

units.la: Sed Nota. ¶Christum, licet abierit, non tamen deposuisse curam suae Ecclesiae. Patet ex eo, quod mandata dedit discipulis. Huc facit parabola Matt 25. Item Matth.24. In primis quod habetur Matt. 28.Mar.16.Luc.24.Interim hoc singuli fidelis accommodent, & meminerint illum aliquando rediturum: Vigilent ergo, ut parati sint,Luc.12.
units.tr: But note. ¶ Although Christ has departed, he has not laid down the care of his Church. This is clear from the commands he gave to his disciples. The parable in Matt. 25 is relevant here, and likewise Matt. 24; especially what is found in Matt. 28, Mark 16 and Luke 24. Meanwhile let each faithful person apply this to himself and remember that he will one day return. Let them therefore watch, that they may be ready (Luke 12).

units.la: ¶2. Authoritatem doctrinae Apostolicae, non solum generali electione, quoad salutem aeternam (Eph. 1.)sed etiam spirituali, ut testes essent,&c. Ioh.15.1.Cor.4.
units.tr: ¶ 2. The authority of apostolic doctrine: not only by general election, as regards eternal salvation (Eph. 1), but also by a spiritual one, so that they might be witnesses, etc. (John 15; 1 Cor. 4).

units.la: 2. Mandata acceperunt vnà cum signis, quæ fuerunt literæ credentiū,Mar.16. Ergo doctrina illorum non est incerta.3.Spiritum sanctum habuerunt ducem.Fuit ergo totum hoc negotium, quod obierunt, diuinum:& Christi legati fuerunt, 2.Cor. 5,Luc.10.21. Ista nos excitent hodie,ne aspernemur verbum gratiæ, iram verò eiusdem, quæ propter peccata se cœlitus ostendit (ad Rom.1.)feria pœnitentia pręueniamus,& assiduè Oremus.
units.tr: 2. They received their commands together with signs, which were the credentials of the believers (Mark 16). Therefore their doctrine is not uncertain. 3. They had the Holy Spirit as their guide. The whole work they undertook was therefore divine, and they were Christ's envoys (2 Cor. 5; Luke 10). These things should stir us today, so that we do not despise the word of grace, but rather anticipate by timely repentance the wrath of the same God, which reveals itself from heaven on account of sins (Rom. 1), and that we pray constantly.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: HOMILIA II.

units.la: 3 Quibus (Apostolis) etiam seir, sum, postquam ipse possus fuit, repræsentârat vivum, multis indubitatis signis, per dies quadraginta conspectus ab eis, & dicens quæ ad regnum Dei spectant.
units.tr: 3 To these (the apostles) he also presented himself alive after his suffering, by many infallible proofs, being seen by them over forty days and speaking of the things that pertain to the kingdom of God.

units.la: Lvcas Apostolorum Acta cum Evangelio de Christo connectit, idq; singulari Spiritus sancti consilio, vt constet, ea quæ illi tradiderunt & fecerunt,etiam ad Christi regnum pertinere,cuius illi ministri fuerunt, & qui suo spiritu in illis egit,Matthæi 10. Id ergo seruiat: 1. Institutioni, ne de illorum doctrina dubitemus, Lucæ 10 21. 2.Consolationi, quando do hinc patet, Ecclesiam ipsi cordi esse, qui vt olim Apostolos dedit,ita illi adhuc prospicit.Ephes.4.Isa.49.59. Quia autem huc maximè facit actus eius postremus, hunc diligenter describit Lucas, & habet is tria praecipuè,ex quibus duo in praesen ti videbimus.
units.tr: Luke joins the Acts of the Apostles to the Gospel about Christ, and he does so by the singular counsel of the Holy Spirit, so that it is established that what they taught and did also pertains to the kingdom of Christ, whose ministers they were, and in whom his Spirit worked (Matt. 10). This therefore serves: 1. for instruction, so that we need not doubt their teaching (Luke 10:21); 2. for consolation, since it is plain from this that the Church is dear to him, and that he who once gave apostles still watches over her (Eph. 4; Isa. 49; 59). Now because his last act bears most directly on this, Luke describes it carefully, and it has three principal parts, of which we shall see two at present.

units.la: I. Resurrectionis assertio. Is enim qui pasus erat (non alius) seipsum illis exhi- buit viuentem per quadraginta dies. Huc pertinent quae habentur Matthaei vigesi- mo octauo,Lucae vigesimo quarto, Iohan nis 20.21. priori ad Corinthios 15. Quae omnia docent, illum vero corpore resurrexisse : & in primis quidem tempus 40. dierum.
units.tr: I. The assertion of the resurrection. For he who had suffered (not another) showed himself to them alive for forty days. To this belong the passages in Matthew 28, Luke 24, John 20 and 21, and 1 Corinthians 15. All of these teach that he rose again in body, and especially the period of forty days.

units.la: Sed Nota. ¶ 1. Causas, cur hoc fecerit. Quia hic versatur cardo nostrae salutis. Passim enim resurrectionem & vitam pollicetur Iohan 5.6.11. Imò ideo illi fidimus, quòd eum corporis & animae seruatorem esse audimus. At quis hoc potuisset credere,si ipse in morte mafifset? Quis eundem in Zion regnare,ad Dei dextram sedere (Psal.2. 110.) crederet, nisi de eius resurrectione nobis constaret.Ideo statim resurrexit, & id argumentis infinitis testatus est, vt discipulos certa spe confirmaret in suo munere, ne quid dubita-
units.tr: But note: 1. The causes why he did this. Because here the hinge of our salvation turns. For everywhere he promises resurrection and life (John 5, 6, 11). Indeed we trust in him precisely because we hear that he is the saviour of body and soul. But who could have believed this if he had remained in death? Who would believe that he reigns in Zion and sits at the right hand of God (Ps. 2; 110), unless the fact of his resurrection were established for us? Therefore he rose at once, and attested it by countless proofs, so that he might confirm his disciples in their office with a sure hope, lest they doubt his promises (John 14:16; Matt. 28).

units.la: Resurrectio Christi fulta, tis nostrae cardo. rent de eius promissionibus, Iohan.14.16. Matth.28.
units.tr: The resurrection of Christ, the pivot of our salvation.

units.la: {1} 2. Quis nobis etiam resurrectionis Christi vsus esse debeat? Vt nimirum non dubitemus de salute nostra. Non fallent enim promissiones, quas dedit, Ioh.14.12. 17. Vide i.Cor.15. Et hinc constat, nos ple nè esse redemptos, Rom.4.8. Deinde vt intrepidi stemus in omni periculo, & cum Paulo clamemus ad Romanos 8. Hofeæ decimo tertio. Arguuntur, qui ad quæuis trepidant.
units.tr: {1} 2. What use we ought to make of the resurrection of Christ: namely, that we should not doubt our salvation. For the promises he gave will not fail (John 14:12, 17; see 1 Cor. 15). And from this it is clear that we have been fully redeemed (Rom. 4:8). Then, that we may stand fearless in every danger, and with Paul cry out (Rom. 8; Hos. 13). Those who tremble at every thing are rebuked.

units.la: II. Disseruit cum illis de regno Dei. Sic dicitur nostræ redemptionis negotium, eó quód huius finis est, vt qui natura peccatores & sub potestate tenebrarum eramus, ex hac asserti, quoad hic viuimus, Dei spiritu regamur, & tandem cum Deo viua mus in cœlis.
units.tr: II. He spoke with them about the kingdom of God. The business of our redemption is so called because its end is that we who by nature were sinners and under the power of darkness, once set free from this, may, as long as we live here, be ruled by the Spirit of God, and at last live with God in the heavens.

units.la: De hoc cum discipulis tam diu agere voluit: partim quód huius regni administros fecerat, & ideo opus erat, vt eius mysteria intelligerent: partim quód sciebat eos Iudæorum errore esse imbutos, & regnum terrenum somniare ex prophetijs perperam intelleƈtis. Est hoc vetus diaboli ftratagema, quo ipsum Christum est aggressus, Matthæi 4. & hodie multos, qui deinde aduersis offendun tur, Luc.9. Matth.13.
units.tr: He wished to deal with the disciples about this for so long: partly because he had made them ministers of this kingdom, and so it was necessary that they understand its mysteries; partly because he knew that they had been steeped in the error of the Jews and dreamed of an earthly kingdom, having misunderstood the prophecies. This is the old stratagem of the devil, with which he attacked Christ himself (Matt. 4), and which today entangles many who afterwards stumble when troubles come (Luke 9; Matt. 13).

units.la: NOTA.
units.tr: NOTE.

units.la: Notis. Quod discipulos tam diligenter instituit. Atqui triennio toto cum ipso versati erant, praedicarant, miracula viderant & fecerant. Matt. 10. Luc. 22. Vbi docemur, multa institutione opus esse ijs, qui regnum Dei debent prouehere, nec temere cuiuis hoc munus debere committi. Simile pretiosi depositi. At nihil est pretiosius Euangelio. Matt. 13. Habet enim salutis aeternae verbum. Actor. 11. Et qui hic peccant vel negligentia, vel malitia, aut ignorantia, non sibi solis peccant. Ezech. 3. 33. 13 Matth. 24. Ministri ergo attendant sibi ipsis, &c. Act. 20. Legant, vigilent. 1. Tim. 4. 2. Tim. 3. Nec vnquam excidat, ipsos thesaurum hunc gestare in vasis testaceis. 2. Cor. 4. 5. &c.
units.tr: Notes. That he instructed the disciples so diligently. Yet they had lived with him for the whole of three years, had preached, had seen and performed miracles (Matt. 10; Luke 22). Here we are taught that those who are to advance the kingdom of God need much instruction, and that this office should not be rashly committed to anyone. It is like a precious deposit. But nothing is more precious than the Gospel (Matt. 13), for it contains the word of eternal salvation (Acts 11). And those who sin here, whether through negligence, malice or ignorance, do not sin against themselves alone (Ezek. 3; 33; 13; Matt. 24). Let ministers therefore attend to themselves, etc. (Acts 20). Let them read and keep watch (1 Tim. 4; 2 Tim. 3). And let it never slip from mind that they carry this treasure in earthen vessels (2 Cor. 4:5, etc.).

units.la: Meminerint huius, qui ius habent eligendi, ne cui temere manus, &c. 1. Tim. 5. Obseruandum hoc ipsum in magistratuum electione. Exod 18.
units.tr: Let those who have the right of choosing remember this, that they should not lay hands rashly on anyone (1 Tim. 5). This same thing is to be observed in the election of magistrates (Exod. 18).

units.la: ¶ 2. Qualia debeant esse Christiano-rum colloquia. Christus ex mortuis redie-rat. At neque ipse nugatur de paradiso aut de regno Dei, inferis, neque discipuli de his quaerunt. Sed de regno Dei cum illis agit. Ita videmus in historia Lazari. Ioh. 12. Procul ergo facessant fabulatores. Discant autem singuli ea meditari & loqui, quae ad regnum Dei fa-
units.tr: 2. What sort of conversation Christians ought to have. Christ had risen from the dead. Yet he does not trifle about paradise or the kingdom of God in the underworld, nor do the disciples ask about such things. Rather, he deals with them about the kingdom of God. So we see in the history of Lazarus (John 12). Let the fabulists therefore keep far away. Let each one learn to meditate on and speak of those things which pertain to the kingdom of God.

units.la: Christianorum colloquia quia sint de regno Dei. ciunt.1. Inspiciant seipsos, & agnoscant quàm infelix fit seruitus, in qua natifunt Gen.5. Pfal.51. Rom.5.Ioh.8. Ita concipi-entfalutis desiderium. 2.Expendant Chri-fti beneficium,qui redemit,& deuicto dia-bolo, nos in libertatem asseruit. Matth.12. Ioh'8 Gen.3 1.Pet.2.&c.'3.Officium suum considerent, quod est,vt stent in liberta-te.Gal,5. Hanc non conuertant inlicenti-am,sed Deo locum dent, vt is in ipsis re-gnet Rom.6.12.Matth.6.Istis sermonibus fe mutuo ædificent, fugiant autem praua colloquia. 1.Corinth.5. At hic feré pecca-tur.Pleriq; seipsos ignorant. Ideo neque Christi beneficium agnoscunt. Et cùm Christiani dicátur, diabo'o militant. Hinc ira Dei,quæ indies aggrauatur: neq; spes est salutis,nisi conuertamur, Col.3. Ifa. 9. Amos 4.
units.tr: The conversations of Christians should be about the kingdom of God. 1. Let them examine themselves, and recognise how wretched is the servitude into which they were born (Gen. 5; Ps. 51; Rom. 5; John 8). So the desire for salvation is conceived. 2.
