units.la: No T. ¶ 1.Quàm vani sint conatus hostium contra regnum Christi. Quò magis hi furiunt, eò magis propagatur, & quidem dem in ipsorum ordine. Sic Iohan.3.7.12. 19.Idem factum Neroni, Phil.4. Similia hodie fiunt, quae nos debent consolari bifariam. 1. Ne terreamur hostium minis, Psalm.110. 2. Ne desperemus in peccatis. Qui hos recepit in gratiam, cur nos negligat, qui vocantem sequimur? Matth.11. Iohan.6.7. &c. Vide item Rom.8. & 5.Pf. 103. &c.
units.tr: NOTE 1. How vain are the attempts of enemies against the kingdom of Christ. The more they rage, the more it spreads, and indeed within their very order. So John 3:7, 12, 19. The same happened to Nero, Phil. 4. Similar things happen today, which ought to console us in two ways. 1. That we not be terrified by the threats of enemies, Ps. 110. 2. That we not despair over our sins. He who received these into grace, why would he neglect us who follow his call? Matt. 11; John 6 and 7, etc. See also Rom. 8 and 5; Ps. 103, etc.

units.la: {2}Quibus studijs Ecclesia propagetur? Doctrina pura & disciplina sancta, qua errores & vitia itidem corrigantur. Ita multi trahuntur, quos prius offendebat novitas. Hodie quia negligentes sumus, & insuper licentia regnat, nö mirum, si in peius proficiamus. Oremus.
units.tr: {2} By what studies is the Church propagated? By pure doctrine and holy discipline, by which errors and vices are likewise corrected. Thus many are drawn in, whom novelty had previously offended. Today, because we are negligent, and licence moreover reigns, it is no wonder if we make progress for the worse. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA XLV.
units.tr: HOMILY XLV.

units.la: 8 Stephanus verò plenus fide & potentia edebat miracula & signa magna in populo.
units.tr: Acts 6:8: And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and signs among the people.

units.la: 9 Exorti sunt autem quidam è Synagoga quae dicitur Libertinorum, & Cyrenaeorum, & eorum qui sunt ex Cilicia & Asia, altercantes cum Stephano, & cadfinem vsque cap.
units.tr: Acts 6:9: But there arose certain of the synagogue which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and of the Cyrenians, and of those of Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen, (and so on) to the end of the chapter.

units.la: VT Christus per crucem in gloriam ingressus est, ita persecutionem feferent,quicunque in ipso pie viuere & regni sui participes fieri volunt, 2. Tim.2. Quia autem cruce offendimur, prodest scire, quid olim passi sint credentes. Et huc facit in primis sequens historia. Audimus enim felicem progressum Euangelij, & quod Sacerdotes aliquot crediderint. Poterant ergo omnia tuta videri. Sed ecce certamen oritur, quo nullum grauius hucusque fuit, &c. Vius,vt tunc quoq; praeparemur ad crucem, quando pax alta esse videtur, neque lubitis tempestatibus offendamur. Vide Isa. 57 48. Sed singula videamus.
units.tr: As Christ entered into glory through the cross, so all who want to live godly in him and become sharers in his kingdom must endure persecution (2 Tim. 2). Because we are offended by the cross, it is useful to know what believers have suffered in the past, and the following history bears on this in the first place. For we hear of the happy progress of the Gospel, and that several priests have believed. All things could therefore seem safe. But behold, a conflict arises, greater than any until now, etc. Let us learn from this to prepare ourselves for the cross even when deep peace seems to prevail, and not be shaken by sudden storms. See Isa. 57 [and] 48. But let us look at the individual points.

units.la: 1.Stephanus describitur. Primus Diaco nus. Plenus fide, quae zelo accendit. Potentia adendi mircula. Et apparet illum docuisse etiam ita enim solebant Diaconi,vt sibi bonu gradu acquirent 1.Tim.3. Confirmatur promissio Matth.25. Benevfus est donis Dei quo ad temporaria. Ergo augentur. Imitemur. Hodie plerique languent. Ideo proficimus in peius.
units.tr: 1. Stephen is described. He was the first deacon, full of faith, which kindles zeal, and of power to work miracles. It appears that he also taught, for deacons were accustomed to do so, so that they might acquire for themselves a good standing (1 Tim. 3). The promise of Matt. 25 is confirmed: he was faithful with the gifts of God as far as temporal things go, and so they are increased. Let us imitate him. Today many languish, and therefore we make progress for the worse.

units.la: II. Hostes Sunt hi ex collegio Libertinorum. Erat enim Ierusal vniuersalis Schola, & proinde diuersa collegia, &c. Hi infur gunt ex diuersis nationibus. Ita fit,vt veritas fere a doctis oppugnetur, & tunc conuenire possunt, qui inter se sunt diuersi fiffimi,vt Luc.23.Ne offendamur, sed vigilemus.Quid vero agunt?
units.tr: II. The enemies are these, from the college of the Libertines. For Jerusalem had a universal school, and therefore various colleges, etc. They rise up from different nations. So it happens that the truth is generally attacked by learned men, and then those who are most at odds with one another can come together (Luke 23). Let us not be offended but keep watch. But what do they do?

units.la: ¶ 1. Disputant: Nimirum, si qua ratione ipsum irretire possint, vt Scribæ, Matt.21. 22. Quia enim rudem putabant, facilem fi- bi pollicentur victoriâ Sed secus fit. Non ergo deest suis promissis Christus, Ioh. 14. Luc.21. Matt.10. Præstitit in Apostolis. Nunc in Stephano. Nec adhuc exhaustus est fons gratiæ. Neminem ergo terreat mundi sapientia. Causa Christi est, &c.1. Cor.1 Col.2 1.Ioh.4.
units.tr: ¶ 1. They dispute. Surely, if they could somehow entangle him, as the scribes did (Matt. 21, 22), since they thought him untrained, they promise themselves an easy victory. But it turns out otherwise. Christ therefore does not fail in his promises (John 14; Luke 21; Matt. 10). He has shown it in the apostles, and now in Stephen. Nor is the fountain of grace yet exhausted. Let no one therefore be frightened by the wisdom of the world. The cause is Christ's, etc. (1 Cor. 1; Col. 2; 1 John 4).

units.la: ¶ 2. Falsos testes subornant, vt Matt.26 Mar.14. Vide quid possit veritatis odium Sciebant legem Dei, Deut.19. Exod.20. Prou.6. Et communis sensus horret istud scelus. Attamen sponte illud designant. Ita dantur in reprobum sensum veritatis hostes, vt nullus flagitij eos pudeat. Hodie multa similia fiunt: quando quidnis licet contra fideles. Violantur fœdera, pax publica. Simus cauti, Luc.16. Non autem offendamur nimium.
units.tr: ¶ 2. They suborn false witnesses, as in Matt. 26 and Mark 14. See what hatred of the truth can do. They knew the law of God (Deut. 19; Exod. 20; Prov. 6), and common sense shudders at such a crime. Yet they plan it deliberately. So enemies of the truth are given over to a reprobate mind, so that they feel no shame at any wickedness. Today many similar things happen, when people think nothing of acting against the faithful. Covenants and public peace are violated. Let us be cautious (Luke 16), but let us not be too much offended.

units.la: ¶ 3. Quia pauci nihil poterant, populum commouent vnà cum Scribis & fe- nioribus, vt captus per tumultum in Concilio abripiatur. Vetus diaboli stratagema seditionib. obruere eos, contra quos non valent leges. Sic cum Christo actum,
units.tr: ¶ 3. Since few of them could accomplish anything, they stir up the people together with the scribes and elders, so that he may be seized in a tumult and dragged before the council. It is an old stratagem of the devil to overwhelm with sedition those against whom the laws have no force. So it was done with Christ (John 19), with the apostles (Acts 16, 17, 18, 19, 21).

units.la: Ioh.19.Cum Apostolis, Act 16.17.18 19 21. Sed tales ferè seditionib. perceunt. Et obseruanda vulgi leuitas. Prius magni fecerunt. Nunc ab his Sophistis decepti, contra Stephanum insurgunt. Sic Christo accidit. Ioh.6. Matth.21.27. Luc.23. Paulo, Act. 14.28. Nemo igitur auram popularem vemetur. Studeamus Deo placere, qui non mutatur, Num 23. If.40.
units.tr: But such men usually perish by their own sedition. We must also observe the fickleness of the crowd: they had earlier held him in high regard, but now, deceived by these sophists, they rise up against Stephen. So it happened to Christ (John 6; Matt. 21, 27; Luke 23), and to Paul (Acts 14, 28). Let no one therefore court popular favour. Let us strive to please God, who does not change (Num. 23; Isa. 40).

units.la: § 3. De quibus accusant: Blasphemiae in locum sanctum & legem: idque pertinaciter. Templi & urbis meminerunt: quia intolerabile erat contra haec loqui propter promissionem, Pf.132. Ier. 26 Probant: Audiuimus dicentem, &c. Detorquent bene dicta. Docebant Apostoli, homines gratis iustificari absque operibus legis. Christum legem abrogasse. Ideo omnes hunc debere amplecti: alioqui perituros cum templo. Calumniantur ergo, quod solius excidij meminerunt, & huius authorem Christum faciunt.
units.tr: § 3. The charges they bring: blasphemy against the holy place and the law, and that persistently. They recall the temple and the city, because it was intolerable to speak against these, given God's promise (Ps. 132; Jer. 26). They prove it: "We have heard him say," etc. They twist well-spoken words. The apostles taught that men are justified freely, without the works of the law. [They claimed] that Christ had abrogated the law, and so everyone must embrace him, otherwise they would perish along with the temple. They therefore slander him by saying that he spoke only of the destruction [of the temple], and make Christ its author.

units.la: ¶ Obseruemus, veritatem mendacijs oppugnari, nec posse tam cordatè praedicari, quin impij habeant calumniandi occasionem. Ita hodie, quando gratia praedicatur, clamat prohiberi bona opera. Cum Christus dicitur vnicus Mediator, dicunt Dijos proscindi. Quando traditiones tolluntur,Isa 29 Matth. 15. dicunt nos damnare veterem religionem, patres, sacramenta. Quando ite contumacibus ira Dei denuntiatur, clamant seditiosos esse, &c. Amos 7. 1. Reg 18. Sed neminem ista offendant. Vetus mundi mos. Deus autem suorum offaseruat, Psalm 34 112. Prouerb. 10. Calumniatores autem non ferent impune Psal 64 120 140. &c.
units.tr: ¶ Let us observe that the truth is attacked with lies, and that it cannot be preached so wisely that the wicked will not find occasion to slander. So today, when grace is preached, they cry out that good works are forbidden. When Christ is called the only Mediator, they say the gods are being torn down. When traditions are removed (Isa. 29; Matt. 15), they say we condemn the old religion, the fathers, and the sacraments. When the wrath of God is announced to the obstinate, they cry that they are seditious, etc. (Amos 7; 1 Kings 18). But let none of these things offend us. It is the old custom of the world. God, however, watches over his own (Ps. 34, 112; Prov. 10). Slanderers, however, will not go unpunished (Ps. 64, 120, 140), etc.

units.la: III. Quid Stephanus? Ouis in medio luporum, Matthaei 10. Num timet? veniam petit? &c. Imo rationem fidei reddit, & illos arguit. Et ne quis ex affectu locutum putet, conscientiae & spiritus Dei praesentis indicium vultu praefert, &c. Voluit Dei hostes docere, quàm non timeantur. Et haud dubie animo sensit singularem consolationem, adeoque gustum suae clarificationis, qua martyres animantur, 2. Tim 4.
units.tr: III. What does Stephen do? He is in the midst of wolves (Matt. 10). Does he fear? Does he ask for pardon? Not at all: he gives an account of his faith and rebukes them. And lest anyone think he spoke from passion, he shows by his face the sign of a good conscience and of the present Spirit of God, etc. He wished to teach God's enemies how little they are to be feared. And undoubtedly he felt in his mind a singular consolation, and so a foretaste of the glory with which martyrs are encouraged (2 Tim. 4).

units.la: ¶ Obseruemus fidei nostrae gloriam, quae tunc maximè solatur & exhilerat, quando omnia videntur desperata. Exemplafunt passim obuia. In hac igitur maneamus constanter, vt ipsi quoq; gaudeamus cum Christo, &c. Oremus.
units.tr: ¶ Let us observe the glory of our faith, which consoles and cheers most especially when all things seem hopeless. Examples are met everywhere. Let us therefore remain steadfast in this, so that we may also rejoice with Christ, etc. Let us pray.

units.la: O
units.tr: O

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 7.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 46.

units.la: DIxit autem Pontifex maximus: Num hæc ita habent?
units.tr: And the high priest said: Is it so?

units.la: 2 Ipse verò dixit: Viri fratres & patres, audite. Deus illegloriæ visus est patri nostro Abrahæ, cum esset in Mesopotamia, priusquam habitaret in Charram.
units.tr: Then he said: Men, brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.

units.la: 3 Et dixit ei: Exi e terra tua, & ex cognatione, &c. ad ver. 5. v. 3.
units.tr: And he said to him: Go out from your land and from your kindred, etc., to verse 5. Verse 3.

units.la: DIuinus Stephanus ab aduersa-rijs per falsos testes accusatus su-it, quòd in Deum & legem blas-phemus, vrbi & templo excidi-um minetur. Proponuntur hæc, vt in pri-mo martyre videamus, quæ ministrorum veritatis fors sit, adeoq; omnium, qui publicæ saluti, & gloriæ Dei consultum volunt: nimirum qualem Christus prædixit, Matth. 5. 10. Ioh. 15. 16. Sic factum prophetis, Ier. 26. Amos 7. 1. Reg. 18. Matth. 23. Neminem ergo ista hodie offendant. Sequitur.
units.tr: The divine Stephen was accused by his adversaries through false witnesses, on the charge that he blasphemed God and the law and threatened the destruction of the city and the temple. These matters are set out so that we may see in the first martyr what the lot of the ministers of truth is, and so of all who seek public welfare and the glory of God: namely, the kind of lot Christ foretold, Matt. 5:10; John 15:16. So it happened to the prophets, Jer. 26; Amos 7:10; 1 Kings 18; Matt. 23. Let no one therefore be offended by these things today. It follows:

units.la: Quærit Pontifex, num hæc ita se habeant, sicuti dixerant accusatores? Vbi No-
units.tr: The high priest asks whether these things are so, just as the accusers had said. Note:

units.la: NOT. ¶ Exemplum astutiæ, quà falsi antistites contra ministros veritatis vtuntur. Idec non quærit, vt iustitiam simulet, quasi per leuiceat Stephano causam dicere, & veritatem tueri. Atqui ratum adhuc erat decretum, Actorum tertio 4 Ideo-que de solo facto simpliciter, non de iure quærit. Idem hodie fit, quando æquitas summa exercetur, neque aliter audiuntur Christiani, quàm vt ex ipsorum ore constet, num quid contra receptos abusus, & Antichristum dixerint. Hoc si constet, mox capitis sententia fertur, nec vllæ aliuntur rationes. Sunt exempla. Ne ergo nobis fucum fieri sinamus, quando dicendi potestatem facturos pollicentur. Christum audi, Matth. 10. Luc. 10.
units.tr: NOTE. An example of the cunning that false leaders use against the ministers of truth. He does not ask this in order to feign justice, as if he were going to hear Stephen's case fairly and defend the truth. Yet the decree in Acts 3:4 was still in force. He therefore asks only about the fact, plainly, and not about the law. The same happens today, when the greatest injustice is practised: Christians are heard only so far as it is established from their own mouth whether they have said anything against the accepted abuses and against Antichrist. If this is established, the sentence of death is passed at once, and no reasons are heard. There are examples. Let us not therefore allow ourselves to be deceived when they promise us the power of speaking. Hear Christ, Matt. 10; Luke 10.

units.la: Respondet Stephanus narratione, quam gentis origine contexit, beneficia Dei patribus collata, & quicquid ab his bene aut male factum est, narrans. Scopus exaccusatione petendus. Diluit enim crimina impietatis, quòd neque in Deum neq; in legem blasphemus fit. 1. Quia illum Deum agnoscat, qui olim cum patribus egerit. 2. Quia eam ipsam fidem tradat, qua patres olim sine lege & sacrificijs Deo placuerint. 3. Ex eo colligit, longè alium finè esse legis, quàm vt per eam iustificemur, Imò
units.tr: Stephen replies with a narrative, which he weaves from the origin of the nation, recounting the benefits of God conferred on the fathers and whatever was done well or badly by them. The aim must be sought from the accusation. For he refutes the charges of impiety, that he is not a blasphemer either against God or against the law. (1) Because he acknowledges the God who once dealt with the fathers. (2) Because he sets forth that same faith by which the fathers of old pleased God without law and sacrifices. (3) From this he infers that the end of the law is far other than that we should be justified through it. Indeed,

units.la: Oratio Stephani argumentum
units.tr: The argument of Stephen's oration

units.la: Cap.6. Imo in hac eam adumbrari salutis rationem,quæ solo Christo nititur,in quo omnia impleta,&c 4.Vt patrum fiduciam ex⁠cuteret, horum impietatem & pertinaciam illis exprobrat:quodque horum potius imitatores sint,quàm illorum veré veterum,qui Deo placuerint per fidem,&c. Heb.11.
units.tr: Chapter 6. Indeed, in this he foreshadows the manner of salvation that rests on Christ alone, in whom all things are fulfilled, etc. (4) To shake the confidence of the fathers, he upbraids their descendants with impiety and obstinacy, and says that they are rather imitators of these than of those truly ancient men who pleased God through faith, etc. Heb. 11.

units.la: In quibus Not. ¶ Qua constantia fidei agendum sit contra veritatis hostes. Et soletur nos virtus singularis spiritus sancti, qui Stephanum tanta rerum diuinarum cognitione instruxit,sicuti Christus promiserat,Ioh.14.Luc.21.Matth.10. Mar.13.Pertinent ista ad nos etiam. Videa⁠mus singula.
units.tr: Here, Note: with what constancy of faith one must act against the enemies of truth. And we are comforted by the singular virtue of the Holy Spirit, who instructed Stephen with such knowledge of divine things, as Christ had promised, John 14; Luke 21; Matt. 10; Mark 13. These things pertain to us also. Let us look at each point.

units.la: 1.Breui exordio attentos & benevolos reddit. Fratres dicit propter cognationem,ex more.Patres, propter officij dignitatem, quam in eis agnoscit ex Dei insttutione, licet corruptissimos esse sciret, Deut.17. Mal.2.Interim nō seruiliter blanditur, vt nefas putet ab eis dissentire.
units.tr: (1) With a brief opening he makes his hearers attentive and well disposed. He calls them brothers on account of kinship, as is customary; fathers, on account of the dignity of their office, which he recognises in them from God's institution, although he knew them to be most corrupt, Deut. 17; Mal. 2. Meanwhile he does not flatter them servilely, so as to think it wrong to dissent from them.

units.la: Not.¶1.Fidem Christianam non abrogare ciuilitatis officia, quæ debemus cum reuerentia præstantioribus. Licet enim in Christo non sit ὑποταγή (Gal.3. Col.3.)manent tamen Dei leges, Exod.20. 22.Leu.19.Rom.12. Arguuntur Anabaptistæ, Aliter Apostoli,&c. ¶2.
units.tr: Note. (1) The Christian faith does not abolish the duties of civility, which we owe with reverence to those who are superior. For although in Christ there is no subjection (Gal. 3; Col. 3), God's laws nevertheless remain, Exod. 20, 22; Lev. 19; Rom. 12. The Anabaptists are refuted. The Apostles were otherwise, etc. ¶2.

units.la: {1}2. Non ita venerandos esse homines, vt in illorum gratiam dissimulemus veritatem Huius confessio exigitur, Mar.8. Mat thaei 10 Rom.10. Et ratum erit semper illud Christi, Matth 22. Act.4.5. Obser.propter eos qui nefas putant dissentire a sede Romana propter vetustatem & Reges amicos. Atqui Apostolis licuit dissentire ab iis, quorum munus sciebant a Deo institutum, & quos dicebant Patres, &c. Arriftotelis d ftum. Stulti & iniqui in Christum, qui huic praeferunt homines, lsa.vige simo nono.
units.tr: (2) Men are not to be so venerated that we dissemble the truth for their sake. This confession is required, Mark 8; Matt. 10; Rom. 10. And that saying of Christ, Matt. 22, Acts 4, 5, will always stand. Observe this on account of those who think it wrong to dissent from the Roman see because of its antiquity and its friendly kings. Yet the Apostles were permitted to dissent from those whose office they knew was instituted by God, and whom they called Fathers, etc. The saying of Aristotle. Foolish and unjust towards Christ are those who prefer men to him, Isa. 29.

units.la: II. Orditur ab Abrahamo, quo patre su perbiebant, Matthaei 3. Ioh.8. Docet ergo huius exemplo, legis cultum non esse ad salutem necessarium, &c. quando fine hoc Abraham Deo placuerit. Ad amplificationem facit temporis & loci circumstantia: quia in Mesopotamia cum adhuc idolatra esset (Iosf.24.) fit vocatus: & ne tunc quidem mox venerit in hanc terram. Inde colligit, quod Paulus ad Romanos 4.
units.tr: II. He begins from Abraham, in whom they boasted as their father, Matt. 3; John 8. He teaches therefore, by this example, that observance of the law is not necessary to salvation, etc., since Abraham pleased God without it. The circumstance of time and place adds to the amplification: for he was called while still an idolater in Mesopotamia (Josh. 24), and even then he did not come at once into this land. From this he infers what Paul says, Rom. 4.

units.la: NOT.1 Vocationem Abrahami, Gen.ii.12 Nihil praecessit, cuius gratia meruerit vocari, Iosf 24 Rom 4. Vid Epiph. Deinde nihil subjicitur oculis, sed nudum Dei verbum proponitur. Obseruandum, 1. Ex mera gratia nos vocari, nec aliquem esse in salutis causa nostrorum operum respectum. Vide Eph.1. i.Cor. 4. Imo potius quam vocemur, non magis cogitamus de coelesti patria, quam Abraham de Chanaan. Quid quod caro fugit Deu vocantem Gen.3 ii Vocationem & salutem nostram a verbo solo Dei pendere: & proinde so la fide percipi. Animalis homo, &c. i.Cor. 2. Ioh. 6. Sola fides percipit, quae sensus non capit. Heb. ii. Obierunt, quibus leui culum videtur, nos per solā fidē iustificari. Atqui haec omnes hostiū vires superat.
units.tr: NOTE. (1) The calling of Abraham, Gen. 12. Nothing preceded by which he merited being called, Josh. 24; Rom. 4. See Epiphanius. Then nothing is set before the eyes, but the bare word of God is put forward. To be observed: (1) that we are called by pure grace, and there is no regard to our works in the cause of our salvation. See Eph. 1; 1 Cor. 4. Indeed, before we are called we think no more about the heavenly fatherland than Abraham did about Canaan. What of the fact that the flesh flees from God calling, Gen. 3? (2) That our calling and salvation depend on the word of God alone, and are therefore received by faith alone. The natural man, etc., 1 Cor. 2; John 6. Faith alone perceives what the senses cannot grasp, Heb. 11. Those who think it a light matter that we are justified by faith alone go astray. Yet this overcomes all the strength of enemies.

units.la: 2 Abrahami fidem, & obedientiam. Multa illum remorabantur: Patria, Cognati, Pater senex, honores, incerta promissio, &c. Sed mox sequitur. Ita fecit, Rom. 4 Gen. 22. Haec il a fidei obedientia est, de qua, 2.Cor. 10. Ad hanc regulam examinemus nos, Luc. 14. Oremus.
units.tr: (2) Abraham's faith and obedience. Many things held him back: his homeland, his kinsfolk, his aged father, honours, an uncertain promise, etc. But at once it follows: he did so, Rom. 4; Gen. 22. This is that obedience of faith of which 2 Cor. 10 speaks. By this rule let us examine ourselves, Luke 14. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVII.

units.la: 5 Et non dedit illi haereditatem in ea, neque vestigium quidem pedis: & promisit illi eam se daturum in posterum, & semine eius post ipsum, cum illi non esset filius.
units.tr: 5 And he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth; but he promised to give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him, when he had no child.

units.la: 6 Locutus est autem Deus sic: Semen men tuum inquilinum erit in terra alie na, & subijcient illud seruituti, & male tractabunt annis quadraginta.
units.tr: 6 And God spoke thus: Thy seed shall be a sojourner in a strange land, and they shall bring it into bondage, and entreat it evil, forty years.

units.la: 7 Sed gentem cui seruierint puniam ego, dicit Deus: & posthæc exibunt, & seruient mihi in loco isto.
units.tr: 7 But the nation whom they serve I will judge, saith God: and after that they shall come forth, and serve me in this place.

units.la: QVoniam Stephanus, vt publicus diuini cultus hostis accusatus fuit, hunc suæ responsionis statum habet, vt ostendat se, licet legis & ceremoniarum abrogationem doceat, non tamen ideo gloriæ Dei derogare, aut patribus. Id vero non verbis inanibus, sed reipsa probat. Narrat enim quæcunque Deus olim cum patribus egit: partim vt constet, se non alium Deum agnoscere, quàm quem patres coluerint: partim iustificationem & salutem non esse alligatam ceremonijs, quando sine his patres Deo placuerint & seruati sint. Orditur autem ab Abrahamo, quia hoc illi potissimum gloriabantur. Mat.3. Io.8. Docet ergo hunc ex gratia esse vocatum, ex terra idol. Iof.24. priusquàm vllæ essent ceremoniæ. Deinde sola fide placuisse D. qua hunc secutus fit. Vt ita intelligant, fidem solam adhuc esse organum salutis. ¶ Quia autem hoc carni videtur leuiculum,Abrahami fidem magnificè prædicat, vt conltet hanc vires hominis superare. Et huc pertinent præcedentia, Gen.12.Sequitur.
units.tr: Since Stephen was accused as a public enemy of the divine worship, his answer has this purpose: to show that, although he teaches the abrogation of the law and the ceremonies, he does not on that account detract from the glory of God or from the fathers. He proves this not by empty words but by the facts. For he recounts whatever God once did with the fathers: partly so that it is clear he acknowledges no other God than the one the fathers worshipped; partly so that justification and salvation are not tied to ceremonies, since the fathers pleased God and were saved without them. He begins with Abraham, because this was the man they most gloried in (Matt. 3; John 8). He teaches, therefore, that Abraham was called by grace out of the land of idolaters (Josh. 24) before any ceremonies existed. Then that God was pleased by faith alone, the faith by which Abraham followed him, so that they may understand that faith alone is still the instrument of salvation. ¶ Because this seems a trifle to the flesh, he magnifies Abraham's faith, so that it is clear that faith surpasses human strength. The preceding passages pertain to this as well (Gen. 12). Follows.

units.la: 1.Amplior illustratio, qua illa ad hu'us imitationem excitet, &c. Tria dicit. 1. Vbi eo venit,non inuenit vacuam, sed a Chananæis possessam. Imo ne veftig um pedis illi dedit, sed variis sedibus iactatus tandem locum sepulturæ emit,Genef. 12.13. 14. 20. 23. &c. 2.Quid ergo illum sustentauit? Sola promissio Dei. At graue est promissioni credere, fi euentus non respondeat.3.Promisit femine eius,cum nullum haberet, iam fere centenarius. Gen. 17 18. Videbatur ergo Deum cum eo ludere.Nihilominus tamen credidit contra spem. (Rom.4) & hæc fides ei imputata fuit ad iustitiam,Gen 15.At quia hæc scripta sunt propter nos (Rom.4.) debemus singula nobis applicare.
units.tr: 1. A fuller illustration, by which he stirs them to imitate Abraham, etc. He says three things. 1. When Abraham came there he found the land not empty but possessed by the Canaanites. Indeed God gave him not even a foot's breadth; tossed about among various dwellings, he at last bought a place of burial (Gen. 12, 13, 14, 20, 23, etc.). 2. What, then, sustained him? The sole promise of God. But it is hard to believe a promise when the outcome does not correspond. 3. He promised him a seed when he had none, Abraham being by then nearly a centenarian (Gen. 17, 18). It seemed, therefore, that God was playing with him. Nevertheless he believed against hope (Rom. 4), and this faith was imputed to him for righteousness (Gen. 15). But because these things were written for our sake (Rom. 4), we ought to apply each one to ourselves.

units.la: Quare No T.1. Vt Deus suorum fidem exerceat, dum eis omnia eueniunt promissioni contraria.Idem enim Ifaaco accidit,Gen.25. Iacobo item,Ge.27 28.29 &c. Sic cum Dauide actum 1.Sam 16.17 18 19 &c.Pfal 2. Eadem fere omnium nofi um fors. Promittitur nobis in Christo victoria, pax,gaudium, salus, Ioh.14.16. Luc.2.
units.tr: Wherefore Note 1. That God exercises the faith of his own while everything that happens to them is contrary to the promise. For the same befell Isaac (Gen. 25), likewise Jacob (Gen. 27, 28, 29, etc.). So it went with David (1 Sam. 16, 17, 18, 19, etc.; Ps. 2). Nearly the same lot falls to all of us. Victory, peace, joy and salvation are promised us in Christ (John 14, 16; Luke 2).

units.la: 1 Cor.1. Rom.5.14. &c. Interim publico omnium consensu damnamur, opprimimur, crucem ferimus, 1.Cor.4. Ro.8. Matthaei 16. Iohan.15. & 16. Actorum 14. 2. Timoth. 3.
units.tr: (1 Cor. 1; Rom. 5, 14, etc.) Meanwhile, by the public agreement of all, we are condemned and oppressed, and we bear the cross (1 Cor. 4; Rom. 8; Matt. 16; John 15 and 16; Acts 14; 2 Tim. 3).

units.la: ¶ 2. Quid tunc faciendum? Cogitemus regnum Christi non esse de hoc mundo, Iohan.18. Ideo ne iudicemus de eo secundum externam rerum faciem. Sed respiciamus in promissiones Dei, quae non fallent. Vult se ruatas, Psal.89. Isa 40. Iere.33. Potest item, Matth.11.28 16. Hac fide sufulti omnia facile vincemus, 1. Iohan.5. Roman 8. &c.
units.tr: ¶ 2. What, then, must be done? Let us consider that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world (John 18). Therefore let us not judge of it by the outward appearance of things, but let us look to the promises of God, which will not deceive. He wills to save (Ps. 89; Isa. 40; Jer. 33); he is able also (Matt. 11:28; 16). Supported by this faith, we will easily overcome all things (1 John 5; Rom. 8, etc.).

units.la: II. Adducit oraculum de seruitute Ægyptiaca, quod in primis facit ad Abrahami fidem illustrandam, Ge.15. Interim docet fuisse illic Ecclesiam, quam Deus respexerit, cum neq; lex esset neque templum. Unde rursus colligit, abfq; his nos iustificari & seruari posse. Comprehendit autem paucis verbis Deus, quaecunq; de eius Ecclesia possunt dici.
units.tr: II. He adduces the oracle about Egyptian servitude, which chiefly serves to illustrate Abraham's faith (Gen. 15). Meanwhile he teaches that there was a Church there, which God regarded, when there was neither law nor temple. Whence he again concludes that we can be justified and saved apart from these things. God, in a few words, comprehends whatever can be said of his Church.

units.la: Vbi NOTA. ¶ 1. Quod semen Abrahami extra terrā promissam seruire debuit. Vide Exod.1.2.3.5. Adumbratur sors Ecclesiae in terris. Est ei destinata patriae coelestis hereditas, Luc.10.22. Ioh.12.14 17. Phil.3. Sed interim exulat in terris, nec
units.tr: Where NOTE. ¶ 1. That Abraham's seed had to serve outside the promised land (see Exod. 1, 2, 3, 5). The lot of the Church on earth is foreshadowed. An inheritance in the heavenly fatherland is destined for her (Luke 10:22; John 12, 14, 17; Phil. 3), but meanwhile she is an exile on earth, and not

units.la: Locus Ge. 15.
units.tr: Passage Gen. 15.

units.la: Ecclesia in mundo peregrinatur & affligitur. habet ciuitatem permanentem, Hebr. 11. Gen.47.Pf.39.1.Par.29. Ideo vt peregrini premuntur fideles Sed meminerimus,nihil nobis fortuitum accidere,Matt.10. Lu cæ12.Ioh.16. Mereri item hoc nostram vi tiofitatem,& opus esse, &c.1. Corinth.11. 1.Petri 4.
units.tr: The Church wanders as a pilgrim in the world and is afflicted. She has an abiding city (Heb. 11; Gen. 47; Ps. 39:1; 1 Chr. 29). Therefore, like pilgrims, the faithful are oppressed. But let us remember that nothing happens to us by chance (Matt. 10; Luke 12; John 16). Likewise, that our sinfulness deserves this, and that it is necessary, etc. (1 Cor. 11; 1 Pet. 4).

units.la: ¶ 2. Quod se iudicem fore promittit Deus.Est enim iudex totius terræ,Ge.18. Non potest ergo suos negligere,Zacha.2. 12. Exempla sunt ab orbe condito. Vide Ægypt.Exo.7.8.9.10.12.14.Assyrios,Ifa.37. Babylo.Ifa.13.14.Dan.5. Reliquas monarchias,&in primis Romanos.Nec dubitemus hodie etiam requisiturum Deum fan guinem suorum,Apoc.6.18.&c. Interim singuli abstineant ab iniurijs.
units.tr: ¶ 2. That God promises to be judge. For he is the judge of all the earth (Gen. 18). He cannot therefore neglect his own (Zech. 2:12). Examples are found from the beginning of the world: see Egypt (Exod. 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14); the Assyrians (Isa. 37); Babylon (Isa. 13, 14; Dan. 5); the remaining monarchies, and especially the Romans. Let us not doubt that today too God will require the blood of his own (Rev. 6:18, etc.). Meanwhile, let each one abstain from injuries.

units.la: ¶ 3. Finem liberationis : Seruient mihi in hoc loco.Est hæc vniuersalis lex, vt qui Dei populus esse voluntexeant ex Ægypto & Babylon.&illi seruiant,Apoc.18.If. 52.Et perierunt,qui ad ollas Ægypti respi ciebant,Exod.16.Num.11.21.Idem monet Christus exemplo vxoris Lothi,Luc.19. Gen.19.Huc faciunt,quæ habentur Rom. 6. Tit.2.3.1.Theffal.4 Ephef.1 1.Petri 2. Idem priuatim obseruent quotquot ex ali quo periculo grauiori liberati sunt, Psal. 50.In summa, agnoscamus nos ex gratuita Dei ta Dei misericordia seruari, & simus grati. Oremus.
units.tr: ¶ 3. The end of the liberation: they shall serve me in this place. This is a universal law: those who wish to be God's people must come out of Egypt and Babylon and serve him there (Rev. 18; Isa. 52). And those perished who looked back to the pots of Egypt (Exod. 16; Num. 11, 21). Christ admonishes the same by the example of Lot's wife (Luke 19; Gen. 19). To this pertain the things found in Rom. 6; Titus 2, 3; 1 Thess. 4; Eph. 1; 1 Pet. 2. Whoever has been delivered from some graver danger should likewise observe the same privately (Ps. 50). In sum, let us acknowledge that we are saved by the free mercy of God, and let us be thankful. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVIII.

units.la: 8 Deditq ei pactum circumcisionis, & ita Abraham genuit Isaac, & circumcidit eum octauo die: Isaac autem genuit Iacob, & Iacob duodecim Patriarchas.
units.tr: 8 And he gave him the covenant of circumcision; and so Abraham begat Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day: and Isaac begat Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs.

units.la: 9 Patriarchæ vero inuidia moti, Ioseph um vendiderunt abducendum in Aegyptum, sed erat Deus cum eo.
units.tr: 9 And the patriarchs, moved by envy, sold Joseph to be carried away into Egypt; but God was with him.

units.la: 10 Et eruit eum ex omnibus ipsius oppressionibus, deditq ei gratiam & sapientiam coram Pharaone rege Aegyptiorum, qui constituit eum præfectum Aegypto, & toti domui suæ.
units.tr: 10 And he delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him grace and wisdom before Pharaoh king of the Egyptians, who made him governor over Egypt and over all his house.

units.la: QVamuis Apostoli non aliam fidem prædicarent, quàm quæ patribus promissò Seruatore nititur, & qua isti omnes seruati sunt, à sacerdotibus tamen accusati sunt, ac si nouam religionem tradere rent, & non sine patrum contumelia vete rem cultum abolerent. Occasio hæc fuit, quòd legales ceremonias in Christo abolitas esse docerent: ideoque nunc illo vno nos debere esse contentos. Stephanus ergo suam Apologiam ita instruit, vt prima
units.tr: Although the apostles preached no other faith than that which rests on the Saviour promised to the fathers, and by which all of them were saved, they were nevertheless accused by the priests, as if they were handing down a new religion and abolishing the old worship, to the dishonour of the fathers. The occasion for this was that they taught the legal ceremonies had been abolished in Christ, and that therefore we ought now to be content with him alone. Stephen, then, arranges his apology so that, in the first part, he

units.la: parte doceat, patribus nullam fieri iniu-riam, quando constet hos sine illis fuisse seruatos. Et orditur ab Abrahamo, nar-rans, vt hunc Deus ex gratia vocâuit, vt idem Deo vocanti ex fide paruerit, & ea fide sit iustificatus. Obijciebant illi: At-qui Abrahamo data Circumcisio, quæ po-stea ad Legis obseruationem Patres om-nes obstrinxit: Ergo tam hæc quàm illa ijs necessaria sunt, qui Abrahami filij vo-lunt dici. Ad ista iam respondet.
units.tr: teaches that no injury is done to the fathers, since it is clear that these were saved without those. He begins with Abraham, relating how God called him by grace, so that he obeyed God calling by faith, and was justified by that faith. They objected to him: But circumcision was given to Abraham, and it afterwards bound all the fathers to the observance of the Law. Therefore both this and that are necessary for those who wish to be called sons of Abraham. He now answers these objections.

units.la: I. Et dedit illi, &c. Fatetur Circumcisio nem à Deo mandatam, & huius obseruan-tissimum fuisse Abrahamum, Ge.17. & 21. Sed fiduciam eius confutat, dum hanc tunc demum institutam esse ostendit, cum ille iam iustificatus esset ex fide, Ge. 15 Vide Rom 4.
units.tr: I. And he gave him, etc. He admits that circumcision was commanded by God, and that Abraham was most faithful in observing it (Gen. 17 and 21). But he overthrows their confidence in it, while he shows that it was instituted only when Abraham was already justified by faith (Gen. 15). See Rom. 4.

units.la: Sed Not. ¶1 Locutionem, Dedit ei testamentum Circumcisionis. Ita loquitur ex Dei ore, Gen.17. Dicitur autem Circumcisio fœdus, certa cum ratione. Etenim præ-cedunt alij articuli fœderis, qui magis vr-gentur, Exod.20 Deut.6.10. Ierem 4. Et queritur de Circumcisis Dei, vt fœd fra-gis, Ierem.31. Ita ergo dicuntur propter Analogiam. Et eadem est ratio omnium Sacramentorum. Sacrificia, Leuit 4. & 5. Manna & petra, 1.Cor.10. Arca fœderis, Psalm 68. &c. Baptismus, Tit. 3. Actor 22. 1. Petri 3, 1. Iohannis 1. Idem si in Coena observemus, finis erit contentionum.
units.tr: But note the phrase, He gave him the covenant of circumcision. So God speaks from his own mouth (Gen. 17). Circumcision is called a covenant for a good reason. For other articles of the covenant come first, and these are more pressing (Exod. 20; Deut. 6, 10; Jer. 4). And God complains of the breaking of his covenant by the uncircumcised (Jer. 31). So they are called this by analogy. And the same reasoning applies to all the sacraments: sacrifices (Lev. 4 and 5); manna and the rock (1 Cor. 10); the ark of the covenant (Ps. 68), etc.; baptism (Titus 3; Acts 22; 1 Pet. 3; 1 John 1). If we observe the same in the Supper, there will be an end to the disputes.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quod circumcisio promissionem & iustitiam fidei secuta est. Ergo Sacramenta inania sunt, nisi praecedant promissiones, quibus fides nitatur. Simile silli, quod literis prius scriptis appendi-tur. Errant ergo turpiter, qui nudis signis inhaerent, ut olim Iudaei, &c. Oportet prius Christum aprehenderimus, & huius vi ua simus epistola, 2. Cor. 3. Quod si vero fine fide non prosunt Sacramenta a Deo tradita, multo minus ceremoniae, quae sollis hominum traditionibus nituntur. Nam his non potest adesse fides, Rom. 10. Vide Isa. 29. Matth. 15. Hic ergo ruit totus Papatus.
units.tr: 2. That circumcision followed the promise and the righteousness of faith. Therefore sacraments are empty unless promises go before, on which faith may rest. It is like a seal that is attached to letters written beforehand. Those therefore err shamefully who cling to bare signs, as the Jews once did, etc. We must first lay hold of Christ and be his letter (2 Cor. 3). But if sacraments given by God do not profit without faith, much less do ceremonies, which rest on the mere traditions of men. For faith cannot be present in these (Rom. 10; see Isa. 29; Matt. 15). Here the whole Papacy collapses.

units.la: II. Patriarcharum exemplo probat, Circumcisionem non prodesse ad iustitiam. Nam paucis attingit illos, ut ostendat Patres in foedus potius quam in circumcisionem respexisse: & sic perstringit prepo steram ipsorum gloriationem, qui huic considebant neglectis articulis foederis, & ita simul eripit fiduciam Patrum. Vide hi storiam, Gen. 37. Paucis exprimit sceleris atrocitatem. 1. Fons, inuidia. Ergo Caini similes, Gen. 4. 2. Voluerunt occidere, &
units.tr: II. He proves by the example of the patriarchs that circumcision does not avail for righteousness. For he touches on them only briefly, to show that the fathers looked to the covenant rather than to circumcision. In this way he strikes at the perverse boasting of those who relied on circumcision while neglecting the articles of the covenant, and at the same time he takes away the confidence of the fathers. See the history (Gen. 37). He expresses the atrocity of the crime in a few words. 1. The source is envy; therefore they are like Cain (Gen. 4). 2. They wished to kill him,

units.la: Cap.6. proinde rei sanguinis, Matth.5. Gene. 22. 3. Vendiderunt in Aegyptum, quod perse capitale, Exod.21. Accesit impietas in patrem, dolus, &c. Quo exemplo docemur, quid posint inuidia, superbia, dominandi cupido & alij affectus, si ijs indulgeas. Et vtinam hodie non similia facerent, qui suos ciues vendunt exteris. Qui item arma sumunt contra fratres, eiusdem fidei professores, & eos iuuant, qui arma breui in nos conuertent.
units.tr: (chap. 6) and so were guilty of blood (Matt. 5; Gen. 22). 3. They sold him into Egypt, which is a capital crime (Exod. 21). Impiety towards their father was added, and deceit, etc. From this example we are taught what envy, pride, the lust for domination and the other passions can do, if you indulge them. And would that today those who sell their fellow citizens to foreigners did not do similar things! Likewise those who take up arms against brothers, professors of the same faith, and help those who will soon turn those arms against us.

units.la: ¶ Finis, vt intelligant, se ex gratuita Dei misericordia habere quicquid habeant, nec posse patribus gloriari, qui hoc vno facto meruerint, vt abijcerentur à Deo.
units.tr: The aim is that they may understand that whatever they have, they have from God's free mercy, and that they cannot boast of the fathers, who by this one deed deserved to be cast off by God.

units.la: Caeterum Nota. ¶ Inanem esse gloriationem ex maioribus. Si boni sint, non prodest hoc nisi imitemur, Ezech 18. Ioh. 8. Mat.3. Adhaec quicquid illi habuerunt, hoc Deus dedit, 1.Cor.4. Vtinam hodie istud consideremus, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, note that glorying in one's ancestors is empty. If they were good, this profits nothing unless we imitate them (Ezek. 18; John 8; Matt. 3). Besides, whatever they had, God gave it (1 Cor. 4). Would that we considered this today, etc.

units.la: III. Quia in Iosephum incidit, cuius exemplo fuerunt virtutes, docet etiam hunc ex gratia habuisse quicquid habuit, & qui dem quando inter Aegyptios agebat sine templo, &c.
units.tr: III. Since he comes to Joseph, in whose example there were virtues, he teaches also that this man had from grace whatever he had, and indeed when he was living among the Egyptians without a temple, etc.

units.la: Vbi Not. ¶1. Deum illi adfuisse. Non ergo obfuit ei fratrum iniquitas, Putipharis ris vxor, &c. Commune hoc pijs omnibus. Psa.34. Imo quando deserimur ab intimis, adest nobis Deus. Psalm.27. Ioh.16. 14. Matthaei 28. Obseruandum autem, ita Deum suis adesse, vt tamen patiatur af fligi variè, Psalm.34. Ioh 16. Ne ergo desperemus ideo, quasi afflictiones argumen tum sint Dei nobis infensi. Permittit hoc, quia nobis vtile, 1. Corinth. 11. Quia hoc exigit eius iustitia, 1. Petri 4. Conformes facit suo Filio, Rom. 8. 2. Timot. 2. Lucae 22.
units.tr: Here note, first, that God was present with him. Therefore the wickedness of his brothers, the wife of Potiphar, and so on, did him no harm. This is common to all the godly (Ps. 34). Indeed, when we are deserted by our closest friends, God is present with us (Ps. 27; John 16; Matt. 28). It must be observed, however, that God is so present with his own that he nevertheless allows them to be afflicted in various ways (Ps. 34; John 16). Let us not therefore despair, as if afflictions were a sign that God is hostile to us. He permits this because it is useful to us (1 Cor. 11), because his justice requires it (1 Pet. 4), and he makes us conformed to his Son (Rom. 8; 2 Tim. 2; Luke 22).

units.la: ¶ 2. Deum dedisse Iosepho sapientiam & gratiam. Est hoc etiam generale. Ex nobis ipsis nihil habemus, 2. Corinth. 8. Genes. 8. 1. Cor. 4. Ne ergo superbiamus donis alienis, sed bene vtamur, Mat. 25. &c Accommodent haec sibi, quibus hodie datur in pace & otio viuere. Meminerint hoc diuinitus dari. Vsus, vt Deo seruiant, & fratribus egentibus succurrant. At nos hodie diuersum facimus. Puniet ergo Deus, nisi sterio resipiscamus & Oremus.
units.tr: 2. That God gave Joseph wisdom and grace. This too is a general truth. We have nothing of ourselves (2 Cor. 8; Gen. 8; 1 Cor. 4). Let us therefore not be proud of gifts that are not our own, but use them well (Matt. 25), etc. Let those to whom it is given today to live in peace and leisure apply this to themselves. Let them remember that this has been given from heaven, and that the purpose of it is that they serve God and help needy brothers. But we today do the opposite. God will therefore punish us, unless we repent in time. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIX.

units.la: II Venit autem fames in vniuer-sam terram Aegypti & Chanaan, & op-presso magna, & non inueniebant cibos patres nostri.
units.tr: Then there came a famine over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers found no food.

units.la: 12 Cum audisset autem Iacob esse frumentum in Aegypto, misit Patres nostros primum.
units.tr: 12 When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time.

units.la: 13 Et in secunda profectione agnitus est Ioseph a fratribus suis, et innotuit Pharaoni gens Ioseph.
units.tr: 13 At the second visit Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh.

units.la: 14 Mittens autem nuntijs Ioseph accersiit patrem suum Iacob, omnemque cognationem suam in animabus septuaginta quinque.
units.tr: 14 Then Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his kindred, seventy-five souls.

units.la: 15 Descendit ergo Iacob in Aegyptum, obijt ipse et patres nostri.
units.tr: 15 So Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers.

units.la: 16 Qui translati sunt in Sichem, et positi in sepulchro, quod emit Abraham pretio argenti a filijs Emmor patris Sichem.
units.tr: 16 They were carried over to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a price in silver from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem.

units.la: Stephanus diligenter narrat quid Deus cum patribus egerit. Scopus est, ut ostendat, se veterum religionem tenere, qui sine templo & ceremonijs Deo placuerint & seruati sint. Unde colligit, Templum ne nunc quidem necessarium esse, sed eum debere spectari, qui illo sit figuratus, Gal 3. Hebr. 9.10. Inter alia vero diligenter de Iosepho agit, eo quod hic fuit Christi typus. Subijcit modo descensum Israelitarum in Aegyptum, cuius etiam author fuit Iosephus. Idem scopus qui supra, Salutem adeo non esse alligatam terrae Chanaan & templo, vt pa-tres olim fame inde expulsi in Ægyptum venerint, vbi annis 210. Deo seruierint & placuerint sine templo & ceremoniis. Pos-se ergo etiam nunc ipsos sine iustis seruari, &c. Historia extat Gene. 42. 43. 44. 45. 47. Videamus.
units.tr: Stephen carefully recounts what God did with the fathers. His aim is to show that he holds to the religion of the ancients, who pleased God and were saved without temple and ceremonies. From this he infers that the temple is not necessary even now, but that one should look to him who was prefigured by it (Gal. 3; Heb. 9–10). Among other things he treats carefully of Joseph, because he was a type of Christ. He then adds the descent of the Israelites into Egypt, whose author too was Joseph. The aim is the same as above: salvation is not so bound to the land of Canaan and the temple that the fathers, driven out from there by famine, came into Egypt, where for 210 years they served God and pleased him without temple and ceremonies. Therefore those without the temple too can be saved even now. The history is in Genesis 42, 43, 44, 45 and 47. Let us look at it.

units.la: I. Causam descensionis in Ægyptum, quae terram Chanaan vexat, & quod sola Ægyptus haberet frumentum gurauit hoc quoq; Christum, in quo vno inuenitur panis, &c. Ioh. 6. Isa. 55. Vnde fames venerit, vide Psalmo 105. Deus ergo immittit famem (Leuit. 26. Deuter. 28. 1. Reg. 8. Amos 4.) vt puniat ingratos, & in primis luxum, &c. Sunt exempla quae docent iudicare de nostris temporibus.
units.tr: I. The cause of the descent into Egypt: the famine that afflicts the land of Canaan, and that Egypt alone had grain. This too signifies Christ, in whom alone bread is found (John 6; Isa. 55). For the source of the famine, see Psalm 105. God therefore sends famine (Lev. 26; Deut. 28; 1 Kings 8; Amos 4) to punish the ungrateful, and above all luxury. There are examples that teach us to judge our own times.

units.la: Sed No T. 1. Quod Iacobus quoq; laborauit. Sic prius Abrahamus & Isaac, Gene. 12. 26. Vnde patet sanctos etiam interdum exerceri vniuersalibus poenis, non quod ipsis etiam irascatur Deus, sed quod vel paterne castigat, 1. Cor. 11. vel praeuenit lapsus graviores: vel quod sua iudicia vult exequi, vt in praesenti, &c. Genes. 15. Ista nos consolentur, ne contra Deum murmuremus, Psal. 62.
units.tr: But note first that Jacob too suffered it. So before him Abraham and Isaac (Gen. 12, 26). From this it is clear that the saints too are sometimes exercised by general punishments, not because God is angry with them, but because he chastises them as a father (1 Cor. 11), or forestalls graver falls, or because he wishes to carry out his judgments, as in the present case (Gen. 15). Let these things console us, so that we do not murmur against God (Ps. 62).

units.la: 2. Quod Iosephum praemisit, cuius
units.tr: 2. That he sent Joseph ahead, whose

units.la: operaferuarentur,Pfalm.105 Habet ergo Deus rationem suorum, & fere prosunt quę nocentis ma videntur Exempla sunt pasim. Intellexit hoc Iosephus, Gen.45. 50. Interim non excusantur fratres, qui parricidiali odio accensi illum vendiderant. Imo vlciscitur illos Deus, &c.
units.tr: work they were preserved by (Ps. 105). God therefore takes account of his own, and things that seem to harm the innocent often profit them. Examples are everywhere. Joseph understood this (Gen. 45, 50). Meanwhile the brothers are not excused, who, inflamed with a parricidal hatred, had sold him. Indeed God takes vengeance on them.

units.la: ¶ 3. Quàm prosit bonos euehere. Vt nius Iosephi opera feruatur totaÆgyptus, & finitimæ regiones. Sic propter eundem benedixit Deus Putiphari,Gen.39. Similia habes de Lotho,Gen.14.Elia,1.Regum 17.Paulo, Actorum 27. Ita econtra vnius impietas in multos redundat. Achan, Iof. 7. Ionas Cap 1. Erant hęc obseruanda hodie in tanta scelerum licentia & impunitate. Miramur pertinacem Dei iram. Sed quid opus mirari? Fiunt propter quæ venit ira Dei,Colof.3.Ebrietas regnat, Isaiæ 5. Ecclef.10. Scortatio, imo incæstus, Leui. 20. Abusus nominis Dei,Exo.20.Leuit.18 24. Sabbathi prophanatio,Leuit.26. Ezechielis 20 22.23. Homicidia,Num.35. His iam additur sanguis fidelium Christi, & quod arma nostra iungimus cum horum persecutoribus. Quid ergo sperenus quàm quòd dicitur Matthæi 25. Genefeos 4.
units.tr: 3. How much it profits to raise up good men. Through the work of Joseph the whole of Egypt and the neighbouring regions were preserved. For his sake God blessed Potiphar (Gen. 39). You have similar things about Lot (Gen. 14), Elijah (1 Kings 17) and Paul (Acts 27). Conversely, the impiety of one man spreads to many: Achan (Josh. 7), Jonah (ch. 1). These things ought to be observed today, in such great licence of sins and impunity. We marvel at God's stubborn wrath. But why marvel? The things occur on account of which the wrath of God comes (Col. 3): drunkenness reigns (Isa. 5; Eccl. 10), fornication, indeed incest (Lev. 20), abuse of God's name (Ex. 20; Lev. 18, 24), profanation of the Sabbath (Lev. 26; Ezek. 20, 22–23), murders (Num. 35). To these there is now added the blood of Christ's faithful, and the fact that we join our arms with the persecutors of these people. What then do we hope for, except what is said in Matthew 25 and Genesis 4?

units.la: II. Denfcenfum ipsum. Vocatur tota gens,
units.tr: II. The descent itself. The whole nation is called

units.la: gens, & additur numerus LXXV. Genef. 46. Nemo igitur mansit in Chanaan, sed omnes simul exultârunt tanto tempore, & sola Dei gratia seruati sunt absque cultu legali.
units.tr: a nation, and the number seventy-five is added (Gen. 46). No one therefore remained in Canaan, but all of them went down together into Egypt, and for so long a time were preserved by the grace of God alone, without legal worship.

units.la: No T. ¶ Veritatem promissionum Dei, quas nemo potest impedire. Promiserat Deus multam sobolem Abrahamo, Gene. 15.17. Sara diu sterilis, Gene.18. Sic Rebecca, Gene.25. Iacob variè iactatur, Gene.49 Pharao vult extinguere, Exod.1.2. Ita tamen creuerunt, vt in exitu numerentur 630550 armatorum, Numer. 1. Ita factum in spirituali Israelis Ecclesia, sicuti prædictum, Ifaiæ 54. Rom 15 Colof. 1. Ista nos solentur hodie publicè & priùa tim, &c.
units.tr: Note: the truth of God's promises, which no one can hinder. God had promised Abraham a great offspring (Gen. 15, 17). Sarah was long barren (Gen. 18), and so was Rebekah (Gen. 25). Jacob is variously tossed about (Gen. 49). Pharaoh wishes to extinguish them (Ex. 1, 2). Yet they grew so that at the exodus they were counted as 603,550 armed men (Num. 1). So it happened in the spiritual Church of Israel, as foretold (Isa. 54; Rom. 15; Col. 1). These things console us today, both publicly and privately, etc.

units.la: III. Patres omnes in Ægypto mortui abfq; templo, &c. Ergo etiam fine hoc & aliis ceremonijs seruati fuerunt per idem, quam in morte testati sunt per sepulturas, Heb.11.
units.tr: III. All the fathers died in Egypt, without the temple. Therefore they too were saved without this and the other ceremonies, through the same faith which they attested in death by their burials (Heb. 11).

units.la: No T. ¶ 1. Non referre vbi moriamur. Omnis terra Domini, Pfal.24. Ex omni loco patet credentibus cœli ianua, Ioh 5.10. 14. Apoc.14. & 20. Sunt ergo ridiculi, qui salutem certis locis alligant, contra illud Matt.24 Item qui sepulchris certis fidunt vel superbiunt, Ifa.22.
units.tr: Note. 1. It makes no difference where we die. "The earth is the Lord's" (Ps. 24). From every place the gate of heaven lies open to believers (John 5, 10, 14; Rev. 14, 20). Therefore they are ridiculous who tie salvation to certain places, against that saying (Matt. 24). Likewise those who trust in, or pride themselves on, certain tombs (Isa. 22).

units.la: ¶2. Obijcitur, Atqui Patres voluerunt in terram promissam transferri, & Iosephı de ossibus suis dedit singulare mandatum Gen.49 50.Iof.24 R. Nihil hoc superstitiosis illis patrocinari. 1.Fidei opus fuit, (Hebr.11) qua respexerunt in promissiones,Gen.12 15.17. 46.2. Posteris exemplū præbuerunt, vt ipsi quoque de reditu cogitarent, & egressi semel non redirent in Ægyptum. Quod quàm necessarium fuerit,apparet ex ijs quæ post acciderunt, Exod.14.16.Num.11.14.20 21.&c.Item Iere. 42.43.Discamus bonitatem Dei agnoscere,qui mortem Filij merito vicit,vt nobis transitus sit ad vitam æternā, Ioh.5.Rom. 8.14.In hoc constantes,Oremus.
units.tr: 2. It is objected: but the fathers wished to be carried into the promised land, and Joseph gave a special command concerning his bones (Gen. 49, 50; Josh. 24). I reply that this favours nothing for those superstitious people. 1. It was a work of faith (Heb. 11), by which they looked to the promises (Gen. 12, 15, 17, 46). 2. They provided an example for posterity, that they too should think of returning, and, having once left, should not go back to Egypt. How necessary this was appears from what happened afterwards (Ex. 14, 16; Num. 11, 14, 20, 21, etc.), and likewise from Jer. 42, 43. Let us learn to acknowledge the goodness of God, who by the merit of his Son conquered death, so that for us there is a passage to eternal life (John 5; Rom. 8, 14). Standing firm in this, let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA L.
units.tr: HOMILY L.

units.la: 17 Cum autē appropinquaret tempus promissionis,quam iurauerat Deus Abrahamo,creuit populus,& multiplicatus est in Ægypto.
units.tr: 17 But when the time of the promise drew near, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt.

units.la: 18 Vsque quo exortus est alius rex, qui non nouerat Iosephı
units.tr: 18 Until another king arose who did not know Joseph.

units.la: 19 Hic aduersus genus nostrum in geniosus, malè acceperunt Patres nostros, adeò vt exponerent infantes suos neso bolesciere.
units.tr: 19 This man, crafty against our race, dealt badly with our fathers, so far as to expose their infants, so that they would not survive.

units.la: 20 Quo tempore natus est Moses, qui fuit gratus Deo: & nutritus fuit tribus mensibus in domo patris sui:
units.tr: 20 At that time Moses was born, who was pleasing to God, and he was nourished for three months in his father's house.

units.la: 21 Expositum autem illum sustulit filia Pharaonis, et nutriuit eum sibi pro filio.
units.tr: 21 When he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter took him up and brought him up as her own son.

units.la: 22 Et eruditus est Moses omni sapientia Aegyptiorum: erat, potens dictis & factis.
units.tr: 22 And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; he was mighty in words and deeds.

units.la: POstquam Diuus Stephanus Iudaicae gentis originem vsq; ad descensum in Ægyptum exposuit, pergit modo & illius mirabilem multiplicationem, oppressionem & liberationem narrat. Vtitur autem singulari diligentia, eo quod ista typum habent communis redemptionis in Christo factae. Itaq; horum idem scopus est, qui superiorum. Iudeos nimirum non per legem & sacra legalia, sed ex gratuita misericordia tunc seruatos & auctos fuisse, secundum Dei promissiones. Vnde colligit, Dei cultum & salutem nostram ex fide pendere, quia illius gratiam & promissiones apprehendimus. Videamus ergo singula ex ordine.
units.tr: After Saint Stephen has set out the origin of the Jewish people down to their descent into Egypt, he now goes on to describe their remarkable increase, their oppression and their deliverance. He takes particular care over this, because these things are a type of the common redemption made in Christ. So the aim of these events is the same as that of the earlier ones: to show that the Jews were preserved and multiplied not through the law and the legal ceremonies, but by God's free mercy, according to his promises. From this he concludes that the worship of God and our salvation depend on faith, because we lay hold of his grace and promises. Let us therefore look at the individual points in order.

units.la: I. Causam omnium indicat, Dei gratiam & fidem, qui promissis fare voluit: Vt appropinquauit tempus, &c. Atqui promis-
units.tr: I. He shows the cause of all things, namely God's grace and faithfulness, who willed to keep his promises: "When the time drew near," etc.

units.la: fio ista fasta fuit,priusquam haberet filios Abrahamus,Gene.22.15.17.&c. Ergo gratuita fuit,vt nihil vel dignitati vel meritis maiorum possit tribui.Eodem argumento nos quoq; ex gratia seruatos esse doce mur,Eph.1 Rom.9.&c.
units.tr: But this promise was made before Abraham had sons (Gen. 22.15–17, etc.). Therefore it was free, so that nothing can be attributed either to the dignity or to the merits of the forefathers. By the same argument we are taught that we too are saved by grace (Eph. 1; Rom. 9, etc.).

units.la: II. Conditionem populi describit.Surrexit Rex qui non nouerat Iosephum.Is dolo suo genus nostrum circumuenit,&c. Vide Exod 1.2.5. &c. Praetexuit iussuum Pharao. Iniquum vt peregrini gaudeant immunitate. Periculum ex bellis Lucrifpes. Interim obliuiscitur pastorum, &c. Finis, vt doceat contra Regis voluntate auctos fuisse, & ideo hoc etiam fuisse opus singulare Dei, qui promisiones praestare voluerit ex mera misericordia.
units.tr: Here note: 1. That it is said the king did not know Joseph, though barely fifty years had passed since his death. So the memory of benefits is fleeting among kings. For when men are intoxicated by fortune, they grow arrogant and then think nothing is unlawful for them. There are similar examples everywhere: so Saul (1 Sam. 17, 18, 24, 26), and even David (2 Sam. 11, 23, etc.). Rightly, then, he warns us (Ps. 146; 118).

units.la: Vbi Not. ¶ 1. Quod dicitur Rege non nouisse Iosephum. Atqui 50 anni vix effluxerant ab huius morte. Est ergo fluxa beneficiorum memoria apud Reges. Nam fortuna ebrij insolescunt, & tunc nihil sibi non licere putant. Sunt pasim similia exempla. Sic Saul, 1.Sam. 17.18.24 26. Imo Dauid, 2.Sam. 11. 23. &c. Merito ergo ille nos admonet, Psal. 146.118.
units.tr: 2. How harmful is the forgetting of past deeds, and likewise of laws and privileges. This destroyed the Egyptians, and the Jews themselves (Judg. 2). Today it destroys us in matters of state and religion. Hence it comes about that we hand ourselves over to foreign kings, and even bear arms against our own country, and those whose duty was to forbid this allow it. The custom of the Medes was most praiseworthy (Esther 6).

units.la: ¶ 2. Quam noceat veterum a ctorum obliuio, legum item & priuilegiorum. Haec Aegyptios perdidit. Iudaeos ipsos, Iud 2. Hodie eadem nos perdit quoad rempub. & religione. Hinc fit vt nos mancipemus exteris Regibus. Imo vt contra fidem pro priam arma geramus, & hoc permittant quorum erat prohibere. Laudatissimus fuit mos Medeorum, Hesterae 6.
units.tr: 3. God permitted this when the time of the promise was drawing near. So he is accustomed to mix sad things with joyful ones, partly to test the faith of his people, and partly to check their sense of security and confidence. So it happened at the Exodus (Exod. 14:17); to David (Ps. 2); at the restoration of the city (Neh. 4). Let us not be surprised, then, today. This is the last attempt of Satan, etc. (Luke 11; Rom. 16).

units.la: ¶ 3. Deum, cum promisionu tempus appropinquaret, hoc permisisse. Ita solet lae tristia mis-iis tristia miscere, partim vt fidem suorum ... exerceat,partim vt securitati & confidentiae occurrat. Sic factum in exitu, Exod.14.17. Dauidi, Psalm.2. In vrbis restitutione, Nehem.4. Ne miremur ergo hodie. Elt hic postremus Satanae conatus, &c. Lucae 11. Rom.16.
units.tr: II. He deals with Moses, in whom the Jews gloried as their deliverer and lawgiver (John 6). He teaches, moreover, that this man too was preserved and brought up by the grace of God before the Law existed, etc. He proves this:

units.la: II. De Mose agit, quo vindice & legislatore Iudaei gloriabantur, Ioh.6. Docet autem etiam hunc Dei gratia seruatum & euestum fuisse, priusquam Lex effet, &c. Id vero probat.
units.tr: 1. From the time: "was born," when affairs were desperate, and while still an infant he was pleasing to God. Let us observe that the deliverer was born when there was scarcely any hope of liberation left. So it happened at Christ's birth (Luke 2). Let no one rashly despair of God (Isa. 28; Philo).

units.la: ¶ 1. A tempore, Natus, quando res peri clitabantur, & infans adhuc gratus fuit Deo. Obseruemus, tunc natum vindicem, quando vix aliqua spes liberationis reliqua erat. Sic factum in Christi natiuitate, Lucae 2. Nemo temere de Deo desperet, Isa.28. Philo.
units.tr: 2. His parents nourished him in secret. This was a work of faith (Heb. 11). So this preserved Moses. Meanwhile Christians should imitate them, and not obey tyrants in matters which cannot be done without loss of piety (Acts 4, 5). Consider how dreadful the guilt is of those who, against the edicts of their own princes, hire out their services to foreign tyrants for the oppression of Christ's faithful (Zech. 2:12). It will be hard for them, etc. (Acts 9). Let them also see Matt. 25.

units.la: ¶ 2. Parentes illum aluerunt clam. Fuit hoc fidei opus, Hebr.11 Haec ergo Mosem seruauit. Interim imitentur illos Christiani, ne tyrannis obediant in ijs, quae salua pietate non possunt praestare, Act.4 5. Ob seruandum, quam horribilis illorum culpa sit, qui contra suorum principum edicta tyrannis peregrinis suam operam locant, in opprimendis Christi fidelibus, Zachar 2.12. Durum erit illis, &c. Act.9. Videant item Matth.25.
units.tr: 3. Exposed at last, he is preserved by Pharaoh's daughter, who adopted him. Thence he is brought up and instructed in all wisdom, etc. Yet this could have wholly corrupted Moses. That he later came to true faith and became a servant of God he had from the free mercy of God, who does not allow his own to be snatched from him (John 10).

units.la: § 3. Expositus tandem seruatur per fili- am Pharaonis, quæ illum adoptauit. Inde educatur & instituitur in omni sapientia, &c. Id vero poterat Mosem totum corrumpere. Quod ergo postea ad veram fidem peruenit, Dei seruus factus est, id habuit ex gratuita Dei misericordia, qui suos non finit sibi eripi. Ioh. 10.
units.tr: § 3. Finally, exposed, he is saved through the daughter of Pharaoh, who adopts him. Thence he is brought up and instructed in all wisdom, etc. Yet this could have wholly corrupted Moses. That he afterwards came to true faith and became a servant of God, he owed to God's free mercy, who does not allow his own to be snatched from him (John 10).

units.la: Ludificat ergo Deus mirifice tyrannos, Psal. 2. Pharao in suo sinu alit, erudit & instruit vindicem eius populi, quem oppressum volebat. Sic Saul Ionathanum. Achab Abdiam. 1. Reg. 18. Herodes, &c. Matth. 2. Saulus, Act 9.8. Imperatoribus idem accidit sæpe. Et hodie interdum Euangelium prouehunt, qui volunt extinctum, Fidamus ergo Deo, & Oremus
units.tr: God therefore marvellously mocks tyrants (Ps. 2). Pharaoh nurses in his own bosom, educates and trains the avenger of the people whom he wished to see oppressed. So Saul (with) Jonathan; Ahab (with) Obadiah (1 Kings 18); Herod (Matt. 2); Saul (Acts 9.8). The same has often happened with emperors. And today too they sometimes advance the Gospel, though they wish it extinguished. Let us therefore trust in God, and pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LI.
units.tr: HOMILY LI.

units.la: 23 Ut vero impletum est ei quadraginta annorum tempus, subiecit in core ius ut viseret fratres suos, filios Israel.
units.tr: 23 But when forty years had been completed for him, it came into his heart to visit his brethren, the children of Israel.

units.la: 24 Et cum vidisset quendam iniuria affici, tutatus est, & percussò Aegyptio vindicaut eum, qui opprimebatur.
units.tr: 24 And seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him, and striking down the Egyptian, avenged the one who was being oppressed.

units.la: 25 Existimabat autem fratres sua intelligere Deum per manum ipsius dare eis salutem: at illi nō intellexerunt
units.tr: 25 For he supposed that his brethren understood that God was giving them salvation through his hand, but they did not understand.

units.la: 26 Porro sequenti die visus est ip*sis pugnantibus, & compulit os in pacem, dicens, Viri, fratres estis vos: cur ergo alij alios iniuria afficitis?
units.tr: 26 On the next day he appeared to them as they were fighting, and urged them towards peace, saying, "Men, you are brothers; why do you wrong one another?"

units.la: 27 Is autem qui iniuria afficiebat proximum, repulit eum dicens: Quis te constituit principem & iudicem super nos?
units.tr: 27 But he who was wronging his neighbour thrust him away, saying, "Who made you a ruler and judge over us?

units.la: 28 Num tu me vis intermittere quemadmodum interemisti heri Aegyptium.
units.tr: 28 Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?"

units.la: 29 Ad hunc sermonem Moses fugit, & factus est aduena in terra Madiam, vbi genuit duos filios.
units.tr: 29 At this saying Moses fled, and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he begot two sons.

units.la: OVoniam Stephanus in Mosis mention incidit, illius historiam diligentissimè tractat, partim quidem quod Moses liberationem populi ex Ægypto typum Christi gessit, de quo testatus est Iohannes, Cap.5. Deutronom.18. partim vero vt sE ab illius contemptu vindicet, cuius accusabatur, eo quod contra templum & sacra Leuitica esset concionatus. Vtq; horum fiduciam omnem auferat, ostendit ne Mosem quidem habere quod glorietur, quando gratiæ opera fuerint, quæcunque gesta sunt. Id nunc plenius patebit. Narrat enim vt officium suum coeperit obire,vtque Patres illum reiecerint.
units.tr: Since Stephen came upon the mention of Moses, he treats his history very carefully: partly because Moses' deliverance of the people from Egypt was a type of Christ, of whom John testified (ch. 5) and of whom Deut. 18 speaks; and partly so that he may clear himself of the contempt for that man of which he was accused, because he had preached against the temple and the Levitical sacred rites. And so that he may take away all confidence in these charges, he shows that Moses himself has nothing to boast of, since whatever was done was the work of grace. This will now be clearer. For he tells how Moses began to undertake his office, and how the fathers rejected him.

units.la: 1. A Caula & tempore orditur: Cum ef- set quadragenarium iubijt cor, &c. Ergo totis animis quadraginta in aula vixit, nec fui populi rationem habuit. Fuit ergo hic motus diuinus, qui illū excitauit, Vide Heb. 11. Vbi istud fidei tribuitur, quod donum Dei est, ad Eph 2. Ioh.6.
units.tr: 1. He begins with the cause and the time: When he was forty years old, it came into his heart, etc. Therefore for forty years he lived wholly at court and took no account of the people. This motion, then, was divine, which stirred him up; see Heb. 11, where this is ascribed to faith, which is the gift of God; Eph. 2; John 6.

units.la: NOT. ¶ 1. Quòd non nisi a Deo exci-tatus fratrum curam suscepit. Nam mun-do immersi nihil recti faciunt, nisi Deus extrahat, 1 Cor.2. Ioh 3. 2. Cor.3. Cant.1. Nostrum vero est, non reluctari trahenti Deo, & simul huic omnem gloriam transcribere, 1. Cor.4.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. That he took up the care of his brethren only when roused by God. For those immersed in the world do nothing right unless God draws them out: 1 Cor. 2; John 3; 2 Cor. 3; Song 1. It is our part, however, not to resist God drawing us, and at the same time to ascribe all glory to him: 1 Cor. 4.

units.la: ¶ 2 Quanta diuinæ vocationis vis fit a-pud electos. Agnoscunt sui pastoris vo-cem, Ioh. 10. Ita ergo hanc sequuntur, vt abijciant omnia quæ ipsos remorantur, nec aliquid graue putant, quod Deus requirit. Ita Moses relinquit delicias, otium, opes, honores. Eligit inopiam, labores, pericula, infamiam. Sic Apostoli, Matth. 4. 9. 19. In primis Paulus Act 9. Phil.3. Zacheus. Luc. 19. Et hæc est abnegatio illa, quæ exigitur, Mat. 16. Fidei item obedientia, Rom.1 16. At ista arguunt nostram socordiam, qui nihil amittere aut pati volumus: Vxor Lothi. Gen.19.
units.tr: 2. How great is the power of divine calling among the elect. They recognise the voice of their shepherd (John 10), and so they follow it in such a way that they cast off everything that holds them back, and do not think anything hard that God requires. Thus Moses leaves pleasures, leisure, wealth and honours; he chooses poverty, labours, dangers and infamy. So did the apostles (Matt. 4, 9, 19), and above all Paul (Acts 9; Phil. 3), and Zacchaeus (Luke 19). This is the self-denial that is demanded (Matt. 16), and likewise the obedience of faith (Rom. 1:16). But such examples expose our sloth, for we want to lose or suffer nothing: think of Lot's wife (Gen. 19).

units.la: II.Ne quis Patres ita meruisse dicat, vt ipsis Moses vindex daretur, occurrit, & ostendit illos adeo non agnouisse Dei visi-tantis bonitatem, vt potius Mosem indig-nissimè reiecerint. Id probat historia, Exod 2. Nam in vnius facto apparet, quales illi omnes fuerint: ingrati nimirum, murmuratores, &c. Exod 5.14.16.17. Num.11. 14.16.21. Ita vero pulchrè contempti Mo-sis crime in Patres retorquet, vt ipsos iam horum imitatores esse ostendat: Sic Christus, Mat.23,
units.tr: II. Lest anyone say that the fathers deserved to have Moses given to them as their deliverer, he goes on to show that they had so little recognised the goodness of God visiting them that they most unworthily rejected Moses. The story proves this (Exod. 2). For in that one deed it appears what sort of people they all were: ungrateful, murmurers, and so on (Exod. 5, 14, 16, 17; Num. 11, 14, 16, 21). And so beautifully does he turn the crime committed against the rejected Moses back upon the fathers, to show that they are now imitators of those same men. So Christ did (Matt. 23).

units.la: NOT. ¶ 1. Mosem & in eo boni magistratus officium. 1. Non puduit eum popu-li, cuius vindex erat constitutus. Ita non pudeat te eorum, quos tibi Deus credidit. Sunt enim ij, pro quibus ille Filium tradidit, Ioh.3. De quibus idem loquitur Zach.2. Simile depositi ab amico 2. Tuetur oppressum contra apertam vim, non sine periculo vitae. Est hoc proprium officium magistratus, Psalm.72. ad Romanos, decimo tertio. Id vero imprimis pertinet ad religionem, Isa.49. Psalm.2. Iniquissimi, qui hanc negligunt, aut etiam iniquitoribus permittunt miseros, &c. 3. Litigantes studet ad concordiam reducere. Hac imprimis opus est, Matthaei 22.&c.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. Moses, and in him the office of a good magistrate. (1) He was not ashamed of the people whose deliverer he had been appointed. So let it not shame you of those whom God has entrusted to you. For these are the ones for whom he handed over his Son (John 3), and of whom the same speaks (Zech. 2). It is like a deposit from a friend. (2) He defends the oppressed against open violence, not without danger to his life. This is the proper office of the magistrate (Ps. 72; Rom. 13). It pertains above all to religion (Isa. 49; Ps. 2). Most unjust are those who neglect this, or even allow the wretched to be handed over to the unjust, and so on. (3) He strives to reduce litigants to concord. This above all is needed (Matt. 22, etc.).

units.la: ¶ 2. Quam gratum retulit Moses? Pefsimam. Conuitia, quasi regnum affectet. Item vt latroni cædes exprobratur. Denique defertur apud Pharaonem, & cogitur fugere. Ita solet mundus. Sensit idem Samuel, 1. Sam. 8 12. Dauid, &c. 2. Sam. 15. 16. 20. 1. Reg, 12. Gentium heroes. Ne ergo offendantur boni principes, si quid huius accidit, vt propter ea velint ab officio suo recedere. Dei seruifunt (Rom. 13. Psalm. 72.) qui remunerator est fidelis, Hebr. 11. Matth 25.
units.tr: 2. How gratefully did Moses get repaid? Most wickedly. He is reproached as if he aimed at kingship; likewise, as a murderer is thrown in a robber's face. Finally he is informed against to Pharaoh and is forced to flee. So the world usually behaves. Samuel felt the same (1 Sam. 8, 12), and David (2 Sam. 15, 16, 20), and Rehoboam (1 Kings 12), and the heroes of the Gentiles. So let good princes not be offended if anything of this kind happens to them, so that they do not for that reason wish to withdraw from their office. They serve God (Rom. 13; Ps. 72), who is a faithful rewarder (Heb. 11; Matt. 25).

units.la: ¶ 3. Vt Moysis exemplum conueniat Christi & Christo, Deuteronom. 18. Hic cum esset in gloria Patris (Iohannis iprimo) nos inuisit, Philip. 2. Victo Satana nos vindi-cauit, Iohannis 12. 16. Ephes. 4. Genes. 3. Charitatem praecipit, Iohannis decimoquinto. Hic plerique ingrati sunt, oggan-niunt, gloriam quae ipsi debetur, transferunt alio, Ier. 2. Isa. 55.
units.tr: 3. That the example of Moses agrees with Christ and with Christ's office (Deut. 18). He, though he was in the glory of the Father (John 1), visited us (Phil. 2). Having conquered Satan, he delivered us (John 12, 16; Eph. 4; Gen. 3). He enjoins love (John 15). Here many are ungrateful: they grumble, and transfer to another the glory that is owed to him (Jer. 2; Isa. 55).

units.la: III. Moses fugit in Madian, vbi quadraginta annos mansit. Vidit enim ex re-pulsa ista, nondum adesse tempus liberationis. Ideo seruat se melioribus temporibus. Ita Christus saepe, Iohan. octauo, de cimo, &c. Postea imperterritus obuiam it morti, Ioh. 11. 18. Ita nobis licet aliquando fugere, Matth. decimo. Interea autem If.
units.tr: III. Moses fled into Midian, where he stayed forty years. For from that rejection he saw that the time of liberation was not yet at hand, and so he preserved himself for better times. So Christ often did (John 8, 10, etc.). Afterwards he met death fearlessly (John 11, 18). So we too may sometimes flee (Matt. 10). Meanwhile the Israelites are afflicted.

units.la: Poenae ingratorum.
units.tr: Punishment of the ungrateful.

units.la: autem Israelitæ affliguntur. Fuit hæc digna pœna ingratitudinis. Sic etiam factum Numer. decimoquarto. Ita fit ingratis & contumacibus, vt ipsi remorentur suam salutem. Exempla hodie palsim extant. In omnibus istis ergo agnosce Dei bonitatem & fidé in seruandis promissis. Huic fidamus, & Oremus.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Israelites are afflicted. This was a worthy punishment for their ingratitude. So it also happened (Num. 14). Thus it happens to the ungrateful and obstinate that they themselves delay their own salvation. Examples are found everywhere today. In all these things, then, recognise the goodness of God and his faithfulness in keeping his promises. Let us trust in this, and pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LIII.

units.la: 30 Expletis vero annis quadraginta, visus est ei in deserto montis Sinai Angelus Domini in flammeo igne rubi:
units.tr: 30 When forty years had been completed, there appeared to him in the desert of Mount Sinai an angel of the Lord, in the flame of a burning bush.

units.la: 31 Moses autem vt conspexit admiratus est visum, & cum accederet ad considerandum, extitit ad eum vox Domini, dicentis.
units.tr: 31 But Moses, when he saw it, was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look more closely, the voice of the Lord came to him, saying:

units.la: 32 Ego sum Deus illè patrum tuorum, Deus Abrahami, & Deus Isaac, & Deus Iacob. Tremefactus autem Moses, non audebat considerare.
units.tr: 32 I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Moses, trembling, did not dare to look.

units.la: 33 Dixit autem ei Dominus: Solue soleas pedum tuorum: locus enim in quo stas, terra sancta est.
units.tr: 33 And the Lord said to him: Loose the sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.

units.la: 34 Vidi, vidi vexationem populi mei, qui est in Aegypto, & suspiria eorum audiui, vt eruam eos: nunc ergo veni, mittam te in Aegyptum.
units.tr: 34 I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, so that I may deliver them. Now therefore come, I will send you into Egypt.
