To make this clearer, he first set out: (1) what kind of man Saul was, breathing out slaughter and so on; (2) that he set out for Damascus, armed with public authority, equipped of course with weapons, servants and so on; (3) his purpose, which was to bring men and women in chains to Jerusalem, that is, to make them either deny the faith there or be put to death (Acts 26).

units.la: ¶ Est haec communis sors piorum, de qua nos Christus admonuit, Matt. 10. 24. Ioh. 16. Luc. 12. 2. 2. Tim. 3. Non ergo offendamur hodie, quasi quid nouum & insolens accidat, 1. Pet. 4. Quin nos praeparemus, vt Christus iubet Luc. 14. Matt. 16. Soletur autem, quod Christi crucem ferimus, qui nos suae gloriae olim consortes faciet. Luc. 22. Iohan. 14. 17. 2. Tim. 2. Et ne nunc quidem Ecclesiam suam negligit, Iohan. 10. Matt. 10. 28. Patet hoc in sequentibus. Narratur enim vt Saulum compescuerit, &c.
units.tr: This is the common lot of the godly, of which Christ warned us (Matt. 10:24; John 16; Luke 12:2; 2 Tim. 3). So let us not be offended today, as if something new and strange were happening (1 Pet. 4). Rather, let us prepare ourselves, as Christ commands (Luke 14; Matt. 16). And this is consoling, that we bear the cross of Christ, who will one day make us partakers of his glory (Luke 22; John 14, 17; 2 Tim. 2). Nor does he now neglect his Church (John 10; Matt. 10:28). This will appear in what follows, for it is told how he restrained Saul, and so on.

units.la: I. Tempus & locus: Cum iam appropinquaret, &c. Ergo iam in conspectu habuit vrbem & vt lupus ouili viso totus infremuit, trepidantibus interea pijs.
units.tr: I. The time and place: "when he was now drawing near," and so on. So he already had the city in view, and like a wolf that has seen the sheepfold, he raged on every side, while the godly trembled meanwhile.

units.la: NOT. ¶ Quoniam Deus saepe hostes progredi patiatur? Similia exempla sunt in Pharaone, Exod. decimoquarto & decimoquinto. In Saule, 1. Sam. 23. 24. In Sena nacheribo, Isa. 36. 37. Trepidant tunc pij, & cum Dauide clamant, Psalm. 13. Hab. 1. Ieremiae duodecimo, &c. Sed ita solet Deus alienum opus facere, vt suo operi locum faciat (Isa 28.) & illustrior sit eius gloria. Debet hoc publice obseruari hodie. quando similia exempla non semel vidi‣ mus. Priuatim item in quauis angustia. Nec enim abbreuiatur manus Domini, Isa.59. Pfalm.136 Exspectemus modo il—lum constanti fide.Pfalm.72.62.Habacuk. secundo.
units.tr: NOTE: Why does God allow enemies to advance so far? Similar examples are in Pharaoh (Exod. 14 and 15), in Saul (1 Sam. 23 and 24), and in Sennacherib (Isa. 36 and 37). Then the godly tremble and with David cry out (Ps. 13; Hab. 1; Jer. 12), and so on. But God is accustomed to do his alien work so as to make room for his own work (Isa. 28), and so that his glory may be more illustrious. This ought to be observed publicly today, when we have seen similar examples more than once, and privately in every distress. For the hand of the Lord is not shortened (Isa. 59; Ps. 136). Let us only wait for him with steadfast faith (Ps. 72, 62; Hab. 2).

units.la: II.Modus.Lux repente circumfulget. Ac cedit vox instar fulminis, quæ scelus ox‣ probrat.Prostratus ille iacet.Fuit hæc terribilis rerum faciesfed sic narrantur, vt videas Deum hæc absque labore fecisse. Ipse lucis Creator, Genesis 1. Pfal.19. Hic vero subitam educir,vt magis terreat. Ad prosternendum sola vox sufficit. Facit enim quæ vult, Pfalm.115.Rom.4. &c. Sic Ioh.18.
units.tr: II. The manner: suddenly a light shone round about him. And a voice comes like a thunderclap, which rebukes his crime. He lies prostrate on the ground. That scene was terrible, yet it is narrated in such a way that you see God doing these things without any labour. He is the Creator of light himself (Gen. 1; Ps. 19). Here indeed he sends it suddenly, so as to terrify more. A voice alone is enough to prostrate him, for he does what he wills (Ps. 115; Rom. 4, and so on). So also in John 18.

units.la: Itaque Not. ¶ Facillimum esse Deo hostes suos vincere. Quia enim est exer‣ cituum Dominus, creaturas quasuis po—teftarmare. Sic olim aquis vsus est, Gen. 6 7 Linguarum diuisione, Genel.vndeci—mo.Igne & sulphure, Genef.19. Infects, &c.Exod.7.8.9.10. &c. Serpentibus, Nu—mer.vigefimo primo. Muribus,1.Samuel. 5.6.Pediculis,vt Antioch.2.Machab.9.Herodem Magnum Agrippam, Actor. duodecimo.Et Deo suam manum extenden—te,omnes vires 1 buntur. Quid nunc iu‣ uant Saulum Pontificum literæ,satellites, ius Romanæ ciuitatis? Quibus verò armis prostratus iacet? Luxsola & Domini vox eum deiecit. Quid ergo fiat, si potentia sua Deus vtatur? Tunc hostes interse committere potest. Iud. 7. 1. Sam. 31. Ita nos solentur hodie, Psal. 33. 2. &c.
units.tr: Hence, NOTE: It is very easy for God to overcome his enemies. For he is the Lord of hosts, able to command any creatures whatever. So once he used the waters (Gen. 6, 7); the division of tongues (Gen. 11); fire and brimstone (Gen. 19); plagues (Exod. 7, 8, 9, 10, and so on); serpents (Num. 21); mice (1 Sam. 5, 6); lice, as in Antiochus (2 Macc. 9); Herod Agrippa the Great (Acts 12). And when God stretches out his hand, all powers are overthrown. What now does the Pontiff's letter help Saul, or his attendants, or the right of Roman citizenship? With what weapons is he laid low? The light alone and the voice of the Lord cast him down. What then will happen if God uses his power? Then he can set enemies against one another (Judg. 7; 1 Sam. 31). So today we are consoled in this way (Ps. 33; 2, and so on).

units.la: ¶ Officij item admoneant, vt coram tanto Deo humiliemur. Magnum enim nostræ vitiofitatis argumentum, quòd plerique ab illo datis donis insolescunt. Cogita semper qui sis, Genef. tertio, decimo octauo. Vnde acceperis? priori ad Corinthios quarto. Quòd Deus superbis resistit, &c. Luc. secundo, decimoquarto, 1. Pet. 5. Iac. 4.
units.tr: It also admonishes us in duty to humble ourselves before so great a God. For it is a great proof of our wickedness that most people grow proud over the gifts they have received from him. Always consider who you are (Gen. 3; 18). Where did you receive it from? (1 Cor. 4). That God resists the proud (Luke 2, 14; 1 Pet. 5; James 4).

units.la: III Saulus mitior quærit, Quis es Domine? O socordiâ! Audit se ab eo peti, quem persequebatur, & adhuc quærit, &c. Frequens hodie, quòd cum Dei iram & manus quotidie irritemus, adhuc quærimus, vnde mala nobis accidant? Sic ægroti, qui intemperantia & libidine sibi morbus accessuerunt. Sic in publica egestate & rerum penuria. Causa, quia semper alias causas malorum fingimus.
units.tr: III. Saul, being gentler, asks: "Who are you, Lord?" O sluggishness! He hears that he is being sought by the one whom he was persecuting, and yet still asks, and so on. It is common today that, while we daily provoke the wrath and hand of God, we still ask whence evils come upon us. So sick people, whose illness has been brought on by intemperance and lust, do the same. So it is in public want and scarcity of goods. The reason is that we always invent other causes for our troubles.

units.la: ¶ Obseruemus ergo Deum esse, cuius nutu omnia fiunt, Matthæi 10. Eundem scelerum vindicem esse, Exodi 20. Psalmo quinto, &c. Deinde in nos ipsos descendamus, & examinemus vitam an-teactam.Ita mox patebit, quis nos percutiat.
units.tr: NOTE: Let us therefore observe that God is the one at whose nod all things happen (Matt. 10), that he is the same avenger of crimes (Exod. 20; Ps. 5, and so on). Then let us descend into ourselves and examine our past life. So it will soon be plain who is striking us.

units.la: IV. Respondet Dominus, Ego sum Ie-sus, &c. Duo dicit: 1. Scelus arguit, quasi dicat. Putas tibi cum hominibus vilissimis rem esse, &c. At tibi mecum res est, qui illos pro meis agnosco, & mihi factum pu-to, &c. Matthaei 25. Zachr. 2. Isa. 62. Vide quem habeant tyranni. Psalm. 2. Soletur nos. Interim hoc sibi applicent, qui mono polijs, vsuris, &c. alios opprimunt, & de pauperant.
units.tr: IV. The Lord answers: I am Jesus, and so on. He says two things: (1) He rebukes the crime, as if he said: You think you have to do with the most worthless men, but you have to do with me, who acknowledge them as mine and reckon what is done to them as done to me (Matt. 25; Zech. 2; Isa. 62). See what tyrants have. Ps. 2. Let this console us. Meanwhile, let those who oppress others with monopolies, usuries and so on, and impoverish them, apply this to themselves.

units.la: 2. Poenam minatur: Durum est tibi, &c. Metaphora a bobus, qui recalcitrando seipsos laedunt. Ita fit aduersus Christum & Ecclesiam pugnantibus. Vide Zach. 12. Matt. 21. Luc. 20. Exempla passim occurrunt. Simus ergo obfirmato animo. Vi uit adhuc Christus ille, & regnat, neq; Ecclesiam suam vnquam deseret. Matth. 28. Ioh. 14. Oremus.
units.tr: 2. He threatens punishment: It is hard for you, and so on. The metaphor is from oxen, which hurt themselves by kicking back. So it happens to those who fight against Christ and the Church. See Zech. 12; Matt. 21; Luke 20. Examples occur everywhere. Let us therefore be steadfast in mind. Christ still lives and reigns, and will never desert his Church (Matt. 28; John 14). Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIV.
units.tr: HOMILIA LXXIV.

units.la: 6 Tum (Saulus) tremens & patiens dixit: Domine quid me vis facere? Et Dominus ad illum: Surge, & ingredere in urbem, & dicetur tibi quid te oporteat facere. 7 Viri autem qui cum illo iter faciebant, stabant attoniti, audientes quidem vocem, neminem autem videntes,
units.tr: 6 Then Saul, trembling and astonished, said: Lord, what do you want me to do? And the Lord said to him: Arise, and go into the city, and it will be told you what you must do. 7 But the men who were travelling with him stood astonished, hearing indeed the voice, but seeing no one.

units.la: 8 Surrexit autem Saulus a terra, et cum aperti essent ipsius oculi, nemo nem videbat: itaque manu ducentes eum introduxerunt Damascum.
units.tr: 8 Saul rose up from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one; so, leading him by the hand, they brought him into Damascus.

units.la: 9 Vbi fuit tribus diebus, non videns, et non comedit neque bibit.
units.tr: 9 Where he was for three days, not seeing, and he neither ate nor drank.

units.la: VT Saulus, priusquam ad Christum converteretur, Ecclesiam crudeliter persecutus est: Ita in eo exemplo proponitur, quo docemur: 1. Salutem nobis ex gratia obtingere, neque nos aliquid habere quo gloriemur. Etsi enim non omnes similli immani tate contra Christum saeviant, omnium tamen ea conditio est, ut Dei manu habeant opus. 1.Cor. 2. Gen.6. 8.Phil.2.2.Cor.3. Gratuita ergo misericor dia nobis subuenitatur oportet. 2. Quàm facile sit Deo hostes suos vincere, & Ecclesiam suam liberare. Fuit Saulus potentissimus, crudelissimus, & iam videri poterat victor. Sed Deus momento aeternit & ex lupo agnum facit, imò pastorem, vt in praesenti narratur.
units.tr: As Saul, before he was converted to Christ, persecuted the Church cruelly, so in this example is set before us a lesson by which we are taught: 1. That salvation comes to us from grace, and that we have nothing in which to glory. For although not all rage against Christ with such monstrous cruelty, yet the condition of all is such that they have their work from the hand of God. 1 Cor. 2; Gen. 6; 8; Phil. 2; 2 Cor. 3. Therefore we must be helped by free mercy. 2. How easily God overcomes his enemies and frees his Church. Saul was most powerful and most cruel, and already he could seem to be the victor. But God in a moment makes a lamb out of a wolf, indeed a shepherd, as is related in the present passage.

units.la: I. Paulus tremens quaerit, Domine quid me, &c. Exemplum extremè humiliati & ad omne obsequium parati. Nam Domi-num agnoscit, quem oderat, quemque ab aliis nolebat agnosci. Et priusquam aliquid præcipiatur, quærit vt seruulus.
units.tr: I. Paul, trembling, asks: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" etc. An example of one utterly humbled and ready for every obedience. For he acknowledges as Lord the one whom he hated and whom he had been unwilling to have acknowledged by others. And before anything is commanded, he asks like a servant.

units.la: Not. ¶ 1. Quid eos deceat, qui a Deo castigantur. Agnoscant se a Deo castigari, & quidem suo bono. Heb.12. 1.Cor. 11.Pf. 94.1.Sam.2.Deinde Dominum suu agnoscant, & de eius voluntate interrogent, vt norint, quibus studijs placetur. Est hoc proprium electis, Pfalm.25.119. Secus reprobi, qui etsi cogantur interdum Deo cedere, fremunt tamen, & ideo ad ingenium mox redeunt. Pharao, Exod.8. 9.10. Saul, 1.Samuelis 24.26. Ita seruiPontificum, Iohan.18.
units.tr: Note. 1. What befits those who are chastised by God. Let them acknowledge that they are chastised by God, and indeed for their own good. Heb. 12; 1 Cor. 11; Ps. 94; 1 Sam. 2. Then let them acknowledge their Lord, and ask about his will, so that they may know by what pursuits he is pleased. This is characteristic of the elect: Ps. 25; 119. Otherwise the reprobate, who, although they are sometimes compelled to yield to God, nevertheless rage, and therefore soon return to their nature. Pharaoh, Exod. 8; 9; 10. Saul, 1 Sam. 24; 26. So the servants of the Pontiffs, John 18.

units.la: Itaque nos Paulum imitemur quandocunque castigamur. ¶ 2. Quid possit seueri-rior castigatio in causa fidei quoq; & falsitis. Multi enim nisi cogantur, non cedunt Deo. Hinc illud Luc.14. Talis Paulus & multi hodie. Falluntur, qui in religione ne minem cogi debere clamant, &c. Est quidem fides Dei donum, Eph.2. Ioh.6 1.Cor 3. Sed largitur hanc per verbum, &c. Rom. 10. Hoc igitur audire oportet. Si quis non lint, cogantur. Coerceantur item supersti-tiones, idololatria, &c. Deut.13. Zach.13. Ideo Apostolos, cum non essent Christiani mani magistratus, virtute maiori Deus arma uit 2 Cor 10.13 1 Tim.1. AStor.13, Eadem enim hic ratio est, quae in alijs sceleribus. Et exempla iunt passim obuia.
units.tr: Therefore let us imitate Paul whenever we are chastised. 2. What a more severe chastisement can do also in the cause of faith and falsehood. For many, unless they are compelled, do not yield to God. Hence that saying of Luke 14. Such was Paul, and many today. They are mistaken who cry out that in religion no one ought to be compelled, etc. Faith indeed is a gift of God, Eph. 2; John 6; 1 Cor. 3. But he bestows it through the word, etc. Rom. 10. Therefore this must be heard: if some are not willing, let them be compelled. Superstitions likewise, idolatry, etc., are to be restrained: Deut. 13; Zech. 13. Therefore God armed the Apostles with greater power when there were not yet Christian magistrates: 2 Cor. 10; 13; 1 Tim. 1; Acts 13. For the reason here is the same as in other crimes, and examples are everywhere at hand.

units.la: II. Quid Dominus? Mox benignum se praebet humiliato, secundum promissio-nem Matth 11.Ioh. 6. Remittit autem ad Ananiam, partim vt eius modestiam probet, dum ad eos relegat, quos prius odérat: partim vt seruet a se institutum ordinem, & verbi ministerium contra contemptores commendet, Rom 10 Sic factum cum Æthiope supra 8. Sic fiet cum Cornelio, infra 10 &c.
units.tr: II. What does the Lord do? Immediately he shows himself kind to the humbled one, according to the promise of Matt. 11; John 6. But he sends him back to Ananias, partly so that he may test his modesty, in that he sends him to those whom he had previously hated; partly so that he may preserve the order he has instituted, and commend the ministry of the Word against despisers: Rom. 10. So it was done with the Ethiopian above, chapter 8; so it will be done with Cornelius, below, chapter 10, etc.

units.la: Nota. ¶ Non debere verbi praedicationem pro superuacanea negligi, & noua quaeri reuelatio. Vide Lucae 16, Gal. 1. Neque etiam contemnantur ministri obscuriores. Nam verbo Dei authoritas exseip so constat, &c.
units.tr: Note. The preaching of the Word ought not to be neglected as superfluous, and new revelations sought. See Luke 16; Gal. 1. Nor should the less distinguished ministers be despised. For the authority of the Word of God is established from itself, etc.

units.la: III Interfertur narratio de Sauli comitibus. Steterunt attoniti. Sed prius etiam ciderunt, vt patet, Act. 26. Vbi dicuntur vocem non audiuisse: nimirum quod non in tellexerint, cum ad ipsos non pertineret.
units.tr: III. The narrative about Saul's companions is inserted. They stood astonished. But they had also fallen down before, as is plain, Acts 26, where they are said not to have heard the voice: namely because they did not understand it, since it did not pertain to them.

units.la: Vbi Not. ¶ Quid eos maneat, qui Christi sti hostibus se coniungunt. Cum ijsdem poenas dant, siue ferui, siue subditi, siue filij sint. Omnibus enim praeiudicat obedientia,quam Deo debemus,Actor.4.5.Lu-cæ 14. Notus est apologus de Ciconia.E-rat hoc obseruandum hodie, quando in Christum ferè omnes peccant.Alij crude-liter persequuntur. Alij persecutorum a-micitias quærunt. Alij Ipestatores sunt o-tiosi.Multi arma quoque cum eis coniun-gunt.Excusant se egestate, & quòd bella hæc geri dicunt, licet ipsi quiescant. Ege-nis respondet Paulus,Eph.4.Alteris Chri-stus quando loquitur Iudæ, Matthæi 26. Vide ergo Prou.1.Psal.1.
units.tr: Here note: what awaits those who join themselves to the enemies of Christ. They pay the same penalties with them, whether they are servants, subjects, or children. For obedience, which we owe to God, takes precedence over all: Acts 4; 5; Luke 14. The fable of the stork is well known. This ought to be observed today, when almost all sin against Christ. Some persecute cruelly. Others seek the friendships of the persecutors. Others are idle spectators. Many also join arms with them. They excuse themselves by poverty, and by saying that these wars are waged, although they themselves are at rest. Paul answers the poor: Eph. 4. To the others Christ speaks when he speaks to Judas: Matthew 26. See therefore Prov. 1; Ps. 1.

units.la: IV. Quid Paulus accepto responso Do-mini Surrexit, quia surgendi copiam fa-ciebat Christus. Sed appertis oculis nihil vidit.Ideo ducitur, &c. Triduo nihil edit nec bibit, &c.
units.tr: IV. What Paul does, having received the Lord's answer: he rose, since Christ was granting him the power to rise. But with his eyes opened he saw nothing. Therefore he is led, etc. For three days he ate nothing and drank nothing, etc.

units.la: NOTA ¶ Vt Christus hostium co-natus soleat eludere, vt in foueam, quam fecerunt,incidant Psalm.7. Visus est præ alijs videre Saul.Galat.1.Phil.3.Nunc ani-mo & corpore cœcutit.Venit cum feruis, qui Christianos captiuos ducerent Hie-rosolymam.Nunc ab illis plus quàm capti sunt ducitur Damascum. Multos fame af-flixit:nunc ipse inædia vexatur.Sunt simi-lia exempla in Ægyptijs.Exod.1.& 12.Ba-laamo, Num.23.24. Hamano, Heft. 5.6.7. Hoc illud est,quod habetur Psal.2.
units.tr: NOTE. How Christ is wont to mock the attempts of enemies, so that they fall into the pit they have dug: Ps. 7. He seemed to see more than the others: Gal. 1; Phil. 3. Now he is blind in mind and body. He came with servants who would lead captive Christians to Jerusalem. Now he is led by them to Damascus, more than captive. He afflicted many with hunger; now he himself is vexed by fasting. There are similar examples among the Egyptians: Exod. 1; 12. Balaam, Num. 23; 24. Haman, Esther 5; 6; 7. This is that which is found in Ps. 2.

units.la: Agnoscamus nos potentiam Christi, & ex ea consolationem petamus contra hostium minas, 1.Ioh.5.2.Par.32,Rom.8. Inter rim sub eius manu potenti humiliemur, & ei vni viuamus, qui pro nobis est mortuus, 2.Cor.5. Oremus.
units.tr: Let us acknowledge the power of Christ, and from it let us seek consolation against the threats of enemies: 1 John 5; Ps. 32; Rom. 8. Meanwhile let us be humbled under his mighty hand, and let us live to him alone, who died for us: 2 Cor. 5. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY 75.

units.la: 10 Erat autem quidam discipulus Damasci, nomine Ananias, ad quem dixit per visum Dominus, Anania. Et ille ait: Ecce, ego adsum Domine.
units.tr: 10 Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias, to whom the Lord said in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Behold, I am here, Lord."

units.la: 11 Tum Dominus ad eum, Surge & proficiscere in vicum, qui vocatur Rectus, & quære in domo Iudæ Saulum, nomine Tarsensem. Ecce enim orat.
units.tr: 11 Then the Lord said to him, "Arise and go to the street called Straight, and seek in the house of Judas a man of Tarsus named Saul. For behold, he is praying."

units.la: 12 Et vidit in visione Virum, Ananiam nomine, introeuntem & imponentem sibi manum, vt visum reciperet.
units.tr: 12 And in a vision he saw a man named Ananias come in and lay his hand on him, so that he might receive his sight.

units.la: 13 Respondit autem Ananias: Domine, audiui ex multis de viro hoc, quanta mala fecerit sanctis tuis Hierosolymis: & hic habet potestatem a summis sacerdotibus vinciendi omnes, qui invocant nomen tuum.
units.tr: 13 But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem; and here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon your name."

units.la: Christus in Scriptura describitur, qui inter inimicos regnet,& ex cuius manib. nemo possit oues rapere,Pfal.iio Mat.io. Ioh.10. Est hæc dulcis & necessaria consolatio,propter hostium rabiem, & credentium infirmitate.Ideo exemplis quoque confirmatur: inter quæ eximium est, quod in Paulo habemus. Fuit is à pueris institutus in lege fecundùm Pharifæorum doctrinam, Act.26. Hinc zelum concepit prepofterum,qui crudelissimum fidei per secutorem fecit, Phil.3. Accessit potentia & authoritas.At quia illum Deus fegre gàrat ab vtero, vt Filij sui Apostolus esset, (Galat.1.) decretum hoc ratum esse opor tuit,& non solum Ecclesiam contra illum defendit Christus,sed ita cicurat, vt se ad omne obsequium offerat humiliter. Sequitur, vt plene conuersus & ad Apostoli munus ordinatus fit.
units.tr: Scripture describes Christ as reigning in the midst of his enemies, and as the one from whose hands no one can snatch the sheep (Psal. 110; Matt. 10; John 10). This is a sweet and necessary consolation, on account of the raging of enemies and the weakness of believers. It is therefore also confirmed by examples, the most outstanding of which we have in Paul. From boyhood he was instructed in the law according to the teaching of the Pharisees (Acts 26). From this he conceived a perverse zeal, which made him the most cruel persecutor of the faith (Phil. 3). Power and authority were added. But because God had set him apart from the womb to be an apostle of his Son (Gal. 1), this decree had to be ratified: Christ not only defended the Church against him, but so tamed him that he offered himself humbly to every obedience. It follows that he was fully converted and ordained to the office of apostle.

units.la: I. De Anania agitur, cuius opera Christus vti voluit. Fuit is ex vulgo discipulorum probatæ pietatis & innocentiæ, Act. 22. Hunc per visionem excitat Dominus, & interea Paulum quoq; alia visione præparat, vt ad se venientem non auersetur.
units.tr: I. The story concerns Ananias, through whose work Christ wished to act. He was one of the ordinary disciples, of proven piety and innocence (Acts 22). The Lord rouses this man by a vision, and meanwhile prepares Paul also by another vision, so that he would not shrink from one coming to him.

units.la: Vbi Not.1. Studium Christi pro no ftra salute, maximè pro ouibus perditis. Vide Ifa.42.Matth.11 12.9.18.&c. Item Lucæ 15.Idem in præsenti facit. Sic infrà 10.
units.tr: Note 1: Christ's zeal for our salvation, especially for lost sheep. See Isa. 42; Matt. 11, 12, 9, 18, etc. Likewise Luke 15. He does the same here, as also below at 10.

units.la: Item Matth.9.Soletur hoc nos publicè & priuatim.Excitet item vt imitemur Christum, & ipsi quoque deseruandis potius quàm perdendis hominibus cogitemus.
units.tr: Likewise Matt. 9. This should comfort us both publicly and privately. It should also stir us to imitate Christ, and to think of ourselves as those who ought to save people rather than destroy them.

units.la: 2. Quod Ananiæ ministerio vtitur.Est ordinarius Dei mos,vt sæpe dictum. Ne ergo contemnamus hunc ordinem, neque fastidiamus ministros propter externam speciem. Sufficit abundè quisquis à Deo ordinatur. Poterat Paulus mirari, cur nō Petrus aut alius mittatur.Sed Deo fesæ commodat,qui ferè abiectis vtitur,vt nos modestiæ admoneat, 1.Cor.1.
units.tr: 2. That he uses the ministry of Ananias. It is God's ordinary way, as has often been said. Therefore let us not despise this order, nor disdain ministers because of their outward appearance. Whoever is ordained by God is quite sufficient. Paul might have wondered why Peter or someone else was not sent. But God accommodates himself to what is weak and uses what is almost despised, to remind us of modesty (1 Cor. 1).

units.la: ¶ 3. Quòd vterque præparatur peculiari visione.Opus eo. Nisi enim ministri recte vocetur,vt de sua vocatione certi sint: & auditores quoq; præparentur, nō potest fructus sequi.Quid enim prædicabunt, qui neque misi sunt, neque aliquid in mandatis habent,Rom.10. Icre.23 Quomodo item stabit adaerfus minas & conatus hostium? Vocatio certè olim prophetas aut mauit,Amos 7.Iere.1.Apostolos, Act.4.5. 2.Cor.5.1.Corin.9. Rursus auditores,nisi præparentur(Ge.6 8.)(semen illud nō excipient,vt fructum ferat. Est enim eadem illorum ratio,quæ terræ,Gen.3.Luc.8.Hinc patet, cur hodie nihil proficiatur. Mini-
units.tr: ¶ 3. That both are prepared by a special vision. The reason is this: unless ministers are rightly called, so that they may be certain of their calling, and unless hearers are also prepared, fruit cannot follow. For what will they preach who have neither been sent nor have anything in their commission (Rom. 10; Jer. 23)? How will he stand against the threats and attempts of enemies? Calling indeed once made prophets (Amos 7; Jer. 1) and apostles (Acts 4, 5; 2 Cor. 5; 1 Cor. 9). Again, hearers, unless they are prepared (Gen. 6, 8), will not receive that seed so that it bears fruit. For their condition is the same as that of the ground (Gen. 3; Luke 8). From this it is clear why nothing progresses today. Ministers

units.la: ftri sponte currunt plerique, & ventri ftu dent,Phil.3. Idem de multis in magistratu ʼpoteft dici, qui debebant Ecclesiæ nutri- tij efle & Filium Dei exosculari,Ifa.49 Pf. 2.Deuter.17.Auditores sunt, quales Eze- chiel.33.
units.tr: very many run of their own accord and devote themselves to their bellies (Phil. 3). The same can be said of many in the magistracy, who ought to be nursing fathers of the Church and to kiss the Son of God (Isa. 49; Psal. 2; Deut. 17). The hearers are such as those in Ezekiel 33.

units.la: II.Paulum ergo videamus, qui interea orauit:Assiduè nimirum toto illo triduo. Fuerunt causæ multæ.1. Senserat grauem Christi manum,Heb.10. 2. Accusatus vt publicus hostis. 3. Obuersabantur animo quæcunque fecerat credentibus. Hinc conscientiæ terrores, de quibus Ifa.6.38. 39 &c. 4.Exspectat promissionum reuela tionem,&c.
units.tr: II. Let us see Paul, then, who meanwhile prayed: assiduously, of course, through all those three days. There were many causes. 1. He had felt the heavy hand of Christ (Heb. 10). 2. He was accused as a public enemy. 3. Whatever he had done against believers hovered before his mind. Hence came terrors of conscience, of which Isa. 6, 38, 39, etc. 4. He awaited the revelation of the promises, etc.

units.la: NOT. ¶ 1.Quid nos deceat hodie,quan do eædem causæ nos vrgent. In nobis in- uenimus peccata,vt omnibus idem dicen dum fit,quod Psal.143.150. Sentimus Dei manum. Opus habemus institutione.Assi duè ergo orandum,1.Thef.5.vt Deus pro pitius fit nobis,vt in vijs suis dirigat, Psal. 25.119.vt nos tueatur.
units.tr: NOTE ¶ 1: What befits us today, when these same causes press upon us. In ourselves we find sins, so that the same thing must be said to all as in Psal. 143, 150. We feel the hand of God. We need instruction. Therefore we must pray continually (1 Thess. 5), that God may be gracious to us, direct us in his ways (Psal. 25, 119), and keep us safe.

units.la: ¶ 2.Interim non præscribamus Deo ex impatientia. Differt opem aliquando,vt etiam hic.Id vero,vt fidem nostram exer- ceat. Vide Abrahamum,Gen.15.17 Rom. 4 Cananæam,Mat.25.Ita nos,Luc.18. Sed ferè segnes sumus, quasi non opus fit Dei auxilio. Aut si non cito audiat, deficimus, vt Mal.3.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Meanwhile let us not prescribe to God out of impatience. He sometimes delays help, as here, and he does so in order to exercise our faith. See Abraham (Gen. 15, 17; Rom. 4), the Canaanite woman (Matt. 25), and so with us (Luke 18). But we are mostly sluggish, as if there were no need of God's help. Or if he does not hear quickly, we lose heart, as in Mal. 3.

units.la: III. Quid Ananias? Tergiuersatur ini-tio ex metu. Sed ridiculum se prębet, dum ista Deo exponit.
units.tr: III. What of Ananias? At first he shrinks back out of fear. But he makes himself ridiculous while he sets these things out before God.

units.la: Nota. Quid posit metus etiam in sanctis: nimirum vt contra Dei mandata ex seipsis consilia capiant. Sic Abraham, Gen.12.20. Sic Moses impeditur, Exod.3. & 4. Ionas, cap.1. Elias, 1. Reg. 19. Est hæc humana infirmitas, ob quam neq; nos desperare, neque alios damnare debemus, cùm in Christo quoque locum habuerit, Ioh.12 Luc.22. &c. Interim videndum, ne huic indulgeamus contra Dei mandatum. Hæc hodie omnis diffidentiæ & inobedientiæ causa est. Qui nihil timent quando seruiendum est mundo & carni, timere incipiunt, si quid faciendum ex Dei mandato. Hinc ratiocinationes mirificæ, &c. Cogitemus ergo huius nutu omnia regi, Math.6:10. Eundem esse iustum, sapientem, bonum, qui in suis vijs ambulantes non deserat, Ioh.14. Mat.28. Huic ergo fidamus (Rom.1.16.) & Oremus.
units.tr: Note: what fear can do even in the saints, namely, that they take counsel from themselves against God's commands. So Abraham (Gen. 12, 20). So Moses is hindered (Exod. 3 and 4), Jonah (ch. 1), Elijah (1 Kings 19). This is human weakness, on account of which we ought neither to despair nor to condemn others, since it found a place even in Christ (John 12; Luke 22, etc.). Meanwhile we must take care not to indulge it against God's command. Today this is the cause of all distrust and disobedience. Those who fear nothing when they must serve the world and the flesh begin to fear if anything must be done by God's command. Hence come wonderful rationalizations, etc. Let us therefore consider that all things are ruled by his will (Matt. 6:10), and that he is the same just, wise and good God who does not forsake those who walk in his ways (John 14; Matt. 28). Let us therefore trust in him (Rom. 1:16). And let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXVI.

units.la: 15 Dixit autem illi Dominus: Va de, quia organum electum mihi est iste, ut portet nomen meum coram gentibus & Regibus, & filijs Israel.
units.tr: 15 But the Lord said to him: Go, for this man is a chosen instrument to me, to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel.

units.la: 16 Ego enim ostendā ei, quàm multa oporteat eum pati pro nomine meo.
units.tr: 16 For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name.

units.la: QVoniam Dei Filius Apostolos totius orbis doctores fecit (Mar.16) Euangelistæ non abfq; causa narrant, qui & quales initio fuerint, quomodo conuersi sint, & quid postea fecerint. Primò quidem, vt Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qua eum erga illos, tum erga totum mundum vsus est: Partim verò, vt maior sit doctrinæ eorum authoritas, ne eos pro vulgaribus hominibus contemnamus, sed semper meminerimus dicti Christi, Iohan. 15. Mat.10. Luc.10.21. Vtrumque in primis in Paulo obseruari debet. Quia enim hic nō solùm à Christo alienus, sed hostis quoq; fuit, in eo Deus singulare bonitatis exemplum edidit, 1.Timot.1. Deinde cùm præ alijs laborauerit (1.Cor.15. Rom.15.) & nul lius scripta frequentius adducantur, necesse est scire, quis & qualis fuerit. Hunc maximè facit præsens hoc de illo Christi testimonium.
units.tr: Since the Son of God made the apostles teachers of the whole world (Mark 16), the evangelists do not narrate without reason who and what sort of men they were at the beginning, how they were converted, and what they did afterwards. First, that we may acknowledge God's goodness, by which he dealt with them and, through them, with the whole world. Second, so that the authority of their teaching may be greater, and we do not despise them as ordinary men, but always remember Christ's saying (John 15; Matt. 10; Luke 10:21). Both points should be observed especially in Paul. For since he was not only alien to Christ but also his enemy, God displayed in him a singular example of goodness (1 Tim. 1). Then, since he laboured more than the others (1 Cor. 15; Rom. 15), and since no one's writings are cited more often, it is necessary to know who and what sort of man he was. This present testimony of Christ about him makes this especially clear.

units.la: Huius occasio fuit, quòd Ananias eum accedere noluit, quòd propter anteacta sibi ab eo timeret. Nam sancti quoq; non semper intelligunt quid Deus velit aut agat: & ideo interdum sibi timent, vt Moses Exod 3 4. &c. Ita hic Ananias. Sed Deus vt eum: Vade. Perinde ac si herus seruulo cunctatori loquatur.
units.tr: The occasion was that Ananias was unwilling to go to him, because he feared him on account of what Paul had done before. For the saints too do not always understand what God wills or does, and so they sometimes fear for themselves, as Moses (Exod. 3, 4) and others did. So too Ananias here. But God says to him: Go. It is as if a master spoke to a hesitant servant.

units.la: NOT. ¶ Deum non admittere nostras rationes, vt ut carni plausibiles videantur. Sc actum Exod 4. Iere. 11. Reg 19. Ita Lucas 9. Et sanè ridiculi sunt, qui cum Deo disputationem instituunt. Scit ille omnia melius quàm nos. Singuli ergo hoc sibi applicent.
units.tr: NOTE. That God does not admit our reasons, however plausible they may seem to the flesh. So it was done in Exodus 4, Jeremiah 11, and 1 Kings 19; likewise in Luke 9. Indeed, those are ridiculous who enter into debate with God. He knows all things better than we do. Let each one apply this to himself.

units.la: ¶ Obseruemus tamen eius bonitatem, qui interdum suorum mandatorum ratio nem nobis reddit, vt etiam in praesenti: Quia organum, &c. Sensus: A deo nihil peri cui esse à Saulo, vt potius fidem ipse praedicaturus sit, & propter illam nihil non passurus. Sed singula excutiamus, quia multa insunt, quae nostrae institutioni & consolationi seruiunt.
units.tr: Let us nevertheless observe his goodness, who sometimes gives us the reason for his commands, as also in the present case: "Because the instrument..." The sense is: nothing is to be feared from Saul by God, so that he himself should rather preach the faith and, on account of it, suffer everything. But let us examine the particulars one by one, since many things are contained in them which serve our instruction and consolation.

units.la: I. Organum electum dicit. Sic dicuntur Electum homines, quia Deus per eos agit & sua instrumenta dicia exequitur. Ita vasa gloriae & irae dicuntur, Rom. 9.2. Tim. 2. In praesenti Paulus organum electum, quia illum Deus ab utero matris segregarat (Gal. 1.) vt eo vte retur praealijs, &c.
units.tr: I. He says "a chosen instrument." Men are so called because God acts through them and carries out his instruments as designed. So vessels of glory and of wrath are called such (Rom. 9; Tim. 2). In the present case Paul is a chosen instrument, because God had set him apart from his mother's womb (Gal. 1), so that he might be used before others, and so on.

units.la: NOT. ¶1. Vt nos quoq; de Dei seruis eximijs debeamus iudicare. Agnoscamus organa Dei fuisse. Vt ergo opus non instrumento, sed opifici tribuitur : ita nos, quæ illi fecerunt ad Deum authorem referamus. Sic ipsi docuerunt, Actor. 3. 14. 1.Cor.15.Errant ergo, qui ita ab illis pendent,vt pro Dijs habeant, aut propter illos in sectas scindantur. Videi.Cor.3.1.Auguft.in 1.Ioh.2.&c.
units.tr: NOTE. (1) That we too ought to judge concerning God's distinguished servants in this way. Let us acknowledge that they were instruments of God. Just as a work is ascribed not to the tool but to the workman, so we should refer to God as author what they have done. Thus they themselves taught (Acts 3:14; 1 Cor. 15). They err, therefore, who depend on them so much that they regard them as gods, or who split into sects on account of them. See 1 Cor. 3; Augustine on 1 John 2, etc.

units.la: ¶ 2.In nobis ipsis idem obseruemus,ne efferamur ijs,quæ fecimus præclarè. Cogitemus,qui fimus natura,Pfal 51. Gen.6. 8.1.Tim.6.2.Cor.3. Quicquid ergo habemus,accepimus, &c.1.Cor.4.Phil.3. Cur vero aecepimus? 1.Vt Deum veneremur Matt.25.2.Vt proximo benefaciamus,Leuit.19.1.Corin.12. Ad ista fi nos examinemus,tantum nobis deerit,vt potiùs humiliari nos deceat,quàm superbire,Roma.7. Dauid,2.Sam.7.
units.tr: (2) In ourselves too let us observe the same, that we not be puffed up by what we have done well. Let us consider what we are by nature (Ps. 51; Gen. 6, 8; 1 Tim. 6; 2 Cor. 3). Whatever we have, we have received (1 Cor. 4; Phil. 3). But why have we received it? First, that we may worship God (Matt. 25); second, that we may do good to our neighbour (Lev. 19; 1 Cor. 12). If we examine ourselves by these standards, so much will be lacking to us that it becomes us to be humbled rather than to be proud (Rom. 7; David, 2 Sam. 7).

units.la: ¶ 3. In reprobis quoque & impijs hoc obseruemus, ne horum furoribus terreamur,aut successibus offendamur. Sunt enim hi quoque organa Dei, Ifaiæ 10.Pharao,Rom. 9. Exod. 9. Non possunt ergo plus quàm hic velit, Iob 38. Non intelligunt quidem hoc, & ideo superbiunt, Exod.5.Ila 10.Hab.1.Dan. 4. Sed hæc illis suæ ruinæ causa est,Prou,16.
units.tr: (3) In the reprobate and the impious too let us observe this, that we not be terrified by their rages or offended by their successes. For these too are instruments of God (Isa. 10; Pharaoh, Rom. 9; Exod. 9). They therefore cannot do more than he wills (Job 38). Indeed they do not understand this, and so they are proud (Exod. 5; Isa. 10; Hab. 1; Dan. 4). But this is the cause of their ruin (Prov. 16).

units.la: II. Quale organum: Vt ferat nomen me-um, id est, praedicet, quis sim &c. Nominat se natum ad autem gentes, quia Doctor gentium esse praedicatio debebat, i. Tim. 2. Et de eo oportebat nunc ne Christi mentionem fieri propter Iudaeos, Act. 10, 11.21. &c. ¶ Obseruemus, quod sit officium ministrorum: Vt nimirum portent nomen Christi, id est, doceant, hunc esse Seruatorem unicum, &c. Non alia nomina, Acto. 4. Gal. 1. Et quidè apud omnes, adeo vt ne coram regibus quidem illos Christi & Euangelij pudeat, Mar. 8. Rom. 1. 10. Pf. 119. Sic fecit Petrus, Act. 26. Phil. 4. 2. Tim. 4. Hinc factum, vt veteres Episcopi munus per imaginem Christophori expresse rint. Quem typum ad fores templorum proposuerunt, vt & Georgij, qui principis Christiani typus est, &c. Postea res in ido lolatriam degenerauit: vt vel hoc exemplo discamus quid sit, velle aliunde quàm ex Dei verbo discere, Hab. 2. Recte Apostolus, 1. Ioh. 3.
units.tr: II. What sort of instrument: "that he may carry my name", that is, preach who I am, and so on. He names the Gentiles because he was to be the preacher and teacher of the Gentiles (1 Tim. 2). And it was necessary that Christ's name be mentioned to the Jews at that time (Acts 10, 11, 21, etc.). Let us observe what the duty of ministers is: namely, to carry the name of Christ, that is, to teach that he is the only Saviour, and so on, and not other names (Acts 4; Gal. 1). And they must do so before all, indeed without shame even before kings, concerning Christ and the gospel (Mark 8; Rom. 1, 10; Ps. 119). So Peter did (Acts 26; Phil. 4; 2 Tim. 4). Hence it came about that the ancient bishops portrayed this office expressly through the image of Christopher. They set up this figure at the doors of churches, as also of George, who is a type of the Christian prince, and so on. Afterwards the thing degenerated into idolatry, so that from this example at least we may learn what it means to wish to learn from anywhere other than God's word (Hab. 2). Rightly the apostle says (1 John 3).

units.la: III. Ostendam ei, &c. Videtur commina tio, sed potius promissio est non simplex.
units.tr: III. I will show him, etc. This seems like a threat, but it is rather a simple promise.

units.la: 1. Merebatur Paulus affligi vt hostis Christi. Sed poenas meritas conuertit ei Deus in Filij sui crucem. 2. Promittit vires & fortitudinem, vt inuictus maneat, &c. Ad expositionem facit 2. Cor. 11.
units.tr: 1. Paul deserved to be afflicted as an enemy of Christ. But God turned the punishment he had earned into the cross of his Son. 2. He promises strength and courage, so that he may remain unconquered, etc. Compare 2 Cor. 11 for the exposition.

units.la: {*}NOTA. ¶ 1. Crucepiorum, & in primis ministrorum Christi neminem debere offendi. Eadem omnium conditio, quæ Paulì. Deinde non est hæc insolens, &c. Matt. 5.10. Ioh.15.16. 2 Tim.3. Neque aliter poterit fieri propter mundi ingenium, Ioh 3. Stulti, qui hoc non obseruant, & putant Euangelium sine cruce prædicari posse. Hæc opinio tepidos facit, &c. Apoc 3. Gal. 1. Itaque præparemus nos ad crucé, Luc.9 Mat.16. Luc.14.
units.tr: NOTE. (1) That none of the crucified, and especially none of the ministers of Christ, ought to be offended. Their condition is the same as Paul's. Moreover, this is not something strange, etc. Matt. 5.10; John 15.16; 2 Tim. 3. Nor can it be otherwise, given the nature of the world, John 3. Fools who do not observe this and think the Gospel can be preached without the cross are mistaken. This opinion makes people lukewarm, etc. Rev. 3; Gal. 1. Therefore let us prepare ourselves for the cross, Luke 9; Matt. 16; Luke 14.

units.la: ¶ 2. Soletur, quod Christi crucem ferimus (vt Simon Mar.15.) & quod ille noster, is est Agonothetes, qui simul vires suficit, dum suam charitate diffundit in cordibus nostris, Rom.5.8. Phil.4.1. Ioh.5. De his cogitemus hodie in hac mundi sene-cta, &c. Oremus.
units.tr: (2) Let us be comforted that we bear the cross of Christ (as Simon did, Mark 15), and that he is our contender, who is also the one who supplies strength, while he pours out his love in our hearts, Rom. 5.8; Phil. 4.1; John 5. Let us think of these things today in this old age of the world, etc. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 77.

units.la: 17 Abijt igitur Ananias, et introi-uit domum illam, & impositis manibus, dixit: Saul frater, Dominus misit me (Iesus scilicet, qui tibi apparuit in via, qua veniebas) vt visum recipias, & im-pleatis Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: 17 So Ananias went away and entered that house. Laying his hands on Saul, he said: "Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me (Jesus, of course, who appeared to you on the road by which you were travelling), that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit."

units.la: 18 Et continuo deciderunt ab oculis eius tanquam squamæ, & visum recepit: ac surgens baptizatus est. 19 Quumq; cœpisset cibum, corro- boratus est.
units.tr: 18 And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He rose and was baptized. 19 And when he had taken food, he was strengthened.

units.la: SIcuti Paulus plus alijs Apostolis labo- rauit in propagando Christi regno (1. Cor.15. 2. Cor.11.) ita eius historia maiori diligentia,quàm aliorum describitur.1.Vt in ea agnoscamus Dei gratuitam miseri- cordiam, qua is peccatores ad se conuer- sos complestitur,Ezech 18.2. Vt in ea ma ior fit eius doctrinæ authoritas, de qua il- le tam grauiter protestatur,Act 20. Gal.1. Ad vtrumq; in primis facit illustre de illo Christi testimonium. Vocat enim ele- ctum organum eum,qui vas iræ dici & se- se merebatur, quod ipse fatetur 1.Cor 15. primo ad Timotheum primo.Deinde tri- buit ei fidem & dexteritatem in rebus a- gendis, constantiam item & patientiam, &c. Nemo igitur eius doctrinam con- temnere potest,nisi in ipsum Christum ve lit esse iniurius, & ipsum leuitatis infimu- lare. Sed faciunt ad istorum confirma- tionem, quæ de eius restitutione dicun- tur hoc ordine.
units.tr: Just as Paul laboured more than the other apostles in spreading Christ's kingdom (1 Cor. 15; 2 Cor. 11), so his history is described with greater care than theirs. First, that in it we may recognize God's free mercy, by which he embraces sinners converted to himself (Ezech 18.2). Second, that the authority of his teaching may be greater, a point on which he protests so solemnly (Acts 20; Gal. 1). For both purposes that remarkable testimony of Christ about him is especially useful. For Christ calls him a chosen instrument, though he deserved to be called a vessel of wrath, as he himself confesses (1 Cor. 15; 1 Tim. 1). Then Christ attributes to him faith and skill in carrying out his tasks, and constancy and patience as well. No one therefore can despise his teaching without wishing to wrong Christ himself and charge him with levity. But what is said of Paul's restoration serves to confirm these points, and it does so in the following order.

units.la: I. Ananias producitur,de quo hæc di- cuntur. 1. Abijt & domû illam ingressus est. Obsequitur ergo nunc mandato Do- mini, quod priûs ex metu detrectabat.
units.tr: I. Ananias is brought forward, and of him these things are said. (1) He went away and entered that house. He therefore now obeys the Lord's command, which before he had refused out of fear.

units.la: Ita omnes sanȼti.Moses,Exod 4.5 &c.Ioô nas,cap.1.2.3.Iere.1.Imitemur.T mere hu manum est, & in sanctissimos cadit hic affectus. Imo in Christo locum habuit,Iob. 12.Matth.26.Luc.23.Sed inexcusabile sceleus est, ex metu officium deserere.Simile militis.Id ne faciamus,plurimum prodest prouidentiæ Dei consideratio. In eius manu sunt nostræ sortes,Psal.31. Matt.10. Idem sapientia ipsissima est. Iustus item. Et in suis præceptis ambulantes potest tueri,Ioh.10. Hæc qui tenent,cum Dauide aiunt Psalm.23.Item cum Paulo, Rom.8.14.
units.tr: So all the saints have done: Moses (Exod. 4.5 etc.), Jonah (chapters 1, 2, 3), Jeremiah (chapter 1). Let us imitate them. To tremble is human, and this feeling falls upon the most holy; indeed it had its place even in Christ (John 12; Matt. 26; Luke 23). But to desert one's duty out of fear is an inexcusable crime. Consideration of God's providence greatly helps us to avoid this. Our lots are in his hand (Ps. 31; Matt. 10). He is also wisdom itself, and he is just. He can protect those who walk in his precepts (John 10). Those who hold this say with David (Ps. 23), and with Paul (Rom. 8.14).

units.la: ¶2. Imponit ei manus. Ceremonia ex veteri Testamento petita. Victimæ ad aram,Sacerdos nomine populi imponebat manum,quæ concionis nota erat, & eandem sic Deo consecrabat.Ea nunc ex Christi mandato vtitur Ananias, & ita imponit Paulo curam Ecclesiæ & eundem consecrat Christi seruitio. Agnouit hoc ipse, 2.Cor.11.1.Cor.9.Idem obseruent omnes ministri,& sibi dictu putent illud, 1.Tim.4.2.Tim.1. O si deisto omnes cogitarent diligentius!
units.tr: ¶ 2. He lays his hands on him. The ceremony is taken from the Old Testament. When a victim was brought to the altar, the priest laid his hand on it in the name of the people; this was a sign of the sermon, and so he consecrated it to God. Now Ananias uses the same rite by Christ's command, and thus lays on Paul the care of the Church and consecrates him to Christ's service. Paul himself acknowledged this (2 Cor. 11; 1 Cor. 9). Let all ministers observe the same, and take that saying (1 Tim. 4; 2 Tim. 1) as addressed to themselves. Oh, if only everyone would consider this more diligently!

units.la: ¶3. Annuntiat ei quæ in mandatis habebat,& intrepide Iesu v,nomen eius seruum profitetur apud eum, qui hostis paulò ante fuerat. Ita non pudeat nos Christi, Rom. 1. Mar. 8. Econtrà quia Christi de illo testimonium audierat, immemor iniuriarum fratrem dicit. Imitemur ipsi quoq; Matt. 18.6. Hodie in utroq; pecca tur turpissimè.
units.tr: ¶ 3. He announces to him what he had been commanded, and fearlessly confesses Jesus' name to him as his servant, before one who had lately been an enemy. So let us not be ashamed of Christ (Rom. 1; Mark 8). On the contrary, because he had heard Christ's testimony about Paul, Ananias calls him brother, forgetful of injuries. Let us also imitate him (Matt. 18.6). Today we sin shamefully in both respects.

units.la: II. Effectus. Fit quod promissum. Deci dunt squamæ ab oculis, & accipit Spiritum, vt sequentia docent) vt corpore animoq; videat. Squamæ docent, non leuem fuisse caecitatem, qualis ex fulgure, sed miraculosam. Ita etiam restitutio.
units.tr: II. The effect. What was promised comes to pass. Scales fall from his eyes, and he receives the Spirit, as what follows shows, so that he may see with body and soul. The scales show that his blindness was not slight, such as comes from lightning, but miraculous. So too the restoration was miraculous.

units.la: ¶ Seruit autem vtraq; praesenti negotio. Vilus sibi erat oculatissimus in lege, Gal. 1. Phil. 3. Sed mera haec caecitas erat, pendente adhuc velo ob oculos, &c. 1. Corin. 3. Isto nunc per Christum sublato videt. Eadem omnium ratio. Quotquot sibi ipsis videntur sapere extra Christum, reuera caeci sunt, 1. Cor. 2. Vide gentes Ro. 1. Sic in Papatu. Solus Christus squamas ignorantiae aufert, & illuminat. Vide Ioh. 1. 8. 12. If. 49. 42. 1. Cor. 1. Col. 2. Hunc ergo sequamur.
units.tr: ¶ He served both purposes in the present business. He seemed to himself most keen-sighted in the law (Gal. 1; Phil. 3). But this was mere blindness, with the veil still hanging over his eyes (2 Cor. 3). Now that the veil is removed through Christ, he sees. The reason is the same for all: whoever seems wise to himself apart from Christ is really blind (1 Cor. 2). See the Gentiles (Rom. 1). So it is under the Papacy. Christ alone takes away the scales of ignorance and enlightens. See John 1, 8, 12; Isa. 42, 49; 1 Cor. 1; Col. 2. Let us therefore follow him.

units.la: III. Quid Paulus? ¶ 1. Surgit & baptizatus est. Hoc enim quoq; iusserat Ana-nias, Act. 22. & ita ablutionem ei in Christo monstrauerat. Atqui poterat hoc videri superuacaneum in eo, quem Christus iam fecerat electum organum,&c. Sed sanctì nihil superuacaneum ducunt quod Deus tradidit. Sentiunt in seipsis infirmitatem, quæ adminiculis opus habet, Roman. 7. Iisdem gaudent & orant. Supra 8.Psal.25. 119.1. &c. Nòrunt,quia cum seueritate prę cepta fuerat obseruatio veterum rituum, qui tamen debebant aboleri,Hebr. 9. Vide Gen.17,Exod. 4. 12. Arguuntur,qui fidem ostentant cum Sacramentorum con temptu.
units.tr: III. What did Paul do? ¶ 1. He rose and was baptized. For Ananias had also commanded this (Acts 22), and so had shown him the washing in Christ. Yet this might seem superfluous for one whom Christ had already made a chosen instrument. But the saints regard nothing as superfluous that God has handed down. They feel in themselves a weakness that needs supports (Rom. 7). They rejoice in these same things and pray (Acts 8; Ps. 25; 119). They know that the observance of the old rites, which nevertheless had to be abolished, had been enjoined with severity (Heb. 9). See Gen. 17; Exod. 4, 12. Those are rebuked who display faith while despising the sacraments.

units.la: ¶ 2.Sumpto cibo recuperat vires.Prius toto triduo nihil ederat,&c. Nunc ipsum restituente Domino,edit, &c. Ergo non cibi modo à Deo dantur,sed etiam facultas edendi & nutriendi vis. Docent hoc quotidiana exempla. Huc refer Ezechiel.4 5.14. Leuit.26. Recte ergo ille rusticus gratias agebat Deo, qui dedisset cibandi & edendi facultatem.Vtinam obseruarent lurcones, qui turpiter abutuntur. Sed quia faciunt quod habetur Isaiæ 5. Amos 6.vnâ cum Dei donis seipsos perdunt, & sibi multorum scelerum sunt authores.
units.tr: ¶ 2. After taking food he recovers his strength. Before this he had eaten nothing for three whole days. Now, with the Lord himself restoring him, he eats. So food is given by God not only as food, but also the power of eating and the strength of nourishing. Daily examples teach this. Refer here Ezech. 4, 5, 14; Lev. 26. Rightly, then, that countryman gave thanks to God, who had given the ability to feed and to eat. Would that gluttons, who shamefully abuse this, would observe it! But because they do what is described in Isa. 5 and Amos 6, they destroy themselves along with God's gifts, and become the authors of many sins for themselves.

units.la: ¶ Obseruemus item,sanctos non aspernari solita naturæ subsidia. Edit Paulus, & neq; sub prouidentiæ , neq; religionis prætextu à cibo abstinet. Ita monet Timotheus.
units.tr: ¶ Let us also observe that the saints do not spurn the usual aids of nature. Paul eats, and under neither the pretext of providence nor that of religion does he abstain from food. Timothy advises the same.

units.la: motheus,1 Timoth.5. Stulte superstitiosi sunt, qui se sanctiores putant, si seipsos inedia conficiunt, Zach.8 Rom.14. Videitem Deut 14.16. Stultiores, qui ciborum discrimina & delectum observant ex lege reda ctum, quem Christus sustulit, Mat.15 Act. 10 Vnde Apostolus, Col 2.Heb.13.1.Tim. 4 &c. Vtamur ergo libertate nostra, sed sic, nec in licentiam exeat, Gal 5. Vtq; nos Deus illuminet & corroboret, Oremus.
units.tr: Timothy (1 Tim. 5). Foolishly superstitious are those who think themselves holier if they wear themselves out by fasting (Zech. 8; Rom. 14). See Deut. 14, 16. More foolish still are those who observe distinctions and a choice of foods drawn from the law, which Christ abolished (Matt. 15; Acts 10). Hence the Apostle (Col. 2; Heb. 13; 1 Tim. 4, etc.). Let us therefore use our liberty, but in such a way that it does not turn into licence (Gal. 5). And may God enlighten and strengthen us. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXVIII.

units.la: 19 Fuit autem Saulus cum discipulis, qui erant Damasci per dies aliquot.
units.tr: 19 And Saul was with the disciples who were at Damascus for some days.

units.la: 20 Et statim in Synagogis praedicauit Christum, nempe eum esse Filium Dei.
units.tr: 20 And straightway in the synagogues he preached Christ, namely that he is the Son of God.

units.la: 21 Obstupescebant autem omnes qui audiebant, & dicebant: Nonne hic est qui populatus est in Ierusalem eos, qui invocabant nomen istud: & huc idcirco venit, ut vinctos eos abduceret, ad Principes Sacerdotum.
units.tr: 21 But all who heard were amazed and said: Is this not he who destroyed in Jerusalem those who called upon this name? And he came here for this purpose, that he might lead them away bound to the chief priests.

units.la: 22 Saulus autem magis invalescebat & confundebat Iudaeos, qui habitabant Damasci, collatis testimoniis demonstrans eum esse Christum.
units.tr: 22 But Saul grew all the stronger and confounded the Jews who dwelt at Damascus, proving by the comparison of testimonies that he is the Christ.

units.la: OVemadmodum in Pauli conuer‑sione exemplum singulare miseri cordiæ Dei proponitur, quo docemur e‑um peccatores ad se conuersos recipere in gratiam: ita in illius exemplo officij sui omnes admonentur, qui recte conuerti volunt. Primo enim prostratus quærit, Quis es Domine? Inde, quid ipsum velit facere? Iussus ire in vrbem, paret, ibi triduum exspectat. Adhæc Ananiam antea ignotum, & ex vulgo Christianorum non saftidit. Deniq; baptizatur, per omnia se Dei voluntati accomodans. Ita nos, quan do Deus peccantes vel foris castigat, vel intus conscientias terret, quæramus de illo & voluntate eius, Isa. 55. Amos 5. Edo‑ni hanc obediamus, & nullius nos morae aut laboris pigeat, Pf. 62. Hab. 2. In primis non pudeat nos seruorum Dei & huius mandatorum, Luc. 10. Mar. 8. Quia vero non sufficit reliquisse prauos mores, nisi insuper nouae vocationi satisfaciamus, sequitur vt Paul. suo officio cœperit fungi, &c.
units.tr: Just as in the conversion of Paul a singular example of God's mercy is set before us, by which we are taught that he receives into grace sinners who turn to him, so in his example all are admonished in their duty who wish to be converted aright. For first, prostrate, he asks, "Who are you, Lord?" Then he asks what the Lord wishes him to do. Bidden to go into the city, he obeys, and there he waits three days. Moreover, he did not disdain Ananias, previously unknown to him and one of the common sort of Christians. Finally he is baptized, accommodating himself in all things to the will of God. So we too, when God either chastises us in our sins outwardly or terrifies our consciences inwardly, should seek him and his will (Isa. 55; Amos 5), and that we may obey, let no delay or labour weary us (Ps. 62; Hab. 2). Above all let us not be ashamed of the servants of God and of his commands (Luke 10; Mark 8). But because it is not enough to have abandoned wicked morals unless we also satisfy the new calling, it follows that Paul began to discharge his office, etc.

units.la: I. Coniungit se discipulis, non Iudæis vel gentibus. Atqui illi erant, quos capere debebat, & qui plerisque erant inuisi. Itaq; horum consuetudo non solum periculosa esse poterat, sed insuper ei perfidiæ notam inurere. Sed Ecclesiæ societatem pluris facit, memor nimirum eorum, quæ olim dicta, Psal. 3. 84.
units.tr: I. He joins himself to the disciples, not to the Jews or the Gentiles. Yet those were the men whom he was to seize, and who were for the most part hateful to him. Therefore association with them could not only be dangerous but would also brand him with the mark of treachery. But he sets a higher value on fellowship with the Church, mindful surely of those things said long ago (Ps. 3; 84).

units.la: NOT. Quid deceat eos, qui ad Christum verè conuerti volunt? Separent sese a mundo, cum ipsos Christus ex hac sele-gerit, Ioh. 15. Vide Act. 2. Licet quidem necessaria commercia exercere, &c. 1. Cor. 5. 7. Item occasiones quærere alios conuertendi. Ita Christus neminem fastidit, Matth. 9. Luc. 7. 14. At a non necessariis & periculosis commercijs abstinendum. Talia sunt eorum, de quibus nihil potest sparari, vt Abbatū & similium. Quid horum sociis & conuiuis accidat, vnius Petri exemplum docet. Matth. 26. Semper ergo in mentem veniat quod habetur, Psal. 16. 15.
units.tr: NOTE. What befits those who truly wish to be converted to Christ? Let them separate themselves from the world, since Christ has chosen them out of this world (John 15; see Acts 2). It is indeed permitted to carry on necessary dealings, etc. (1 Cor. 5:7). Likewise to seek occasions of converting others; so Christ disdains no one (Matt. 9; Luke 7, 14). But one must abstain from unnecessary and dangerous dealings. Such are those of whom nothing can be spoken well, such as abbots and their like. What happens to the companions and table-fellows of such men is taught by the example of Peter alone (Matt. 26). Let there therefore always come to mind what is written (Ps. 16; 15).

units.la: II. Non latet, sed ingreditur Synagogam, & illic prædicat. Id verò ostendit, sicut conuersum fuisse. Caeterum NotQuid prædicârit? Duo dicuntur. 1 Quòd Iesus sit Filius Dei. 2. Quòd sit Christus. Postea fatetur se nihil quàm Iesum Christum nouisse, 1. Cor. 2. Et debet hic nobis quoq; sufficere, 1. Cor. 1. Col 2. Act. 4.
units.tr: II. He does not hide himself but enters the synagogue and preaches there. This indeed shows that he had been converted. Note what he preached. Two things are stated: (1) that Jesus is the Son of God; (2) that he is the Christ. Afterwards he confesses that he knows nothing but Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 2. And this should suffice for us too, 1 Cor. 1; Col. 2; Acts 4.

units.la: Vt autem salutaris sit eius cognitio, tenere oportet: 1. Quis sit, quoad persona & essentiam. Paulus eum prædicauit, quem ex Maria natum fuisse, & verum hominem vixisse simul & mortuum esse, om
units.tr: So that the knowledge of him may be saving, we must hold two things: (1) who he is, as to person and essence. Paul preached him who was born of Mary, and who lived as a true man and died, which all

units.la: Paulus prædicat Iesum. Salutaris cognitio est in duobus consistit, de persona et officio. nes sciebant, & ipse quoq; fatetur, Rom. 1. Eundum vero Dei Filium dicit: verum fi licet & æternum. Rom. 9. Col 1. 2. 2. Cor. 5. &c. Docuit ergo illum esse Deum & Hominem verum. Ita omnes Apostoli, 1. Ioh. 4. Necessarium hoc, quia fi alterum negetur, non poterit pro Seruatore vero agno sci. ¶ 2. Quis fit, quoad officium? Christus, id est, vnctus: & proinde promissus ille Redemptor. Vngebantur enim olim Sacerdotes & Reges, Num. 8. 1. Sam 10. 16. &c. Hinc promissus ille Seruator dicitur Vnctus, quia Sacerdotem & Regem esse oportebat, Pfal. 110 2. 72. 45. &c. Vtriusque vero officium praestitit IESVS Vt Sacerdos, docuit, Deuter. 18. Ifa. 61. Matth. 16. Mar. 1. Luc. 4. Eph. 4. Obtulit seipsum, Iohan. 6. Apo. 1. Intercedit, 1. Iohan. 2. Heb. 4 1. Tim. 2. Benedicit, Gen. 22. Eph. 1. &c. Vt Rex, asseruit ex diaboloi potestate, Luc. 11. Legibus instruit. Regit & tuetur. Beat opibus æternis. Hic ergo prædicandus, & in eodem nobis acquiescendum, Ioh. 6.
units.tr: knew, and he himself confesses too, Rom. 1. He calls him the Son of God, true and also eternal, Rom. 9; Col. 1, 2; 2 Cor. 5, etc. He taught, therefore, that he is God and true Man. So all the apostles, 1 John 4. This is necessary, because if either nature is denied, he cannot be acknowledged as the true Saviour. Paul preaches Jesus. Saving knowledge consists of two things: the person and the office. (2) What is he, as to office? Christ, that is, anointed; and therefore the promised Redeemer. For priests and kings were anointed of old, Num. 8; 1 Sam. 10. 16, etc. Hence that promised Saviour is called the Anointed, because he had to be both Priest and King, Psal. 110. 2; 72; 45, etc. Jesus performed the office of each. As Priest, he taught, Deut. 18; Isa. 61; Matt. 16; Mark 1; Luc. 4; Eph. 4. He offered himself, John 6; Rev. 1. He intercedes, 1 John 2; Heb. 4; 1 Tim. 2. He blesses, Gen. 22; Eph. 1, etc. As King, he asserted his power against the devil, Luc. 11. He instructs with laws, rules and protects, and enriches with eternal goods. He is therefore to be preached, and in him we must rest, John 6.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quomodo prædicauit Paulus? Sic vt Iudæos confutaret, qui illum negabant. Ita hodie oportet contradicentes convinci, Tit. 1. Obseruatum hoc omnibus fe culis, & necessarium hoc est propter mundi pertinaciam,Ifa.53.Luc 1.Ideo Apofto- li de futuris quoque admonuerunt,2.Pet. 2.Actor.20.1.Timoth.42.Tim.3. 2.Theff. 2. 2.Iohan.2.4. Turpiter errant, qui hodie istud indignè ferunt. Quàm verò necesse fit,experientia docet.
units.tr: 2. How did Paul preach? So as to confute the Jews who denied him. So today the contradictors must be convinced (Titus 1). This has been observed in all ages, and it is necessary because of the obstinacy of the world (Isa. 53; Luke 1). Therefore the apostles also warned concerning future things (2 Pet. 2; Acts 20; 1 Tim. 4; 2 Tim. 3; 2 Thess. 2; 2 John 2, 4). They err shamefully who today bear this indignantly. How necessary it is, experience teaches.

units.la: III.Effectus.Obstupuerunt omnes.Pij autem anteacta repetunt, & glorificant Deum, Gal.1. Itaque in gaudium conuersus fuit eorum terror & metus.
units.tr: III. The effect. All were astonished. But the godly recall past things and glorify God (Gal. 1). And so their terror and fear were turned into joy.

units.la: NOT. ¶1. Vtnos quoque Sanctorum egregiè factis affici debeamus? Agnoscamus in eis Dei bonitatem, virtutem,veritatem, & hunc glorificemus. Sic ipsi omnia ad Deum referunt, 1. Cor.3.15. Errant, qui in illos transferunt honorem, qui Christo debetur.
units.tr: NOTE. (1) Should we too be moved by the excellent deeds of the saints? Let us acknowledge in them the goodness, power and truth of God, and glorify him. Thus they themselves refer all things to God (1 Cor. 3:15). They err who transfer to those men the honour that is owed to Christ.

units.la: ¶2. Ne pudeat nos renuntiare affuetis erroribus,imo oppugnare. Errare & peccare humanum est,Iac.3.Prouerb.24.Roman.7. At pertinaciter tueri errores atque scelera, & eadem propagare ad alios, diaboli opus. Meminerint singuli, quid Deo, quid proximo debeant. Vide Iosuæ septimo.Dauidem, Psalmo quinquagesimo primo. Similibus argumentis nos quoque nostram refipifcentiam testemur. Oremus.
units.tr: (2) We should not be ashamed to renounce accustomed errors, indeed to oppose them. To err and to sin is human (James 3; Prov. 24; Rom. 7). But to defend errors and wickedness obstinately, and to propagate the same to others, is the work of the devil. Let each remember what he owes to God and what to his neighbour. See Joshua 7, and David in Psalm 51. By similar arguments let us also testify to our repentance. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILIA LXXIX.

units.la: 23 Expleto autem multo tempore, miuerunt inter se Iudæi consilium interimendi.
units.tr: 23 When many days had passed, the Jews took counsel together to kill him.

units.la: 24 Sed intellectæ sunt insidiæ eorum. Adseruabant autem portas die ac nocte, vt eum interimerent.
units.tr: 24 But their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates day and night so that they might kill him.

units.la: 25 Acceptum igitur eum discipuli nocte per murum demiserunt funesummissum in sporta.
units.tr: 25 So the disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall in a basket.

units.la: VT Pauli conuersionem diligenter Lucas descripsit. Ita mox quæ eius doctrina fuerit, exposuit: Nimirum, Iesum esse Dei Filium & Christum, id est, Regem & Sacerdotem, adeoque promissum humani generis Seruatorem. Conuenit hæc cum Apostolorum confessione, Mat. 16. Ioh. 6. & ea doctrina est, quæ perpetuo seruari debet in Ecclesia, &c. Gal. 1.2. Ioh. 1. Quia autem Paulum organum electum fore Christus præDixerat, incipit Lucas nunc eius res gestas narrare, &c. Discipulus, quàm multis quamque grauibus casibus exerceantur Christi fideles, & vt hic eis adsit.
units.tr: Luke described Paul's conversion carefully, and then straightaway he set out what Paul's teaching was: namely, that Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ, that is, King and Priest, and so the promised Saviour of mankind. This agrees with the confession of the Apostles, Matt. 16; John 6, and it is the doctrine which must always be kept in the Church, etc. Gal. 1, 2; John 1. But because Christ had foretold that Paul would be a chosen instrument, Luke now begins to narrate his deeds, etc. Learn from this how many and how grievous trials Christ's faithful are tested by, and how Christ is present with them.

units.la: Quia vero Lucas noluit omnia narrare, sed quæ sufficiebant Ecclesiæ institutioni, omisit quædam, & ideo quoque hic dicit; Post multos dies, &c. Oportet ergo hûc referre, quæ habentur, Gal. 1. 2. Cor. 11 Conuersus & baptizatus, quia sciebat se Apostolum gentium factum, mox in Arabiam abijt prædicatum. Inde fere post annos tres redijt Damascum, & cum rursus sedulò doceret, Iudæos magis irritauit. Et Aretas Rex propter res in Arabia nouatas ipse quoq; ei fuit infensus, & præsecto vrbis mandauit, &c. Audiuerunt hunc Iudæi, & portas munierunt præsidijs, vt non posset elabi. Tunc ergo accidit quòd hic narratur. Vbi hæc veniunt consideranda.
units.tr: Since Luke did not wish to relate everything, but only what sufficed for the instruction of the Church, he omitted some things, and therefore he also says here, "after many days," etc. It is necessary, then, to bring in here what is recorded in Gal. 1, 2; 2 Cor. 11. Once converted and baptized, knowing that he had been made apostle to the Gentiles, he at once went away into Arabia to preach. From there, after about three years, he returned to Damascus, and when he again taught diligently, he provoked the Jews even more. King Aretas also, on account of the new affairs in Arabia, was hostile to him, and commanded the governor of the city, etc. The Jews heard of this and fortified the gates with guards, so that he could not escape. Therefore what is related here came to pass. Here the following points are to be considered.

units.la: I. Quàm duro tyrocinio Deus Paulum probârit. Qui cum comitatu terribili Damascum venerat, nunc solus, aut cum paucis in Arabiam ad barbaros homines abit prædicatum. Damascum reuersus vt quie sceret, de vita periclitatur. Sentit ergo inti o statim, quod Christus dixerat.
units.tr: I. With how harsh an apprenticeship God tested Paul. He who had come to Damascus with a terrifying escort now goes alone, or with a few companions, into Arabia, to barbarous people, to preach. Returning to Damascus, hoping to rest, he is endangered for his life. He therefore immediately experiences what Christ had said.

units.la: Est autem hæc communis Christia- norum fors Matth. 16. Ioh. 16. 2. Tim. 3. Act. 14. Neque possumus aliud nobis demun- do polliceri, Ioh. 3. 15. Experimur hodie. Sed tunc vetera exempla animo repetamus, Abraham, Gen. 12. 13. 14. &c. Isaac & Iacob, Gen. 28. 47. &c. Israelitarum egressum ex Ægypto excipit deserto, &c. Quid
units.tr: This is the common lot of Christians: Matt. 16; John 16; 2 Tim. 3; Acts 14. Nor can we promise ourselves anything else in this world, John 3:15. We experience this today. But let us now recall the old examples to mind: Abraham, Gen. 12, 13, 14, etc.; Isaac and Jacob, Gen. 28, 47, etc.; the wilderness receives the Israelites when they leave Egypt, etc. What [was done] to Christ? Matt. 3, 4, etc.

units.la: Christo factu? Mat.3.4.&c. Sunt haec dura carni, & Paulo quoque dura visa sunt. Sed vicit fidei constantia, 1.Cor.4. Eadem nos quoque armemur, Luc.22.&c. Et soletur, quod Deus nostrae infirmitatis memor fo let inducias dare, vt hic Paulo quoque fecit: simulque consolationibus confirmat, 1.Cor.10.2.Cor.1.Ioh.14.
units.tr: These things are hard for the flesh, and they seemed hard to Paul too. But the constancy of faith prevailed, 1 Cor. 4. Let us arm ourselves with the same, Luke 22, etc. And let us be comforted by this, that God, mindful of our weakness, is accustomed to grant respite, as he did here for Paul too; and at the same time he strengthens us with consolations, 1 Cor. 10; 2 Cor. 1; John 14.

units.la: 2. Vt mundus veritatis doctrinae refi- stat. Paulus neque armis neque militibus instructus erat, sed verbo Dei pugnabat. Hoc quia non possunt illi confutare, ad vim & arma conuertuntur. Ita hodie.
units.tr: 2. That the world resists the doctrine of truth. Paul was equipped neither with arms nor with soldiers, but fought with the Word of God. Since the adversaries cannot refute this, they turn to force and arms. So it is today.

units.la: Sed No r. Praeposterum mundi studium. Quando Paulus cum publica authoritate & satellitibus veniebat Damascum, tunc timere debuisset insidias Sacerdotum Rex Aretas. Sed tunc nemo obstitit venienti. At nunc quando nihil periculi est praesidium portis imponitur, & omnia habent spec e belli. Fit idem hodie. Quan do Pontificij sibi aperte ius sumunt in Regum subditos per inquisitores, &c. admittuntur absq; contradictione. Vt primum vero aliquis pauperculus Euangelium praedicat, & huic populus aures praebet, nos armis agitur, concurritur. Ita praedictum Psalm.2. Ita cum Christo actum, Lucae 22. Similes eorum qui contra lepores resārmati exunt, lupos & vrsos sinunt grassari.
units.tr: But note the perverse zeal of the world. When Paul came to Damascus with public authority and attendants, then King Aretas ought to have feared the plots of the priests. But then no one opposed his coming. Now, when there is no danger, a guard is placed on the gates, and everything has the appearance of war. The same thing happens today. When the Papists openly assume for themselves the right over the subjects of kings, through inquisitors, etc., they are admitted without objection. But as soon as some poor man preaches the Gospel, and the people give ear to him, they are roused to arms and rush together. Thus the Psalm (Ps. 2) foretold, and thus it was done with Christ, Luke 22. They are like those who arm themselves against hares and let wolves and bears roam free.

units.la: 3. Vt Deus talium conatus eludat. Fratres Paulum in sporta demittunt, &c.Erat hoc periculosum. Rebellio videtur eum seruare, quem princeps extinctum vult. Et timendi erant excubitores. Deinde moenia sacrosanēta erant, &c.Sed qui scie-bant Sabbathum debere cedere charitati, hic quoq; faciunt quod hæc iubebat,Luc. 14.Mar 2.3.Fuit ergo hoc non vulgaris fi-dei exemplum.
units.tr: 3. That God mocks the attempts of such men. The brothers let Paul down in a basket, etc. This was dangerous. A rebellion seems to be saving the man whom the prince wants dead. And the sentinels had to be feared. Moreover, the walls were inviolable, etc. But those who knew that the Sabbath must give way to charity, here too did what these things commanded, Luke 14; Mark 2, 3. This was therefore no ordinary example of faith.

units.la: ¶ Imitentur Christiani, vt pios sub ty-rannis laborantes seruent si possunt, neque se ministros præbeant crudelitatis, &c. Hoc nomine laudantur obsterrices, Exod.1. Rahab, Iof. 2. Heb.11. Arguunt hæc nostri seculi ignauiam. Dum pij prey-muntur plerique genio indulgent, Amos 6. Requisiti, sese excusant rationibus fri-uolis. Sed puniuntur tales lege talionis. Quales vero, qui ministrorum capitibus suum otium redimunt.
units.tr: ¶ Let Christians imitate this, so that they protect the godly who suffer under tyrants, if they can, and do not make themselves ministers of cruelty, etc. For this reason the midwives are praised, Exod. 1; Rahab, Josh. 2; Heb. 11. These things expose the idleness of our age. While the godly are oppressed, most men indulge their own pleasure, Amos 6. When called upon, they excuse themselves with frivolous reasons. But such men are punished by the law of retaliation, and so much the more those who buy off their own leisure with the heads of ministers.

units.la: 4.Paulus hoc officium admisit. Non di-cit,Ne resistatis malo, Mat.5. Neq; garrit de prouidentia, Matth.10. Psalm.56. 91. Sed oblata ope per se pia & sanēta vtitur. Ita alibi Actorum 16,22.23 25. ¶ Neminem ergo moueant fanatici Anabaptistæ. Est
units.tr: 4. Paul accepted this duty. He does not say, "Resist not evil," Matt. 5; nor does he chatter about providence, Matt. 10; Ps. 56, 91. But when help is offered, he uses it, being in himself pious and holy. So also elsewhere, Acts 16:22, 23, 25. ¶ Therefore let not the fanatical Anabaptists move anyone. For there is a twofold way of resisting: the lawful and the unlawful.

units.la: enim duplex resistendi modus, legitimus, & illegit: ¶ 2. Fugam quoque licitum esse constat. Quod hïc Paulus facit, hoc Chri-ftus quoq;, &c. Matt.2. Luc.4. Ioh.8. Imò discipulos iussit fugere, Mat.10. Sed tunc vide, ne quid fiat cum detrimento gloriæ Dei. Item ne præter officium negligan-tur, quos ipsis credidit Deus. Denique in omni causa spectetur gloria Dei & proxi-mi salus, &c. Oremus
units.tr: ¶ 2. It is also established that flight is permitted. What Paul does here, Christ also did, etc. Matt. 2; Luke 4; John 8. Indeed he commanded his disciples to flee, Matt. 10. But then take care that nothing is done to the detriment of God's glory. Likewise, that those whom God has entrusted to them are not neglected beyond their duty. Finally, in every cause let the glory of God and the salvation of the neighbour be regarded, etc. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXX.

units.la: 26 Cùm verò Saulus aduenisset Hierosolymam, tentabat fe adiungere discipulus: sed omnes timebant eum, non credentes eum esse discipulum.
units.tr: 26 And when Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples, but they all feared him, not believing that he was a disciple.

units.la: 27 Barnabas autem acceptum eum duxit ad Apostolos: & narrauit quomodo in via vidisset Dominum, qui loquutus effet ei, & quomodo Dama-sci liberè loquutus effet in nomine Iesu.
units.tr: 27 But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and related how on the road he had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.

units.la: 28 Versabatur ergo eum eis in Hie-rufalem.
units.tr: 28 So he moved about among them in Jerusalem.

units.la: 29 Et liberè in nomine Domini Iesu loquebatur & disceptabat aduer-sus Græcos: illi verò conabantur eum interimere.
units.tr: 29 And he spoke boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus and disputed against the Grecians, but they tried to kill him.

units.la: VT Christus Paulum sibi præ alijs de-legit, vt eius ministerio regnum suum per orbem propagaret: Ita eiusdem templo docuit, quàm multis & grauibus aduersis suos exercere soleat, & facilè fit eosdem feruare. Expertus est hoc Paulus mox ab initio. Postquam enim ex Arabia redijt Damascum, de vita periclitatur, Iudaeis cum Areta contra eum conspiranti-bus. Seruatur autem mirificè per discipulos. Vbi consolationis plenum est, quod vt pij vbique hostes habent, ita vbiq; fratres inueniunt. Mar. 10. Sequitur quid fecerit elapsus. Summa, quòd Hierosolymam venerit, ibi rursus docuerit, denuò item periclitatus & per fratres seruatus sit. Sed singula ex ordine consideremus.
units.tr: Just as Christ chose Paul above others, so that through his ministry he might spread his kingdom throughout the world, so in the same person he has taught how many and grievous adversities he is accustomed to exercise his people with, and how easily he keeps those same people safe. Paul experienced this right from the beginning. For after he returned from Arabia to Damascus, he was in danger of his life, the Jews conspiring against him together with Aretas. But he was wonderfully preserved through the disciples. Here there is comfort: as the godly have enemies everywhere, so they find brothers everywhere. Mark 10. Next follows what he did after his escape. In short, when he came to Jerusalem he taught there again, was again in danger, and was preserved by the brothers. But let us consider the particulars in order.

units.la: I. Hierosolymam redit, unde exierat ut lupus & persecutor. Magnum argumentum fidei fortis Dominabantur illic hostes Christi, & hi nunc præ aliis Paulum oderant. Erat ergo ei periculosum venire in eorum consperctum. Sed vincit metum fides, quæ simul mouet, vt qui priùs inter magnates in precio fuerat, nunc discipulis, id est, Christianis se cupiat coniungere. Vide Phil. 3.
units.tr: I. He returns to Jerusalem, whence he had gone out as a wolf and persecutor. This is a great proof of strong faith. Christ's enemies held sway there, and they now hated Paul more than others. It was therefore dangerous for him to come into their sight. But faith overcomes fear, and at the same time moves him, who before had been held in high esteem among the great, now to desire to join the disciples, that is, the Christians. See Phil. 3.

units.la: NOT. Commune hoc votum esse de bere iis, qui seruari cupiunt, vt Ecclesiæ coniungantur. Est quidem pusillus grexferè ex quibus mactationis constans, Lu-
units.tr: NOTE. This is a common wish among those who desire to be saved, that they join themselves to the Church. Indeed the little flock is for the most part made up of those destined for slaughter, Luke 12.
