units.tr: II. Those who were of the circumcision, that is, who, though called Christians, were still addicted to the law. These dispute with him and accuse him as though he had committed a crime, looking, no doubt, to the tradition of the fathers and the accepted custom. See John 4.

units.la: NOT. ¶ 1. Quàm noxium sit imbui erroribus. Feré enim pertinacia sequitur, ne videamur errauisse. Hinc illi damnant, de quo potius debebant gaudere. Similes, qui hodie papisticas sordes tuentur contra nos, cum interim Euangelium iactent.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. How harmful it is to be steeped in errors. For obstinacy usually follows, lest we seem to have been wrong. Hence those men condemn him for what they ought rather to have rejoiced in. Like those who today defend papistical filth against us, while all the while boasting of the gospel.

units.la: ¶2.Neminem posse omnibus placere, & feré accusari eos,qui laudem mereban tur.Vide Mosem,Exod 2 5.14.16.Num.11. 16.20.21.&c. Prophetas 1. Reg 18 22. Am. 9.Christum,Matt 9 11.&12. Mar.2 3 Luc. 13.14.Ioh.11 Idem nunc fit Petro. Patien- tes ergo fimus, & Deo nos approbare ftu deamus.
units.tr: 2. No one can please everyone, and those who deserve praise are almost always accused. See Moses (Exod. 2, 5, 14, 16; Num. 11, 16, 20, 21, etc.), the prophets (1 Kings 18, 22; Amos 9), Christ (Matt. 9:11–12; Mark 2:3; Luke 13, 14; John 11). The same now happens to Peter. Let us therefore be patient, and take care to please God.

units.la: Petrus respondit,& facti rationem red dit diligenter.Vbi obseruabimus.
units.tr: Peter answered and gave an account of the matter carefully. Here we shall observe:

units.la: 1.Petri modestiam. Poterat bonitate causæ fretus dedignari eos responso, vel etiam cū eis expostulare. Sed agnoscit ad fe pertinere,quod aliis præscribit 1.Pet.3.
units.tr: 1. Peter's modesty. Relying on the goodness of his cause, he could have disdained to answer them, or even reproached them. But he acknowledges that what he prescribes to others applies to himself (1 Pet. 3).

units.la: Arguitur Pontifi c.Rom.insolentia,qui Petri successione, superbi,quiduis pro li- bidine faciūt.Vide dift.40.Ca.Si Papa.At quod hic fit,etiam alibi, Gal.2. Sic Victor reprehensus ab Irenæo, &c. sed sic oportet Antichristum agere,Dan.7.2.Theff.2.
units.tr: The arrogance of the Roman Pontiff is reproached, who, proud of his succession from Peter, do whatever they please. See dist. 40, c. Si Papa. But what happens here happens elsewhere too (Gal. 2). So Victor was reproved by Irenaeus, etc. But this is how Antichrist must act (Dan. 7:25; 2 Thess. 2).

units.la: 2.Quo argumento fe excuset?Nimirum quod nihil factum nisi ex Dei mandato, qui hoc ita fieri voluerit. Id probat dili- genti narratione, quid sibi,quid Cornelio acciderit.
units.tr: 2. With what argument does he excuse himself? Namely, that nothing was done except by God's command, since God wished it to be done thus. He proves this by a careful narrative of what happened to himself and to Cornelius.

units.la: Vbi Not. ¶ Quod simplici narratio- ne contentus,nullos adhibet colores. Sa- tis ergo excusati sunt Christiani, qui con tra receptas consuetudines aliquid faciunt ex D. iussu. Nam perpetuo ratum erit quod habetur, Act. 4 5. Sufficiat ergo ratio hæc nobis contra papistas, qui æquo morosiores ea accusant, quæ ex Dei verbo fecimus: Vt Missæ abrogationem. Vide Ioh.19.Heb.9.10.Zach.3. Imaginum de molitione. Sed habes Exod.20.Deut.7. If. 40.44 Hab.2.1.Ioh.5 &c. Nuptias, 1.Cor. 7.Heb.13.1.Tim.3. Ciborum discrimina, Matt.15.1.Cor.8.Rom 14.1.Tim.4.Purgatorium. Vide 1.Ioh.5.1.Ioh.1. Quod illi ob ijciunt, Ecclesiam ita constituisse, respondemus ex Isa 29.Matt.15.Et quod Euangelium hic commendatur, quo seruemur. Sic Ioh.6.Rom.1.10. Act. 16. In eo igitur simus constantes, Matt.24.
units.tr: Note that he, content with a simple narrative, adds no embellishments. So Christians are sufficiently excused when they do something against received customs by God's command, for what has been established will always stand (Acts 4:5). So this reason is enough for us against the papists, who unjustly take more offence at those things we have done from God's word, such as the abolition of the Mass (see John 19; Heb. 9, 10; Zech. 3), and the making of images. But you have Exod. 20; Deut. 7; Isa. 40, 44; Hab. 2:1; John 5, etc. Marriage (1 Cor. 7; Heb. 13; 1 Tim. 3). Distinctions of foods (Matt. 15; 1 Cor. 8; Rom. 14; 1 Tim. 4). Purgatory: see 1 John 5; 1 John 1. As to what they object, that the Church has so established it, we answer from Isa. 29 and Matt. 15. And that the gospel is commended here, by which we are kept (so John 6; Rom. 1, 10; Acts 16). Let us therefore be constant in it (Matt. 24).

units.la: 3. Confirmationis loco subtexit Spiritus sancti missionem, cuius finem & vsum exponit ex verbis Baptiste & Christi, Matthæi 3.Act 1.Et hinc colligit, illum gentes pro suis agnoscere. Et infert: Quis ego, qui possem prohibere Deum? Quasi diceret: Impium per se est, damnare quod Deus probat. At quanto magis impium, se etiam ponere contumaciter eius decretis?
units.tr: 3. As confirmation he adds the mission of the Holy Spirit, whose purpose and use he explains from the words of the Baptist and of Christ (Matt. 3; Acts 1). And from this he gathers that God acknowledged the Gentiles as his own. And he infers: "Who was I, that I could hinder God?" As if he said: it is in itself wicked to condemn what God approves. But how much more wicked is it to set oneself obstinately against his decrees?

units.la: Arguuntur, qui totas Ecclesias damnant, in quibus luculenta sunt Spiritus sancti indicia. Grauior tamen eorum culpa est, qui falsa doctrina seducunt, aut etiam
units.tr: Those are rebuked who condemn whole churches in which there are clear signs of the Holy Spirit. Yet guiltier still are those who lead people astray with false doctrine, or who even attack Christ's sheep with open violence.

units.la: aperta vi in Christi oues grassantur.Sen-tient isti omnes vindicis Dei manum.Oremus.
units.tr: All such men will feel the hand of God the avenger. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 96.

units.la: 18 His autem auditis quieuerunt, & glorificauerunt Deum dicentes: nempe etiam gentibus Deus refipifcen-tiam dedit in vitam.
units.tr: 18 And when they heard these things, they were quieted and glorified God, saying: Then God has also given repentance unto life to the Gentiles.

units.la: 19 Illi vero qui dispersi fuerant ex oppressione, orta ob Stephanu.per-uenerunt vsque in Phœnitiam & Cy-prum & Antiochiam, nemini loquen-tes sermonem Dei nisi solis Iudæis.
units.tr: 19 Now those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose over Stephen travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word of God to none but the Jews alone.

units.la: 20 Quidam autem ex illis Cyprij et Cyrenenfes, quum introissent Antio-chiam locuti sunt Græcis, Euangelizan-tes Dominum Iesum.
units.tr: 20 But some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, when they came to Antioch, spoke to the Greeks, preaching the Lord Jesus.

units.la: 21 Fuit autem manus Domini cum eis, multusque numerus credenti-um conuersus est ad Dominum.
units.tr: 21 And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.

units.la: VT Petrus fidelis serui Christi ossi-cio functus est, quando Cornelio ex Dei iussu Euangelium prædica-uit.Ita cum eius factu quidam reprehen-derent, eximium Christianæ modestiæ exemplum præbuit. Facti enim sui ration-em ijs reddit, a quibus ipse poterat ra-tionem exigere. Omissis autem omnibus alijs argumentis, hoc vrget, se nihil expriuato consilio, sed omnia ex Dei iussu fecisse. Vbi discamus quibus argumentis hoc excusare debeamus ea, quae secundum Dei verbu fiunt. Quibus enim huius authoritas sordet, indigni sunt quorum ratio habeatur. Sequitur.
units.tr: Just as Peter, the faithful servant of Christ, discharged his office when by God's command he preached the Gospel to Cornelius, so when some found fault with his deed, he gave an outstanding example of Christian modesty. For he gave account of his action to those who could have demanded it of him. Setting aside all other arguments, he presses this one alone: that he had done nothing on his own plan, but everything by God's command. Here we learn with what arguments we ought to defend what is done according to the word of God. For those who scorn its authority are unworthy to have their reasoning taken into account. It follows:

units.la: I. Vt Apologiam hanc acceperint. ¶ 1. Quemadmodum Petri, ut Petrus et fratres ac ceperint. Hinc apparet, eos hanc litem apologiam non malitiole, sed incolulto zelo mouisse. Interim discant hos imitari, qui zelum ho die praetexunt. Prorsus est acquirere verbo Dei, neque praeter hoc aliud quaerere; etiam si nobis non certa omnium ratio constet. Deut. 28. Hoc fidei proprium exercitium est, Rom. 1. 16. 4. Gen. 15. 22. Heb. 11. Qui contra Deum disputare audent, se a fide alienissimos esse docent.
units.tr: I. That they accepted this apology. ¶ 1. As in the case of Peter, that Peter and the brothers accepted it. From this it is clear that these men raised this dispute not from malice but from a sincere zeal. Meanwhile let them learn to imitate those who today put forward a pretext of zeal. It is absolutely necessary to acquiesce in the word of God and to seek nothing beyond it, even if the reason for everything is not clear to us. Deut. 28. This is the proper exercise of faith, Rom. 1. 16. 4. Gen. 15. 22. Heb. 11. Those who dare to dispute against God show that they are utterly alien to faith.

units.la: ¶ 2. Glorificant Deum. Euidentius testantur, sibi satis factum esse. Sunt enim qui tacent, sed animo dolorem coquunt. Imitemur autem, ut ipsi quoque ijs gratulemur, quos Deus conuertit. Requirit hoc Dei gloria & charitas. Vicissim doleamus aliorum interitu, 1. Cor. 5. 1. Sam. 15. 16. Quales ergo, qui cŏuersos petunt armis?
units.tr: ¶ 2. They glorify God. They bear more evident witness that they were fully satisfied. For there are those who keep silent but nurse grief in their hearts. Let us imitate them, so that we too rejoice with those whom God converts. The glory and love of God require this. In turn let us grieve at the ruin of others, 1. Cor. 5. 1. Sam. 15. 16. What then of those who seek to bring the converted down by force of arms?

units.la: ¶ 3. Ergo & gentibus dedit poenitentiam ad vitam. Bifariam hoc fit: quando vel loco & tempus poenitentiae dat Deus, vel corda emollit. Ezech.11. Vtrumque hic factum, & vt sic fiat necesse est, 2.Cor.3. Tren.4. Psalm.51. Vnde sequitur,ea etiam quæ conuersi faciunt,ad Deum referri debere,vt huic omnis gloria cedat, 1.Cor.4. Obseruemus autem poenitentiam dari nobis per Euangelium, & quidem ad vitam dari. Vult enim Deus non mortem peccatoris,sed, &c. Ezech.18. Ier.18. Zach.1. Matth.11. Ista nos hodie excitent, vt Euangelium audiamus, neque dubitemus de Dei gratia. Quod miseri & calamitosi sumus,ex eo est, quod poenitentiae doctrinam reijcimus, adeoque cum Deo nos castigante certamen suscepimus, Isa.9. Amos 4.
units.tr: ¶ 3. Therefore he has also given the Gentiles repentance unto life. This happens in two ways: when God either gives the time and place for repentance, or softens the hearts. Ezek. 11. Both have happened here, and it must be so for this to occur, 2 Cor. 3. Lam. 4. Psalm 51. Hence it follows that even what the converted do must be referred to God, so that all glory may be yielded to him, 1 Cor. 4. Let us note, moreover, that repentance is given to us through the Gospel, and indeed given unto life. For God wills not the death of the sinner, but, etc. Ezek. 18. Jer. 18. Zech. 1. Matt. 11. Let these things stir us today to hear the Gospel and not to doubt the grace of God. That we are wretched and miserable comes from this, that we reject the doctrine of repentance, and so we have entered into a contest with God who chastises us, Isa. 9. Amos 4.

units.la: II. Redit ad intermissam historiam amplius docens, vt Christi regnum ad gentes propagatu fit. Et in praesenti loca nominat: Phoeniciam, quae Syriae vicina erat, regio olim celeberrima Cyprus, insula diues & voluptatibus dedita, & ideo Veneri sacra. Antiochia item, Syriae vrbium celeberrima, & quę Ecclesiam habuit frequentissimam, in qua Christianorum nomen primo coepit.
units.tr: II. He returns to the interrupted narrative, teaching further how the kingdom of Christ was spread to the Gentiles. And in the present passage he names places: Phoenicia, which was near Syria, a region once very famous; Cyprus, a rich island given to pleasures, and therefore sacred to Venus; likewise Antioch, the most famous of the cities of Syria, which also had a very large congregation, and where the name of Christians first began.

units.la: Quia autem rem maximi momenti pau cis Lucas comprehendit, singulas circumstantias videamus.
units.tr: But since Luke has summed up a matter of the greatest importance in few words, let us look at the individual circumstances.

units.la: NOT. ¶ 1. Qua occasione in istis locis coeptum praedicari. Fuit haec, persecutio exorta propter Stephanum. Vide Acto 8. Fuit tunc miserrima Ecclesiae facies, & lacerata prorsus videbatur. Sed ex singulis membris fere novum corpus nascitur. Et voluit primitivam Ecclesiam hoc exemplo Deus confirmare, ut omnes posteri hinc consolationem habeant. Factum idem deinceps. Simile tempestatis. Hodie similia vidimus. Ne ergo desperemus.
units.tr: NOTES. ¶ 1. By what occasion preaching began in these places. It was this: a persecution arose over Stephen. See Acts 8. At that time the Church's appearance was most wretched and it seemed utterly torn apart. Yet from almost every torn member a new body is born. And God willed to strengthen the primitive Church by this example, so that all posterity might have consolation from it. The same happened afterwards. Similar storms have occurred. Today we have seen similar things. Let us not therefore despair.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quorum ministerio hoc factum Obscurorum hominum, quorum nomina ignorantur. Ita solet Deus, 1. Cor. 1. Accedit, quod neque illis per omnia conuenit. Plerique enim solis Iudaeis praedicarunt, ignari nimirum eorum, quae Petro & Cornelio acciderant. Aliqui tamen Antiochiae gentibus Euangelizarunt. Profuit ergo haec dissensio. Simile exemplum infra 15. Ne ergo offendamur hodie dissensionibus, quae etiam suum vsum habent. Probantur fideles, 1. Cor. 11. Ventilatur veritas. Obseruent modo Dei verbum omnes & horum constantiam imitentur, qui vix elapsi ad officium redeunt. Hac conditione fuga concessa, Matt. 10. Non ipsi nobis ferias faciamus.
units.tr: ¶ 2. By whose ministry this was done: obscure men whose names are unknown. So God is accustomed to act, 1 Cor. 1. Moreover, it did not altogether suit them. For most preached to the Jews alone, plainly ignorant of what had happened to Peter and Cornelius. Yet some at Antioch preached the Gospel to the Gentiles. So this disagreement was useful. A similar example occurs below, chap. 15. Let us not therefore be offended today by disagreements, which also have their use. The faithful are tested, 1 Cor. 11. The truth is sifted. Let all only observe the word of God and imitate the steadfastness of those who, scarcely escaped, return to their duty. Flight is permitted on this condition, Matt. 10. Let us not grant ourselves holidays.

units.la: ¶ 3. Quid praedicarunt? Iesum Christum.
units.tr: ¶ 3. What did they preach? Jesus Christ.

units.la: Huius solius fit mentio, quia in eo omnis salus, Act.4.Ioh.14.4.Act.5. 1.Cor.1.Ideo Paulus hoc vno gloriatur, 1.Cor.2. Gal.6. 1. Obseruemus hoc propter eos, qui nobis vitio vertunt, quod vnum Christum praedicemus. Atqui non alius datus est no bis. Neq; potest de illo nimium dici. Quin ergo Petrum audimus? Ioh.6.
units.tr: Only this is mentioned, because in him is all salvation, Acts 4. John 14. 4. Acts 5. 1 Cor. 1. For this reason Paul glories in this one thing alone, 1 Cor. 2. Gal. 6. 1. Let us note this on account of those who blame us for preaching Christ alone. Yet no other has been given to us, nor can too much be said of him. Why then do we not listen to Peter? John 6.

units.la: {4}. Profectus. Erat manus Domini cum illis, & multus numerus, &c. Ne quis ilto- rum industriae quid tribueret, Deo hoc omne tribuit. Obseruandum hoc omnibus ministris. Vide 2. Cor. 2. 3. 1. Cor. 3. Eodem faciunt, Ioh. 6. Matth. 1. Ifa 54. Iere 31. Ne ergo insolescant ministri, &c. Idem peri-net ad alios quoque publice & priuatim Psal. 127.
units.tr: {4}. Progress. The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number, etc. Lest anyone attribute anything to their diligence, God attributes all of this to himself. This must be observed by all ministers. See 2 Cor. 2. 3. 1 Cor. 3. They do the same, John 6. Matt. 1. Isa. 54. Jer. 31. Let ministers therefore not grow proud, etc. The same applies to others too, both publicly and privately, Psalm 127.

units.la: In primis obseruemus. Finem totius negotij Euangelici: Vt qui ignorantia, suppers-titione, sceleribus a Deo fuerunt auersi, ad eum conuertantur. Vide 2. Cor. 5. Vendicatur igitur homo totus Deo, &c. Eph. 1. Rom. 12. 1. Pet. 2. Deut. 6. Et huc pertinet regula Christi, Matthaei 16. Lucae 9.14. Nequicquam ergo gloriantur Euangelio, qui adhuc pristinis sordibus inhaerent. Vide Iacob. 2. Quid item relapsos maneat, gentium illarum exempla docent, & in primis Cypri expugnatio aute biennium à Turcis facta. Istos ergo imitemur, & indesinenter Oremus.
units.tr: First let us observe the aim of the whole Gospel enterprise: that those who were turned away from God by ignorance, superstition and wickedness may be converted to him. See 2 Cor. 5. Therefore the whole man is claimed for God, etc. Eph. 1. Rom. 12. 1 Pet. 2. Deut. 6. To this also belongs the rule of Christ, Matt. 16. Luke 9. 14. Therefore those who still cling to their former filth boast of the Gospel in vain. See James 2. What also awaits those who relapse, the examples of those nations teach, and above all the capture of Cyprus by the Turks about two years ago. Let us therefore imitate these men and pray without ceasing.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XCVII.

units.la: 22 Peruenit autem rumor ad aures Ecclesiæ quæ erat Hierosolymis. Miserunt igitur Barnabam, ut pergeret Antiochiam usque.
units.tr: 22 But the report reached the ears of the Church which was at Jerusalem. So they sent Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch.

units.la: 23 Qui cum aduenisset & vidisset gratiam Dei gaudens est, & hortatus est omnes ut proposito cordis permanerent in Domino.
units.tr: 23 Who, when he had come and seen the grace of God, rejoiced, and exhorted them all that with purpose of heart they should remain in the Lord.

units.la: 24 Nam erat vir bonus et plenus Spiritu sancto & fide: & adiuncta est multa turba Domino.
units.tr: 24 For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith; and a great crowd was added to the Lord.

units.la: 25 Abiit autem Tarsum ut requireret Saulum: & inuentum duxit Antiochiam.
units.tr: 25 Then he went to Tarsus to seek Saul; and having found him, he brought him to Antioch.

units.la: CHristus non modo pro peccatis nostris mori debuit, sed simul filios Dei dispersos in vnum colligere, Ioh. 11. 10. Id vero impossibile videbatur, quod mundus non solum in diuersas religiones distractus, sed Dei cognitio inter gentes omnino extincta erat, diabolus autem omnes sub tenebrarum potestate premebat, Coloss. 1. Ephes. 5. Ideo Prophetæ de eo sæpe varicinati sunt, Ifa.2.42. 49.54. 60,Mich.4.Pfal.2.72 Zach.9. &c. Vt vero hoc coeperit fieri,Lucas diligenter narrat. Cum enim res ista Apostolis etiam initio absurda videretur,Petrus visione excita tur,vt Cornelio prædicet.Interea quidam Hierosolyma eiecti prædicant in Phœni-cia,Cypro,Syria,& quidem in huius vrbe celeberrima, cuius conuersionem Lucas diligentissimè exponit.1. Per quos factu: Vulgares quosdam & obscuros:Nimirum vt constaret Dei hoc opus fuisse,1.Cor.1. 2.Quid prædicârint? Solum Christum.Id toto hoc libro inculcatur. Idem ergo hodie etiam solus prædicetur. Solus enim verba vitæ æternæ habet, Ioh. 6.4.Act.4. Idem fundamentum est Prophetarum & Apostolorum,Eph.2.1.Cor.3.Ifa.28.1.Pet. 2.Act.3.Sequitur.
units.tr: Christ ought not only to die for our sins, but at the same time to gather together into one the scattered children of God, John 11:10. Yet this seemed impossible, since the world was not only split into diverse religions, but the knowledge of God had been wholly extinguished among the nations, and the devil oppressed all under the power of darkness, Colossians 1; Ephesians 5. Therefore the prophets often prophesied about him: Isaiah 2, 42, 49, 54, 60; Micah 4; Psalm 2, 72; Zechariah 9, etc. But Luke carefully relates how this began to happen. For when this matter seemed absurd to the apostles even at the beginning, Peter was roused by a vision so that he might preach to Cornelius. Meanwhile some who had been driven out of Jerusalem preached in Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Syria, and indeed in that most famous city, whose conversion Luke expounds most diligently. 1. By whom it was done: certain common and obscure men; plainly so that it might be evident that this work was God's, 1 Corinthians 1. 2. What did they preach? Christ alone. This is pressed throughout this whole book. So let the same be preached alone today also. For he alone has the words of eternal life, John 6; Acts 4. The same is the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, Ephesians 2; 1 Corinthians 3; Isaiah 28; 1 Peter 2; Acts 3. It follows:

units.la: I. Vt fe gesserint erga nouam Ecclesiam Hierofolymitani, inter quos præcipui fuerunt Apostoli. Miserunt illuc Barnabam, nimirum vt eos confirmaret, & Ecclesias inter fe conciliaret. Sic factu cum Samaria,Act.8.Idem animus omnium,qui Pauli,2.Cor.11.
units.tr: I. How the Jerusalem people behaved toward the new Church, among whom the apostles were chief. They sent Barnabas there, namely so that he might strengthen them and unite the churches with one another. So it was done with Samaria, Acts 8. The same spirit belonged to all who were of Paul's company, 2 Corinthians 11.

units.la: No T.q Christianorum esse,vt Ecclesias etiam procul dissitas consilio & opera iuuarent,& laudem mereri eos,qui hoc fe dulo faciunt. Est enim vnum omnium corpus, 1. Cor. 12. Eph. 1. 4. Item fi Deus remuneratur officium vni praestitum (Matt. 25. 10.) quanto magis illud &c. Obseruandum hoc Magistratibus quoq;. Nec est quòd eorum calumnijs moueamur, qui hoc dicunt esse seditiosum. Idem poterat objici Apostolis, & quidem obijciebatur, Actor. 16. 17. &c. Sed nihilominus perrexerunt.
units.tr: It is the duty of Christians to help churches even far distant by counsel and work, and to deserve praise, those who do this with diligence. For there is one body of all, 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 1, 4. Likewise, if God rewards a service rendered to one (Matthew 25:10), how much more that... This is to be observed by magistrates also. Nor are we to be moved by the slanders of those who say this is seditious. The same could be objected to the apostles, and indeed it was objected, Acts 16:17, etc. Yet they nevertheless went on.

units.la: II. Barnabas quis & qualis? Vir bonus, plenus spiritu & fide.
units.tr: II. Who and what sort of man was Barnabas? A good man, full of the Spirit and of faith.

units.la: Ingens laus, qua non poterat maior fingi. Nec falsam fuisse ex actis apparet, Act. 4. 13. 14. &c.
units.tr: A great praise, than which none greater could be invented. And from the Acts it appears that it was not false, Acts 4:13-14, etc.

units.la: Vbi Not. ¶ 1. Quales debeant adhiberi publicis officijs maximè ijs, qui ad religionem spectant. Tales nimirum: quorum probitas perspecta est. Ita factu cum Diaconis, Actor. 6. Huc faciunt quae de Ministris habentur, 1. Tim. 3. Tit. 1. De Magistratibus, Exod. 18. Qui improbis & ineptis res committunt, ijs idem accidit quod Noe, Gen. 6. Vide Prouer. 26. &c.
units.tr: Note here: (1) what sort of men ought to be employed in public offices, especially those who have to do with religion. Namely such men whose uprightness has been thoroughly tested. So it was done with the deacons, Acts 6. To this pertain the things said about ministers, 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1. About magistrates, Exodus 18. Those who entrust affairs to the dishonest and unfit suffer what happened to Noah, Genesis 6. See Proverbs 26, etc.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quid requiratur, vt quis fit vir bonus. De Barnaba dicitur. A. Plenus Spiritu sancto. Hoc opus ante omnia, quia ex feip- so nemo bonus praeter vnum Deum, Mat. 19 Pfal. 5. Gen. 6. 8. 2. Cor. 3. B. Fide plenus. Additur hoc, quia sola fides nos iustificat, & Christo insitos foecundat, vt quæ Deo placent faciamus, Ioh. 15. Rom. 12. Ex eo sequitur, eos qui fide carent, neque bonos esse, neque aliquid bonum facere, ad Romanos 14.
units.tr: (2) What is required for someone to be a good man. Of Barnabas it is said: (a) full of the Holy Spirit. This is the chief thing, because no one is good of himself except God alone, Matthew 19; Psalm 5; Genesis 6:8; 2 Corinthians 3. (b) Full of faith. This is added because faith alone justifies us, and grafts us into Christ and makes us fruitful, so that we do what pleases God, John 15; Romans 12. From this it follows that those who lack faith are neither good nor do anything good, Romans 14.

units.la: III. Quid fecit Barnabas? ¶ 1. Vi fagra tia Dei, id est, fidei profectum & gratuita Spiritus dona, gaudet ... est. Vtitur autem gratiæ vocabulo Lucas vt ostendat, hoc omne Dei opus & beneficium fuisse, Mat. 11 Ioh. 6.1 Cor. 3. Obseruandum hoc in similibus passim.
units.tr: III. What did Barnabas do? (1) He saw the grace of God, that is, the progress of faith and the free gifts of the Spirit, and rejoiced. Luke uses the word grace so as to show that this whole thing was God's work and benefit, Matthew 11; John 6; 1 Corinthians 3. This is to be observed in similar passages everywhere.

units.la: Est autem hoc viri boni & Christiani argumentum, quod gaudet aliorum profectu. Huius seculi filij alij alijs inuident. Cain, Gen. 4. Saul, 1 Samuel. 17.18. &c. Aliter pij, eo quod Dei gloriam quærunt, & quosuis saluos cupiunt ex vera dilectione. Vide Mosem, Num. 11. Paulum, Rom. 1. 1. Cor. 1. Phil 1. &c. Imitemur. E contra autem contristemur, si secus fiat. Vide Paul. 2. Cor. 11. 12. 1. Cor. 5.
units.tr: Now it is a mark of a good man and a Christian that he rejoices in the progress of others. The sons of this age envy one another: Cain, Genesis 4; Saul, 1 Samuel 17-18, etc. Otherwise it is with the godly, since they seek God's glory and desire that all be saved out of true love. See Moses, Numbers 11; Paul, Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 1; Philippians 1, etc. Let us imitate them. On the contrary, let us be saddened if it happens otherwise. See Paul, 2 Corinthians 11-12; 1 Corinthians 5.

units.la: ¶ 2. Hortatus est, vt propositio cordis adhærerent Domino. Perseuerantia enim opus est in omnibus, in primis in religione, Lucæ 9. Matt. 24. 2. Timot. 4. 2. Ne tamen inanem professionem putarent suffi cere, cordis propositum exigit. Vide Isaiæ 29. Qui ex corde Domino adhærent, hos nihil potest reuocare,Phil.3. Iohan.6. At quia sciebat Barnabas multa esse quae nos auocant,hortatur. Ita opus est, 2.Tim.4. Faliuntur, qui hoc putant superuacaneum.
units.tr: (2) He exhorted them that they should cleave to the Lord with purpose of heart. For perseverance is needed in all things, especially in religion, Luke 9; Matthew 24; 2 Timothy 4. Yet lest they think an empty profession sufficed, he demands a purpose of the heart. See Isaiah 29. Those who cleave to the Lord from the heart, nothing can call them back, Philippians 3; John 6. But because Barnabas knew there were many things that draw us away, he exhorts them. So it is needful, 2 Timothy 4. They are mistaken who think this superfluous.

units.la: ¶ 3. Profectus Tarsum quæsiuit Paulum & adduxit. Aliud argumentum magni zeli & modestiae. Sciebat quatus esset Paulus, & quantum sibi decessurum esset per hunc. Sed Christi gloriam suae praefert. Qui suam quaerunt, fide destituuntur, Ioh.
units.tr: (3) He went to Tarsus, sought Paul and brought him. This is another mark of great zeal and modesty. He knew how great Paul was and how much of his own standing would be yielded to him through this man. But he prefers Christ's glory to his own. Those who seek their own are destitute of faith, John 5.

units.la: 5. Imitantur ergo Barnabam omnes in republica & Ecclesia Lacedaemm. Interim docemur Ecclesias ministris opus habere, Rom.10. De his cogitent, qui illas volunt propagatas. Hodie secus multi, &c.
units.tr: Therefore all in the commonwealth and Church should imitate Barnabas. Meanwhile we are taught that churches need ministers, Romans 10. Let those who wish them to be propagated think on these things. Today many act otherwise, etc.

units.la: III. Fructus huius studij. Multa turba fidelium addita fuit Domino. Ergo non sibi, sed Christo lucrifecerunt homines, Matth.25.28.1.Cor.9.
units.tr: III. The fruit of this zeal: a great crowd of believers was added to the Lord. Therefore men gained not for themselves but for Christ, Matthew 25:28; 1 Corinthians 9.

units.la: NOTA. ¶ Fidelium ministrorum labores non esse inutiles. Nec enim sterile est verbum Dei, & vbiq; inuenit terram bonam,&c.Isaiae 55.Lucae 8. Et Deus ipse dat incrementum. Oferuent omnes,quibus aliquid publice mandatum. Oremus.
units.tr: NOTE. The labours of faithful ministers are not in vain. For the word of God is not barren, and everywhere it finds good ground, etc., Isaiah 55; Luke 8. And God himself gives the increase. Let all to whom something has been publicly entrusted take note. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCVIII.

units.la: Factum est autem vt annum
units.tr: It came to pass that for a whole year

units.la: totum convenirent in Ecclesia, docentq; turbam multam, & discipuli nominarentur primum Antiochiae, Christiani.
units.tr: they gathered together in the Church, and taught a great multitude; and the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.

units.la: LVcas diligenter describit conuersionem Antiochiae, & Ecclesiae illic collectae constitutionem, partim quia illic Christianorum nomen coepit, partim quod formam Ecclesiae praebet, quam omnes imitentur. Inter alia vero commendat Barnabę illuc missi studium, de quoditu: 1. Quod nihil nouârit, sed ad perseuerantiam hortatus fit. Imitandum hoc, ne temere mutetur quod bene constitutum est. Id enim vt odiosum est, ita causam totam suspectam facit. 2. Quod cum videret pluribus ministris opus esse, quaesierit Paulum & adduxerit, neque eum abstulerit, quod hunc se praestantiorem esse sciret. Obseruandum hoc quoque, vt idonei doctores sint, & ne priuatae gloriae causa cuiquam locus negetur. Sequitur.
units.tr: Luke describes carefully the conversion at Antioch and the constitution of the Church gathered there, partly because the name of Christians began there, and partly because it provides a pattern of the Church which all should imitate. Among other things he commends the zeal of Barnabas, who was sent there, and notes two things about him: (1) that he did not change anything, but exhorted them to perseverance. This is to be imitated: what has been well established should not be changed rashly. For such change is odious, and it makes the whole cause suspect. (2) That, seeing that more ministers were needed, he sought out Paul and brought him, and did not take him for himself, although he knew that Paul was the more excellent. This also is to be observed: that teachers should be fit, and that no one should be denied a place for the sake of private glory. It follows.

units.la: I. Quid vterque antiquitatem fecerint: Tria dicuntur. 1. Annum totum manserunt illic. Constantiae argumentum. Non potuit enim hoc fieri absque labore atque periculo. 2. Congregarunt in Ecclesia. De coetibus loquitur, quos frequentes coegerunt. 3. Docuerunt, &c.
units.tr: I. What the two of them did in that time: three things are told. (1) They remained there a whole year. This is evidence of constancy, for this could not be done without labour and danger. (2) They gathered in the Church. He speaks of the assemblies, which they held frequently. (3) They taught, etc.

units.la: Nota. Quid fieri debeat in Ecclesijs. Ante omnia opus perseuerantia mini strorum. Multa enim obijciuntur. Sed me minerint dicti, Lucae 9.2.Tim.2.4. Obseruemus hoc in omni alia re, in primis in magistratu. Qui hoc negligunt seipsos prostituunt. 2. Coetus cogantur. His in primis Deus deleftatur. Ideo olim instituit, Exod.23. Leuit.23. Deut.16. Christus item, Matth.18. Frequantarunt hos pij diligenter, Psal.42.43. Prophani nimis, qui contemnunt. Doceantur publice omnes. Sub doctrina comprehenduntur Sacramenta & preces. Haec sunt Ecclesiae exercitia, in quibus agnosci debet Christi erga illam facilitas.
units.tr: Note. What ought to be done in the churches. Before all things there is need of the perseverance of ministers, for many objections are raised. But remember the words of Luke 9 and 2 Tim. 2:4. Let us observe this in every other matter, especially in the magistracy. Those who neglect this prostitute themselves. (2) Assemblies should be convened. God especially delights in these, and therefore he instituted them long ago, Exod. 23, Lev. 23, Deut. 16. Christ likewise, Matt. 18. The godly have attended these diligently, Ps. 42, 43. The profane, who despise them, are too many. Everyone should be taught publicly. The sacraments and prayers are included under doctrine. These are the exercises of the Church, in which Christ's kindness towards it ought to be recognised.

units.la: II. Discipuli illic primum Christiani dicti. Initio discipuli dicti ad exemplum apostolorum. Vide Act 6.9. Ita vero officij admonebantur, ut audirent Christum, Deuter.18. Matthaei 17. Iohan.8. 10. Licet ergo nomen mutatum sit, rata tamen manet eius significatio & eius vsus: ne nobis dicatur, quod extat Malach.1. At nunc Christianorum nomen coepit, vel potius reuocatum, &c. Psalm.105. Id vero vt singulare quid Lucas annotat, quia tale quid promissum, Isa.62.
units.tr: II. The disciples were first called Christians there. At first they were called disciples after the example of the apostles; see Acts 6 and 9. Yet they were reminded of their duty in this way, that they should hear Christ, Deut. 18, Matt. 17, John 8 and 10. Although therefore the name has been changed, its meaning and its use nevertheless remain fixed, so that it may not be said to us what is found in Mal. 1. But now the name of Christians began, or rather was recalled, etc. Ps. 105. Luke notes this as something singular, because something of the kind was promised, Isa. 62.

units.la: Decet ergo nos in eo considerando diligenter versari.
units.tr: It is fitting, therefore, that we dwell carefully on this consideration.

units.la: I. Quando & vbi coeperit. Antiochiae, & quidem sub annum octauum post ascensionem Christi. Atqui poterat hoc Hierosolymis fieri:sed in vrbe ethnica fit, vt videamus Christianismum non esse loco alligatum, vt hodie illud Romanenses clamant. At quanto rectius hoc Antiochae ni fecissent?
units.tr: I. When and where it began: at Antioch, and indeed about the eighth year after the ascension of Christ. Yet this could have happened at Jerusalem; but it happens in a heathen city, so that we may see that Christianity is not bound to a place, which the Romanists now cry out against. But how much more rightly would they have done this at Antioch, had they not?

units.la: Interim Not. Quàm parum prosi-ciant hostes Christi persecutionibus. Noluerunt Christi nomen ferre Hierosolymis. Nunc illud per totum orbem propagatur, vt vbique audiant. Simile incendij, Luc.12. Fit idem hodie, & exempla multa sunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile note: how little the enemies of Christ profit by persecutions. They were unwilling to bear the name of Christ at Jerusalem. Now it is spread throughout the whole world, so that it is heard everywhere. Like a fire, Luke 12. The same thing happens today, and there are many examples.

units.la: 2. Quod à nullo Apostolorum denominantur, sed ab vno Christo. Causa: quia ex eo nobis obtingunt, quaecunque ad salutem faciunt. Docet hoc ipsum Christi no men. Olim Sacerdotes & Reges vngebantur. Quia verò Deus seruatorem promiserat, qui suorum Rex & Sacerdos esset, (Psal.2 .110.) hic χρίστος Christus est dictus, Psal.45. Ioh.1. Act.10. At quia idem suos quoque spiritu donat, & reges & sacerdotes fecit, iure ab eo Christiani sunt dicti, Apoc.15.
units.tr: 2. That they are named after no apostle, but after Christ alone. The reason: because from him come to us all things that serve our salvation. The name of Christ itself teaches this. Formerly priests and kings were anointed. But since God had promised a Saviour who would be the King and Priest of his people (Ps. 2, 110), he was called Christ, [χρίστος], Ps. 45, John 1, Acts 10. And because he also endows his own with the Spirit, and has made them kings and priests, they are rightly called Christians by him, Rev. 1 [sic; cf. Rev. 1:6, 5:10].

units.la: Not.¶ Christi potentiam & maiestatem cum bonitate coniunctam. Quis Monarcha narcha suos omnes potuit aut voluit reges facere? Imo plerique mancipia ambi tionis fuerunt, seque ipsos perdiderunt. At Christus cupit habere confortes, Luc. 22. Ioh. 12. 14. 17. Matth 19. Et suos armat hic quoque, vt ad hoc sufficiant, Ioh. 14. Phil. 4.
units.tr: Note: the power and majesty of Christ joined with goodness. What monarch has been able or willing to make all his own subjects kings? Indeed most have been slaves of ambition and have ruined themselves. But Christ desires to have companions, Luke 22, John 12, 14, 17, Matt. 19. And he equips his own here also, so that they may be sufficient for this, John 14, Phil. 4.

units.la: 3. Vsus huius nominis. 1. Christo nos totos consecrat, vt hunc solum agnoscamus Seruatore, & apud hunc quaeramus omnia. Exigit hoc ipse Deus, Matth. 17. Christus item, Matth. 11. Ioh. 7. 4. Isaiae 42. Matth. 23. Et hue facit baptismus, in quo ei nomen damus, Matth. 28. Simile ciuitatis. Arguit hoc Sectarios, qui alia sibi nomina acceperunt. Coepit error hic Apostolorum tempore, 1. Cor. 3. Neque aliter huic medebimur, quam si vno Christo simus contenti. Augusti in 1. Ioh. 2.
units.tr: 3. The use of this name. 1. It consecrates us wholly to Christ, so that we may acknowledge him alone as Saviour, and seek all things from him. God himself requires this, Matt. 17. Christ likewise, Matt. 11, John 7, Isa. 42, Matt. 23. Baptism also bears on this, in which we give him our name, Matt. 28. Like a city's name. This convicts the sectaries, who have taken other names for themselves. This error began in the time of the apostles, 1 Cor. 3. Nor shall we remedy it otherwise than by being content with Christ alone. Augustine on 1 John 2.

units.la: 2. Officij admonet, vt nos Reges & Sacerdotes praebeamus. Regis est liberum esse, vincere, regere, tueri, beneficum esse, Lu 22. Sacerdotis autem docere (Malach. 2.) offerre, orare & benedicere, Num. 6. His studeant Christiani Libertatem suam tueantur, (Gal. 5.) ne serui sint peccati & superstitionum. Vincant diabolum & huius suggestiones, 1 Pet. 5. Ephes.
units.tr: 2. It reminds us of our office, that we should show ourselves as kings and priests. It is the mark of a king to be free, to conquer, to rule, to protect, and to be generous, Luke 22. But it is the office of a priest to teach (Mal. 2), to offer, to pray and to bless, Num. 6. Let Christians strive for these things: let them guard their liberty (Gal. 5), lest they be slaves of sin and superstitions. Let them conquer the devil and his suggestions, 1 Pet. 5, Eph.

units.la: 6. Regant seipsos & sibi creditos Verbo
units.tr: 6. Let them rule themselves and those entrusted to them by the Word

units.la: Dei, Psalm. 19. 119. Benefici sint, Iohan. 15. Matth. 5. Praeterea doceant alij alios pro suae vocationis ratione, Matth. 18. Exod. 23. Deut. 22. Sacrificent laudem & gratiarum actionem, Heb. 13. Seipsos, Rom. 12. Preces per Christi nomen, Ioh. 14. 16. Eleemosynas, Matth. 25. Heb. 13. Hos. 6.
units.tr: of God, Ps. 19, 119. Let them be generous, John 15, Matt. 5. Besides, let them teach one another according to the reason of their calling, Matt. 18, Exod. 23, Deut. 22. Let them offer sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving, Heb. 13; themselves, Rom. 12; prayers through the name of Christ, John 14, 16; alms, Matt. 25, Heb. 13, Hos. 6.

units.la: ¶ Qui haec praestant, Christiani sunt. Qui negligunt, ex eorum sunt numero, de quibus Matth. 7. Singuli ergo sese examinent, & si quid deest, sarciant, & indies proficiant in melius. Oremus.
units.tr: ¶ Those who do these things are Christians. Those who neglect them are of the number of those of whom Matt. 7 speaks. Let each therefore examine himself, and if anything is lacking, let him supply it, and let him make progress daily for the better. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIX.
units.tr: HOMILIA XCIX.

units.la: 27 Per id tempus autem descenderunt Hierosolymis Prophetae Antiochiam.
units.tr: 27 About that time, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.

units.la: 28 Et unus eorum Surgens, nomine Agadus, significavit per Spiritum, famem magnam futuram in toto terrarum orbe: quae etiam fuit sub Claudio Caesare.
units.tr: 28 And one of them, named Agabus, stood up and foretold by the Spirit that a great famine would come over the whole world, which also happened under Claudius Caesar.

units.la: 29 Singuli autem discipulorum, prout cuique suppetebat, decreverunt subsidio mittere aliquid fratribus habitantibus in Iudaea.
units.tr: 29 Each of the disciples, as much as he was able, resolved to send relief to the brothers living in Judea.

units.la: 30 Quod & fecerunt mittentes ad seniores per manum Barnabae & Saulí.
units.tr: 30 And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

units.la: SEmper quidem Ecclesiæ suę Christus sadest (Iohannis 14. Matthæi 28.) at eandem varijs casibus exerceri finit, Iohannis 16. Causa, vt partim nos in officio contineat: partim vt discamus illum suos non minus in aduersis quàm secundis ser uare posse. Vidimus id hucusque. Initio Hierosolymis felicitèr colligitur Ecclesia: Sed mox disipatur persecutione, Actor. 8.9. Excipit hanc pax insperata, & ad gentes quoque extenditur, & Antiochiæ inci pit Christianorum nomen. Sequitur noua calamitas, fames, quæ totum orbem af flixit, & procul dubio fidelibus fuit mole stissima, Heb. 10. Vsus, ne offendamur eiusmodi vicissitudinibus. Et quia hic locus plurimùm nos docet atque consolatur, videamus singula ex ordine.
units.tr: Christ is always present with his Church (John 14, Matthew 28), yet he allows it to be exercised by various trials (John 16). The cause is partly to keep us in our duty, and partly that we may learn that he can preserve his people no less in adversity than in prosperity. We have seen this so far. At first the Church is happily gathered at Jerusalem, but soon it is scattered by persecution (Acts 8, 9). Then an unhoped-for peace follows, it spreads also to the Gentiles, and at Antioch the name of Christians begins. A new calamity follows, a famine, which afflicted the whole world and was doubtless very burdensome to the faithful (Heb. 10). Let us use this so that we are not offended by such changes. And since this passage teaches and comforts us greatly, let us look at its parts in order.

units.la: I. Ipsa fames, de qua Suetonius etiam & Iosephus. Immissa procul dubio diuini tus Amos 3.4. Leuit.26. Deuter.28. Nec enim aliquid temerè contingit, Matthæi 10.
units.tr: I. The famine itself, of which Suetonius also writes, and Josephus. It was doubtless sent by divine judgment (Amos 3:4; Lev. 26; Deut. 28). For nothing happens by chance (Matt. 10).

units.la: Sed NOTA. Causam Hanc Lucas ceu digito monstrat, dum Claudij meminit: Nimirum vt eius seculi statum & mores inde colligamus. Fuit ille corruptissimus à pueris, vt à matre diceretur, hominis portentum. Primus imperium emit à
units.tr: But NOTE: Luke points to the cause as with a finger when he mentions Claudius, namely so that we may gather from this the state and morals of that age. He was most corrupt from boyhood, so that his mother called him a monster of a man. He bought the empire from the soldiers first,

units.la: militibus,vorax & ebriosus. Libidinis infa-tiabilis. Factum ergo quod fieri solet, vt eius mores reliqui imitarentur, Eccle.10. Monebat Deus & hortabatur ad poeniten-tiam. Sed eius verbum reijciebatur. Itaque famem Deus immisit, in qua ipse etiam Claudius periclitatus.
units.tr: greedy and a drunkard, insatiable in lust. So what usually happens happened: others imitated his morals (Eccl. 10). God warned and exhorted them to repentance, but his word was rejected. And so God sent the famine, in which Claudius himself was also endangered.

units.la: ¶ Discamus iudicare de nostri seculi fa-me & alijs calamitatibus. Constat fibijpsi Deus in suis iudicijs, Ierem.5. Atqui ho-die passim regnant Claudij ebriosi & ver-bi contemptores. Habent sui similes prae-fules papisticos & multos ex Euangelij ministris, vt olim, Isaiae 56. Imitatur vul-gus, & fit quod futurum Christus praedi-xit, Matth.24. Lucae 21. Et licet vbique cer-nantur irae Dei signa, plerique tamen con-temnunt. Quid ergo miru, si Deus puniat?
units.tr: Let us learn to judge the famine of our own age and other calamities by this. God is consistent in his judgments (Jer. 5). Yet today drunken Claudiuses and despisers of the Word reign everywhere. They have prelates like themselves, the Papists, and many of the ministers of the Gospel, as once (Isa. 56). The common people imitate them, and what Christ foretold comes to pass (Matt. 24; Luke 21). And although the signs of God's wrath are seen everywhere, most people despise them. What wonder, then, if God punishes?

units.la: II. Vt Deus Ecclesiam de fame futura praemonuerit? Veniunt Prophetae quidam Hierosolyma Antiochiam. Inter hos Aga-bus istam praedicit. Nota. ¶ Bonitatem Dei, qui poenas meritas non immittit nisi praemonitis: Nimirum, vt sciamus has non temere accidere, & vt conuertamur, Amos 3. Sic factum omnibus seculis. Ante diluuium, Gen. 6. 2. Petri 2. Sodomae, Gene.13.14.18.&19. In Aegypto, Genef.
units.tr: II. How God forewarned the Church of the coming famine: certain prophets come from Jerusalem to Antioch, and among them Agabus predicts it. Note the goodness of God, who does not send deserved punishments unless they are announced beforehand, namely so that we may know that these things do not happen by chance, and that we may be converted (Amos 3). So it has been done in all ages: before the flood (Gen. 6; 2 Pet. 2); at Sodom (Gen. 13, 14, 18, 19); in Egypt (Gen. 4; Exod. 5).

units.la: 4. Exodi 5. Ante captiuitatem Babylo-nicam, nicam, Paral. 36. Sic quoad postremum excidium, Matthæi 23.24. Lucæ 19. Vide Iosephum & Egesippum. Huc refer generales prædictiones, quas singuli possunt sibijpsis applicare, Leuitici 26. Deuteronom. 28. Item quotidianas conciones, & quòd omnino fit quod Christus prædixit, Marci 13. Obseruemus nos hanc bonitatem Dei.
units.tr: Before the Babylonian captivity (2 Chron. 36). So also with regard to the final destruction (Matt. 23, 24; Luke 19). See Josephus and Hegesippus. To this belong the general predictions, which each may apply to himself (Lev. 26; Deut. 28), likewise the daily sermons, and the fact that everything Christ foretold comes to pass (Mark 13). Let us observe this goodness of God.

units.la: III. Antiocheni quid? ¶ Non contemnunt admonitionem, sed credunt, vt ex factis apparet.
units.tr: III. What did the Antiochenes do? They did not despise the warning but believed it, as their deeds make clear.

units.la: Poterant conijcere ex præsenti statu, orbem terrarum sic meruisse. Sic Niniuitæ, Ionæ 3. Est hoc initium salutis, Isaiæ 7. Qui nolunt credere, experiuntur. Ita prædicitur, Matthæi 24. 2. Petri 3.2. Thessalon. 5. Ideo quo maior aliorum securitas eo magis fiat, &c. Luc. 21.
units.tr: They could conjecture from the present state of things that the whole world had deserved this, as the Ninevites did (Jonah 3). This is the beginning of salvation (Isa. 7). Those who are unwilling to believe experience it. So it is foretold (Matt. 24; 2 Pet. 3:2; 1 Thess. 5). Therefore the greater the complacency of others, the more it comes about, etc. (Luke 21).

units.la: ¶ 2. Deliberant de mittendo subsidio in Iudæam, vbi maior inopia propter persecutionem. Heb 10. Id vero faciunt contra morem huius seculi, Amos 8. Lucæ 12. &c. Ita vero testantur, quanti faciant Euangelium, quod à Iudæis ad ipsos deuenerat, Iohannis 4 Roman. 15 Hodie ingratissimi sunt mortalium, qui suis doctoribus inuident, quæ dantur ab aliis, 1.Cor. 9 1. Tim. 5.
units.tr: 2. They deliberate about sending aid into Judea, where there was greater want because of the persecution (Heb. 10). Indeed they do this against the custom of this age (Amos 8; Luke 12, etc.). In this way they testify how highly they value the Gospel, which had come to them from the Jews (John 4; Rom. 15). Today people are most ungrateful, who begrudge their teachers what is given by others (1 Cor. 9; 1 Tim. 5).

units.la: ¶ 3. Quomodo hoc fecerint. 1. Decreuerunt singuli. Voluntarium officium innuitur. Sic 2. Corinth. 9. Matthæi 6. Excitet nos, quod hoc officij genus est minimum, quod ditiores egenis debent. Luc. 16. 2. Cor. 8.
units.tr: 3. How they did this. First, each decided for himself, so a voluntary duty is indicated (2 Cor. 9; Matt. 6). Let it stir us up that this kind of duty is the least that the richer owe to the needy (Luke 16; 2 Cor. 8).

units.la: 2. Pront quisque poterat, Nec enim plus exigitur, 2. Cor. 8. Id vero inexcusabiles facit, si ne hoc quidem præstemus.
units.tr: Second, each gave as he was able, for nothing more is required (2 Cor. 8). This makes them inexcusable if we do not even do this much.

units.la: 3. Mittunt per Paulum & Barnabam ad Seniores Iudæorum. Ita cauere voluerunt, ne fraus fieret, & ne indignis cederent, ne glectis dignioribus quod fere fit, vbi promiscua est turba mendicantium.
units.tr: Third, they send it through Paul and Barnabas to the elders of the Jews. In this way they wished to guard against fraud, and lest the gift fall to the unworthy while the more deserving were neglected, which usually happens where the crowd of beggars is mixed.

units.la: Estque hic vetustissimus mos subueniendi pauperibus, Deuteron. 15. Actorum 4. 5. 6. 1. Corinth. 16. Docet autem hic locus, quid debeamus afflictis fratribus & quousque debeat beneficentia extendi, Galat. 6. Lucæ 10. Quid ergo de ijs dicendum, qui suos negligunt, imo qui vt Iudas (Iohannis 12. 13.) ab alijs data suffurantur. Imitemur hos. Meminerimus nos puniri merito. Emendemus corruptos mores. Benefici sumus erga omnes, Matthæi 25. 26. Luc. 16. Oremus.
units.tr: This is also the most ancient custom of helping the poor (Deut. 15; Acts 4, 5, 6; 1 Cor. 16). This passage teaches what we owe to afflicted brothers and how far beneficence should extend (Gal. 6; Luke 10). What then must be said of those who neglect their own, or who, like Judas (John 12, 13), steal what has been given by others? Let us imitate the good, not these. Let us remember that we are rightly punished. Let us amend our corrupt morals. Let us be beneficent to all (Matt. 25, 26; Luke 16). Let us pray.

units.la: CAPVT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Homilia c.
units.tr: Homily C.

units.la: Odem autem tempore iniecit Herodes Rex manus, vt affligeret quosdam ex Ecclesia.
units.tr: Now at that same time King Herod laid hands on some members of the Church to harm them.

units.la: 2 Intercmit autem Iacobum fratrem Iohannis, gladio.
units.tr: He also put James, the brother of John, to death with the sword.

units.la: 3 Et cum vidisset hoc gratum esse Iudaeis, perrexit comprehendere etiam Petrum: (erant autem dies azymorum.)
units.tr: And when he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to seize Peter also. (Now it was the days of unleavened bread.)

units.la: 4 Quem etiam prehensum coniecit in carrerem, traditum quaternis militibus, vt eum seruarent: volens post pascha producere eum populo.
units.tr: He seized him too and put him in prison, handing him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending to bring him out before the people after the Passover.

units.la: 5 Petrus igitur seruabatur in custodia: preces autem assiduae fiebant ab Ecclesia ad Deum pro ipso.
units.tr: So Peter was kept in custody, but the Church made constant prayer to God for him.

units.la: DEscripsit antea Lucas persecutiones Ecclesiae motas a Sacerdotibus. Fuerunt hę graues, sed grauior est quę modo narratur. Author est potentissimus Rex, penes quę summa potestas. Et cum Apostoli hucusque intacti fuerint, nunc vnus ex praecipuis (Gal. 2.) cadit. Vsus omnium, vt Ecclesiæ forte agnoscamus & ad similia præ paremur. Quia autem hic nimiu tardi su- mus, præstat singulas circumstantias excu- tere.
units.tr: Luke has already described the persecutions of the Church stirred up by the priests. Those were grievous, but the one now narrated is more grievous. Its author is a most powerful king, in whose hands lies supreme power. Until now the apostles had been untouched, but now one of the chief of them (Gal. 2) falls. The purpose of all this is that we may recognise the Church's condition and prepare ourselves for similar things. Since we are here rather slow, it is worth going through the individual circumstances.

units.la: I.Tempus.Eodem tempore,quo, fames exorta fuit. Concurrunt ergo duo mala maxima. NOT. Sortem Ecclesiæ & pio rum, plenam tribulationum,Psal.34. Sic Abraham iactatus, Gen.12.13.14 &c. Ita Isaac,Gen.26.Iccob, Gen.28.31.33 34.42. 43 47.&c. Hodie nobis non possumus me liera polliceri,Iohannis 16.Matth.24.præ paremur ergo ad patientiam,memores iu dicium Dei incipere a domo eius, 1.Pet 4 Causam vide,Heb.12. 1.Corinth.11 Rom. 7. Falluntur qui ex euentis de fide & religione iudicant.
units.tr: I. Time. At the same time that a famine broke out, so two very great evils meet. NOTE. The lot of the Church and of the godly is full of tribulations (Ps. 34). So Abraham was buffeted (Gen. 12, 13, 14, etc.), and so Isaac (Gen. 26), Jacob (Gen. 28, 31, 33, 34, 42, 43, 47, etc.). Today we cannot promise ourselves freedom (John 16; Matt. 24). Let us therefore prepare for patience, mindful that the judgment of God begins at his own house (1 Pet. 4). See the cause in Heb. 12, 1 Cor. 11 and Rom. 7. They are mistaken who judge faith and religion by outcomes.

units.la: II.Author Herodes.Commune nomen regum Iudæorum, ortum ex Herode Magno, qui ex alienigenis primus regnauit. Alioqui Agrippa fuit, Herodis primi nepos ex Ariftobulo Princeps calidissimus qui miris artibus se apud Caium primo, deinde apud Claudium insinuauit, vt tandem fere aui regnum tenuerit, &c.
units.tr: II. Author Herod. This is the common name of the kings of the Jews, taken from Herod the Great, who was the first of foreign origin to reign. Otherwise it was Agrippa, grandson of the first Herod through Aristobulus, a most crafty prince who ingratiated himself by remarkable arts, first with Caius and then with Claudius, so that at last he held his grandfather's kingdom, and so on.

units.la: NOT. Quod tantum hostem Deus excitauit Ecclesiæ: Nimirum vt magis e- lucerct potentia Christi, & quam yana fit totius mundi potentia, si cum illo conse- conse. ratur. Imó constat potentissimos Reges cadere, vt primum cum Christo bellum suscipiunt. Sic factum Herodi Magno, Matth 2. Antipas, de quo Mar. 6. Luc. 13. Isti nunc. Iuliano. Nec desunt hodie exempla. Neminem ergo terreat tyrannorum potentia. Fortior est, qui a nobis stat, 1. Ioh. 4. Psal. 2. 110. Ioh. 16.
units.tr: NOTE. God roused so great an enemy against the Church, surely so that the power of Christ might shine more clearly, and so that one may see how empty the power of the whole world is when weighed against him. Indeed it is established that the most powerful kings fall as soon as they take up war with Christ. So it happened to Herod the Great (Matt. 2), and to Antipas, of whom we read in Mark 6 and Luke 13, and now to Julian. Nor are examples lacking today. Let no one, therefore, be terrified by the power of tyrants. He is stronger who stands on our side (1 John 4; Ps. 2, 110; John 16).

units.la: III. Causae persecutionis.
units.tr: III. Causes of the persecution.

units.la: ¶ 1. Afflixit eos, qui erant de Ecclesia. Ita verò dicebantur Christiani, qui a Synagogis deficiebant. Ergo indignè tulit scisma in religione. Sciunt enim tyranni religionum diuersitate animos vehementissimè disiungi, & ideo licet omnem religionem contemnant, volunt tamen vniformem esse inter suos. Vide 1. Regum 12. 1. Machab. 1. Interim scismatis culpa semper adscribitur Christi cultoribus, qui vnum Deum agno sciunt per vnum Mediatorem, Eph. 4. Causa, quod ijdem consensum mundi in superstitiones scindunt, Lucae 12. Hoc praetextu olim Iudaei & gentes pugnârunt. Ita hodie, qui sectas inuehunt, &c. 2. Pet. 2. Apologus ouiculae & lupi. Nemo autem offendatur, modo in Christo vniamur.
units.tr: ¶ 1. He afflicted those who were of the Church. Those who were leaving the synagogues were called Christians. Therefore he took the schism in religion badly. For tyrants know that minds are most violently divided by diversity of religion, and so, although they despise every religion, they want uniformity among their own people. See 1 Kings 12 and 1 Macc. 1. Meanwhile the blame for schism is always laid on the worshippers of Christ, who acknowledge one God through one Mediator (Eph. 4). The reason is that they split the agreement of the world over superstitions (Luke 12). Under this pretext the Jews and the Gentiles once fought, and so today those who introduce sects, and so on (2 Pet. 2). Consider the fable of the little sheep and the wolf. Let no one take offence, provided we are united in Christ.

units.la: ¶ 2. Videns hoc placere Iudaeis. Voluit ergo Rex nouus gratiam inire apud Iudaeos, gentem seditiosam & Christi inimicam. Itafolent tyranni innocentium sanguinesuam tyrannidem stabilire, contra illud, Psalm.72. Pilatus, Luc.23. Matth.27. Ioh.19. Hodie multi, vt Pontifices sibi demereantur, cum quibus peribunt, Apoc. 17. & 18.19.20.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Seeing that this pleased the Jews. The new king therefore wished to win favour with the Jews, a seditious people and enemies of Christ. So tyrants are accustomed to establish their tyranny with the blood of the innocent, contrary to Ps. 72. Compare Pilate (Luke 23; Matt. 27; John 19). Today many, in order to win the favour of the priests, perish along with them (Rev. 17, 18, 19, 20).

units.la: IV. Quid fecit? Iacobum occidit gladio. Petrum capit, etiam occisurus nisi festum obstitisset, &c.
units.tr: IV. What did he do? He put James to death with the sword. He seized Peter, intending to kill him too, had the feast not stood in the way.

units.la: No T. Dei prouidentiam tunc quoque non cessare, quando tyranni omnia faciunt pro libidine. Iacobus tantus Apostolus (Matt.4. Mar.5. &c.) occiditur, Petrus feruatur: quo diutius voluit vti Deus. Sic cum Prophetis factum, 1.Reg.19. Cum Iohanne item, Ioh.21. Et si quos feruare vult Deus, facile occasionem inuenit. Petrus custoditur seuerissimè, dum alij festu agunt, & ita fit quod praedictum, Ioh.16. Sed ea occasione interim vtitur Deus in eo feruando. Ne ergo nos offendat aliquid: sed in Domino speremus, Isa.28.&c.
units.tr: NOTE. God's providence does not cease even when tyrants do everything at their pleasure. James, so great an apostle (Matt. 4; Mark 5, etc.), is killed, while Peter is kept, because God wished to use him for longer. So it was with the prophets (1 Kings 19), and likewise with John (John 21). And if God wishes to keep anyone, he easily finds an opportunity. Peter is guarded most strictly while the others keep the feast, and so what was foretold comes to pass (John 16). Yet God uses that occasion to preserve him. Let nothing therefore offend us, but let us hope in the Lord (Isa. 28, etc.).

units.la: V. Interea Ecclesia quid? Num Petri causam nihil ad se pertinere putant? Num calumniantur? Num arma corripiunt? Nihil horum: sed coetus agunt, orant, &c.
units.tr: V. Meanwhile what did the Church do? Did they think Peter's cause had nothing to do with them? Did they complain? Did they take up arms? None of these. Rather they gather, pray, and so on.

units.la: NOTA 1. Fidei constantiam. Propter religionem exorta persecutio. Non tamen men intermittunt huius exercitia. Sicut pra Cap. 4.5. & 8. Arguuntur, qui ceden-dum putant, & dissimulandum. Imitemur, neque pudeat, &c. Rom. 1.
units.tr: NOTE 1. The constancy of faith. The persecution arose on account of religion, yet they do not give up its exercises, as before in chapters 4, 5 and 8. Those are rebuked who think one should yield and dissemble. Let us imitate them, and not be ashamed (Rom. 1).

units.la: 2. Gratitudinis exemplum. Agnoscunt Petrum in causa communi periclitari, & quid ei debeant, ut suo doctori. Ideo pro eius salute solliciti sunt: & cum liceret in festo gaudere (Deut. 14. 16.) ipsi lugent, precantur. Hoc officii Paulus requirebat, Eph. 6. Fortissima arma Ecclesiae, fides invicta (1. Ioh. 5.) conuersio feria ad Deum preces, &c. Iac. 5. Ita montes quoque transferuntur, Mar. 11. Heb. 11.
units.tr: 2. An example of gratitude. They recognise that Peter is in danger in a common cause, and what they owe him as their teacher. Therefore they are anxious for his safety, and although they might have rejoiced at the feast (Deut. 14, 16), they themselves mourn and pray. Paul required this duty (Eph. 6). The strongest weapons of the Church are invincible faith (1 John 5), unceasing prayer to God, and so on (James 5). So mountains too are moved (Mark 11; Heb. 11).

units.la: In his nos hodie esse oportebat, Heb. 13. At tot periclitantibus nos lasciuimus, Bachi, Veneris, Martisfesta celebramus. Fiet ergo quod olim, Amos 6. Matt. 24. Moueant saltem pericula priuata, ut conuertamur & Oremus
units.tr: We ought to be among these people today (Heb. 13). Yet while so many are in peril, we indulge ourselves, celebrating the feasts of Bacchus, Venus and Mars. So what happened of old will happen again (Amos 6; Matt. 24). Let private dangers at least move us, that we may turn back and pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CI.
units.tr: HOMILY CI.

units.la: 6 Quum vero esset producturus eum Herodes, nocte illa dormiebat Petrus inter duos milites, vinctus catenis duabus: et custodes ante ostium observabant carcerem.
units.tr: Now when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping that same night between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while guards kept the prison before the door.

units.la: 7 Et ecce, Angelus Domini superuenit et lux splenduit in carcere: et percussato pulsato latere Petri excitauit eum, dicens: Surge velociter. Et exciderunt ei catenæ ex manibus.
units.tr: And behold, an angel of the Lord came upon him, and a light shone in the prison. Striking Peter on the side, he roused him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell from his hands.

units.la: 8 Dixitq; ei Angelus, Præcinge te & subliga sandalia tua. Fecit autem ita. Tum ille dixit ei, Indue pallium, & sequere me.
units.tr: The angel said to him, "Gird yourself and put on your sandals." He did so. Then the angel said to him, "Put on your cloak and follow me."

units.la: 9 Itaq; egressus Petrus sequebatur eum, nec sciebat verum esse quod fiebat per Angelum: sed putabat se videre visum.
units.tr: So Peter went out and followed him, not knowing that what was done through the angel was real; he thought he was seeing a vision.

units.la: 10 Quum autem transissent primam ac secundam custodiam venerunt ad portam ferream, quæ ducit in civitatem: quæ sponte aperta est eis: & egressi sunt vicum unum, & statim abscessit Angelus ab eo.
units.tr: When they had passed the first and second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city. It opened to them of its own accord. They went out and passed along one street, and at once the angel left him.

units.la: 11 Tum Petrus ad se reversus dixit: Nunc vere agnosco Dominum misisse Angelum suum, & eruisse me e manu Herodis, & ex omni exspectatione populi Iudæorum.
units.tr: Then Peter, coming to himself, said, "Now I truly know that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people."

units.la: HIstoria hæc tria continet præcipua, quæ nostræ institutioni & consolationi seruiunt. 1. Quæ sit Ecclesiæ & credentium sors in terris. Ioh.15.16. Matt.16. 2. Tim. 3. 2. Quid tunc faciant Memores Christianæ communionis causam suæ agi putent singuli. Heb.13.1. Cor.12. Cœtus agant &
units.tr: This history contains three main points, which serve our instruction and comfort. 1. What the lot of the Church and of believers is on earth. John 15:16; Matt. 16; 2 Tim. 3. 2. What they then do: each one, mindful of Christian fellowship, thinks that his own cause is being pursued. Heb. 13:1; 1 Cor. 12. Let them gather and

units.la: Cap.12.
units.tr: Chapter 12.

units.la: & orent Ephef.6. 3. Exemplum, vt Deus suos feruet, quando omni auxilio destitu-ti sunt, Psal. 34. 1. Corinth. 10. 2. Corinth. 1. Iohan. 14. 16 Et de isto nunc agetur. Expo-nitur enim precum effectus : Miraculosè enim liberatur Petrus, & omnis potentia & prudentia Herodis cedit precibus pio-rum, &c. Iacob. 5. Id vt melius pateat, om-nes circumstantiæ describuntur.
units.tr: and pray. Eph. 6. 3. The example of how God keeps his own safe when they are deprived of all help. Ps. 34; 1 Cor. 10; 2 Cor. 1; John 14:16. And this will now be discussed. For the effect of prayer is set forth: Peter is miraculously freed, and all the power and cunning of Herod yields to the prayers of the godly, etc. James 5. So that this may be clearer, all the circumstances are described.

units.la: I. Quando? Ea nocte, postquam Herodes illum producere voluit. Fuit ergo mora aliqua. Interea Petrus detinetur, pij orant, Iudæi auidè exspectant. Sed in tempore adest Deus, Not. ¶ Differri aliquando opem, non quòd nostri obliuiscatur Deus, sed vt nos exerceat & exploret (1. Pet. 1. 4.) viqué eius beneficium sit illustrius: quando in ipso articulo temporis liberat, &c. Sic factum, Exod. 2 3. 14. Item Isa. 36. 37. Typum habes, Mar. 4. Discamus ergo patienter exspectare Deum, non præscri-bere, Psalm. 27. 62. Hab. 2. Iudith. 8. Obser-uandum hoc priuatim in morbis & aliis aduersis.
units.tr: I. When? On that night, after Herod had wished to bring him out. There was therefore some delay. Meanwhile Peter is held, the godly pray, and the Jews wait eagerly. But God is present at the right time. Note: help is sometimes deferred, not because God forgets us, but so that he may exercise and test us (1 Pet. 1:4), and so that his benefit may be the more illustrious, since he delivers at the very moment of crisis, etc. So it happened, Exod. 2 3. 14. Likewise Isa. 36, 37. You have a type in Mark 4. Let us learn therefore to wait patiently for God, not to dictate to him: Ps. 27, 62; Hab. 2; Judith 8. This is to be observed privately in sicknesses and other adversities.

units.la: II. Quid tunc Petrus. Putari poterat exanimatus metu, vel eiulare & coqueri. Sed duabus catenis vinctus, dormit inter duos milites. Id vero non socordiæ, sed fidei opus est, Act. 5.
units.tr: II. What did Peter then do? One might suppose he was dead with fear, or wailing and lamenting. But bound with two chains, he sleeps between two soldiers. This is indeed the work not of carelessness but of faith, Acts 5.

units.la: Caeterum Not. ¶ Opponi Petrum Herodi. Hic anxius est, ne ille elabatur. At Petrus suauiter dormit. Ita solet fieri, &c. Impij fibijpsis laborum authores sunt, quia putant omnia suis viribus perfici oportere. Interim vel inuiti sentiunt, sibi cum eo rem esse, contra quem nihil possunt. Hinc illa Psal. 2. Isa. 8. 48. 57. Econtra pij in Dei prouidentia recumbunt, & in hunc curas suas reijciunt (Psal. 55.) quae causa est, vt in medijs periculis pace fruantur, Rom. 5. 8. Phil. 4. Neminem igitur impiorum concursiones & conatus terreant.
units.tr: Moreover, note: Peter is set against Herod. Here the one is anxious lest the other escape, but Peter sleeps soundly. So it usually happens, etc. The wicked are the authors of their own troubles, because they think everything must be accomplished by their own strength. Meanwhile, though unwillingly, they feel that they have to do with one against whom they can do nothing. Hence those words of Ps. 2; Isa. 8; 48; 57. On the contrary, the godly rest in the providence of God and cast their cares upon him (Ps. 55). This is why they enjoy peace in the midst of dangers, Rom. 5:8; Phil. 4. Therefore let no attempts and assaults of the ungodly terrify anyone.

units.la: III. Modus liberationis describitur. ¶ 1.
units.tr: III. The manner of the deliverance is described. ¶ 1.

units.la: Angelus Dei aflitit, vt supra 5. cap. Fit ergo quod promisi. Psal. 34. 91. Similia exempla habes, Gen. 19. 24. 48. Item, Exod. 14. 23. 32. Helisaeus, 2. Reg. 6. Dan. 6. Sic Matt. 1. 2. Dignitas hominis magna (Heb. 1.) cuius consideratio nos confirmet, vt nobis applicemus quod Helisaeus dicebat, 2. Regum 6. Officij item admoneat 1. Cor. 11.
units.tr: The angel of God stands by, as above in chapter 5. So what I promised comes to pass. Ps. 34, 91. You have similar examples: Gen. 19, 24, 48; also Exod. 14, 23, 32; Elisha, 2 Kings 6; Dan. 6. So also Matt. 1, 2. The dignity of man is great (Heb. 1), and the consideration of it should strengthen us, so that we apply to ourselves what Elisha said, 2 Kings 6. It also reminds us of our office, 1 Cor. 11.

units.la: ¶ 2. Lux fulget in carcere, partim vt constaret Angelum lucis esse, partim vt Petrus cerneret quid agendum. Potest autem Deus suis in medijs tenebris lucem accendere, & illos efficaciter consolari. Typus, Gen. 1. Sed & Christus ipse lux illa est la est, Ioh. 1. 8. 12. &c. In ea igitur ambulemus, & læta fient omnia.
units.tr: ¶ 2. A light shines in the prison, partly so that it might be plain that the angel is a messenger of light, and partly so that Peter might see what he had to do. God can kindle light for his own in the midst of darkness and effectively console them. Type: Gen. 1. But Christ himself is also that light, John 1:8, 12, etc. Let us therefore walk in it, and all things will be joyful.

units.la: ¶ 3. Excitat dormientem, nec cogitantem de liberatione. Bonitas Dei semper pro nobis vigilantis. Satan semper insidiatur, 1. Petri 5. Iohan. 8. Qui fit ergo quod non perdit dormientes? Nimirum, quia sub tutela Dei agimus, Psal. 91. Huic ergo nos commendemus semper. Et contra mortis terrorem hoc soletur, Iohan. 5. 11. Matth. 9.
units.tr: ¶ 3. He rouses the sleeper, who was not thinking about his deliverance. The goodness of God is always watchful on our behalf. Satan always lies in wait (1 Pet. 5; John 8). Why then does he not destroy the sleepers? Surely because we live under the protection of God (Ps. 91). Let us therefore always commend ourselves to him. And this should comfort us against the terror of death (John 5:11; Matt. 9).

units.la: ¶ 4. Catenæ cadunt, & facile omnia perficiuntur, custodes vel sopiti vel examines (Matth. 28.) non impediunt, &c. Por ta ferrea patet sponte. Omnia denique successiuè fiunt, vt miraculum fit illustrius, & in minimis quoq; appareat Dei providentia. Vsus, vt videas, quàm facilè sit Deo suos liberare. Huic cedunt, quæ invicta videbantur, Prouerb. 21. Similia exempla, Exod. 14. Iof. 3. Ignis, Dan. 3. Leones, Dan. 6. His fidem confirmemus ad Romanos octauo. Quòd si nolit liberare, feramus patienter, 1. Corinth. 10. 2. Corinth. 1.
units.tr: ¶ 4. The chains fall, and everything is done easily; the guards, either drowsy or stunned (Matt. 28), do not hinder, etc. The iron gate opens of its own accord. Finally, everything happens in succession, so that the miracle is more illustrious and God's providence appears even in the smallest things. The use: that you may see how easily God frees his own. Things that seemed invincible yield to him, Prov. 21. Similar examples: Exod. 14; Josh. 3; fire, Dan. 3; lions, Dan. 6. Let us confirm our faith by these, Rom. 8. But if he is unwilling to deliver us, let us bear it patiently, 1 Cor. 10; 2 Cor. 1.

units.la: IV. Quid Petrus? ¶ 1. Nescit hæc verè agi, sed visionem putat, qualis Supra 10. Exemplum infirmitatis carnis, quæ opera Dei manifesta non semper animaduer-
units.tr: IV. What of Peter? ¶ 1. He does not know that these things are truly happening but thinks it a vision, as above at chapter 10. An example of the weakness of the flesh, which does not always notice the manifest works of God.

units.la: ra Dei manifesta non semper animaduertit.
units.tr: ...does not always notice the manifest works of God.

units.la: tit,Luc.9. Apoc 1. Dan.9.10. Quid ergo gloriamur nostris vi ibus?
units.tr: ...Luke 9. Rev. 1. Dan. 9, 10. Why then do we glory in our own strength?

units.la: ¶ 2. Obtemperat tamen,non contradicit quicquam. Sic supra 10. Imitemur, ad Romanos, 1 16. Quales ergo,qui intra conscientias conuicti, imò percussi non cedunt. Vide Isa 9 10.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Yet he obeys and contradicts nothing. Thus above at chapter 10. Let us imitate, Romans 1:16. Those then who, convicted in their conscience, or rather struck down, do not yield. See Isa. 9:10.

units.la: ¶ 3. Re cognita prædicat Dei beneficium magnificè. Verè scio, quod Deus misit Angelum. Eripuit me ex manu Herodis & expectatione Iudæorum. Idem faciant omnes liberati, Psal.50.107. Sic Paulus 2. Timoth.4. Quanto magis liberatio ex inferis vni Deo debet adscribi per Christum. &c. Gen.3. Apoc.5. Act.4.
units.tr: ¶ 3. Once the matter is known, he proclaims God's benefit magnificently: "I truly know that God sent his angel and snatched me from the hand of Herod and from the expectation of the Jews." Let all who are delivered do the same, Psalms 50, 107. So Paul, 2 Tim. 4. How much more should deliverance from the dead be ascribed to the one God through Christ, etc. Gen. 3. Rev. 5. Acts 4.

units.la: Errant, qui Diuis vota nuncupant & reddunt. Item qui suis viribus & meritis gloriantur, 1.Cor.4. 2.Cor.3. Oremus.
units.tr: They err who make vows to the saints and pay them. Likewise those who glory in their own strength and merits: 1 Cor. 4, 2 Cor. 3. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CII.

units.la: 12 Et re considerata venit domum Mariæ matris Iohannis, qui cognominatur Marcus, vbi erant multi congregati & precantes.
units.tr: 12 And when he had considered this, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John, who was surnamed Mark, where many were gathered together and praying.

units.la: 13 Quum pulsasset autem Petrus ostium vestibuli, prodijt puella vt subauscultaret, nomine Rhode.
units.tr: 13 When Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a servant girl named Rhoda came to listen.

units.la: 14 Quæ agnita voce Petri, præ gaudio non aperuit vestibulum, sed intro currens annuntiauit adstare Petrum ante vestibulum.
units.tr: 14 When she recognised Peter's voice, she was so overjoyed that she did not open the gate, but ran inside and announced that Peter was standing before the gate.

units.la: Illi vero dixerunt ei, Insanis. Illa autem affirmabat itaque rem habere. At illi dicebant, Angelus eius est.
units.tr: They said to her, "You are mad." But she insisted that it was so. And they said, "It is his angel."

units.la: Petrus autem perseverabat pulsare: quum igitur aperuissent, viderunt eum, et obstupuerunt.
units.tr: But Peter kept on knocking. So when they had opened, they saw him and were astonished.

units.la: Quum autem eis indixisset silentium, narravit eis quomodo Dominus ipsum eduxisset e carcere: dixitque, Annuntiate ista Iacobo et fratribus. Et egressus profectus est in alium locum.
units.tr: Having motioned to them for silence, he told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison. And he said, "Report these things to James and the brothers." Then he went out and departed to another place.

units.la: Orto autem die fuit tumultus non parvus inter milites, quidnam factum esset Petro.
units.tr: When day came, there was no small commotion among the soldiers as to what had become of Peter.

units.la: Herodes vero quum eum requisivisset, et non invenisset, quaestione de custodibus habita, iussit eos ad supplicium rapi: et quum descendisset a Iudea Caesaream, ibi commoratus est.
units.tr: Herod, when he had searched for him and not found him, after examining the guards, ordered them to be led away to execution. And he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

units.la: VT Lucas ex Spiritus sancti suggestione persecutione describit, quae docet, quae sit in terris Ecclesiae conditio. Ita bonitat. & providentiae Dei exemplum apponit, qui Ecclesiam inter pericula videt & servat. Huc facit miraculosa liberatio
units.tr: Here Luke, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, describes a persecution which teaches what the condition of the Church is on earth. He sets before us an example of God's goodness and providence, who sees and preserves the Church amid dangers. To this belongs the miraculous deliverance

units.la: Petri, quam nihil potuit impedire. Etsi enim non omnes adhuc modum liberentur, sunt tamen promissiones generales, Deum omnes respicere, qui sibi illi consecrant, Psalm. 34. 91. Matth. 10. Luc. 12. Vt verò magis confirmemur, narrat Lucas, quid porro factum.
units.tr: of Peter, which nothing could hinder. For although not all are delivered in this way, there are nevertheless general promises that God looks upon all who consecrate themselves to him (Ps. 34; 91; Matt. 10; Luke 12). So that we may be the more confirmed, Luke goes on to tell what then happened.

units.la: I. Petrus consilio apud se inito, adit domum Mariæ, quæ fortassis prope erat, & ubi sciebat fideles convenire. Fuit mater Marci Euangelistæ, insigniter pia, quæ fer uente persecutione domum suam Ecclesiæ quasi consecrauit. Pudeat viros principes suæ ignauiæ. Ibi pulsat, quia miraculo non erat opus.
units.tr: 1. Peter, having taken counsel with himself, goes to the house of Mary, which was perhaps near, and where he knew the faithful were gathering. She was the mother of Mark the evangelist, remarkably pious, who, while the persecution raged, as it were consecrated her house to the Church. Let princes among men be ashamed of their cowardice. Peter knocks there, since there was no need of a miracle.

units.la: ¶ Obseruandum quòd ex periculo elapsus redit ad Ecclesiam. Ita cum peccasset abnegando, Ioh. 20. 21. Est hoc Spiritus sancti opus, qui credentes vnit, non dissipat. Vt enim sciunt salutem omnem in vno Christo haberi (Act. 4. Ioh. 1. 4 14.) ita hanc in eos solos deriuari sciunt, qui corporis eius membra sunt, Ephes. 1. 2. 4. Ideo commune omniū votū est, quod habetur, Ps. 122. 84. Arguuntur, qui in persecutione ecclesias deserunt, & semel elapsi nolūt porro periclitari. Dum vitæ consulere volūt, perdunt eam, Mat. 16. Mar. 8.
units.tr: ¶ Note that he, having escaped from danger, returns to the Church. So too, after he had sinned by denying, he was restored (John 20; 21). This is the work of the Holy Spirit, who unites believers and does not scatter them. For as they know that all salvation is had in Christ alone (Acts 4; John 1; 4:14), so they know that it flows to those alone who are members of his body (Eph. 1; 2; 4). Therefore the common prayer of all is the one found in Ps. 122 and 84. Those are condemned who desert the churches in time of persecution, and, once they have escaped, are unwilling to run any further risk. While they wish to look after their life, they lose it (Matt. 16; Mark 8).
