units.la: 3 Ad aperiens & proponens opor tuiffe Christum pati, & resurgere à mortuis, & hunc esse Christum Iesum, Quem ego, inquit, annuntio vobis.
units.tr: Opening and setting forth that Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and that this Christ is Jesus, whom, he says, I proclaim to you.

units.la: 4 Nonnulli igitur eorum assensi sunt & consociati sunt Paulo & Silæ, & religiosoum Græcorum multitudo magna, mulieresq; primariæ non paucæ.
units.tr: Some of them therefore were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, and so did a great multitude of devout Greeks and not a few leading women.

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus, Lucæ 9. ait: Nemo qui manu aratro ad mota respicit à tergo, idoneus est regno Dei. Eodem pertinent, quæ idem dicit, Luc. 14. Docet autem omnibus istis, verbi ministris singulari constantia opus esse, sic vt nullis periculis siue laboribus sese auocari patiantur. Exemplum huius in Paulo habemus, qui ab eo die, quo Christo & Euangelio seruire cœpit, continuis persecutionibus vexatus est, vt hucusque vidimus: perrexit tamen, & nouas subinde quæsiuit occasiones. Et vltimo Philippis, quo per Angelum vocatus erat, suit indignissimè tractatus. Non tamen obmurmurat Deo, non ab officio suo cessat, sed rectà Thessalonicam, Macedoniæ metropolim contendit, & ibi Euangelium prædicat. Inde Berrhæam & Athenas contendit. Videamus locum ordine.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ says in Luke 9: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." To the same point belong the things he says in Luke 14. He teaches, moreover, that those who minister the Word need singular constancy, so that they do not let themselves be called away by any dangers or labours. We have an example of this in Paul, who, from the day he began to serve Christ and the Gospel, has been vexed by continual persecutions, as we have seen so far; yet he persevered and kept seeking new opportunities. And at last at Philippi, to which he had been called by an angel, he was most shamefully treated. Yet he does not murmur against God, nor does he cease from his office, but hastens straight to Thessalonica, the metropolis of Macedonia, and there preaches the Gospel. From there he presses on to Berea and Athens. Let us look at the passage in order.

units.la: I. Paulus vbi Thessalon. venit, citò
units.tr: I. When Paul came to Thessalonica, having quickly

units.la: transmisisalijs oppidis, quòd nullam oc-casionem offerret spiritus, Iudæorum synagogam ingressus ibi docet per tria sab-batha, &c. NOT. 1. Quod Iudæis denuò prædicat, quorum incurabilem pertinaciam iam toties expertus erat, quòsq; reiectos esse nouerat, Act. 13. Sed mouit eum Christi studium, & suæ gentis amor. Hinc illa, Rom. 9. & 10. &c. Et adhuc sperat aliquid iuxta prophetias, Isa. 10. Rom. 11. Habet item exemplum, 1. Reg. 19.
units.tr: passed by the other towns, since the Spirit offered no occasion, he entered the synagogue of the Jews and taught there for three sabbaths, etc. NOTE 1. That he preaches again to the Jews, whose incurable obstinacy he had already tried so often and whom he knew to have been rejected (Acts 13). But the zeal of Christ and his love for his own nation moved him. Hence those passages, Rom. 9 and 10, etc. And he still hopes for something according to the prophecies (Isa. 10; Rom. 11). He has likewise an example in 1 Kings 19.

units.la: Docemur non deferendum esse officium propter hominum ingratitudinem, sed patienter ferendos esse malos, si quo modo lucrifieri possint, 2. Tim. 2. Vide Dei exemplum, Ierem. 7. 11. 2. Par. 36. Matth. 5. Christi item, Matth. 23. Luc. 13. 19. Huius serui sumus, à quo præmium sperari debet. Confutantur qui mox cessant, vbi nihil proficiunt. Obseruent Magistratus. Privatim singuli.
units.tr: We are taught that office must not be abandoned because of men's ingratitude, but that the wicked are to be borne patiently, if in any way they can be won (2 Tim. 2). See God's example (Jer. 7:11; 2 Chron. 36; Matt. 5), and likewise Christ's (Matt. 23; Luke 13, 19). We are the servants of him from whom a reward ought to be hoped for. Refuted are those who soon cease when they accomplish nothing. Let magistrates take note; let individuals take note privately.

units.la: 2. Quod sabbatha & synagogas obseruant. Nil vult in occulto agere, vt etiam Christus, Iohan. 18. Lucæ 22. Interim vides venerabilem tuti-ssimam consuetudinem esse, quod ad sacros cœtus conuenerunt. Propter hos templa & dies festi instituti sunt o-lim Leuit. 25. Necessaria hæc propter do-ctristrinam,preces & externa religionis exer citia. Obseruauit ergo Christus ipse. Vi de 1. Cor. 14. 11. Magna illorum impietas, qui scurriliter contemnunt.
units.tr: 2. That they observe the sabbaths and synagogues. He wishes to act in secret, as Christ also did (John 18; Luke 22). Meanwhile you see that it is a venerable and most safe custom that they assemble for sacred gatherings. On account of these, temples and feast days were instituted of old (Lev. 25). These things are necessary on account of doctrine, prayers and the external exercises of religion. Christ himself therefore observed them. See 1 Cor. 14:11. Great is the impiety of those who scornfully despise them.

units.la: II. Quid in Synagogis egerit Paulus? Docuit. Sed hic singula No t a. §1. Vnde doctrinam suam hauserit? Ex scriptura. Vi des vnde petenda doctrina Ecclesiae? Scri ptura à Deo data, vitam continet, 2. Tim. 3. Ioh. 5. Hinc illa, Ezech. 3 33. 2 Tim. 3. Ro. 15. Impudens illorum improbitas, qui ad Patres & Concilia remittunt, interim scri pturas reijciunt, nec volunt ex illis de salute disputari.
units.tr: II. What did Paul do in the synagogues? He taught. But here note single points. §1. Whence did he draw his teaching? From Scripture. See whence the doctrine of the Church must be sought: Scripture, given by God, contains life (2 Tim. 3; John 5). Hence those passages, Ezek. 3:33; 2 Tim. 3; Rom. 15. Shameless is the wickedness of those who refer us to the Fathers and Councils while meanwhile rejecting the Scriptures, and who do not want questions of salvation to be disputed from them.

units.la: §2. Quomodo tractauit scripturas? Aperuit, id est, interpretatus est, nimirum collatione locorum mutua, & applicauit, &c. Sic Christus, Lucae 4. &c. Docemur non sufficere nudam lectionem scriptura rum. Secari enim oportet verbum Dei, & applicari praesentibus auditoribus, vt inde discant sibi necessaria. Vide 2. Tim. 2. 3. Mat. 24.
units.tr: §2. How did he handle the Scriptures? He opened them, that is, he interpreted them, namely by the mutual comparison of passages, and applied them, etc. So Christ, Luke 4, etc. We are taught that a bare reading of the Scriptures is not enough. For the word of God must be rightly divided and applied to the present hearers, so that they may learn what is necessary for themselves. See 2 Tim. 2:3; Matt. 24.

units.la: §3. Quid docuit? Christum, & quidem huius passionem & resurrectionem, quod que Iesus Mariae filius, quem ipse praedicabat, Christus sit. Erat enim duplex Iudaeorum error. Primo offendebantur cru ce Christi, eo quod prophetias secundum teram intelligebant,& Mesiam exspectabant sine cruce,vt multi hodie. Diuersum ergo docet, quòd facilè potuit ex Isa. 53. Psalm. 22. &c. Deinde Iesum non agnoscebant pro Mesia. Probat ergo & hoc, nimirum quod illi applicat, quæ de Mesia in scripturis habentur.
units.tr: §3. What did he teach? Christ, and indeed his passion and resurrection, and that Jesus, the son of Mary, whom he preached, is the Christ. For the error of the Jews was twofold. First, they were offended by the cross of Christ, because they understood the prophecies according to the flesh and expected a Messiah without a cross, as many do today. He therefore teaches the opposite, which he could easily do from Isa. 53, Psalm 22, etc. Then they did not acknowledge Jesus as the Messiah. He therefore proves this also, namely by applying to him what the Scriptures say about the Messiah.

units.la: Docemur hic: A. Quid in Ecclesia debet praedicari? Vnus Christus. Hic enim caput, rex, sponsus, pastor, &c. est, Eph. 1. 2. 5. 2. Cor. 11. Ioh. 10. Idem sibi vult ad ducì homines, Matth. 28. Hinc illa, Act. 4. 1 Cor. 2. Gal. 6. Arguuntur, qui aliis nænijs obtundunt, &c. Gal. 1. B. Quomodo praedicari debeat Christus? Qualem scripturæ proponunt, qui cùm Deus sit æternus, tamen homo factus, pro nobis mortuus sit & resurrexit, 1. Cor. 15. inq; cœlos subuectus regnet, nobis adsit, &c. Et vt homines agnoscant non alium esse saluatorem quàm hunc. Vt item non terrenum regnum in illo quærant, sed æternæ salutis mysteria. Qui talem agnoscunt, non facilè dimouentur, sed constantes sunt.
units.tr: We are taught here: A. What ought to be preached in the Church? Christ alone. For here he is head, king, bridegroom, shepherd, etc. (Eph. 1, 2, 5; 2 Cor. 11; John 10). He wishes the same thing, that men be led to him (Matt. 28). Hence those passages, Acts 4; 1 Cor. 2; Gal. 6. Reproved are those who weary people with other trifles, etc. (Gal. 1). B. How ought Christ to be preached? As the Scriptures set him forth: that although he is eternal God, yet he was made man, died for us and rose again (1 Cor. 15), and having been carried up into the heavens, reigns and is present with us, etc. And so that men may acknowledge that there is no other saviour than this one. Likewise, that they should not seek in him an earthly kingdom, but the mysteries of eternal salvation. Those who acknowledge him thus are not easily moved, but are constant.

units.la: Hinc vides quomodo doctrinas nostri seculi dijudicare debeas, 1. Ioh. 4. Nemo audiendus, qui aliud tradit quàm Christum, &c.
units.tr: Hence you see how you ought to judge the doctrines of our age (1 John 4). No one is to be heard who teaches anything other than Christ, etc.

units.la: III. Fructus prædicationis. Quidam ex
units.tr: III. The fruit of the preaching.

units.la: ex Iudæis crediderunt, pauciores tamen, quia iam incipiebat excœcatio. Interim ta men fœderis sui veritatem Deus custodit, sicut promisit, Isa. 10. Rom. 10. Et verè qui dem illos credidisse apparet. Plures tamen ex Græcis credunt, qui iam ante cœperant aliquem habere syncerioris religionis gustum ex Iudæorum conuersatio ne. In primis autem commemorantur mulieres aliquot nobiliores credidisse, &c. Habet enim Deus suos in quouis ordine, &c.
units.tr: Some of the Jews believed, though fewer, because the blindness was already beginning. Meanwhile God keeps the truth of his covenant, as he promised (Isa. 10; Rom. 10), and indeed it appears that they did believe. Yet more of the Greeks believed, who had already before begun to have some taste of a purer religion from their association with the Jews. Among the first are mentioned several women of higher rank who believed, etc. For God has his own in every rank, etc.

units.la: NOTA. ¶1. Euangelium nunquam frustra prædicari, Isa. 55. Luc. 8. Excitet hoc ad studium gravans studium.
units.tr: NOTE. (1) The gospel is never preached in vain (Isa. 55; Luke 8). Let this stir you to eager zeal.

units.la: ¶ Interim vides quę sint officia credentium. Adiunguntse Paulo & Silæ, tum ar- dentiori discendi studio, tum quod publicè fidem profitentur. Ita studeant profice re.indies. Non pudeat illos Euangelij & ministrorum, Rom. 1. 2. Tim. 1. Non vult ambidextros cultores dominus, Apoca. 2. Oremus.
units.tr: Meanwhile you see what the duties of believers are. They join themselves to Paul and Silas, both with a more ardent desire to learn and because they openly profess the faith. Let them likewise strive to make progress daily. Let them not be ashamed of the gospel and of the ministers (Rom. 1; 2 Tim. 1). The Lord does not want double-dealing worshippers (Rev. 2). Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXVIII.

units.la: 5 Sed inuidia commoti Iudæi, qui incredulι erant, assumptis quibusdam circumforaneis viris sceleratis: ac turba coaclα, perturbârunt vrbem: et adon ti domum Iasonis, studebant eos adducere ad populum:
units.tr: 5 But the Jews, who were unbelievers, moved by envy, took along certain wicked men from the marketplace, and, gathering a crowd, threw the city into confusion; and they came upon the house of Jason and sought to bring them out to the people.

units.la: 6 Et quum non inuenissent eos, traxerunt Iasonem & quosdam fratres ad praefectos vrbis, clamando, Hi sunt qui orbis terrarum statum subuerterunt: & hic adsunt.
units.tr: 6 And when they did not find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the magistrates of the city, crying out: "These are the men who have turned the world upside down, and they are here as well."

units.la: 7 Quos excepit Iason: qui omnes contra decreta Caesaris faciunt, regem alium dicentes esse, Iesum.
units.tr: 7 Jason received them, and they all act against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.

units.la: 8 Concitarunt autem turbam & praefectos vrbis haec audientes:
units.tr: 8 And they stirred up the crowd and the magistrates of the city, who heard these things.

units.la: 9 Qui tamen quum satis accepissent a Iasone & caeteris, dimiserunt eos.
units.tr: 9 Yet when they had taken sufficient security from Jason and the others, they released them.

units.la: 10 Fratres vero statim per noctem emiserunt Paulum simul & Silam Beraeam: qui quum aduenissent, ierunt in Synagogam Iudaeorum.
units.tr: 10 But the brothers at once sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived, they went into the synagogue of the Jews.

units.la: QVemadmodum Deus filium suum humani generis saluatorem constituit, qui diaboli regnum euertere debeat: Ita ab initio statim praedixit perpetuam inter hunc & illum pugnam fore. Gen. 3. Exempla huius rei passim nobis hic liber exhibet. Vbicunque enim Apostoli per Euangelij praedicationem Christi regnum erigere conati sunt, per sua organa se illis satan oppositu. Factum Hierosol.
units.tr: Just as God appointed his Son to be the Saviour of the human race, who was to overthrow the kingdom of the devil, so from the beginning he foretold that there would be a perpetual struggle between the one and the other. Gen. 3. This book shows us examples of this everywhere. For wherever the Apostles have tried to raise up Christ's kingdom by preaching the Gospel, Satan has opposed them through his instruments. It happened at Jerusalem,

units.la: sol. Acto 3.4.5.7.8. Damasci, Act 9. Antiochiae, & Lystris, Act. 13. 14. Tandem oritur interfinum dissidium, Act. 15. Idem Philippis accidit, & nunc Thessalonicae, &c. Vt sus omnium est, ne similibus offendamur hodiie. Cogitemus hanc esse fortem Eccle siae in mundo, qui suo potius principi seruire vult, Zach 12. Luc. 2. Act. 14. 2. Tim. 3.
units.tr: Acts 3, 4, 5, 7, 8. At Damascus, Acts 9. At Antioch and Lystra, Acts 13, 14. At last a dissension arises among them, Acts 15. The same happened at Philippi, and now at Thessalonica, etc. As is everyone's lot, we should not be surprised that we meet similar things today. Let us consider that this is the lot of the Church in the world, which the world would rather see serve its own prince. Zech. 12. Luke 2. Acts 14. 2 Tim. 3.

units.la: Sed videamus praesentem locum, qui institutioni & consolationi plurimum seruit.
units.tr: But let us look at the present passage, which serves instruction and consolation very well.

units.la: I. Instrumenta nominantur, quibus satan vsus est. Fuerunt duo genera hominum. Primum Iudaeorum est, qui zelo commo-ti dicuntur. Intelliguntur hypocritae, quisfuae contumaciae & incrudelitati zelum legis Dei praetexebant, cum reuera dunta-xat sua quaerent, vt ex conspiratione pa tet. Alterum est circumforaneorum. Sunt hi otiosi homines & venales propter inopiam, & proinde ad quoduis facinus para ti. Mira coniuratio & societas.
units.tr: I. The instruments that Satan used are named. There were two kinds of men. The first were the Jews, who are said to have been moved by zeal. They are understood to be hypocrites, who used the zeal of God's law as a pretext for their obstinacy and cruelty, while in truth they were seeking only their own ends, as the conspiracy makes plain. The second were the loafers of the marketplace. These are idle men, who are for sale on account of their poverty and therefore ready for any crime. A remarkable conspiracy and alliance.

units.la: NOTA. 1. Qui semper praecipui veritatis hostes sint? Hypocritae nimirum, & qui ocium sectantes disciplina oderunt, seq; venales praebent. Illi enim suo quaestui & gloriae timent, Ioh. 5. His ibi fas, vbi plurima merces. Hinc fit quod ob veritatis odium sociantur, qui alioqui dissimili
units.tr: Learn from which class of men you must most guard yourself today. Both insinuate themselves half-openly. The abbots flatter; the nobles court their favours. But if you allow the Caesars too to obtain what they desire, your Gospel is finished.

units.la: sunt, vt hîc & Matth.22. Luc.22. Ioh. 18. 19. Hodie Monachi & nobiles, imò Cæres. Quid quòd inter medias acies vîsuntur Episcopi & Monachi, qui se mundo mor-tuos esse gloriantur?
units.tr: ¶ 2. Not all are excused who pretend zeal for their own pursuits. For there is "zeal not according to knowledge" (Rom. 10). Paul burned with this (Gal. 1; Phil. 3), yet he is called a persecutor and a wolf (Acts 9:1; 1 Cor. 15). Let us test zeal, both our own and that of others, by the Word of God.

units.la: Discè à quo hominum genere tibi maximè cauendum sit hodie. Vtrumq; semi-rifice insinuat. Blandiuntur Abbates. Op-timates illorum munera affectant. Quod si Cares quoq;, quod cupiunt, obtinere si-nas, de Euangelio tuo actum est.
units.tr: II. The pursuits are set forth. They stir up the city, by false rumours spread here and there, as if the Apostles were enemies of public safety. They rush into other people's houses, intending to drag the Apostles off to death. When these are not found, they drag off Jason the host and certain brothers, which could not have been done without open violence, etc. They accuse most falsely.

units.la: ¶ 2. Non excusari omnes eos qui suis studijs zelum prætexunt. Est enim zelus non secundùm scientiam, Rom.10. Hoc Paulus arsit, Gal.1. Phil 3. Attamen persecutor & lupus dicitur, Actorum 9.1. Corinth.15. Examinemus zelū, tum nostrum tum aliorum ad verbum Dei.
units.tr: NOTE. ¶1. With what weapons is the truth attacked? A. With open violence. For in this Satan especially has his stronghold, being a murderer from the beginning (John 8). Thus was war waged against Christ (Luke 22). There are examples in every age. Hence chains, exile, crosses and other afflictions of the godly. B. With lies and evil arts, because all the more prudent men shrink from open force. It is therefore rendered hateful by calumnies. Behold the shamelessness of the impious, who dare to turn upon the godly what they themselves commit. So Ahab (1 Kings 18). Christ himself experienced the same (Luke 23; John 18, 19).

units.la: II. Studia exprimuntur. Concitant se ditionem, nimirum falsis rumoribus hinc indesparsis, quasi publicæ salutis hostes sunt Apostoli. Irruunt in ædes alienas, Apostolos protracturi ad mortem. Non inuentis his, Iasonem hospitem & quosdam fratres protrahunt, id quod sine vi aperta fieri non potuit, &c. Accusant mendacissimè.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. With what weapons is the truth attacked? A. With open violence. For in this Satan especially places his trust, being a murderer (John 8). So the battle was waged against Christ (Luke 22). There are examples in every age. Hence chains, exile, crosses and other afflictions of the godly. B. With lies and wicked arts, because all the more prudent men shrink from open force. Thus the truth is made hateful by calumnies. See the shamelessness of the wicked, who dare to turn upon the godly the very things they themselves have committed. So Ahab (1 Kings 18). Christ himself experienced the same (Luke 23; John 18, 19).

units.la: NOTA. ¶1. Quibus armis oppugnetur veritas? A. Vi aperta. In hac enim maximè præsidium habet satan, vtpote homicida, Iohan.8 Ita contra Christum pugnatum, Luc. 22. Exempla sunt omnibus seculis. Hinc vincula, exilia, cruces & aliæ piorum afflictiones. B. Mendacijs & malis artibus eò quòd prudentiores omnes apertà vim horrent. Calumnijs ergo exosa redditur. Vbi est ea impudentia impiorum, vt quæ ab ipsis committuntur, in pios torquere ausint. Ita Achab, 1. Reg. 18. Idem Christus expertus est, Luc. 23. Ioh. 18.19.
units.tr: 2. One should not readily believe the rumours that are spread about the godly. The truth must be investigated, and men who seemed deserving of any punishment will often be found almost innocent. Consider that Satan and men are by nature liars (John 8; Ps. 116).

units.la: ¶ 2. Non credendum facile rumoribus qui de pijs sparguntur. Inuestiganda veritas, & ferè innocentes deprehendentur, qui quouis supplicio digni videbantur. Cogita satanam & hominies natura mendaces esse, Ioh. 8. Ps. 116.
units.tr: III. The outcome of the whole affair. At first everyone is stirred up, as is characteristic of seditious people. But soon God calms this storm, while he governs the minds of the judges, so that, having received satisfaction from Jason, they let him go, and so on. This council was more prudent and more just than that at Philippi.

units.la: ¶ 3. Quid fiat, vbi otiosi & circumfora nei feruntur, &c. 1. Thess 5.2. Thess 3.
units.tr: But NOTE. ¶ 1. Jason, who, having incurred the danger of death for an act of piety, is so easily set free, indeed has everlasting glory.

units.la: III. Exitus totius negotij. Commouentur primo omnes, quod proprium est sed ditionibus. Sed mox sedat tempestatem hanc Deus, dum iudicum animos moderatur, vt satisfactione ab Iasone accepta, dimittatur, &c. Prudentior & iustior sena tus hic quàm Philippensis.
units.tr: But note: (1) Jason, who was about to perish because of his duty of piety, is so easily set free, and indeed has everlasting glory.

units.la: Sed NoT. ¶ 1. Iasonem, qui ob officiū pietatis iam iam periturus, tam facilè libe ratur, imò sempiternam habet gloriam.
units.tr: But note: 1. Jason, who, though on the point of perishing for an act of devotion, is so easily set free, and indeed has everlasting glory.

units.la: Sic Loth,Genef.19. Impletur promissio Matt. 10. Imitemur,nec pigeat periclitari pro Christi fidelibus.
units.tr: So Lot, Gen. 19. The promise of Matt. 10 is fulfilled. Let us imitate them, and not shrink from running risks for Christ's faithful people.

units.la: ¶ 2 Fratres, qui Paulum & Silam confessim emittunt, & nouum pro his subeunt periculû. Est hoc gratitudinis exemplum. Tale quid in Galatis commendat Paulus,Cap 4 Hodie fideles ministri primi manifestis periculis objiciuntur, imò ad supplicia deposcuntur ab his qui Christi stianissimi videri volunt.
units.tr: 2. The brethren, who at once send Paul and Silas away, and take on new danger on their behalf. This is an example of gratitude. Paul commends something similar in the Galatians, chap. 4. Today faithful ministers are exposed to plain dangers, and indeed are demanded for punishment by those who wish to seem most Christian.

units.la: ¶ 3. Paulum,in quo duo obseruabis.A. Quod consilium fratrum de fuga admittit. Permissa ergo fuga quando nec Dei gloria,nec fratrum salus periclitatur,Mat. 10 Nec enim nos absque vllo fructu perire vult Deus.
units.tr: 3. Paul, in whom you should observe two things. A. That he accepts the brethren's counsel about flight. Therefore, when flight is permitted, when neither God's glory nor the brethren's safety is endangered, Matt. 10. For God does not wish us to perish without any fruit.

units.la: B. Quòd statim diuertit in synagogam Iudæorum,& denuò prædicat. Ita ergo ea uenda pericula, ne officium negligamus. Zelus Dei omnia moderabitur. Oremus.
units.tr: B. That he immediately turns aside into the synagogue of the Jews and preaches again. So we should avoid those dangers that are to be avoided, but not neglect our duty. The zeal of God will govern all things. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXXXIX.

units.la: 11 Fuerunt autem isti generosiores ijs Iudæis qui erant Thessalonicenses, vt qui recepermt sermonem cum omni alacritate, quotidie scrutantes scripturas, an hæc ita se haberent.
units.tr: 11 Now these were more noble than those Jews who were in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all eagerness, searching the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.

units.la: 12 Mil-
units.tr: 12 Mil-

units.la: 12 Multi igitur crediderunt ex eis, & Græcæ mulieres honestæ, & viri non pauci.
units.tr: 12 Therefore many of them believed, and not a few honourable Greek women, and men.

units.la: 13 Vt autem cognoverunt Thessalonicenses Iudai Berrhoeæ quoque annunciatum esse à Paulo sermonem Dei, venerunt etiam illuc, concitantes turbam.
units.tr: 13 But when the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God had also been proclaimed by Paul at Berea, they came there too, stirring up the crowd.

units.la: 14 Sed statim Paulum emiserunt fratres, ut iret velut ad mare: Silas autem & Timotheus subsisterunt illic.
units.tr: 14 But at once the brothers sent Paul away, as though to the sea; but Silas and Timothy remained there.

units.la: 15 Qui verò Paulum susceperant, duxerunt eum Athenas usque: & accepto mandato ad Silam & Timotheum, ut quam celerrimè ad ipsum venirent, abierunt.
units.tr: 15 Those who had escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and, having received a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they departed.

units.la: QVamuis regnū Domini nostri Iesu Christi continuis & assiduis mundi conatibus oppugnetur, adeò tamen euerti non potest, ut potius persecutionibus magis promoveatur. Docet hoc tota huius libri historia. Primò enim Hierosolymis oppugnatum fuit. Sed ea occasione in totam Iudæam & Samariam extenditur, Act. 8. Idem in rebus per Paulum gestis cernitur. Quoties enim loco aliquo ille pellitur, Euangelium alio transfert & eo plures lucrifacit. Id ipsum in Macedonia acci
units.tr: Although the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ is assailed by the constant and unceasing efforts of the world, it cannot be overthrown; rather, it is advanced all the more by persecutions. The whole history of this book teaches this. For first it was attacked at Jerusalem, but on that occasion it spreads into all Judea and Samaria (Acts 8). The same is seen in the things done through Paul. For whenever he is driven out of some place, he carries the gospel elsewhere and wins more people there. The same thing happens in Macedonia.

units.la: dic. Iniquè tractatur Philippis. Sed ita Theffalon.venit. Illinc etiam pellitur per Iudæos.Sed manent feminafidei, quæ mi ræ fructificant, & Berrhoææ plus proficiu tur.
units.tr: It is treated unjustly at Philippi, but it comes to Thessalonica in this way. From there too he is driven out by the Jews. But the women of faith remain, who bear wonderful fruit, and more progress is made at Berea.

units.la: Seruiunt hæc consolationi. Non est con silium contra Dominum,Prou.21. Psal.33. Sed consilium Domini est,vt regnet Christus Psal.110.72.Zach 9 12 Luc.10 Mat.28. Id non fallet. Interim Paulum imitemur, qui subinde ad officium redit.
units.tr: These things serve for consolation. There is no counsel against the Lord (Prov. 21; Ps. 33). But it is the counsel of the Lord that Christ should reign (Ps. 110; 72; Zech. 9; Luke 10; Matt. 28). That will not fail. Meanwhile let us imitate Paul, who from time to time returns to his duty.

units.la: Videamus autem quid Berrhoææ factum sit.
units.tr: Let us see, then, what happened at Berea.

units.la: I. Commendantur Berrhoænses Iudæi, & docetur quàm profecerint apud illos Euangelium. Magis ingenui fuerunt quam Theffalon. Illi enim indignè reiecerant. Hi amplectuntur promptè animo. Deinde domi cum scriptura conferunt quæ à Paulo dicebantur. Ita fit vt & ipsi credant,& suo exèplo plures alios tum viros tum mulieres ad fidem trahant.
units.tr: I. The Jews of Berea are commended, and it is taught how greatly the gospel has advanced among them. They were more well-bred than the Thessalonians. For those had rejected it unworthily; these embrace it readily in mind. Then at home they compare what was said by Paul with Scripture. So it comes about that they themselves believe, and by their example they draw many others to faith, both men and women.

units.la: NOT.qi.Quales esse conueniat Euangelij auditores. Primo promptis animis excipiant.Nisi enim excipiatur femen,fructificare nequit,Luc.8. Impingunt ergo in limine,qui audire nolunt,Ioh.8. Deinde nimia facilitas absit, ne quouis vento doctrinæ circumferamur,Eph.4. Sed semen mentem animo conceptum dijudicemus & conferamus cum scripturis, Lu.8.1.Thes, 5 1.Ioh.4.
units.tr: NOTE: What sort of hearers of the gospel it is fitting to be. First, they should receive it with ready minds. For unless the seed is received, it cannot bear fruit (Luke 8). Therefore those who do not want to hear stumble at the threshold (John 8). Then let excessive credulity be absent, lest we be carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4). Rather, let us weigh the seed conceived in our mind and compare it with the Scriptures (Luke 8; 1 Thess. 5; John 4).

units.la: Arguuntur hoc exemplo: A. Qui scripturarum lectionem laicis prohibent. At- qui has omnibus communes esse vultDe-us. Vide Exod.16 20.Deut.6 Psal.1. Quia ad omnus vita aeterna pertinet quae his continetur,Ioh.5.
units.tr: They are refuted by this example: A. Those who forbid the reading of the Scriptures to the laity. Yet God wills that these be common to all (see Exod. 16; 20; Deut. 6; Ps. 1), because eternal life pertains to all that is contained in them (John 5).

units.la: B. Qui doctrinam suam dijudicari nolunt, sed sibi quiduis docendi ius sumunt. Num Paulo praeferri volunt? Vide Gal. 1.Ioh.8 10.
units.tr: B. Those who do not want their doctrine to be judged, but claim for themselves whatever right of teaching they please. Do they want to be placed above Paul? See Gal. 1; John 8; 10.

units.la: ¶ 2. Credunt multi ex omni hominum genere Iudaei, quorum repudium iam instabat. Sed saluantur reliquiae iuxta promissiones, Isa.10. Mulieres primariae et nobiles. Sic Luc.8. Viri itaque non pauci. Tantum potuit bonum exemplum, &c.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Many Jews from every kind of people believe, although their rejection was already at hand. But the remnant is saved according to the promises (Isa. 10). Women of the first rank and nobility: so in Luke 8. So there were not a few men. So much could a good example achieve, etc.

units.la: Interim patet, Christi gratia ad omnes hominum ordines pertinere, nec quenquam propter patriam vel vitae conditionem excludi, 1 Tim.2.Act 10.Gal.3. Col. 3.Seruiat consolationi simul & institutioni, ne quis alios prae se contemnat, &c.
units.tr: Meanwhile it is clear that the grace of Christ pertains to all orders of men, and that no one is excluded because of his country or condition of life (1 Tim. 2; Acts 10; Gal. 3; Col. 3). Let it serve both for consolation and for instruction, so that no one despises others in comparison with himself, etc.

units.la: II. Quid Berrhoeae tentatum a satana? Idem quod alibi. Sed videtur neminem il lic fuisse suo instituto idoneum. Quare Thessalonica adducit qui turbas exc tent.
units.tr: II. What was attempted at Berea by Satan? The same as elsewhere. But it seems that there was no one there suited to his own purpose. Therefore he brings in men from Thessalonica who stir up tumults.

units.la: Sim le exemplum Lystris æditum, Actor. 14. Hodie sei è Monach s vtitur, qui hinc inde circumcurrentes Euangelij cursum vbique impediunt.
units.tr: A similar example was given at Lystra (Acts 14). Today Satan uses monks, who run about hither and thither and everywhere hinder the course of the gospel.

units.la: Sed No T. ¶ Incurabilem gent s illius malitiam. Non modo ipsi veritati cedere nolunt, sed non possunt ferre vtsaltem alij illuminentur. Recte ergo illos depingit Paulus, 1. Thess. 2. Similes his sunt, quicun que sese organa satanæ præbent ad Christi fidem oppugnandam. Sed obseruent tristem huius gentis exitum, iuxta oracu-la Christi, Matth. 23. 24. Luc. 19. Idem nostris quoq; cuenturum esse generales mi-næ satis docent. Zach 2. 12. Psal. 2. 110. Sunt exempla in potentissimis Imperatoribus & Regibus tum veteratum recentia, &c.
units.tr: But NOTE: the incurable malice of that people. They not only refuse to yield to the truth itself, but cannot bear that others at least be enlightened. Paul therefore rightly portrays them (1 Thess. 2). Those who offer themselves as instruments of Satan to attack faith in Christ are like them. But let them observe the sad end of this people, according to the oracles of Christ (Matt. 23; 24; Luke 19). The general threats show that the same will happen to our own people as well (Zech. 2; 12; Ps. 2; 110). There are examples, both old and recent, among the most powerful emperors and kings, etc.

units.la: III. Quid pij & fideles faciunt? Fratres denuò subducunt Paulum periculo, reli-ctis Berrhœæ, Sila & Timotheo, eò quod illis non ita periculosum erat manere, vt Paulo. Prudenter autem agunt. Nam iter mare versus instituunt, vt Iudæorum insi-dias eludant, mox flexo rui sum itinere Athenas contendunt. &c.
units.tr: III. What do the godly and faithful do? The brothers again withdraw Paul from danger, leaving Silas and Timothy at Berea, because it was not as dangerous for them to remain as for Paul. They act prudently. For they set out on the road towards the sea, so as to elude the snares of the Jews, and soon, turning their route aside, they hasten to Athens, etc.

units.la: In his No T ¶ Pietatis officium, cuod grati pro accepto Euangelij beneficio præ-stant suo doctori. Res erat magni sump-tus & laboris, plenaque periculi. Sed omnia hęc vincunt, eò quod de Euangelio digne iudicant, iuxta illud Pauli, 1.Cor.9. Sic Gal.4.Hoc quia nos no facimus, pericli tari nolumus. Sed fere fiant, ut qui pro Christo nil ferre volunt, postea maioribus ma lis ob causas minus sanctas implicentur.
units.tr: In these things NOTE: the duty of piety, which the grateful render to their teacher for the benefit of the gospel received. It was a matter of great expense and labour, and full of danger. But all these things are overcome, because they judge the gospel worthy, according to that saying of Paul (1 Cor. 9). So also Gal. 4. Because we do not do this, we do not want to be in danger. But it often happens that those who will bear nothing for Christ are afterwards entangled in greater evils, for less holy causes.

units.la: Interim docemur prudentiam non pugnare cum fide. Praecipit hanc Christus, Matth 10. Opus illa propter calliditatem filiorum huius seculi. Luc.16. Curandum tamen ne quid ex carnis ratione praeter officium faciant, sed illam subiiciamus obedientiae fidei, 2.Cor.10. Ita non errabimus. Oremus.
units.tr: Meanwhile we are taught that prudence does not conflict with faith. Christ commands this (Matt. 10). The sons of this age work it through their cleverness (Luke 16). Yet care must be taken that they do nothing beyond their duty out of the reasoning of the flesh, but that they subject it to the obedience of faith (2 Cor. 10). So we shall not go astray. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXL.
units.tr: HOMILY CXL.

units.la: 16 Paulo autem Athenis illos exasperabatur spiritus eius in ipso, quum conspiceret urbem idolis deditam.
units.tr: 16 Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was stirred within him when he saw the city given over to idols.

units.la: 17 Disputabat igitur in Synagoga cum Iudaeis et religiosis, et in foro quotidie cum quibusdam obviis.
units.tr: 17 So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace daily with those who happened to be there.

units.la: 18 Quidam autem ex Epicureis et Stoicis philosophis conferebantur cum eo: et quidam dicebant, Quid vult nugator iste dicere? Alii vero, Peregrinarum deorum videtur annuntiator esse, quia Iesum et resurrectionem annuntiabat eis.
units.tr: 18 Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conferred with him. Some said, "What does this babbler want to say?" Others said, "He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign gods," because he preached to them Jesus and the resurrection.

units.la: 19 Et prehensum eum duxerunt in Areopagum, dicentes, Possumus nescire... re quæ fit ista nova quæ à te dicitur doctrina.
units.tr: 19 And they took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, "May we know what this new teaching is that you speak of?"

units.la: 20 Peregrina enim quædam ingerūt auribus nostris: volumus ergo scire quid nam ista sibi velint.
units.tr: 20 For you bring certain strange things to our ears, so we want to know what these things mean.

units.la: 21 (Cæterum Athenienses & adue næ hospites nulli alij rei vacabant, nisi ad dicendum aut audiendum aliquid noui.)
units.tr: 21 (Now the Athenians and the foreigners living there spent their time on nothing else but telling or hearing something new.)

units.la: EXposuit hucusque Lucas, vt Diuus Paulus Euangelij doctrinâ per mul- tas gentes & vrbes disserminârit, vt non temerè ipse se plus alijs omnibus labora- uisse dicat,1.Cor.15.Porrò ne quis obscu- ros tantummodo & indoctos homines ab illo conuersos putaret,nunc certo diuinę prouidentiæ consilio,Athenas venit, qua nulla fuit vrbs celebrior. Vetustissima vt quæ circa Mosis tempora regem habuit Cecropem. Clara victorijs contra Persas. Clara ingenijs,vt quæ Platonem, Socra- tem,Xenophontem,Cratem, &c. proge- nuit.Schola totius mundi & sapientiæ se- des. Adhæc religione gentilitia præ alijs dementati,eò quod Deos aliquos ex se ge- nitos putarent. Gloriabantur item Palla- dis imagine zelo delapsa,alia item,quęPhi diæ opus esset.
units.tr: Luke has so far set out how the divine Paul spread the doctrine of the Gospel through many nations and cities, so that he could say he had laboured more than all the others, 1 Cor. 15. Lest anyone think that he had converted only obscure and unlearned men, he now comes, by the certain counsel of divine providence, to Athens, than which no city was more famous. It is most ancient, since it had a king, Cecrops, around the time of Moses. It is famous for its victories against the Persians. It is famous for its talents, since it produced Plato, Socrates, Xenophon, Crates, and others. It was the school of the whole world and the seat of wisdom. Moreover, it was driven mad by pagan religion more than others, because its people thought some gods had been born from it. They also boasted of the image of Pallas fallen from heaven, and another likewise, which was the work of Phidias.

units.la: Hvivs conuersionem modò describit Lucas,exemplum proponens tum gratiæ Dei in eminem aspernantis (1. Tim. 2. 1.) tum potentiae Euangelij, quae omnem car nis intellectum debellat & subijcit, Rom. 1. 2. Cor. 10. 1. Cor. 1.
units.tr: Here Luke only describes the conversion, setting forth an example both of the grace of God toward one who was spurning it (1 Tim. 2. 1.) and of the power of the Gospel, which overcomes and subdues all the understanding of the flesh, Rom. 1; 2 Cor. 10; 1 Cor. 1.

units.la: I. Orditur a Paulo, vt se gesserit illic, cum Silam & Timotheum exspectarer, vt bi haec habes: 1. Incandescit spiritu, quod vi- deret tantam vrbem idololatriae immersam. Vt enim nullo scelere magis offendi tur Deus quam idololatria, sic hac etiam maxime irritatur sanctorum zelus: eo quod gloriae Dei prae omnibus studet. Vide Mosem, Exod. 32. Phinees, Num. 25 Helias 1. Reg. 18. Iehu, 2. Reg. 10, Iosias, 2. Par. 34. & 2. Reg. 23. Epiphanius. Prophetae & Apostoli. Exemplum huius in Christo proponitur, Ioh. 2. Psal 68.
units.tr: I. He begins with Paul, how he conducted himself there while he awaited Silas and Timothy, as you have here. 1. He burns in spirit because he sees so great a city immersed in idolatry. For as God is offended by no crime more than idolatry, so the zeal of the saints is most provoked by this, since they strive above all for the glory of God. See Moses, Exod. 32; Phinehas, Num. 25; Elijah, 1 Kings 18; Jehu, 2 Kings 10; Josiah, 2 Chron. 34 and 2 Kings 23; Epiphanius; the Prophets and Apostles. An example of this is set forth in Christ, John 2; Ps. 68.

units.la: NOT. Zelo opus esse Christi ministris. Commendat hunc oratio Domini-ca. Eode singuli flagrare debent, eo quod sine hoc nihil proficitur. Nec Christus eos ferre poterit, qui in religionis causa tepent, Apoc. 3. 1. Reg. 18.
units.tr: NOTE. Christ's ministers must have zeal. The Lord's Prayer commends this. Each one ought to burn with it, since without it nothing is accomplished. Nor will Christ be able to bear those who grow lukewarm in the cause of religion, Rev. 3; 1 Kings 18.

units.la: II. Cogitat de reformanda vrbe, & rem mox aggreditur. Primo cum Iudaeis, tum quia commodius hoc erat, tum quia hunc ordinem Christus docuerat, Act. 1. Deinde cum religiosis, qui iam gustu aliquem habebant. Tandem cum quibusdam obuijs.
units.tr: II. He considers reforming the city and at once sets about the task. First with the Jews, both because this was more convenient and because Christ had taught this order, Acts 1. Then with the devout, who already had some taste of the truth. Finally with certain passers-by.

units.la: Atqui multa auocare poterant. Vrbis celebritas. Ingeniorum subtilitas. Vetustas consuetudinis. Tum quód omnes mutationes periculosæ sunt, maximè peiegi-nis. Sed nihilominus pergit.
units.tr: Yet many things could have called him away: the city's fame, the subtlety of its talents, the antiquity of its customs, and also because all changes are dangerous, especially in religion. Nevertheless he presses on.

units.la: Not. ¶ Nullis rebus nosà vocatione Dei reuocari patiamur. Quòd si carnis rationes voluissent audire Prophetę & Apostoli, omnes fecissent quod Ionas, Cap. 1. Vide Mosem, Exo 4. Cogitemus obedien dum esse Deo, quicquid tandem fiat. Deinde Dei verbum omnibus impedimentis potentius esse, Heb 4. Ier 23 &c.
units.tr: NOTE. Let us not allow ourselves to be called back from anything by the calling of God. For if the reasons of the flesh had been listened to by the Prophets and Apostles, they would all have done what Jonah did, ch. 1. See Moses, Exod. 4. Let us consider that we must obey God, whatever happens in the end. Then, that the word of God is more powerful than all hindrances, Heb. 4; Jer. 23, etc.

units.la: III. Indicatur qui obstinerint Philosophi diuersissimæ sectæ. Epicvrei enim hostes artium & sapientiæ. Voluptatem dicebant summum bonum, quæ ne turbaretur, prouidentiam & vitam æternam negabant. Stoici virtutem vrgebant, & proinde hominis viribus tribuebant fœlicitatem. Docebant indolentiam & Deum subijciebant fato.
units.tr: III. It is shown which philosophers resisted, from the most diverse sects. For the Epicureans were enemies of the arts and of wisdom. They said that pleasure was the highest good, and to keep it undisturbed they denied providence and eternal life. The Stoics pressed virtue, and accordingly attributed happiness to human strength. They taught freedom from passion and subjected God to fate.

units.la: Not. ¶ 1. Qui semper Euangelij hostes futuri sint. Epicuræi voluptuarij, quales hodie mutato nomine multi sunt, vt prædictum, Matth. 24 Luc. 17. 2. Pet. 3. 1. Thess. 5. Hi omnes dicunt quod habetur, Psal. 14. 53. Et proinde Euangelium ferre non possunt. Stoici & Pelagiani, qui suis operioperibus iustitiam & salutem tribuunt. Tales inter Iudaeos Pharisaei, Luc 18. Mat thaei 6. Tempore Apostolorum Nazaraei. Hodie Papistae & Monachi in primis, qui etiam homines ἀπαθεῖς & ἀσόφυεῖς esse volunt, 2. Tim. 3. Hi suo quaestui & exi stimatione timent. Pugnandum cum vi rque genere, afferendus Christus & rectio, quibus capitibus delirium horum omne conturatur.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. Who will always be enemies of the Gospel. The Epicureans were voluptuaries, such as today, under a changed name, there are many, as foretold, Matt. 24; Luke 17; 2 Pet. 3; 1 Thess. 5. All of these say what is written, Ps. 14; 53, and therefore cannot bear the Gospel. The Stoics and Pelagians, who attribute righteousness and salvation to their own works. Among the Jews such were the Pharisees, Luke 18; Matthew 6. In the time of the Apostles, the Nazarenes. Today the Papists and especially the monks, who also want to be impassive [ἀπαθεῖς] and [ἀσόφυεῖς] in their own way. These fear for their gain and their reputation. We must fight against both kinds: Christ and right teaching must be brought forward, and by these heads all their folly is refuted.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quàm impossibile sit absque concertatione Euangelium praedicare. Mundi sapientia, quocunq; inclinet, huic contraria est.
units.tr: 2. How impossible it is to preach the Gospel without contention. Worldly wisdom, whichever way it leans, is opposed to it.

units.la: II. Quomodo iudicârint Athenis de Pauli doctrina.
units.tr: II. How the Athenians judged Paul's teaching.

units.la: 1. Aliqui repudiant cum conuitio. Vocant spermologum ein spiacher Janbiacher/wurtzenframer/&c Hi clau dunt libijpfis viam salutis.
units.tr: 1. Some reject it with abuse. They call him a babbler (spermologus), a "Schwätzer," a "Janbiacher" (a fellow with a hollow tongue), a "wurtzenframer" (a herb-seller), etc. These men shut themselves off from the way of salvation.

units.la: NOT. ¶ Quàm inepta sit ad salutis mysteria percipienda humani ingenij sapientia, 1. Cor 1. Fabulas putant. Si vrgeantur, iam manifesti hostes fiunt. Habes quod respondeas ijs, qui sapientes, religiosos & totum mundi supercilium nobis obijciunt.
units.tr: NOTE. How unsuited human wisdom is to grasp the mysteries of salvation: 1 Cor. 1. They think the gospel is fables. If they are pressed, they at once become open enemies. You have here an answer to those who throw at us their wisdom, their piety, and the whole haughtiness of the world.

units.la: 2. Curiosi quidam putant illum nouam daemonia praedicare. Quare apprehensum ducunt in Martium vicum, vt publicè rationem reddat. Sic Socrati factū. Nouitatis accusant. Confluit magna turba curioforum, quibus vrbs abundat. Bene autem horum vitio vtitur Deus.
units.tr: 2. Some curious people think he is preaching new divinities. So they seize him and lead him to the Areopagus (Mars' Hill), to give an account of himself in public. This is what happened to Socrates. They accuse him of novelty. A large crowd of the curious, with which the city abounds, comes together. God, however, makes good use of their vice.

units.la: NOT. Euangelij sortem in mundo. Vel turpiter exploditur, vel vt hominum affectibus inseruiat trahitur. Multi hodie curiosi sunt, qui quouis vento circumaguntur. Eph.4. Nos constanter persuadere mus, vt Paulus, hac offendamur, 1. Iohan. 2, &c. Oremus.
units.tr: NOTE. The lot of the gospel in the world: either it is shamefully mocked, or it is dragged in to serve men's passions. Many today are curious, and are blown about by every wind: Eph. 4. Let us, like Paul, persuade ourselves constantly not to be offended by these things: 1 John 2, etc. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLI.

units.la: 22 Stans autem Paulus in medio Areopago, dixit, Viri Athenienses, omnino conspicio vos quasi religiosiores.
units.tr: Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' Hill and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious.

units.la: 23 Praeteriens enim et contemplans sacra vestra, inveni etiam aram, cui inscriptum erat, Ignoto Deo. Quem ergo ignorantes colitis, hunc ego vobis annuntio.
units.tr: For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.

units.la: 24 Deus qui fecit mundum et omnia quae in eo sunt, quum sit caeli et terrae Dominus, in manu factis templis non habitat:
units.tr: God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands.

units.la: 25 Nec manibus hominum colitur, alicuius rei egens, quum ipse det omnibus vitam et halitum et omnia.
units.tr: Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things.

units.la: PAulus Apostolus 1. Cor. 1. ait: Praedicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudaeis quidem offendiculum, Graecis vero stulti tiam. Quia enim carnis ratio Christi & spiritus Dei mysteria non capit (Matth. 11. 16. 1. Cor. 2.) stultissimum illi videtur, in Christo crucifixo salutem quaerere, &c. Id tum alibi, tum Athenis maxime Paulus expertus est. Erant illic sapientissimi totius orbis. Sed vix alibi minus profecit. Nam ex illis alij salutis doctrinam ridĕnt & contemnitur, alij ex curiositate suis tantummodo affectibus accommodant. Interim Deus his bene vtitur: quia hac occasione fit, ut in celeberrimo loco Paulus concio natur.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul says in 1 Cor. 1: "We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to the Greeks foolishness." Since the reason of the flesh cannot grasp Christ and the mysteries of the Spirit of God (Matt. 11:16; 1 Cor. 2), it seems most foolish to it to seek salvation in Christ crucified, and so on. Paul found this both elsewhere and above all at Athens. There were the wisest men of the whole world there, yet scarcely anywhere did he achieve less. For some of them mock and scorn the doctrine of salvation, while others, out of curiosity, merely fit it to their own passions. Meanwhile God makes good use of them, for by this occasion Paul comes to preach a sermon in a most famous place.

units.la: Argumentum concionis est, quod a superstitione & idololatria ad vnius veri Dei cultum revocat Athenienses per Christum. Primo enim illos nimiae superstitionis accusat, & institutione opus habere ostendit. Deinde de Deo & vera religione disserit, simul mundi stuporem arguens, qui statuis & simulachris Deum coli posse putet. Tandem ad Christum delabitur, &c.
units.tr: The argument of the sermon is that he calls the Athenians back from superstition and idolatry to the worship of the one true God through Christ. First he accuses them of excessive superstition and shows that they need instruction. Then he discourses about God and true religion, at the same time rebuking the foolishness of a world that thinks God can be worshipped by statues and images. At last he comes down to Christ, and so on.

units.la: I. Exordio breui simul proponit. Amice vero agit, ne initio statim offendéren-tur. Arguit vero superstitionem, quod incerti rerum in religione modum excedant. Probat ex inscriptione altaris. Vide Diog·
units.tr: I. In a brief exordium he states his subject at the same time. He speaks kindly, so that they are not offended at the outset. He attacks superstition, because men who are uncertain about things in religion go beyond due measure. He proves it from the inscription on the altar. See Diogenes Laertius on Epimenides of Crete.

units.la: ginem Laert.in Epimenide Creten. Quasi diceret: Laudatur vestra sapientia, sed in religione minimè sapitis vbi maximè opus erat. Cum non contenti vestris Dijs etiam ignotos colatis, fatemini vobis in re ligione nihil certi esse. Inde verò occasione sumpta promittit se veri Dei cognitionem ipsis traditurum.
units.tr: As if he were saying: your wisdom is praised, but in religion you are least wise exactly where there was greatest need. Not content with your gods, you even worship unknown ones, and so you confess that in religion you have nothing certain. Seizing on this occasion, he promises that he will hand down to them the knowledge of the true God.

units.la: NOT. 1. Quòd præ aliis in religione erra-runt Atheniens. qui sapientiss. homi-num putabantur. Ergo nihil proficit in re ligione carnis sapientia.
units.tr: NOTE 1. That the Athenians, who were thought the wisest of men, erred more than others in religion. Therefore the wisdom of the flesh profits nothing in religion.

units.la: Arguuntur, qui ad studium Theologiæ nō admittunt nisi quos priùs philosophia demetauit, & ineptos per omnia reddidit ¶ 2. Atheniens. eos potiss. nomine falsæ religionis accusari, quòd Deum ignotum colerent. Admonemur ergo: A Religione absque veri Dei cognitione non consistere. Idem enim dicit Christus, Ioh. 4. Vos nescitis, &c. Nam religio in fide & inuocatio ne potissim versatur, Heb. 11. Ps. 50. Rom. 10. 14 Sed neutra sine cognitione Dei sub sistit, Ro. 10. Imò vbi hæc deest, ad ratio- nem carnis coaersi homines, sua figmenta proferunt, & quidè noua quotidie, vt implea- tur Ioh 4. Vide gentes, Ro. 1. Ioh. 1. Ierusalem, 1. Reg 18 Ier. 2. Isa. 55 Papistas, apud quos omnia incerta. Deus Mayzm, Daniel. ii. Imo post mortem adhuc dubitatur maxime.
units.tr: Those are rebuked who admit to the study of theology only those whom philosophy has first driven out of their wits and rendered wholly unfit. Note 2. The Athenians are charged especially with false religion because they worshipped an unknown God. We are therefore admonished that religion does not stand without knowledge of the true God. Christ says the same thing in John 4: "You know not what you worship." For religion consists chiefly in faith and invocation (Heb. 11; Ps. 50; Rom. 10:14). But neither stands without the knowledge of God (Rom. 10). Indeed where this is lacking, men who turn to the reason of the flesh put forward their own inventions, and new ones every day, so that John 4 is fulfilled. See the nations, Rom. 1; John 1; Jerusalem, 1 Kings 18; Jer. 2; Isa. 55; the Papists, among whom everything is uncertain; the god of Mayzm, Daniel ii. Indeed, even after death people doubt most of all.

units.la: B. Quàm miseri sunt, qui veritatis luce carent. Apud seipsos incerti rerum, coram Deo quoque operam ludunt,
units.tr: B. How wretched are those who lack the light of truth! Uncertain about things among themselves, they also trifle with their work before God.

units.la: ¶ 3 Apostolos vnum Deum praedicare. Quare hos audiant, qui saluari volunt, Mar. 16. Act. 1. 16 &c.
units.tr: § 3. The Apostles preach one God. Therefore let those hear them who wish to be saved (Mark 16; Acts 1:16, etc.).

units.la: 11. Proponit veram cognitionem, sic vt simul de cultu admo eat & gentilitios errores refellat. Non autem subtiliter de eius sententia Dei disputat (quia inuestigari nequit, Exod. 33.34.) sed ab operibus illū describit. 1. Deus qui omnia creauit, est omnium quoq; Dominus. Id Epicureorum sententiae opponit, qui mundū aeternum & Deo non curae esse dicebant, Psal. 14.53.
units.tr: II. He sets out the true knowledge in such a way that at the same time he admonishes about worship and refutes the errors of the Gentiles. He does not dispute subtly about God's essence (since it cannot be searched out, Exod. 33, 34), but describes him from his works. 1. God, who created all things, is also Lord of all. He opposes this to the opinion of the Epicureans, who said that the world is eternal and that God takes no care of it (Ps. 14; 53).

units.la: Inde verò colligit illū non habitare in templis manufactis, hoc modo: Qui omni rum Dominus est, vbiq; adsit oportet. Deus omniū Dominus est. Ergo vbiq; est, & per consequens non includitur in templis.
units.tr: From this he infers that God does not dwell in temples made with hands, in this way: whoever is Lord of all must be present everywhere. God is Lord of all. Therefore he is everywhere, and consequently is not confined to temples.

units.la: Nota. ¶ 1. Errare omnes, qui Dei maiestate & gratiam alligant templis. Ita Graeci, quorū templa Persae ideo exustemunt, Iudaei, Ier. 7. Idem faciunt Papistae. Sed aliter scriptura docet, 1. Reg 8. Isa. 66. Ier. 7. Matt 24. Psal. 130. Ioh. 4. Tolluntur peregrinationes.
units.tr: Note. 1. All err who bind the majesty and grace of God to temples. So the Greeks, whose temples the Persians therefore burned; so the Jews, Jer. 7. The Papists do the same. But Scripture teaches otherwise: 1 Kings 8, Isa. 66, Jer. 7, Matt. 24, Psalm 130, John 4. Pilgrimages are abolished.

units.la: § 2. Quis ergo templorum vsus? vt exercitatio ternae religioni & vnanimi pietatis studio seruiant, Coetibus sacris, Leuit.25. Deut. 16. Doctrinae, Ioh.18. Precibus publicis, Matth.18. Sacramentis.
units.tr: § 2. What, then, is the use of temples? That they serve the exercise of true religion and the common zeal for piety: for sacred assemblies (Lev. 25, Deut. 16); for teaching (John 18); for public prayers (Matt. 18); for the sacraments.

units.la: II. Deus non colitur hominum manibus. Probat, quia ipse vitam & halitum quo quelargitur, & ipse nullius indiget. Argumentum tale est. Qui omnia dat omnibus, nec ipse indiget nostris donis, hominum manibus non colitur. At Deus talis. Ergo, &c. Hinc colligit inanem esse cultum, qui in sacrificijs & alijs externis rebus constitit.
units.tr: II. God is not worshipped by human hands. He proves this because he himself gives life and breath to each person, and needs nothing from anyone. The argument runs thus: he who gives all things to all, and does not himself need our gifts, is not worshipped by human hands. But God is such. Therefore, etc. From this he concludes that the worship which consists in sacrifices and other external things is empty.

units.la: Not. §1. Inanem esse sacrificiorum fiduciam. Idem docemur, Psal.50. Isa.1.66. Eodem argumento tota papistica religio damnatur, quae tota constat externis ritibus. Hac decepti homines, egentibus à Christo commendatis, subtrahunt sua officia, & illa non egentibus Diuis offerunt, qui norunt nos, Isa.63. &c. Quid quod simulachris maxima pars cedit, sensu quoque carentibus? Psal.115. & 135. Et sacrificiis luxu & libidine diffluentibus? Imo supplantur Christi membra, vt iis omnia suppetant.
units.tr: Note § 1. That trust in sacrifices is empty. The same is taught in Ps. 50; Isa. 1; 66. By the same argument the whole papistical religion is condemned, since it consists entirely of external rites. Deceived by these, men withhold their duties from Christ, who is commended to us as one in need, and offer them instead to the saints, who need nothing and "know us not" (Isa. 63, etc.). What of the fact that the greater part give themselves to images, which also lack sense (Ps. 115; 135), and to sacrifices that overflow with luxury and lust? Indeed, the members of Christ are trampled down so that everything may be supplied to them.

units.la: § 2. Cur ergo sacrificia olim instituta? Duplicia fuerunt. A. Expiatoria. Non quod quòd his satis fieret pro peccatis, Heb.10. Sed typi erant Christi. Vide 1 Cor 5 Ioh. 1. Deinde docebant mactare pecuinos affectus, &c. Psa. 51. B. Gratulatoria erat pro acceptis beneficijs. Nos expiatorium nullum habemus extra Christum, Heb. 8. 9. 10. 1. Ioh. 1. Apoc. 13. In hoc vetera impleta & abolita, Ioh. 19.
units.tr: § 2. Why, then, were sacrifices instituted of old? They were of two kinds. A. Expiatory. Not because enough was thereby done for sins (Heb. 10), but they were types of Christ (see 1 Cor. 5; John 1). Further, they taught the slaying of the sheep of the passions (Ps. 51). B. Thank-offerings were made for benefits received. We have no expiatory sacrifice outside Christ (Heb. 8; 9; 10; 1 John 1; Rev. 13). In him the old things are fulfilled and abolished (John 19).

units.la: In terim offeramus nosipsos & contrita corda, Rom. 12. Psal. 51. Preces item & erga pauperes beneficentiam, Heb. 13. In his religio versatur. Oremus.
units.tr: Meanwhile let us offer ourselves and contrite hearts (Rom. 12; Ps. 51), likewise prayers and beneficence towards the poor (Heb. 13). In these religion consists. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIII.
units.tr: Homily 143.

units.la: 26 Fecit Deus ex uno sanguine omne genus hominum, ut habitarent per universam superficiem terrae, definiuitq; statuta tempora & terminos habitationis eorum.
units.tr: 26 And he made from one blood every nation of men, so that they might dwell over the whole face of the earth, and he fixed the appointed times and the boundaries of their habitation.

units.la: 27 Ut quaerent Deum, si forte palpando eum invenirent: quanquam profecto non longe abest ab unoquoque nostrum.
units.tr: 27 That they should seek God, if perhaps they might feel after him and find him, though he is indeed not far from any one of us.

units.la: 28 Per ipsum enim vivimus, & movemur, & sumus: sicut & quidam vestratium poetarum dixerunt, Nam huius progenies etiam sumus.
units.tr: 28 For in him we live, and move, and have our being, as some of your own poets have also said: For we are also his offspring.

units.la: 29 Progenies ergo Dei cum simus, non debemus existimare auro aut argento aut lapidi, sculptili artificij aut commentationis hominum numen esse simile.
units.tr: 29 Since then we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like gold or silver or stone, an image carved by human craft and invention.

units.la: Diuus Paulus concione sua, quam in Ariopago habuit, in hoc vnum incumbit, vt Athenien. ab idololatria advocari Dei cultum reuocet per Christum. Id vero fieri non poterat, nisi confutatis eroribus, quibus illi tenebantur. Exillis ergo praecipuos deligit, quos impugnet. Et primo quidem templorum religio e con futat argumentis sumptis ex 1 Regum 8. Isa. 66. Ierem. 23. Deinde sacrificiorum fiduciam euertit, docens his Deum non indigere, Psal. 50. Seruiunt eadem hodie. In praesenti vero caput impietatis impugnat, falsos nimirum Deos & simulachra, aduersus quae magno serio disserit, ostendens plus quam belluinum stuporem esse, quo Dei gloriam in miseros homines transferant, & eundem simulachris fingi & coli posse credant. Producit ergo quic quid amplificationi seruire potest, hoc ordine:
units.tr: The divine Paul, in the sermon he gave at the Areopagus, aims at this one thing: to call the Athenians back from idolatry to the worship of God through Christ. This could not happen unless the errors that held them were refuted, so from these he chooses the chief ones to attack. First he overturns the religion of temples, with arguments taken from 1 Kings 8, Isaiah 66 and Jeremiah 23. Then he overthrows confidence in sacrifices, teaching that God has no need of them, Psalm 50. The same things serve today. But now he attacks the head of impiety, namely false gods and images, against which he argues with great earnestness, showing that it is more than brutish stupidity to transfer the glory of God to miserable men, and to believe that the same God can be shaped and worshipped in images. So he brings forward whatever can serve his amplification, in this order:

units.la: I. Fecit Deus ex vno sanguine omne genus hominum. Patet hoc ex Gen 2. 4. 5. 9.
units.tr: I. God made from one blood every nation of men. This is evident from Gen. 2. 4. 5. 9.

units.la: Colligit autem duo. 1. Non debuisse illos scindi in religione, quorum vnus creator & eadem origo erat. Imo debuisse vnitati reli-
units.tr: He draws two conclusions. 1. Those whose creator was one and whose origin was the same ought not to have been divided in religion; indeed they ought to have devoted themselves to the unity of religion.

units.la: Humani generis ori de vni-us Dei cultu admo-net. religionis studete. Errabant in hoc gentes maximè. NOT. ¶ Naturæ ordinem abijs violari, qui sectas & dissensiones in religio ne inquehunt. Oblitifuæ originis creatorem negligunt. Non ergo potest leue peccatum censeri. Id vero maximè inter Christianos locum habere debebat, qui vnum Deum & vnum Saluatorem faciemur. Vide Eph.4.1.Cor.1.3.
units.tr: Admonition to the human race concerning the worship of the one God. The Gentiles erred most in this. NOTE: Those who stir up sects and dissensions in religion violate the order of nature. They forget the Creator of their origin, so it cannot be counted a light sin. This ought especially to hold among Christians, who confess one God and one Saviour. See Eph. 4. 1 Cor. 1. 3.

units.la: II. Homines non esse pro Dijs habendos, quod frequens erat inter gentes. Putabantur suos Deos omnes fuisse homines. At quomodo ex aliquibus potuerunt Dij fieri, cum eadem omnium origo sit?
units.tr: II. Men are not to be held as gods, which was common among the Gentiles. They thought all their gods had been men. But how could gods be made out of some men, when the origin of all is the same?

units.la: NOT. ¶ Hoc ipso argumento etiam Diuorum cultum cuerti, qui pro Dijs coluntur. Homines fuerunt nobis ὁμοιοπα-θεῖς, Actor 10.14. Peccatores item Isa.53.1. Reg.8. Psalm.31.51.130.143. Rom.1.3.5 Mat.6. Quicquid habent, ex gratia Dei habent per Christum, 1 Cor.4.15. Quin ergo ad hanc contendimus, iuxta ipsorum exemplum & doctrinam &c. Interim noltræ ... ginis consideratio nos modestiæ & eon sordæ admonere debet, &c.
units.tr: NOTE: By this same argument the cult of the deified dead, who are worshipped as gods, is overturned. They were men of like passions with us, Acts 10. 14. Likewise sinners, Isa. 53. 1 Kings 8. Psalms 31, 51, 130, 143. Rom. 1. 3. 5. Matt. 6. Whatever they have, they have from the grace of God through Christ, 1 Cor. 4. 15. Why then do we not strive toward this, following their example and doctrine, etc. Meanwhile, consideration of our origin ought to admonish us to modesty and sobriety, etc.

units.la: II. Deus ille homines in terra collocauit, quam ipsis inhabitandam dedit. Vide Genes.1.9.11. ex Psalmo 115. Ne quis vero Epicurææ dogma inde concluderet,
units.tr: II. That God placed those men on the earth, which he gave them to inhabit. See Gen. 1. 9. 11, and Psalm 115. Lest anyone should draw from this the doctrine of Epicurus,

units.la: Cap. 17. addit, prouidentię Dei certo decreto hoc omne factum esse, & Deum simul præfi-niuisse tempora & locos habitationis ho-minum, nec fortuito in terris res homi-num administrari. Inde vero colligere vult, ab vnius Dei prouidentia debuisse pendere gentes, non fictitijs Dijs & simu-lach. is suam salutem acceptam ferre. Con-uincit eorum deDijs tutelarib. Papatus.
units.tr: he adds in chapter 17 that all this was done by the certain decree of God's providence, and that God at the same time foreordained the times and places of human habitation, and that human affairs are not administered by chance. From this he wishes to conclude that the nations ought to depend on the providence of the one God, and not ascribe their salvation to fictitious gods and images. He refutes the Papists' doctrine of tutelary deities.

units.la: Interim Not. In Deo non præscien-tiam modo, sed prouidentiā esse, quæ om-nia administret. Iuxta huius decretum re-gna oriuntur & occidunt. Vide Dan. 2 7. Amoz 3. Eadem priuatorum quoque ho-minum conditiones compleētitur, Pf. 113. Saul, Dauid, Cyrus, &c. Imo ad minutissi-ma sese demittit, Matth. 6.10. Psalmo 147. &c.
units.tr: Meanwhile note: in God there is not only foreknowledge but providence, which governs all things. By his decree kingdoms rise and fall. See Dan. 2. 7. Amos 3. The conditions of private men too are ordered by it, Ps. 113: Saul, David, Cyrus, etc. Indeed he stoops even to the smallest things, Matt. 6. 10, Psalm 147, etc.

units.la: Seruiat hæc consolationi in aduersis. Institutioni item, ne fortuito res fore pu-temus, vt impij, Psal. 14. 94.
units.tr: This serves for consolation in adversity, and for instruction, lest we think things happen by chance, as the wicked do, Ps. 14, 94.

units.la: III. Indicat finem omnium horum: Vt Deum quærant. Est hoc ipsum agnoscere, obseruare, colere, &c. Ideo conditi homines & in terram collocati. Vide Gen. 2, 9. Inde colligit aduersus finem suæ creatio-nis peccare, adeoque incolatu terræ indi-gnos esse qui Deo neglecto, circa homi-num & simulachrorum cultu occupentur.
units.tr: III. He indicates the end of all these things: that they should seek God. This is to acknowledge, observe, worship, etc. Therefore men were created and placed on the earth. See Gen. 2. 9. From this he concludes that those who, neglecting God, occupy themselves with the worship of men and images sin against the purpose of their creation, and so are unworthy of dwelling on the earth.

units.la: NOT.¶ Corruptionem hominum, qui nihil minus faciunt, quàm quod illos face re decebat. In Deo felicitas omnis, Gen 17 Atillli opes quærunt, voluptates, mundum, &c. Et qui optimi habentur, creaturas quærunt, Ier.2. Isa.55. Omnes creaturæ officium faciunt. Solus homo secus agit, Ier.8. Isa.1.
units.tr: NOTE: The corruption of men, who do almost nothing that befits them. In God is all happiness, Gen. 17. But they seek wealth, pleasures, the world, etc. And those who are thought best seek creatures, Jer. 2, Isa. 55. All creatures do their duty; man alone acts otherwise, Jer. 8, Isa. 1.

units.la: IV. Præoccupatione ijs respondet, qui bus difficile videtur Deum inuenire. Pal- pari potest, nec procul abest, sed passim se sensibus quoq; ingerit. Vide Rom.1. Psal. 19. Imo non opus est, vt extra nos vage- mur. In nobis ipsis inuenitur. In ipso habemus Vitam, Motum, Elfentiam, Psa.22. 139. &c. Conceptio, corporis fabrica, perı-cula, animæ operationes & immortalitas, &c. Denique fumus progenies Dei, nimi rum ad imaginem illius & ad cœlestium bonorum communionem creati, &c. Id verò Arati testimonio probat, vt nagis pudefiant.
units.tr: IV. He answers the prejudice of those for whom it seems hard to find God. He can be felt for, he is not far off, but he thrusts himself on the senses everywhere. See Rom. 1, Ps. 19. Indeed there is no need for us to wander abroad; he is found in ourselves. In him we have life, motion and being, Ps. 22, 139, etc. Conception, the structure of the body, dangers, the operations of the soul and its immortality, etc. Finally, we are the offspring of God, namely created in his image and for fellowship in heavenly goods, etc. He proves this by the testimony of Aratus, so that they may be more ashamed.

units.la: NO T.¶ Inexcusabilem esse hominum cæcitatem & ignorantiam, qui ex seipsis Deos fingunt & simulachra colunt. Qui enim seipsos spectant, Deum agnoscent, Rom.1. Deplorandum ergo hominum corruptio, qui nisi per Dei gratiam restituantur, ipsis brutis animantib. inferiores sunt,
units.tr: NOTE: The blindness and ignorance of men is inexcusable, who fashion gods out of themselves and worship images. For those who look at themselves recognise God, Rom. 1. Therefore the corruption of men is to be deplored, who, unless restored by the grace of God, are inferior even to the brute beasts, Isa. 1, Jer. 8, Ps. 48. Indeed they are inferior even to the devils, James 2, etc.

units.la: Isa.1. Ier 8. Psal.48. Imo dicebolis, Iac.2. &c. Concludit: Cum nos simus genus Dei, et is imaginem suam in nobis esse voluerit, mini meputemus illum auro et argento per villam hominis artem effingi posse. Nam homo, qua tenus Dei imago est (quae in animo haeret) non potest pingi & fingi. Quanto minus Deus, qui spiritus est: Ioh 4. Isa. 40. 66. Non materia, non forma illa neque ars eum exprimet. Simulachra ergo mendacia sunt, ut quae non praestant quod polli-centur, Hab.2.
units.tr: He concludes: since we are the race of God, and he has willed his image to be in us, we should not think that he can be fashioned out of gold and silver by human art. For man, insofar as he is the image of God (which dwells in the mind), cannot be painted or moulded. How much less God, who is spirit: John 4, Isa. 40, 66. Neither matter, nor form, nor art will express him. Images, therefore, are lies, since they do not deliver what they promise, Hab. 2.

units.la: NOT. Atrociorem iniuriam non posse fieri Deo, quam cum simulachris fingitur. Veritas eius commutatur mendacio, Rom.1. adeoque diabolus fingitur, Ioh. 8. Illi fit, quod homo non ferret. Laftan. Hinc illa, Exod.20 Deut 4. Isa.40. 41. 44. Psal. 115. 135. &c. Oremus.
units.tr: NOTE: No more outrageous injury can be done to God than when he is fashioned in images. His truth is exchanged for a lie, Rom. 1, and so the devil is depicted, John 8. What a man would not endure is done to God. Lactantius. Hence that law: Exod. 20, Deut. 4, Isa. 40, 41, 44, Ps. 115, 135, etc. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXLIII.

units.la: 30 Temporibus gitur istius ignorantiae dissimulatis, Deus nunc denuntiat omnibus ubique hominibus ut resipiscant.
units.tr: 30 Therefore, with the times of this ignorance overlooked, God now commands all people everywhere to repent.

units.la: 31 Eo quod statuit diem quo iuste iudicaturus est orbem terrarum, per eum virum quem definit, fide palam fasta omnibus, illo à mortuis excitato.
units.tr: 31 Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, through the man whom he has appointed, having given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead.

units.la: 32 Quum audissent autem resurrectionem mortuorum, alii quidem cauil labantur: alii vero dicebant, Audiemus te rursum de hac re.
units.tr: 32 When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said, "We will hear you again about this matter."

units.la: 33 Et ita Paulus exiuit e medio eorum.
units.tr: 33 And so Paul went out from among them.

units.la: 34 Quidam vero adjuncti crediderunt: in quibus & Dionysius Areopagita, & mulier nomine Damaris, et alii cum eis.
units.tr: 34 But some joined him and believed, among whom were Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

units.la: Diuus Paulus de vero Deo & eius cultu ita disseruit in praecedentibus, vt simul gentium errores diligentissime confutarit. Docuit enim, Deum nec templis includi, nec sacrificijs coli. Imprimis vero simulachra & fictitios Deos impugnauit, docens naturae ordinem ab ijs violari, nec sui finis & dignitatis memores esse, qui neglecto vero Deo iustis occupentur. Sequitur victima pars, qua ad poenitentiam hortatur per Christum, nimirum vt à paganismo resipiscant, & ad veri Dei cultum conuertantur. Quo loco maximè vrget extremi iudicij mentione, propter Epicureos nimirum, qui omnia contemnebant. Ordo hic est:
units.tr: Blessed Paul, in what goes before, discussed the true God and his worship in such a way that he also most carefully refuted the errors of the Gentiles. For he taught that God is not confined to temples nor worshipped with sacrifices. Above all he attacked images and fictitious gods, showing that the order of nature is violated by them, and that those who neglect the true God and occupy themselves with such things forget their own end and dignity. There follows the final part, in which he urges repentance through Christ, namely that they should turn from paganism and be converted to the worship of the true God. In this place he presses especially the mention of the last judgment, chiefly on account of the Epicureans, who despised everything. The order is this:

units.la: I. Praeoccupatione quaestionib. respondet, quae obijci solent, quando veritas
units.tr: I. He anticipates the questions that are usually raised when the truth

units.la: prædicatur: Num hucusque errârint tot sapientes? Cur Deus tot seculis mundum seduci passus sit? Respondet: Deus dissimulauit hucusque, non quod placerent illa, sed quia sic ipsi visum fuit. Nec potuit non errare mundus, quoad dissimulauit Deus, eo quòd per se in diuinis non sapit, 2. Cor. 3. 1. Cor. 2. Nunc autem annuntiat omnibus, vt resipiscant, &c.
units.tr: is preached: Have so many wise men gone astray up to now? Why has God allowed the world to be led astray for so many ages? He answers: God has overlooked these things until now, not because they pleased him, but because so it seemed good to him. Nor could the world help going astray, for as long as God overlooked it, since in divine matters it is not wise by itself (2 Cor. 3; 1 Cor. 2). But now he announces to all that they should repent, etc.

units.la: Not. 1. Quòd simpliciter Dei beneplacitu allegat, non curiosè de causis diuinis putat. Imitandum nobis. Certum nobis sit, Deum iustè & rectè omnia agere, & ne mini ab illo iniuriam fieri, licet id non sen per à nobis intelligatur. Cogitemus esse mysterium à seculo abfconditu, Matthæi 13. Rom. 16. Obedientiæ fidei ergo studeamus, & voluntati Dei subijciamur, 2. Cor. 10. Rom 9. 11. Mat. 6.
units.tr: Note 1. That he simply appeals to God's good pleasure, and does not inquire curiously into the divine causes, is to be imitated by us. Let us be certain that God acts justly and rightly in all things, and that no injustice is done to us by him, even though we do not understand this as we ought. Let us consider that it is a mystery hidden from the ages (Matt. 13; Rom. 16). Let us therefore strive for the obedience of faith and submit ourselves to the will of God (2 Cor. 10; Rom. 9, 11; Matt. 6).

units.la: 11. Finem Euangelij esse, vt homines resipiscant, nimirū aberroribus & vitijs. Ergo non sufficit audiuisse, &c. Hinc illa, Matth. 3. 4. 10. Mar. 1. Luc. 24. Act. 2. 3. Sunt ergo falsi Euangelici, qui in pristinis erroribus & sceleribus manent. Similes ægroti, &c.
units.tr: II. The aim of the gospel is that people repent, namely of their errors and vices. Therefore it is not enough to have heard, etc. Hence those passages: Matt. 3, 4, 10; Mark 1; Luke 24; Acts 2, 3. There are therefore false evangelicals, who remain in their former errors and wickednesses. They are like sick people, etc.

units.la: Interim patet, neminem excusari prioris seculi & patrum ignorantia. Dissimulauit hanc iusto iudicio Deus. At quando veritatem tatem reuelat, certum est illum posthac nolle dissimulare. Audiendus ergo, &c, Pfal.95.Heb.10.12.&c. Qui non obediunt ij oblatam gratiam contemnunt. Arguuntur qui sub titulo Maiorum Euangelium persequuntur.
units.tr: Meanwhile it is clear that no one is excused by the ignorance of the earlier age and of the Fathers. God has overlooked this by a just judgment. But when he reveals the truth, it is certain that he will not wish to overlook it from now on. Therefore one must listen, etc. (Ps. 95; Heb. 10, 12, etc.). Those who do not obey despise the grace offered. They are condemned who pursue the gospel under the title of their forefathers.

units.la: II. Causam allegat,cur nunc ista annun ciet Deus. Quia diem statuit, quo iudicaturus est orbem, &c. Respicit ad veterem morem Dei, qui poenas non exigit, nisi premo nitis prius hominibus, Amos 3. Ante diluuium, Gen.6. Sodomae, Gene.13 14.18.19. Aegyptus, Gen.41.Exod.5.6.7. &c. Iudaei, 2.Par.36.Mat.11.23.24.Luc.19. Sed extremi iudicij rationem propter Epicuraeos.
units.tr: III. He gives the reason why God now announces these things: "Because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world," etc. He looks back to the old custom of God, who does not exact punishments unless he has first admonished people (Amos 3). Before the flood (Gen. 6); Sodom (Gen. 13, 14, 18, 19); Egypt (Gen. 41; Exod. 5, 6, 7, etc.); the Jews (2 Chron. 36; Matt. 11:23-24; Luke 19). But the account of the last judgment is given on account of the Epicureans.

units.la: NOTA. ¶ 1. Statuit Deus diem iudicij. Omnino igitur erit, vtut mundus neget, 2.Pet.2.Vide Dan.12.Ioh 5.Matt.16.24 25. 2.Cor.5.Rom.14.2.Tim.4.Imo necesse est illud esse, alioqui iustitia Dei non consistere. ¶ 2. Quis iudicabitur? Orbis terrarum. Viui & mortui. Nemo igitur subterfugiet, Rom.14 2.Cor.5. Matth.25. Non erit συνπολιτεία, Eph.6. DEBET hoc magnates modestiae & officij admonere.
units.tr: NOTE. ¶ 1. God has appointed a day of judgment. Therefore it will certainly come, however much the world denies it (2 Pet. 2; see Dan. 12; John 5; Matt. 16:24-25; 2 Cor. 5; Rom. 14; 2 Tim. 4). Indeed it must be so, otherwise the justice of God would not stand. ¶ 2. Who will be judged? "The world." The living and the dead. No one therefore will escape (Rom. 14; 2 Cor. 5; Matt. 25). There will be no fellow-citizenship [συνπολιτεία] (Eph. 6). This ought to remind great men of modesty and duty.
