units.la: 32 Qui eo ipso momento acceptis militibus ac centurionibus, &c.
units.tr: 32 He at once took soldiers and centurions, etc.

units.la: QVoniâ Diuinus Paulus apud Hierosolymitanam Ecclesiam pessimè audiebat, quasi legem simpliciter vt malam & noxiam damnaret, Seniores vt se omni suspicione liberet, consulunt. Vbi probandum quidem, quòd tanti viri famę consultum voluntsed improbandū, quòd eiusmodi consilium dant, quod cum inge nua fidei & Christianæ libertatis confessione pugnabat. Hæc enim legis ceremonias per Christum abrogatas esse docet, &c. Heb. 8. 9. 10. Et proinde in cultu quoque nullum harum vsum esse, cum initiò non institutę essent cultus ergo, If.1.Ps.50. Proponitur autem exemplum hoc, vt cari nis prudentiam in religione semper suspe stam habeamus, &c. Sequitur consilij huius exitus, qui diligenter describitur.
units.tr: Since the godly Paul was very badly regarded by the Church at Jerusalem, as if he condemned the law outright as evil and harmful, the elders advised him to clear himself of all suspicion. Here we must approve that such a great man consulted for the sake of his reputation, but disapprove that they gave such advice, which conflicted with the frankness of faith and the confession of Christian liberty. For this teaches that the ceremonies of the law were abrogated through Christ, etc. (Heb. 8, 9, 10). And therefore there is no use of them even in worship, since they were not instituted for worship at the beginning (Isa. 1; Ps. 50). This example is set before us so that we may always be suspicious of the prudence of the flesh in religion, etc. There follows the outcome of this counsel, which is described carefully.

units.la: I. Obtemperat Paulus, qui hactenus ne in minimis quidem cesserat, & qui maiorem habuisset cum ipsis expostulandi oc casionem. Sed vult aliquid illis dare, ne vi deatur contumax, & vt sibi apud illos docendi viam paret. Ingreditur ergo templum. Annuntiat purificationem publicè. Curat vt pro singulis sacrificetur. Manifestus error. Cur non facit, quod ad Gal. 2. Saltem offendiculum timuisset, &c.
units.tr: I. Paul complies, though until now he had not yielded even in the smallest things, and he had had a greater opportunity to argue with them. But he wishes to give them something, lest he seem stubborn, and so that he might prepare a way for teaching among them. So he enters the temple. He publicly announces the purification. He sees that sacrifices are offered for each one. This is a clear error. Why did he not do what he did at Galatians 2? At least he should have feared giving offence, etc.

units.la: ¶ Sed Nota. ¶ Quantum noceat nimia facilitas in religione, maxime si carnis prudentiam adhibeas. Recedit à solita sim plicitate Paulus. Offendiculi causam præbet. Et apud Iudæos nihil proficit. Sic multi ministri hodie peccant, dum omnibus commodi videri volunt. Sed frustrà. Nec enim vllis rebus mouentur, quos ꝛ̄ mouet verbi diuini authoritas.
units.tr: But note: how much excessive ease in religion harms, especially if you apply the prudence of the flesh. Paul departs from his usual simplicity. He gives a cause of offence, and among the Jews he gains nothing. So many ministers sin today, while they wish to seem agreeable to everyone. But in vain, for those whom the authority of the divine Word moves are not moved by any other things.

units.la: Cogitemus causam hanc Dei esse, non nostri iuris. Domini ergo verbum vnicè sectemur, Deut. 4 12. Num. 15. In indiffe-rentibus moderationes eiusmodi locum habent, 1. Cor. 9. &c.
units.tr: Let us consider that this cause is God's, not ours to dispose of. Let us therefore follow the Word of the Lord alone (Deut. 4:12; Num. 15). In matters indifferent such moderations have their place (1 Cor. 9, etc.).

units.la: II. Euentus & finis huius consilij indicatur, qui fuit infelicissimus. Videtur initio succedere res. Sed capitur Paulus, ac praesens vitae discrimen subit, vt nun-quam aliàs.
units.tr: II. The outcome and end of this counsel is indicated, and it was most unhappy. At first the matter seems to succeed. But Paul is seized, and he faces present peril of life, as never before.

units.la: Sed singula ordine suo No T. ¶ 1. Auctores Iudaei qui ab Asia venerunt. Illi ipsi, qui Paulum vbique insecuti fuerant, vt vi-dimus Act.13.14. 17.18. Apparet incurabilis peruicacia gentis, quae merito punita, 1.Thess 2.
units.tr: But let us consider each point in its order. 1. The authors were Jews who came from Asia. These are the very ones who had pursued Paul everywhere, as we saw in Acts 13, 14, 17, 18. The stubbornness of this people is evidently incurable, and it was rightly punished (1 Thess. 2).

units.la: Interim vides quàm laboriosos & auda-ces reddat veritatis odium. Insequuntur vbiq; In aliena vrbe audent tantum facinus,&c Hodie multi similes.
units.tr: Meanwhile you see how laborious and bold the hatred of the truth makes people. They pursue everywhere. In a foreign city they dare such a crime, etc. Today there are many like them.

units.la: ¶ 2. Conturbant totum populum, & quasi ad commune incendium restinguendum excitant. Quid verò opus erat auxilio? Hastenus certè nullas turbas Paulus dederat, nec vim parabat.
units.tr: 2. They stir up the whole people and rouse them as if to put out a common fire. But why was there any need for help? Certainly until now Paul had caused no disturbances, nor was he preparing violence.

units.la: Vides qui seditionum authores sint. Impingitur hocferè ministris verbi, vt etiam Exod.5.1.Reg.18.Amos 7. At reuera tales sunt hostes verbi, qui veritatis lucem non ferunt, Ioh 3. Exempla habuimus Act 14. 16.17.18.19. &c.
units.tr: You see who are the authors of sedition. This charge is commonly laid against ministers of the Word, as also in Exod. 5:1; 1 Kings 18; Amos 7. But in truth such are the enemies of the Word who cannot bear the light of truth (John 3). We have had examples in Acts 14, 16, 17, 18, 19, etc.

units.la: ¶ 3. Accusant trium capitum. A Quod aduersus populum Dei doceat: Nimirum quòd gentes aequaret Iudaeis, & de spiri-tuali Israele loqueretur, vt Iudaeorum fi-duciam reprimeret,Ioh.8 Roman.2.9. B. Quòd legem impiè contemnat. Calumniantur Pauli de lege doctrinam, in primis quòd sacra abrogata doceret,Rom 7. 1.Cor.15.Gal.3.4.5.&c.C.Quod templum prophanet. Id probant, Quia incircumcisum introduxerit. Atqui hoc falsum erat, & calumnia est fusp icione nuda nitens.
units.tr: 3. They accuse him on three counts. A. That he teaches against the people of God, namely, that he made the Gentiles equal to the Jews and spoke of a spiritual Israel, in order to check the confidence of the Jews (John 8; Rom. 2, 9). B. That he impiously despises the law. They slander Paul's teaching about the law, especially that he taught that the sacred things were abrogated (Rom. 7; 1 Cor. 15; Gal. 3, 4, 5, etc.). C. That he profanes the temple. They prove this because he had brought an uncircumcised man in. Yet this was false, and the calumny rests on bare suspicion.

units.la: Discimus hic: 1.Quorum fere accusentur veritatis ministri.Sic Prophetae,Ieremias,Amos. Sic Stephanus, Act.6. Ipse Christus,Luc.23.Ioh.18.Sic hodie fit. Et hæc veritatis fors est,vt nusquam plus possit calumnia.Quia omnes eam oderunt,& praeiudicio occupati,quiduis credunt.Totam ciuitatem hac isti turbat. Vulnerat & incendit,Pf.57.58.140 Iac.3.Hinc illa praecatio Dauidis,Psal.120.&c.
units.tr: Here we learn: 1. By whom the ministers of truth are generally accused. So the prophets Jeremiah and Amos were accused, so Stephen (Acts 6), and Christ himself (Luke 23; John 18). So it happens today. And this is perhaps the lot of the truth, that slander is never more powerful, because all hate it, and, occupied with prejudice, they believe whatever is said. These men throw the whole city into confusion by this. They wound and set on fire (Ps. 57, 58, 140; James 3). Hence that prayer of David (Ps. 120, etc.).

units.la: ¶4. Trahunt e templo,percutiunt,occlusis templi foribus, volunt occidere. Vide quousque procedat impietas. Latet aliquando, sed data occasione erumpit. Sanguinem sitit, & facillime excitantur ad malu, qui in bono sunt difficillimi. Simul vero habemus fucatae sanctimoniae exemplum. Sanguine templum nolunt polluere,cum seipsos polluere non vereantur. Vide similia,Ioh.18.Matth.27.Hoc illud est quod illis Christus exprobrat,Matth.23.Luc.11. &c. Non multo post templum euersum, & tota gens dispersa.
units.tr: 4. They drag him out of the temple, strike him, shut the doors of the temple, and wish to kill him. See how far impiety proceeds. Sometimes it lies hidden, but when an occasion is given it breaks out. It thirsts for blood, and those who are most difficult to move to good are most easily stirred to evil. At the same time we have here an example of pretended holiness. They do not want to defile the temple with blood, though they are not ashamed to defile themselves. See similar things in John 18 and Matt. 27. This is what Christ rebukes them for (Matt. 23; Luke 11, etc.). Not long after, the temple was overthrown and the whole nation dispersed.

units.la: III. Quando iam actum videbatur,subitò liberator aduolat,&c.
units.tr: III. When the matter seemed already done, suddenly a deliverer flies in, etc.

units.la: bunus Paulum sua authoritate affert. Est hoc Magistratus officium, Rom.13. Pec-cant grauissimè, qui quiduis permittunt, aut etiam ipsi opprimunt. Vide Psalm.72, 82 &c.
units.tr: The tribune brings Paul under his own authority. This is the office of the magistrate (Rom. 13). They sin most gravely who permit anything whatever, or even themselves oppress. See Ps. 72, 82, etc.

units.la: Interim obserua fidem Dei & curam paternam, quàsuis nunquam deest, licet nos aliquando deseruisse videatur. Et facilè per quosuis liberare potest. Hic per Ethnicum liberat, vt Ieremiam olim per Nabazardam, Ierc.38.40. Possent huius generis exempla nostro seculo recenseri. Nemo igitur desperet, neque ad media illicita confugiat. Exspectet manum Domini.
units.tr: Meanwhile observe the faithfulness of God and his fatherly care, which never fails, though it may sometimes seem that we have been forsaken. And he can easily deliver through whomever he pleases. Here he delivers through a Gentile, as once he delivered Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan (Jer. 38, 40). Examples of this kind could be recounted in our own age. Therefore let no one despair, nor flee to unlawful means. Let him wait for the hand of the Lord.

units.la: ¶2. Illi conspecto tribuno, Paulum per cutere desinunt. Maiori ergo hominum, quàm Dei metu & reuerentia tanguntur. Est hoc proprium impijs, Psal.14 53. Ideo magistratu opus est, Rom.13. Contra Anabaptistas. Oremus.
units.tr: 2. When they saw the tribune, they stopped beating Paul. They are therefore moved more by fear of men than by fear and reverence of God. This is characteristic of the impious (Ps. 14, 53). Therefore there is need of the magistrate (Rom. 13). Against the Anabaptists. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXI.

units.la: 33 Tunc appropinquans Tribunus prehendit eum, & iussit vinciri catenis duabus, & percontatus est, quis nam essent, & quid fecisset.
units.tr: 33 Then the tribune came up, seized him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.

units.la: 34 Alij autem aliud clamabant in turba. turba, & quum non posset certi quic-quam cognoscere propter tumultum, iussit duci in castra.
units.tr: 34 Others, however, shouted different things in the crowd. Since he could not learn anything certain because of the tumult, he ordered that Paul be taken into the barracks.

units.la: 35 Quum igitur peruenijset ad gra-dus, euenit, vt portaretur à militibus, propter violentiam turbæ.
units.tr: 35 When Paul came to the steps, it happened that he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd.

units.la: 36 Sequebatur enim multitudo po-puli, clamans: Tolle eum.
units.tr: 36 For the multitude of the people followed, shouting: Away with him!

units.la: 37 Et quum iam introducendus ef-set in castra Paulus, dicit Tribuno, Li-cet ne mihi aliquid tibi dicere? Qui di-cit, Græcè nosti?
units.tr: 37 As Paul was about to be taken into the barracks, he said to the tribune: May I say something to you? He replied: Do you know Greek?

units.la: 38 Nonne tu es Aegyptius ille, qui ante hos dies ad seditionem concitasti, & eduxisti in desertum quatuor millia sicariorum?
units.tr: 38 Are you not that Egyptian who, a few days ago, stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins out into the desert?

units.la: 39 Dixit autem Paulus, Ego qui-dem sum Iudæus, Tarsensis, non obscu-ræ Cilicum vrbis ciuis: cæterum rogo te, permitte mihi, vt alloquar popu-lum.
units.tr: 39 But Paul said: I am indeed a Jew, from Tarsus, a citizen of no obscure city of Cilicia. But I ask you, permit me to address the people.

units.la: 40 Quum igitur ille permisisset, Paulus stans in gradibus, manu silen-tium postulauit à plebe, & magno silen-tio facto, loquutus est lingua Hebræa, dicens:
units.tr: 40 When he had granted this, Paul stood on the steps, motioned with his hand for the people to be silent, and when there was great silence, he spoke in the Hebrew tongue, saying:

units.la: DAuid Rex & Propheta ait: Multæ sunt tribulationes iustorum, sed ex omnibus eripit illos Dominus,Pfalm. 34. Consentiunt his quæ habentur Pfal. 94. 1.Cor.10.2.Cor.1.Exemplum horun euidentisimum in præsenti historia propo-nitur. Audiuimus enim Paulum à Iudæis captum fuisse, qui è templo extra stim oc-cidere voluerunt. Repente vero cum ne-mo piorum iuuare queat, per tribunum & milites liberatur, qui ab omni religione alienisimi erant.Fit quod est Apoc.12. &c.Seruiat consolationi.Simul ossi-cij admonentur magistratus:singuli item in necessitatibus fratrum.Sed videamus reliqua.
units.tr: DAVID the king and prophet says: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers them out of them all (Psalm 34). These words agree with what is found in Psalm 94, 1 Cor. 10, and 2 Cor. 1. In the present story we have a most evident example of this. For we have heard that Paul was seized by the Jews, who wanted to kill him at once outside the temple. Yet suddenly, when none of the godly could help, he is set free by the tribune and the soldiers, who were most alien to all religion. Thus what is written in Revelation 12 comes to pass, etc. Let this serve for comfort. At the same time, magistrates are reminded of their duty, and individuals likewise of the needs of the brethren. But let us look at the rest.

units.la: I.Quid Tribunus fecerit? Primum vinciri iubet,tum quod putaret noxium,tum quod seditionem ita demum sedari posse videret. Deinde interrogat quis sit, & quid fecerit.
units.tr: I. What did the tribune do? First he orders him to be bound, partly because he thought him guilty, and partly because he saw that the sedition could be quieted only in this way. Then he asks who he is and what he has done.

units.la: NOT.¶1. Quod præsenti periculo qui dem eripitur Paulus,sed ita vt catenis vinciatur. Poterat omnino afferere Deus. Sed nouerat hoc & Paulo salutarius & ad propagandam gloriam suam vtilius fore. Ita ferè temperare solet liberationis beneficia, maximè cum nobis etiam nō rit capi stro opus esse,Heb.12. Exempla in Dauide, liberatione Ægyptiaca & Babylonica. Discimus patienter ferre ipsius voluntate & iudicia. Nec enim aduersa nos ipsius prouidentiâ eximunt. In morbis & mortis periculo hoc cogitandum,Rom.8.
units.tr: NOTE ¶1. Paul is indeed rescued from the present danger, but in such a way that he is bound with chains. God could certainly have set him entirely free. But he knew that this was more salutary for Paul and more useful for spreading his glory. God usually tempers the benefits of deliverance in this way, especially since we too need chastisement (Heb. 12). Examples are found in David, and in the deliverances from Egypt and from Babylon. We learn to bear patiently what comes by his will and judgment. For his providence does not free us from adversities. In sicknesses and in danger of death we must keep this in mind (Rom. 8).

units.la: ¶ 2.Non vulgi instar insanit Tribunus, sed inquisitionem diligenteinstituit. Est hoc magistratus,nil temerè aut ex affectu facere. Quia nullus excusationi locus est, si læsus sit qui defendi debebat,Deut 1.
units.tr: ¶2. The tribune does not rage like the mob, but conducts a careful inquiry. It is the mark of a magistrate to do nothing rashly or out of passion, because there is no excuse if the one who ought to have been defended has been harmed (Deut. 1).

units.la: II. Quid populus? Primùm vociferatur, & sic quidem vt nihil possit intelligi, quod proprium est seditionibus,Acto 19. Deinde cùm illum in castra iussisset abduci tribunus,vt illic commodiùs res cognosci posset, sequuntur & ea importunitate agunt, vt milites Paulum gestare cogantur. Tandem in hoc omnes consentiunt, quòd ad necem poscunt.
units.tr: II. What did the people do? First they shout, and in such a way that nothing can be understood, which is typical of seditions (Acts 19). Then, when the tribune had ordered him to be led away into the barracks, so that the matter could be examined more conveniently there, they follow with such importunity that the soldiers are forced to carry Paul. Finally, they all agree on this, that they demand his death.

units.la: NOT. ¶1. Nullos veritatis hostes graviores esse quàm hypocritas, qui pietatis zelum crudelitati prætexunt. A. Indicta casa volunt occidere, quem Tribunus liberat, vt causa veriùs cognosci possit. B. Tribunus sedato animo interrogat:Illi cla moribus confusis omnia interturbant, &c. C.Adducţum improbè conculcant, quem milites gestant, ne quid mali patiatur. Præterea veritatem quærente Tribunalo, nihil quàm mortis sententiam oggan- niunt. Ita coram Pilato factum ex Sacerdotum instinctu,Ioh.18.19.Imò Hero. des & Pilatus æquiores fuerunt sacerdo-tibus, Luc.22. Et in cruce pendente Chri-sto, milites ijsdem religiosiores sunt, Mat.27. Hodie non desunt exempla eorum, qui Turcas æquiores iudices senserè.
units.tr: NOTE ¶1. There are no greater enemies of the truth than hypocrites, who put on the pretext of zeal for piety in order to practise cruelty. A. They want to kill without a hearing the man whom the tribune frees, so that the cause may be more truly known. B. The tribune, with a calm mind, questions him; they, with their morals in confusion, throw everything into turmoil, etc. C. They trample shamefully on the man who is carried, while the soldiers carry him so that he may suffer no harm. Moreover, while the tribunal seeks the truth, they strive for nothing but a sentence of death. So it was done before Pilate at the instigation of the priests (John 18, 19). Indeed Herod and Pilate were fairer than the priests (Luke 22). And while Christ hung on the cross, the soldiers were more scrupulous than they (Matt. 27). Today there is no lack of examples of those who have found the Turks to be fairer judges.

units.la: ¶ 1. Non excusari eos, qui fidelibus Christi iniuriá faciunt sub zeli & pietatis prætextu, quod ipse prædixit fore, Ioh.16. Fecit idem Paulus, Act.9. Audi verò quid de se dicat, 1.Tim.1. Eadem est omnis zeli ratio. Scientia illum gubernari & regi oportet, Rom.13.Num.15.1.Sam.15.
units.tr: ¶1. Those who do injury to the faithful of Christ under the pretext of zeal and piety are not excused, as he himself foretold (John 16). Paul did the same (Acts 9). But hear what he says about himself (1 Tim. 1). The whole reasoning of zeal is the same. It must be governed and ruled by knowledge (Rom. 13; Num. 15; 1 Sam. 15).

units.la: III. Quid Paulus? Excusationem medi-tatur in tanto populi furore, tum quod suæ gentis studio tenebatur, Rom.6.10. tum quod non vult causam Christi sufpe-ctam fieri, cuius minister erat. Imitandu.
units.tr: III. What did Paul do? Amid such great fury of the people, he thinks about an excuse: partly because he was held by zeal for his own nation (Rom. 9, 10), and partly because he does not want the cause of Christ, whose minister he was, to be suspected. To be imitated.

units.la: Sed singula Not. ¶ 1. Honorificè di-cendi copiam petit à Tribuno. Non con-temnit, quia miles: sed veneratur, quia ma-gistratus, Rom.13.1.Pet.2. Arguuntur tum Pontifices, qui magistratus proculcant (2. Pet.2.) tum Anabaptistæ, qui omnes sim-pliciter, ut impios solent damnare, &c.
units.tr: But take each point separately. NOTE ¶1. He asks the tribune for the opportunity to speak in an honourable manner. He does not despise him because he is a soldier, but reveres him because he is a magistrate (Rom. 13:1; 1 Pet. 2). Here the Pontiffs are rebuked, who trample on magistrates (2 Pet. 2), and the Anabaptists, who are accustomed to condemn all people indiscriminately, as they do the wicked, etc.

units.la: ¶ 2. Tribunus amicè respondet, quam-uis latronem arbitretur. Vide Iof. de bel. Iud. lib.2. cap.12. Ita implebatur illud Christi, Ioh.5. Matt.24. Vides quantis crimini-bus Deus suos patiatur suspectos fieri. Sic cum Christo astum, Luc.23. Ioh.19. Idem illorum memoriam asserit, Ps.34. &c.
units.tr: ¶2. The tribune answers kindly, although he thinks him a robber. See Josephus, On the Jewish War, book 2, chapter 12. Thus that saying of Christ was fulfilled (John 5; Matt. 24). You see with what accusations God allows his people to be made suspect. So it happened with Christ (Luke 23; John 19). The same thing vindicates their memory (Psalm 34), etc.

units.la: ¶ 3. Paulus non excandescit indigna quæstione, sed modestè quis sit indicat, nobis in exemplum. Ita verò dicendi copiam impetrat à Tribuno, in quo humani tas hæc, magnæ æquitatis argumentum est. Confer cum hoc nostri seculi tyrannos, imò monachos, qui linguas erui curant Christi Martyribus. Sentient olim. Docemur amicè agendum esse cum captiuis. Finis vir ¢ilorum est, ne amplius noceant, & vt aliis exemplo sint. Hoc si fiat, inhumanum est, vlterius grassari & sæuire.
units.tr: ¶3. Paul does not flare up at the unworthy question, but modestly indicates who he is, as an example for us. And he obtains the opportunity to speak from the tribune, and in this humanity is a proof of great fairness. Compare with this the tyrants of our own age, indeed the monks, who take care to have the tongues of Christ's martyrs torn out. They will feel it one day. We are taught that we must deal kindly with captives. The end of punishment is that they may no longer do harm and may be an example to others. If this is done, it is inhuman to rage and rage further.

units.la: ¶ 4. Paulus manu annuens apud populum quoq; silentium impetrat, & orationem instituit fortem & accuratá. Mirum hoc illum potuisse, & populum tacuisse.
units.tr: ¶4. Paul, nodding with his hand, also obtains silence from the people, and begins a speech that is strong and carefully prepared. It is remarkable that he could do this, and that the people kept silent.

units.la: Elucet autem hîc cum potentia Dei, tum fides & veritas promissionum Christi. Vide Matt. 10. Mar. 13. Quid ergo desperemus? Oremus.
units.tr: In this passage there shines forth both the power of God and the faithfulness and truth of Christ's promises (see Matt. 10; Mark 13). Why then should we despair? Let us pray.

units.la: CAPUT XXII. HOMILIA CLXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII. HOMILY CLXXII.

units.la: VIRi fratres et patres, audite meam, qua nunc apud vos vtor, excusationem.
units.tr: Men, brothers and fathers, hear the apology I now make to you.

units.la: 2 ( Quum audissent autem eum Hebraea lingua ipsos alioqui magis praebuerunt silentium: & dixit.)
units.tr: 2 (When they heard him speak in the Hebrew tongue, they gave him all the more silence; and he said.)

units.la: 3 Ego quidem sum Iudaeus, natus Tarsi, vrbe Ciliciae: nutritus vero in hac ipsa vrbe ad pedes Gamalielis, institutus ad exquisitam formam patriae legis: zelo Dei accensus, sicut et vos omnes estis hodie.
units.tr: 3 I am indeed a Jew, born at Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, but brought up in this very city at the feet of Gamaliel, and trained in the strict manner of our fathers' law, zealous for God, as you all are today.

units.la: 4 Qui hoc vitae genus persecutus sum vsque ad mortem, vinciens ac tradens in carcerem tum viros tum mulieres.
units.tr: 4 I persecuted this way of life even to death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women.

units.la: 5 Vt et Pontifex maximus mihi testis est, et totus Seniorum ordo, a quibus etiam epistolis ad fratres acceptis, Damascum proficiscebar, adducturus eos etiam, qui illic essent, vinctos in Hierusalem, vt punirentur.
units.tr: 5 As the high priest also bears me witness, and the whole council of elders, from whom I also received letters to the brethren, I set out for Damascus, intending to bring back to Jerusalem, bound, even those who were there, to be punished.

units.la: Vamuis Dominus noster Iesus Christus suos discipulos in ferendis conuitijs & calumnijs patientes esse velit, Matt.5.10.&c: hoc ipsum tamen non obstat quo minus suam innocentiam afferat. Imo hoc facere conuenit, ne propter ipsos Christus & fides Christiana male audiant. Obseruat hoc in praesenti actione Paulus, Accusaunt Iudaei vt hostem populi, legis & templi, &c. His acceßit suspicio Tribuni, qui putabat esse Ægyptium & sicariorum ducem. Ad ista non trunci instar tacet, sed diligentissimus in hoc est, vt se purgandi copiam impetret. Et hac impetrata, nihil eorum omittit, quæ causam iuuare poterant. Simul habes exemplum promissionis, Luc 21. quo nos consolemur, &c. Sed videamus singula.
units.tr: Although our Lord Jesus Christ wills that his disciples be patient in enduring reproaches and slanders (Matt. 5.10, etc.), this does not prevent them from asserting their innocence. Indeed it is fitting to do so, lest Christ and the Christian faith be ill spoken of on their account. Paul observes this in the present action. The Jews accuse him as an enemy of the people, of the law and of the temple, etc. To these charges was added the suspicion of the tribune, who thought he was the Egyptian and leader of the assassins. Paul does not keep silent like a block of wood in the face of these things, but is most diligent in seeking the opportunity to clear himself. And when this is granted, he omits nothing that could help his cause. At the same time you have an example of the promise (Luke 21), by which we may console ourselves, etc. But let us look at the parts one by one.

units.la: I. Exordium & propositionem paucis verbis simul comprehendit. Vocat enim fratres & patres, quod beneuolentiæ serʼuit. Deinde excusationem promittit. NoTA {Q}uod apertos hostes & tot modis in se iniurios, fratres vocat & patres. Non facit adulandi causa, sed partim quia vt vnus ex vulgo loquitur: partim quia spes erat multos etiam bonos inter hos esse, & ex infidelibus multos adhuc conuerti posse. Arguuntur, qui legitimos titulos honorum damnant, Rom. 12. Peccant tamè, qui in ijsdem inepta adulatione modum excedunt, dum se insinuare conantur.
units.tr: I. In a few words he comprehends both the exordium and the proposition. He calls them brothers and fathers, which serves goodwill. Then he promises an apology. NOTE that he calls them brothers and fathers, though they were open enemies and injurious to him in so many ways. He does not do this for the sake of flattery, but partly because, as one of the common people speaks, and partly because there was hope that many of them were good and that many of the unbelievers could still be converted. Those are rebuked who condemn the lawful titles of honour (Rom. 12). Yet they sin who, in these same matters, go beyond measure with silly flattery while trying to ingratiate themselves.

units.la: Interim officij admonemur, ne propter paucos, qui in nos iniurij sunt, totam aliquam gentem damnemus. Vide quales in Paulum Iudæi fuerint, 1. Thess. 2. Act. 13. 14. 18. &c. Illos tamen amat, honorificè compellat, & saluos cupit Rom.9 10.Imo nunc adhuc verberum dolorem sentiens, ex cae tenis fratres agnoscit.O quàm hodie peccamus praecipit ira & iudicioi&c. Quòd si hoc debemus hostibus, quid obsecro fratribus in necessitate constitutis?
units.tr: Meanwhile we are reminded of our duty not to condemn a whole nation on account of the few who wrong us. See what kind of people the Jews were towards Paul (1 Thess. 2; Acts 13, 14, 18, etc.). Yet he loves them, addresses them with honour, and desires their salvation (Rom. 9, 10). Indeed, even now feeling the pain of the blows, he acknowledges them as brothers from the chains. Oh, how greatly do we sin today by anger and prejudice, etc.! If we owe this to enemies, what, I ask you, do we owe to brothers in need?

units.la: II. Narrationem instituit rerum suarum omnium: non quòd gloriosius sua iactare velit,sed quòd itaque ipsa postularet. Primo enim dum suos natales repetit, diluit crimen à Tribuno obiectum, & se non erronem esse docet. Deinde Iudaeis respondet qui partim religionis mutationem indigne ferebant, partim quòd gentibus praedicaret. Summa omnium est, quòd nihil priuato arbitrio, sed omnia Deo vocante, fecerit. Ita verò progreditur, vt omnibus superstitionibus occurrat.
units.tr: II. He sets out the narrative of all his affairs, not because he wishes to boast of his own things more gloriously, but because the situation itself demanded it. For first, while he recounts his birth, he refutes the charge laid against him by the tribune and shows that he is no vagabond. Then he answers the Jews, who partly took badly the change of religion and partly that he preached to the Gentiles. The sum of it all is that he did nothing by private judgment, but everything at the calling of God. And he proceeds in such a way as to meet every superstition.

units.la: 1. Sunt quos insicitia in religione leues fecit. Orditur ergo à prima institutione, quòd Hierosolymis à puero in patria lege acuratissimè institutus sit.Imo praeceptoris sui mentionem facit, de quo Act. 5. Finis, quod non potuerit esse rerum imperi tus.
units.tr: 1. Some are made light in religion by ignorance. He therefore begins from his first instruction, that at Jerusalem, from boyhood, he was most carefully trained in the law of his fathers. Indeed he mentions his teacher, of whom Acts 5 speaks, so that he could not have been ignorant of these matters.

units.la: NOT. §1. In religione ruditatem fugiendam esse, nec probari qui dicut nos sim pliciter credere debere, Hab.2. Iohan.17. Vult etiam nos à teneris instituì Deus, Exod.13. xod,ij. Deut.6. Pfal.78. Gen.18. Curandum ergo parentibus, vt hoc fiat. Videre est in plantis & animalibus quantum possit educatio. Sed multi canes & equos hac in reliberis præferunt. Singuli item indesinenter discant quæ salutis sunt.
units.tr: NOTE §1. In religion, ignorance is to be avoided, and those are not to be approved who say that we ought simply to believe (Hab. 2; John 17). God also wills that we be instructed from our youth (Exod. 13; Deut. 6; Psalm 78; Gen. 18). Parents must therefore take care that this is done. One can see in plants and animals how much education can do. But many people prefer dogs and horses to children in this respect. Likewise, let each one learn without ceasing what pertains to salvation.

units.la: {2}. Quod Gamalielis meminit, Non pudet ergo illum fui præceptoris, qui tamen in plerisque aberrauerat. Discimus honorare præceptores, Exod.20. &c.
units.tr: {2}. In that he mentions Gamaliel, he is not ashamed of his teacher, although that teacher had gone astray in many things. We learn to honour teachers (Exod. 20, etc.).

units.la: II. Sunt qui prophana mente quamuis religionem ampleftuntur, dum in quauis hominem saluari putant. Hi omnes reli giones probando, omnem damnant. Ne ergo ex horum numero videatur, dicit se zelatore Dei fuisse, &c. Explicat hoc, Phil. 3. Gal.1.
units.tr: II. There are some who embrace religion with a profane mind, while thinking that a man can be saved in any religion. These, by approving all religions, condemn every one. Lest he seem to be one of their number, he says that he was a zealot for God, etc. He explains this in Phil. 3 and Gal. 1.

units.la: NOT. In religione zelum requiri. Licet enim Paulus peccauerit suo zelo, non tamen ille simpliciter damnatur. Nam totos sibi vendicat Deus, Deut.6.10. Mat.6. 22. Arguuntur, qui sultum putant, cum quoqi am contendere. Sunt illi tepidi & sceptici, qui Deo non probantur. Apoc.3. 1.Reg.18.
units.tr: Note: that zeal is required in religion. For although Paul sinned through his zeal, he is nevertheless not simply condemned. For God claims them wholly for himself, Deut. 6.10; Matt. 6.22. Those are rebuked who think it is enough to contend with others as well. There are those lukewarm and doubting people who are not approved by God: Rev. 3.1; 1 Kings 18.

units.la: III. Sunt qui natura ad res nouas pro. cliues, occasione & spe priuati commo. di, quiduis recipiunt. Negat ergo ex illorum genere se esse. Nam fidem hanc aœrri
units.tr: III. There are some who, being by nature inclined to new things, will accept anything for the sake of an opportunity and the hope of private gain. He therefore denies that he belongs to that class. For this faith he persecuted most severely, hastening as far as Damascus, Acts 8.9.

units.la: mè perfecutns sum, Damascum vsque contendens, Act.8.9. Et hic quidem testes stitipsum Pontificem & Seniores, &c. Ex his vero omnibus colligi vult, se diuinitus vocatum imo coactum fuisse, &c.
units.tr: And here indeed he calls the high priest and the elders to witness, etc. From all these things he wishes it to be gathered that he was called, indeed compelled, by God, etc.

units.la: Not. ¶ In religione cauendum esse inprimis, ne prauis affectibus rapti, nostra quaeramus. Qui id faciunt, quouis vento doctrinae rapiuntur, Eph.4. Et licet veram apprehendant, mox tamen resiliunt, Matt.13. Mar 4. Luc.8. Discimus primam religionis curam habere, illam vero innocentia & charitate fraterna testemur. Oremus.
units.tr: Note: In religion one must above all take care not to seek our own things, carried away by wicked desires. Those who do this are swept along by every wind of doctrine, Eph. 4. And although they grasp the true faith, they soon fall away, Matt. 13; Mark 4; Luke 8. We learn that the first concern of religion is to have it, and to bear witness to it by innocence and brotherly charity. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXIII.

units.la: 6 Euenit autem mihi iter facien ti, & appropinquanti Damasco, circiter meridiem, ut repente e coelo circum fulserit me lux multa.
units.tr: 6 And it happened to me, as I was journeying and drawing near to Damascus, about noon, that suddenly a great light shone around me from heaven.

units.la: 7 Cecidique in solum, & audiui vocem dicentem mihi, Saul, Saul, quid me persequeris?
units.tr: 7 And I fell to the ground, and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?"

units.la: 8 Ego vero respondi, Quis es Domine? Dixitque mihi: Ego sum Iesus Nazarenus, quem tu persequeris.
units.tr: 8 And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."

units.la: 9 Porro qui mecum erant, lucem quidem conspexerunt, & expauefacti sunt: vocem autem non audierunt eius qui loquebatur mecum.
units.tr: 9 Now those who were with me saw the light and were terrified, but they did not hear the voice of him who was speaking with me.

units.la: 10 Dixi vero, Quid faciam Domine? Dominus autem dixit mihi, Surge ac proficiscere Damascum, et illic tibi dicetur de omnibus quae constituta sunt tibi ut facias.
units.tr: 10 And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Arise and go to Damascus, and there you will be told about all the things that have been appointed for you to do."

units.la: 11 Quum vero non viderem prae gloria lucis illius, manu deductus ab iis qui mecum erant, veni Damascum.
units.tr: 11 Since I could not see for the glory of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came to Damascus.

units.la: Duus Paulus diligentem rerum abs fe gestarum narrationem contexit: non quidem ut suas virtutes ambitiose iactet, sed ut finitimis suspicionibus occurrat, et notum faciat omnibus, se ex Dei iussu et vocatione, non temere aut privato consilio ad Christi fidem transfuisse, et tandem praedicavisse gentibus. Et huc referri debent, quae de sua educatione, de zelo legis, et Ecclesiae Christi persecutione dixit. Hinc enim quivis conijcere potuit, talem hominem non nisi divina virtute subito mutari potuisse. Id nunc in praesenti aperte docet, dum suae conversionis historiam per omnes circumstantias recensset. Nobis hęc consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: Paul, in relating his deeds in careful detail, does not do so to boast of his own virtues ambitiously, but to meet the suspicions of his neighbours and to make it known to all that he went over to the faith of Christ by God's command and calling, not rashly or on a private plan, and finally preached to the Gentiles. To this belong also the things he said about his upbringing, his zeal for the law, and his persecution of the Church of Christ. For from these anyone might conjecture that such a man could not have been suddenly changed except by divine power. He now plainly teaches this, while he recounts the history of his conversion through all its circumstances. These points come for our consideration.

units.la: I. Quod Paulus religionis mutationem uno hoc argumento excusat, quod huius authorem habuerit Deum.
units.tr: I. That Paul excuses his change of religion by this one argument, that God was its author.

units.la: Nota. Non peccare eos, qui Dei voluntati parere possunt.
units.tr: Note. Those who can obey the will of God do not sin.

units.la: cationem secuti, reliftis superstitionibus adaliam religione transeunt. Quod enim Deus iubet,rectum est,& huic simpliciter obedire debemus,Num.15, i.Sam.15. Nisi hocdemus,omnes Apostoli leuitatis dam nabuntur.
units.tr: ...following the calling, leaving superstitions, they pass over to another religion. For what God commands is right, and we ought simply to obey it, Num. 15, 1 Sam. 15. Unless we grant this, all the Apostles will be condemned for levity.

units.la: Temere ergo accusamur hodie eo quod Rom. Ecclesiam deseruimus, cum idem possimus respondere quod Paulus. Licet enim non eadem forma nobis apparuerit Christus, vocem tamen illius in Euangelio audiuimus,&c. Matt.11.Ioh.7.4.6.8.10 14.If.55.&c.Item Act.4.1.Cor.1.2.&c.Quis ergo vitio vertat, quod ab his difcefferi-mus, qui extra Christum salutem hinc inde monstrant?Si quibus hoc non sufficit, sunt Iudaeis similes.Peccant magis, qui vocem non audiunt,Isa.65.
units.tr: Therefore we are rashly accused today of having deserted the Roman Church, when we could make the same answer as Paul. For although Christ did not appear to us in the same form, yet we have heard his voice in the Gospel, etc. Matt. 11, John 7, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14, Isa. 55, etc. Likewise Acts 4, 1 Cor. 1, 2, etc. Who then could blame us for departing from those who point people hither and thither to salvation outside Christ? If anyone is not satisfied with this, they are like the Jews. They sin more who do not hear the voice, Isa. 65.

units.la: II.Christi potentia, & modus pugnandi cum hostibus. 1.Permittit ut Damasco appropinquet, nec vllum aedit signum suae irae,&c.Ardet ipse vt lupus, pij trepidant.
units.tr: II. The power of Christ and his manner of fighting against enemies. 1. He allows him to approach Damascus, and shows no sign of his anger, etc. He himself burns like a wolf, while the godly tremble.

units.la: NOT. Ingenium Dei,qui impijs multa indulget, vt suos interea castiget,dum illis paratur fouea,Psal.94. Ita enim liberatio fit gloriosior. Simile exemplu, Exo. 14.Item Isa.36.37.Seruiat consolationi, ne desperemus.
units.tr: NOTE. The nature of God, who indulges the impious in many things, so that meanwhile he may chastise his own, while a pit is being prepared for them, Ps. 94. For thus the deliverance becomes more glorious. A similar example, Exod. 14. Likewise Isa. 36, 37. Let it serve for consolation, lest we despair.

units.la: II. Subito sternit, & fine negotio tan*tum hostem.Fulgure examinat.Cadit ille vt nec comites nec Bullæ Pontificum iuuent.Mitis,honorificè alloquitur, & fe ad obsequia promptum offert. Cœcus ducitur in vrbe,vndevt alios duceret,venerat
units.tr: II. He strikes down suddenly, and without trouble, only the enemy. He tests him with lightning. He falls, so that neither companions nor the bulls of the Pontiffs help him. Gently and honourably he addresses him, and offers himself ready for service. The blind man is led in the city, from which he had come to lead others.

units.la: NOT. ¶ Vt hostium suorum consilia Deus facilè deludat,Pfa.33.2.Ita Sanherib, Pharao,& alij persecutores hoc ipsum experti sunt.
units.tr: NOTE. That God easily frustrates the counsels of his enemies, Ps. 33:2. So Sennacherib, Pharaoh, and other persecutors experienced this very thing.

units.la: III.Diferè fatetur sibi fieri, quod mem bris suis fiebat.Ita Zach.2.Summæ coniun ctionis argumentum. Quis hoc putasset videns quæ habes,Act 7.8. Sed vidit,& sibi factum putauit,Zach.2. Seruiat consola tioni piorū, & terreat omnes eos, quibus leue videtur, Christi membra affligere quocunque modo, Matth.15. Exo.22. Interim
units.tr: III. He almost confesses that what was done to his members was done to himself. So Zech. 2. An argument of the closest union. Who would have thought it, seeing what you have, Acts 7:8? But he saw and thought it had been done to himself, Zech. 2. Let it serve as consolation for the pious, and as a terror to all who think it a light matter to afflict Christ's members in any way, Matt. 15, Exod. 22. Meanwhile

units.la: NO.¶ Qualis inter nos quoqʒ σνμπάθεια esse debeat, qui vnum in Christo corpus fumus,1.Cor.12.Ro.12. Arguuturᾶσρρχοι Amoz 6. Peccatur quoad persecutiones, quoad famè:Hodie à multis,quoad peste.
units.tr: NOTE. What kind of sympathy [συμπάθεια] ought to exist among us also, since we are one body in Christ, 1 Cor. 12, Rom. 12. The secure are rebuked, Amos 6. Sin is committed as regards persecutions, as regards famine; today by many, as regards plague.

units.la: III. Conuersionis veræ exemplum: in quo NOT.¶1.Paulum,quis fuerit,& quid fecerit.Lupus, Gen.49.Et quidem rabie plenus pergit: nihil de conuersione cogitans. Perijsset vtiq; nisi cœlitus intonuif-set Deus.
units.tr: III. An example of true conversion, in which NOTE 1. Who Paul was and what he did. A wolf, Gen. 49. And indeed he goes on full of rage, thinking nothing of conversion. He would certainly have perished unless God had thundered from heaven.

units.la: Initium ergo conuetfionis ex Deo est. Natura enim corrupti,omnes ad peccata ferimur,&c. Ifa.53.Pfal.14. 2. Cor,3. Diuinitus ergo conuertamur oportet,vt innó uemur,Ier.31. Thren.5. Pfal.51.Phil.2. Arguntur liberi arbitrij assertores, Ioh.15. 2.Cor.3.
units.tr: The beginning of conversion, therefore, is from God. For by nature we are all corrupt and carried toward sins, etc. Isa. 53, Ps. 14, 2 Cor. 3. We ought therefore to be converted by divine power, that we may be renewed, Jer. 31, Lam. 5, Ps. 51, Phil. 2. Those who assert free will are refuted, John 15, 2 Cor. 3.

units.la: §2. Modum,quo Deus vtitur. Terret exterius fulgure, & humi sternit. Verbo peccatum arguit. Intus humiliat,& spiritus Pharifaicos frangit,vt mitescat. Hæc communis ratio etiam omnibus necessaria. Quia enim securi & insolentes pergimus,deijci nos oportet. Adhibet ergo externas castigationes, & simul verbo nos vrget. Vide Petrum,Matt.26.
units.tr: §2. The manner which God uses. He terrifies outwardly with lightning and throws us to the ground. By the word he convicts us of sin. Inwardly he humbles us and breaks Pharisaic spirits, so that they may become gentle. This common method is necessary for all. For since we go on secure and insolent, we must be cast down. He therefore applies external chastisements and at the same time urges us by the word. See Peter, Matt. 26.

units.la: §3. Quid Paulus? A. Quærit quis fit. Stupiditatis humanæ argumentum. Annon diuinam virtute sentire debebat? Sed ita ferè solemus, vt prostrati à Domino, non tamen illum agnoscamus, & alio con uertamur. Fit hoc in peste. B. Edoctus de Domino,quærit quid faciat? Vox verè humiliati. Imitemur nos. Castigati nos, à Domino castigari cogitemus, & ad illum convertamur, Ifa.9. Pœnitentiam iuxta illius præscriptum instituamus, non nobisipsis, Ifaiæ 29. Pestis. Sed ferè alijs accepta ferimus aduersa, & fit quod Iohannis 8. Hosea 6. Hæc omnium malorum causa.
units.tr: §3. What does Paul do? A. He asks who it is. A proof of human stupidity. Ought he not to have perceived it by divine power? But we are usually such that, though prostrated by the Lord, we still do not acknowledge him and turn to something else. This happens in plague. B. Taught about the Lord, he asks what he should do? The voice of one who is truly humbled. Let us imitate him. Having been chastised, let us consider that we are chastised by the Lord, and turn to him, Isa. 9. Let us institute repentance according to his prescription, not according to our own, Isa. 29. Plague. But mostly we ascribe adversities to others, and what is said in John 8 and Hosea 6 comes to pass. This is the cause of all evils.

units.la: ¶ 4. Dominus in urbem remittit ad Ananiam. Ita vero Pauli modestiam explorat, dum ab illis discere cogitur, quos antea oderat, &c.
units.tr: ¶ 4. The Lord sends him back into the city to Ananias. Thus he tests Paul's modesty, since he is compelled to learn from those whom he had formerly hated, etc.

units.la: Interim sua authoritas asseritur verbi ministerio. Sic Act 8.10.16. Contra reuelationes Anabapt. Conuertamur ipsi quoque ad Deum, & totos nos illi subijcientes, assidue Oremus.
units.tr: Meanwhile his authority is asserted for the ministry of the word, as in Acts 8, 10, 16. Against the revelations of the Anabaptists. Let us also turn ourselves to God, and, submitting ourselves wholly to him, pray constantly. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXIV.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXIV.

units.la: 12 Ananias autem quidam vir pius secundum legem, testimonio ornatus omnium illic habitantium Iudaeorum.
units.tr: 12 Now a certain Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there.

units.la: 13 Veniens ad me, & adstans, dixit mihi, Saul frater recipe visum. Et ego eodem illo momento sum eum intuitus.
units.tr: 13 He came to me, stood by me, and said to me, Brother Saul, receive your sight. And in that very moment I looked up at him.

units.la: 14 Ipse autem dixit, Deus patrum nostrorum delegit te, qui cognoscere ipsius voluntatem, & videres iustum illum, & audires vocem ex ore ipsius.
units.tr: 14 And he said, The God of our fathers has chosen you to know his will, to see that Righteous One, and to hear the voice from his mouth.

units.la: 15 Nam eris ei testis apud omnes homines, eorum quae vidisti & audisti, &c. ad verf. 17.
units.tr: 15 For you will be his witness before all men of what you have seen and heard, etc., to verse 17.

units.la: Quoniam omnis religionis mutatio odiosa est, vt quæ leuem & inCap. 22. constantem animum arguat: Paulus non temere tam multis suum è Iudaismo transitum excusat. Et primo quidem se in illo non perfunctorie versatum fuisse docet, ne quis ipsum vel inscitia deceptum, vel le uitate, vel odio & prophana mente seduc-ctum putaret, &c. Deinde vocationis suae historiam contexuit, ut nō tam vocatum, quam coactum fuisse intelligerent. His in praesenti subijcit, ut ad apostolatum diui-nitus per Ananiae (qui visionis praeceden-tis illi interpres fuerit.) ministerium legi-timè ordinatus sit, ne quis inani phantasia deceptum fuisse diceret.
units.tr: Since every change of religion is hateful, as it suggests a light and inconstant mind, Paul does not lightly offer such a long defence of his passage out of Judaism. First he shows that he was not superficially engaged in that religion, lest anyone think he had been deceived by ignorance, or seduced by lust, or by hatred and a profane mind, etc. Then he sets out the history of his calling, so that they would understand that he was not so much called as compelled. To this he adds that he was lawfully ordained to the apostleship by divine appointment through the ministry of Ananias, who was the interpreter of the earlier vision, so that no one could say he had been deceived by an empty fancy.

units.la: I. Personam Ananiae describit, ne quis ipsum homini leui credid se fuisciparetur. Et quia Iudaei apostatae testimonium non admisissent, à legis observatione illu commendat: testimonio item omnium Iudaeorum, & miraculo. Omnium finis, ut se leui satis suspicione liberet.
units.tr: I. He describes the person of Ananias, so that no one would think he had believed a man of light character. And since the Jewish apostates would not accept testimony, he commends him by his observance of the law, likewise by the testimony of all the Jews, and by a miracle. The purpose of all this is that he might free himself from the suspicion of lightness.

units.la: Nota. 1. In religionis negotio non temere cuiuis credi debere. Vt enim in hoc salus omnis consistit, sic semper fuerunt impostores, & semper erunt, Matth. 24. 2. Tim. 3. 4. r. Tim. 4. &c. Arguitur nostri seculi leuitas, quando in clarissima luce Euangelij quosuis audimus errones, modo ministros & magistratus proscindant improbi.
units.tr: Note: (1) In matters of religion, one should not lightly believe anyone at all. For just as all salvation rests on this, so there have always been impostors, and always will be, Matt. 24; 2 Tim. 3:4; 1 Tim. 4, etc. The lightness of our age is shown when we hear all sorts of errors in the clearest light of the Gospel, provided wicked men tear apart ministers and magistrates.

units.la: {1}2. Quæ vera sit commendatio ministrorum: adeoque omnium, qui in aliquo publico munere versantur. A. Pij sint secundum legem, id est præscriptum Domini. Nec enim sufficit pium esse, sed in Dei verbum respici oportet, ne sit zelus sine scientia. Rom. 10. Vide Num. 15. Isa. 29. Matt. 15.
units.tr: {1} 2. What the true commendation of ministers is, and therefore of all who hold any public office. (A) They should be according to the law, that is, the prescription of the Lord. For it is not enough to be pious, but one must look to the Word of God, lest there be zeal without knowledge. Rom. 10; see Num. 15; Isa. 29; Matt. 15.

units.la: B. Testimonium bonum habeant etiam ab exteris, ne propter ipsos Euangelium maledicatur. 1. Tim 3.
units.tr: (B) They should also have a good testimony from outsiders, so that the Gospel is not blasphemed because of them. 1 Tim. 3.

units.la: C. Vocationem à Deo certam habeant, nec sua sponte currant. Ier 23. Ro. 10. Alio qui nec fortiter, nec cum fructu minus sum obibunt. Prophetæ & Apostoli tales, Tales inquam omnino sunt, quibus credidisti. Dei verbum in omnibus secuti sunt. Vitæ probitas hostibus nota. Vocatio signis probata. Constanter ergo perseuera.
units.tr: (C) They should have a certain calling from God and not run of their own accord. Jer. 23; Rom. 10. Otherwise they will neither discharge their office bravely nor with fruit. The prophets and apostles were such men, truly such men, whom you have believed. They followed the Word of God in all things. The uprightness of their life was known to their enemies, and their calling was proved by signs. Therefore persevere steadfastly.

units.la: II. Ananiæ oratio ponitur, quæ Pauli argumento pulchrè seruiebat: in qua NOTA 1. Authorem totius negotij indicat, Deum. Deus patrum præparauit te. Hinc illud ad Galatas 1. Diserte autem Deum patrum dicit, vt apostasiæ crimen diluat. Sic Stephanus, Actor. 7. Interim patet, ex mera gratia Paulum vocatum fuisse, si nimirum cogites quis fuerit. Ita ipse agnoscit, 1. ad Timoth 1. Galat. 1. Eadem omnium nostrûm est ratio. Tit.3. ad Ephef.2.
units.tr: II. Ananias's speech is given, which serves Paul's argument well. In it, (1) note that he points out the author of the whole affair, God: "The God of our fathers has prepared you." Hence that passage in Galatians 1. He speaks expressly of "the God of our fathers" so as to wipe away the charge of apostasy. So Stephen, Acts 7. Meanwhile it is clear that Paul was called out of pure grace, if indeed you consider who he was. He himself acknowledges this, 1 Tim. 1; Gal. 1. The reason is the same for all of us. Titus 3; Eph. 2.

units.la: § 2. Finem indicat, ad quem ipsum destinârit Deus. A. Vt cognoscere eius voluntatem. Hoc initio opus est verbi ministris, Tit.1. Mal.2.1. Tim.3. Verlatur autem voluntas Dei maxime in duobus, nimirum vt credamus in Christum, & charitatem sectemur, Ioh.6.1. Ioh.3. Gal.5. Hanc antea omnino ignorabat Paulus·
units.tr: § 2. He indicates the end for which God had destined him. (A) That he should know his will. Ministers of the Word need this at the outset, Titus 1; Mal. 2:7; 1 Tim. 3. The will of God is chiefly revealed in two things, namely that we believe in Christ and pursue love, John 6; John 3; Gal. 5. Paul was entirely ignorant of this before.

units.la: B. Vt videres iustum. Intelligit Christum, qui & iustus est, & iustos reddit, Ier.23. Isa. 53.1. Cor.1. Interim apparet, neminem in huius cognitionem venire, nisi reuelante Deo, 1.Cor.2. Matt.11. Ioh.6. Luc.10. &c.
units.tr: (B) That he should see the Righteous One. He means Christ, who is both righteous and makes righteous, Jer. 23; Isa. 53; 1 Cor. 1. Meanwhile it appears that no one comes to knowledge of this except by God's revelation, 1 Cor. 2; Matt. 11; John 6; Luke 10, etc.

units.la: C. Vt audires ex ore eius vocem: adeoque praeter communem morem ab eo edoceris. Huc refer Gal.1.2. Ingens beneficium, Ioh.15. Eo maius autem, quod fuerat hostis. Agnoscamus hoc in nobis hodie. Interim tum Paulus tum alij ministri omnes sui officij admonentur, vt nimirum ex Dei ore doctrinam petant, Ezech.3 33. Ier.1. Matt.28.
units.tr: (C) That he should hear the voice from his mouth: and so be taught by him beyond the common manner. Refer here to Gal. 1:12. This is a great benefit, John 15, and all the greater because he had been an enemy. Let us acknowledge this in ourselves today. Meanwhile both Paul and all other ministers are reminded of their office, namely that they should seek doctrine from the mouth of God, Ezek. 3:33; Jer. 1; Matt. 28.

units.la: D. Vt esses illi testis omnium, &c. Auritus & oculatus. Sic Apostoli quoque nominantur à Christo, Ioh 15. Act.1. Omnium hominum meminit, vt praedicatione inter gentes excusetur.
units.tr: (D) That you should be his witness before all, etc. Both ear-witness and eye-witness. So the apostles too are named by Christ, John 15; Acts 1. He mentions all men so that he may be excused in preaching among the Gentiles.

units.la: Docemur hinc, partim omnium esse, vt veriveritatem cognitam propagent: partim quàm horribile scelus fit, Apoftolorû doctrinæ contradicere. Qui id faciunt, Christum falsi accusant: imò ipsum Deum patrem, i. Ioh. 5.
units.tr: We are taught from this, partly that it is the duty of all to spread the truth once known, and partly how horrible a crime it is to contradict the doctrine of the apostles. Those who do so falsely accuse Christ; indeed they accuse God the Father himself, 1 John 5.

units.la: ¶ 3. Baptismum suadet, & ad hunc suscipiendum hortatur acriter, vt ita publicè Christo nomen det. Ablue peccata tua. Est hæc sacramentalis locutio. Alioqui solus Christi sanguis peccata abluit, 1. Ioh. 1. Psa. 51. Quia autem illa ablutio per baptismum quasi obsignatur, hoc etiam ablui dicitur. Ideo ad fidem in Christum relegat (qui solus dona hæc confert) addens: Invocato nomine Domini. Invocatio enim sine fide consistere non potest, Rom. 10.
units.tr: ¶ 3. He urges baptism and earnestly exhorts him to receive it, so that he might publicly give his name to Christ. Wash away your sins. This is sacramental language. Otherwise only the blood of Christ washes away sins, 1 John 1; Ps. 51. But because that washing is, as it were, sealed through baptism, it is also said to be washed. So he refers him to faith in Christ (who alone bestows these gifts), adding: calling on the name of the Lord. For calling on him cannot exist without faith, Rom. 10.

units.la: Docemur. 1. Sacramenta minimè contemnI vel negligi debere, vt superuaca- nea. Vide Gen. 17. Exo. 4. Similia exempla sunt, Act. 8. 10. 16. Imò Paulum baptizari oportuit. Nil temerè iubet Dominus.
units.tr: We are taught: (1) that sacraments should by no means be despised or neglected as superfluous. See Gen. 17; Exod. 4. There are similar examples in Acts 8, 10, 16. Indeed Paul had to be baptized. The Lord commands nothing rashly.

units.la: II. In sacramentis, non ad externa symbola, sed ad Christum respici debere, qui solus ea cofert, quæ in his adumbrantur.
units.tr: II. In the sacraments, one must look not to the outward signs, but to Christ, who alone bestows what is shadowed forth in them.

units.la: Discamus in religione nihil temerè instituere. In agnita autem & recepta veritate constan rer perseuerare Oremus.
units.tr: Let us learn not to institute anything rashly in religion. But once the truth is acknowledged and received, let us pray to persevere steadfastly.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXV.

units.la: 17 Factum est autem, quum esse me reuersus Hierosolymam, & orarem in templo, vt raperer extra me.
units.tr: 17 It happened, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, that I was caught up out of myself.

units.la: 18 Et vidi eum dicentem mihi, Festina, & exi citò ex Hierusalem, quoniam non acceperunt testimonium tuum de me.
units.tr: 18 And I saw him saying to me, "Make haste, and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive your testimony concerning me."

units.la: 19 Et ego dixi, Domine, ipsi sciunt quia ego eram mittens in carcerem, & caedi per synagogas eos qui crediderant in te.
units.tr: 19 And I said, "Lord, they know that I was throwing into prison and having beaten in the synagogues those who believed in you."

units.la: 20 Et cum funderetur sanguis Stephani martyris tui, ego quoque adstabam, & assentiebar caedi illius, & custodiebam vestimenta eorum qui interficiebant eum.
units.tr: 20 "And when the blood of Stephen your martyr was being shed, I myself was standing by, consenting to his killing and guarding the garments of those who were killing him."

units.la: 21 Et dixit mihi: Vade, quia ego in gentes longe mittam.
units.tr: 21 And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."

units.la: 22 Audiebant autem hunc usque ad hoc verbum: tum vero sublatâ voce suâ dicentes: Tolle de terra hominem istum, non enim decet eum viuere.
units.tr: 22 They listened to him up to this word; then, raising their voices, they said, "Take this man from the earth, for it is not fitting that he live."

units.la: Dicebat Paulus eiusmodi rerum suarum narrationem instituit, quaorum hostium suorum calumnijs & sinistras suspiciones, quibus contra ipsum inuitati erant, occurrere studet. In his præcipua cipua erant duo: Nimirum quod a Iudaismo defecisset, & quod gentibus praedicans, illas Iudaeis aequaret. Ex his enim colligebant, ipsum populi Iudaici hostem, ad haec templi ac Legis prophanum contemptorem esse. Ad primum caput hucusque respondit, hoc unum vrgens, quod nihil temere, sed omnia ex Dei vocatione fecerit: suo exemplo docens, quid nos quoque in mutandis religionibus observare debeamus.
units.tr: Paul set out this account of his affairs in order to meet the slanders of his enemies and the sinister suspicions with which they had been stirred up against him. Two charges were chief: that he had defected from Judaism, and that by preaching to the Gentiles he made them equal to the Jews. From these they concluded that he was an enemy of the Jewish people and a profane despiser of the temple and the Law. To the first charge he has answered so far, insisting on this one point: that he had done nothing rashly, but everything from God's calling. By his own example he teaches what we too ought to observe when we change religions.

units.la: In praesenti ad alterum crimen descendit, hic quoque demonstrans, se diuinitus evocatum fuisse, vt praedicaret gentibus, nec tamen ideo sui populi studium depo fuisse. Et huc quidem praesentis historiae singulae partes faciunt. Vsus, totum Christi & Euangelij negotium per Dei prouidentiam gubernari.
units.tr: Now he comes to the second charge, showing here too that he had been called by God to preach to the Gentiles, and yet had not on that account laid aside his concern for his own people. The individual parts of the present narrative all serve this purpose. The use is that the whole business of Christ and the Gospel is governed by God's providence.

units.la: I Reuersus fnm Hierosolymam: nimirum vt ijs praedicaret, ex quibus prognatus erat. Non ergo per illum stetit, quo minus Iudaei iterum arcentur. Facta hoc 4 anno Coner. Nam ex Damasco venit in Arabiam. Inde redijt Damascum, vnde sporta elapsus est. Inde triennio elapso venit ad Petrum &c. 2. Cor. 12. Gal. 1. 2. Act 9 Finis, quod se gentibus suae impendere cupierit.
units.tr: I. He returned to Jerusalem, namely so that he might preach to those from whom he was descended. It was therefore not through him that the Jews were kept back again. This happened in the fourth year after his conversion. For from Damascus he came into Arabia; from there he returned to Damascus, whence he escaped in a basket. Then, three years having elapsed, he came to Peter, etc. (2 Cor. 12; Gal. 1; Acts 9). The end: that he desired to devote himself to the Gentiles.

units.la: NOT. Ministrios verbi, licet omnibus debitores sint, primam tamen patriæ suæ curam gerere debere. Sic Christus, Luc. 4. Mar. 6.
units.tr: NOTE. Ministers of the Word, although they are debtors to all, ought nevertheless to take first care of their own country. So Christ (Luke 4; Mark 6).

units.la: Obseruandum hoc in ciuilibus quoq; negotijs. Vide Mosem, Exod. 2. Hebr. 11. Magna hodie illorum impudentia, qui pa triam venalem habent. Cogitanda hæc diligenter quando de fœdere agitur. Item in pestis periculo meminerimus conciues non esse deserendos.
units.tr: This is to be observed in civil affairs too. See Moses (Exod. 2; Heb. 11). Great today is the shamelessness of those who have their country for sale. These matters must be considered carefully when a treaty is under discussion. Likewise, in the danger of plague, let us remember that fellow citizens are not to be deserted.

units.la: II. Orauit in templo. Adijcit hoc, ne ipsum latuisse putarent, tum vt templi prophana ti suspicionem diluat. Quid verò orarit potissimum, patet ex Romano 10. Item ex sequenti colloquio cum Deo.
units.tr: II. He prayed in the temple. He adds this so that they would not think he had hidden himself, and so that he might dispel the suspicion that he profaned the temple. What he prayed for above all is clear from Romans 10, and also from the following conversation with God.

units.la: NOT. Ministrorum esse, vt precibus assiduis populi salutem prouehant. Quia suo studio absque Dei incremento nihil proficient, 1. Cor. 3. Samuel, 1. Sam. 12. Ieremias, Cap. 5. 14. Reliqui Prophetæ. Id ipsum verò Magistratus, quoq; obseruent, vt populi salutem precibus Deo commendent, quando sine huius ope nihil proficient etiam ipsi, Psalm. 127. 1. Reg. 3. Moses, Exod. 17. 32. Dauid, 2. Sam. 24. Ezechias.
units.tr: NOTE. It is the task of ministers to advance the people's salvation by constant prayers, since without God's increase they accomplish nothing by their own zeal (1 Cor. 3; Samuel, 1 Sam. 12; Jeremiah, ch. 5 and 14; the other prophets). Magistrates too should observe the same, commending the people's salvation to God in prayer, since without his help they themselves accomplish nothing (Ps. 127; 1 Kings 3; Moses, Exod. 17 and 32; David, 2 Sam. 24; Hezekiah).

units.la: III. Oraculum exponit, quo iussus erat ad gentes proficisci. Fui in ecclesia. Ea fortasse, de qua 2 Corint. 12. Hoc dicit, vt fidem inueniat. Diligenter verò colloquium cum
units.tr: III. He explains the oracle by which he had been ordered to set out for the Gentiles. "I was in the church": perhaps the one of which 2 Cor. 12 speaks. He says this so that he may find faith. He explains carefully the conversation with

units.la: Deo exponit, in quo Not. ¶1. Christus exire iubet illico. Ratio: quia non recipient tuum de me testimonium. Fuit haec grauis tentatio, si cum vocatione conse-ras, Act. 9. Negatur spes omnis profectus, vbi maxime sperauerat, &c. Sed ita suos exercere solet Deus, Exod 2. Discamus non succumbere, licet profectus modo conatui non respondeat. Vide Eliam, 1. Reg. 19. Interim obseruemus Deum verbum gratiae ab ijs auferre, qui non recipiunt. ¶2. Paulus respondet, & quasi disputat cum Deo. Putat repentinam & miraculosam conuersionem aliquid momenti habituram. Frequens hoc vt sancti disputent cum Deo. Sic Iere. 12. Psalm. 73. 13. Hab 1. &c. Permittit Deus, quia fidem confirmat. Confutantur qui Diuis interceffloribus opus esse putant. Curandum tamen, ne Deo plus sapere velimus & contendendo ad inobedientiam & murmur vsq; progrediamur. ¶3. Vrget Dominus, & di serte ad gentes ablegat. Voluit enim rata esse oracula, Deut 32. Hos. 2 Rom. 10. Vi-des qualescunq; sint rationes nostrae, Deum tamen non mutare sententiam suam. Nec enim opus habet, vt a nobis demum discat, &c. Neq; semper de euentu nos cer-tiores facit. Tu obedire discito.
units.tr: God, in which: NOTE 1. Christ bids him leave at once. The reason: "because they will not receive your testimony concerning me." This was a grave temptation, if you compare it with the calling (Acts 9). All hope of progress is denied him just where he had hoped most, etc. But God is accustomed to exercise his own in this way (Exod. 2). Let us learn not to give way, although progress may not match our effort. See Elijah (1 Kings 19). Meanwhile let us observe that God takes the word of grace away from those who do not receive it. 2. Paul answers, and as it were disputes with God. He thinks that a sudden and miraculous conversion will carry some weight. It is frequent for the saints to dispute with God in this way (Jer. 12; Ps. 73:13; Hab. 1, etc.). God permits it because he confirms faith. Those are refuted who think that intercessors of the saints are needed. We must take care, however, not to want to be wiser than God, and not to advance by contention into disobedience and murmuring. 3. The Lord presses on and plainly sends him away to the Gentiles. For he wished his oracles to stand (Deut. 32; Hos. 2; Rom. 10). You see that however good our reasons are, God does not change his decision. Nor does he need to learn from us in the end, etc. Nor does he always inform us of the outcome. Learn to obey.

units.la: Iudæi audita gentium mentione, inter rumpunt orationem furiosis clamoribus & ad necem poscunt. Causa erat, nimia fuę gentis seducta ex scripturis malè intelle-ctis, Exod.5.19. Amos 3.&c. Ideo gentes omnino fastidiebant, & eas sibi æquiparari putabant intolerabile, Actor 11. Nota. ¶ Quantum malum sit superbia. Hæc etiamnum hodie Iudæos dementat, vt nul-lis calamitatibus posint corrigi. Eadem ratio omnium hypocritarum. Quia enim suis operibus omnia tribuunt, nō possunt in salutis consortio ferre peccatores. Vide Matt.9.10.Luc.18.Nouatiani. Dictum Conft.de Accessio.Hoc nomine etiam hodie multi contra Euangelium insaniunt. Anabaptistæ. Sed idem cum Iudæis sentient, Rom.10.Non pudeat nos salutis fo-cios habere peccatores, Matt.9.Oremus.
units.tr: When the Jews heard mention of the Gentiles, they broke off his speech with frenzied shouts and demanded his death. The cause was the excessive pride of that nation, their Scriptures badly understood (Exod. 5:19; Amos 3, etc.). Therefore they utterly despised the Gentiles and thought it intolerable to be made equal to them (Acts 11). NOTE: how great an evil pride is. Even today it drives the Jews mad, so that no calamities can correct them. The same is true of all hypocrites: because they attribute everything to their works, they cannot endure sinners in the fellowship of salvation (Matt. 9 and 10; Luke 18). Compare the Novatians, and the saying at Constance concerning Accession (obscure). On this account many even today rage against the Gospel: the Anabaptists. But they will feel the same as the Jews (Rom. 10). Let us not be ashamed to have sinners as partners in salvation (Matt. 9). Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXVI.

units.la: 23 Vociferantibus autem eis, & proicientibus pallia, & pulverem iactantibus in aerem.
units.tr: 23 And as they cried out, threw off their garments and tossed dust into the air,

units.la: 24 Iussit Tribunus eum duci in castra, dixit, vt in eum verberibus inquiri, ut sciret quam ob causam sic clamarent contra eum.
units.tr: 24 the tribune ordered him to be taken into the barracks and said that he should be examined under the lash, so that he might learn why they shouted so against him.

units.la: 25 Quum autem adstrinxissent eum loris, dixit astanti Centurioni Paulus, Num hominem Romanum, et indemnatum licet vobis flagellare?
units.tr: 25 When they had bound him with thongs, Paul said to the centurion who stood by: "Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen, and one who has not been condemned?"

units.la: 26 Hoc vero cum audijssct Centurio, adijt Tribunum, & annunciauit ei, dicens: vide quid facturus sis: homo enim iste Romanus est.
units.tr: 26 When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and reported it, saying: "See what you are about to do, for this man is a Roman."

units.la: 27 Accedens autem Tribunus dixit ei, Dic mihi, num tu Romanus es? At ille dixit, Etiam.
units.tr: 27 Then the tribune came up and said to him: "Tell me, are you a Roman?" He said, "Yes."

units.la: 28 Et respondit Tribunus, Ego multa summa civitatem istam acquisiui. Paulus autem ait: Ego vero etiam natus sum ciuis.
units.tr: 28 The tribune answered: "I obtained this citizenship for a large sum." But Paul said: "I was born a citizen."

units.la: 29 Statim igitur abscesserunt ab eo qui fuerant in quos ipse timuit, cognito eum Romanum esse, quoniam eum vinxerat.
units.tr: 29 Immediately, therefore, those who were about to examine him withdrew from him, and the tribune himself was afraid when he learned that Paul was a Roman, since he had bound him.

units.la: 30 Postero autem die volens pro certo scire cuius rei accusaretur a Iudaeis, soluit eum e vinculis, et iussit principes sacerdotum venire, totumque ipsorum consessum: ac deductum Paulum statuit coram eis.
units.tr: 30 On the next day, wishing to know for certain what he was accused of by the Jews, he released him from his bonds, ordered the chief priests and their whole council to assemble, and, bringing Paul down, set him before them.

units.la: Quamuis Paulus Apostolus de iis, quae in ipso Iudaei accusabant, ita respondERIT, ut pijs omnib. potuerit satisfacere, utpote qui Dei mandatu in omnibus al'egarit: Iudæis tamen adeo non satisfecit, vt illum ne audire quidem volue rint amplius.Causa,quod fe ad gentes ablegatum esse diceret. Id enim putabant in dignisimè fieri, vt gentes ipsis præferren tur, qui ab initio Dei peculium fuissent, Exod.19.Amos 3.Pfal.147. Est enim hoc proprium hypocritis iuftitiarijs,quod pec-catores in salutis consortio ferre non pof sunt,Matth.9.Luc.7. Exempla sunt hodie quoque.
units.tr: Although the apostle Paul answered the charges the Jews brought against him in such a way that he could satisfy all the godly, since he had acted in everything by God's command, he did not satisfy the Jews at all; they would not even hear him any longer. The reason was that he said he had been sent to the Gentiles. For they thought it most unworthy that the Gentiles should be preferred to them, who from the beginning had been God's own people (Exod. 19; Amos 3; Ps. 147). It is indeed the mark of self-righteous hypocrites that they cannot bear sinners in the fellowship of salvation (Matt. 9; Luke 7). There are examples of this today too.

units.la: Sequitur quid porro factum fit, vbi sin gulæ personæ nobis considerandæ veniunt.
units.tr: What followed next is to be considered as each person comes before us.

units.la: I. Iudæi.Ad necem poscunt priusquam perorauerit. Et quidem Ethnico obijcient eum,qui ex ipsis erat oriundus.idque propter causam religionis & doctrinam. Deinde rem agunt clamoribus, vestium & pulueris iactatione,vt insani solent.
units.tr: I. The Jews. They demand his death before he has finished speaking. And indeed they accuse him, a man of their own stock, before a Gentile, and do so on account of religion and doctrine. Then they carry on with shouting, tossing of garments and dust, as madmen usually do.

units.la: Not. Quantum possit odium Veritatis. Facit homines obliuisci omnis moderationis,æquitatis,charitatis, &c. Sic Ioh. 18.19. Vsurpatur idem hodie.
units.tr: Note: how great the power of hatred of the truth is. It makes men forget all moderation, fairness, charity, and so on (John 18–19). The same thing happens today.

units.la: Simul patet hic,quibus argumentis oppugnentur Christi cultores. Clamoribus. Minis.Supplicijs, &c. O quam multi sunt Iudæorum similes hodie! Discant quæso in religionis causa, vbi salus periclitatur prudenprudenter agere, quando in prophanis importunitas hæc damnatur.
units.tr: At the same time it is clear here by what means the worshippers of Christ are assailed: by shouting, threats, punishments, and so on. O how many are like the Jews today! Let them learn, I beg, to act prudently when salvation is in danger in a matter of religion, when such importunity is condemned even in secular affairs.

units.la: II. Tribunus. Primo iubet Paulum in custodiam ducti: quod prudentiæ fuit. Huic enim gratia ad conspectu subducto facilius fuit furentes compescere. Deinde autem illum flagris examinari iubet pro veteri more. Id vero iniquissimè facit & inhumaniter. Quia nihil dum probarant Iudæi, Paulus autem cordatissimè responderat.
units.tr: II. The tribune. First he orders Paul to be led into custody, which was prudent, for by removing him from sight it was easier to restrain the raging crowd. Then, however, he orders him to be examined by the lash, according to the old custom. But he does this most unjustly and inhumanly, since the Jews had not yet proved anything, while Paul had answered very wisely.

units.la: Sed Notr. 1. Mores impiorum magi stratuum. Prudentia quidevtuntur, qua etiam filios lucis superant, Luc. 16. Interim iustitiæ speciem modo habent, & hanc pro suo arbitrio & commodo versant. Sic Pilatus, Lucæ 23. Ioh. 18.19. Sed fere tales suorum factorum postea pœnitet, vt mox videbimus. Meminerint magistratus, Pf. 72.82. Deut. 1. &c. Admoneantur in primis exemplo hoc, ne in tormentis nimium vel præcipites vel crudeles sint. Quia innocentem torquere scelus est: deinde multi ex dolore fatentur, quod non fecerunt. Vide Psal. 72. Pretiosum ducent sanguinem, &c.
units.tr: But note, first: the ways of ungodly magistrates. They use a prudence by which they even surpass the sons of light (Luke 16). Meanwhile they have only the appearance of justice, and bend it to their own judgment and convenience, as Pilate did (Luke 23; John 18–19). Yet such men usually later repent of their deeds, as we shall soon see. Let magistrates remember Ps. 72, Ps. 82, Deut. 1, and so on. Let them be warned above all by this example not to be either too hasty or too cruel in torture, for to torture an innocent man is a crime; moreover, many confess under pain to what they have not done. See Ps. 72: "They will count their blood precious," and so on.

units.la: 2. Qui fit sanctorum fors in hoc mundo. Cum facinorosis deputantur & vilisimis, in quorum vita ludere liceat. Sic Prophetis factum. Sic Christo euenit, Isaiæ 53.
units.tr: Second: what lot the saints have in this world. They are reckoned among criminals and the most worthless, in whose lives it is permitted to make sport. So it happened to the prophets, and so it befell Christ (Isa. 53).

units.la: Luc.23. Iohanni Baptistæ, Mar.6. Apostolis, 1.Cor.4. Ioh.16.15. Non offendamur ergo hodie, quando Deus suam memoriam asserit, nec latet diu veritas, Psal 34. Lucæ 12. Matt 10.
units.tr: Luke 23; to John the Baptist, Mark 6; to the apostles, 1 Cor. 4; John 16:15. Let us not be offended today when God vindicates his own memory, nor does the truth stay hidden for long (Ps. 34; Luke 12; Matt. 10).

units.la: III. Paulus. Num trunci instar racet? Minime. Imo ad Leges recurrit, & Romanæ ciuitatis ius allegat, quo etiam defenditur.
units.tr: III. Paul. Does he stand like a stump? By no means. Rather he has recourse to the laws and claims the right of Roman citizenship, by which he is also defended.

units.la: Nota. Quæ sit sanctorum patientia? Non ignaua aut belluina stupiditas. Para ti quidem sunt quiduis ferre pro Christo, Phil 1. Interim legitimam defensionem, quæ non pugnat cum fide, non negligunt. Vt reliquis creaturis, sic legibus uti licet. Huius Christus admonet, Mat.10. Luc.12. Imo videmus hic licere, ut politicas quoque leges præexamus, &c.
units.tr: Note: what is the patience of the saints? It is not lazy or brutish stupidity. They are indeed ready to bear anything for Christ (Phil. 1). Meanwhile they do not neglect a lawful defence, which does not conflict with faith. As we may use other created things, so we may use the laws. Christ warns of this (Matt. 10; Luke 12). Indeed we see here that it is permitted to make use of political laws too, and so on.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quanto iniquior fit hodie sanctorum conditio. Centurio licet sciret causam religionis hic agi: patitur tamen ut Rom. Priuilegijs Paulus utatur. Hodie omnes leges & publica iura silent, si quando de religione concertatur. Et hoc quidem Pontificibus debemus.
units.tr: Second: how much less favourable the condition of the saints is today. The centurion, though he knew that the cause of religion was at stake here, nevertheless allowed Paul to use his Roman privileges. Today all laws and public rights fall silent whenever religion is disputed, and for this we are indebted to the Papists.

units.la: IV. Exitus primi Actus huius Tragoediæ subijcitur. Tribunus timet, ut Philippen. Act.16. Nō quidem Deum, sed Rom. fœueritatem. Ita solent impij. Interim emendare volens errorem, crastino produ cit in Concilium, quod quidem putabat sanctissimum. Sed fallitur vt hodie multi, qui sibi nescio quid de Conciliis pollicentur.
units.tr: IV. The outcome of the first act of this tragedy is now set out. The tribune is afraid, as at Philippi (Acts 16): not indeed of God, but of Roman severity. So the wicked usually are. Meanwhile, wishing to correct his error, he brings Paul before the council on the next day, which he indeed thought most holy. But he is deceived, as many today are, who promise themselves I know not what from councils.

units.la: Interim NOTA. ¶ 1. Quàm prosit fenciter Leges obseruare. Claudius bestia erat. Quia tamen adhuc vigebat neruus legum, aliqua superstitionis defensio bonis. Vbi Legum authoritas intercidit, actum est. Pudeat suae ignauiae magistratus Christianos, qui suos opprimi patiuntur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, NOTE: first, how useful it is to observe the laws faithfully. Claudius was a beast. Yet because the force of the laws still flourished, there was some defence of the good against superstition. When the authority of the laws has perished, it is all over. Let Christian magistrates be ashamed of their cowardice, who allow their own people to be oppressed.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quid euenit, vbi iudicia vel in vulgi, vel aliorum gratiam praecipitantur. Sequitur pudor, timor, & saepe mirifica confusio. Exempla passim extant.
