units.tr: Second: what happens when judgments are rushed either to please the crowd or to gratify others. Shame follows, then fear, and often a wondrous confusion. Examples are found everywhere.

units.la: Obseruent hoc quotquot cum virtute & laude respublicas administrare volunt. Consoletur autem pios, quod persecutores tam facile possunt terreri. Oremus.
units.tr: Let all who wish to administer commonwealths with virtue and praise observe this. And let it comfort the godly that persecutors can be so easily terrified. Let us pray.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII. HOMILIA CLXXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. HOMILY CLXXVII.

units.la: INtentis autem oculis in Concilium Paulus ait: Viri fratres, ego omni conscientia bona conuersatus sum coram Deo vsque in hodiernum diem.
units.tr: And fixing his eyes on the council, Paul said: Men, brothers, I have lived in all good conscience before God up to this day.

units.la: 2 Ananias autem Pontifex maxi- mus imperauit iis qui ipsi adstabant, vt os eius caederent.
units.tr: 2 But the high priest Ananias commanded those standing beside him to strike his mouth.

units.la: 3 Tum Paulus dixit ei: Percussurus es te Deus, paries dealbate: Et tu sedes iudicans me secundum legem, et contra legem me iubes percuti?
units.tr: 3 Then Paul said to him: God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit in judgment over me according to the law, and yet order me to be struck contrary to the law?

units.la: 4 Qui vero adstabant, dixerunt, Summo Sacerdoti Dei conuitiaris?
units.tr: 4 But those who stood by said: Do you revile God's high priest?

units.la: 5 Dixit autem Paulus: Nescieham fratres, quod Pontifex esset. Scriptum est enim: Principi populi tui non maledices.
units.tr: 5 And Paul said: I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest. For it is written: You shall not curse the ruler of your people.

units.la: VT Paulus electum fuit Iesu Christi organum: Ita illius exemplo suos omnes Christus docere voluit, quid ipsos in hoc mundo maneat, & quomodo sese gerere debeant. Aetor 9. Primo enim hostes acerrimos sensit Iudaeos, pro quorum salute dies noctes excubabat, Ro. 10. 9. Euenit hoc ipsum omnibus Pauli successoribus, Matth. 10. &c. Deinde illi contra ipsum Romanos arma commouent. Ita hodie fit. Sed intrepidus Paulus Dei verbo sese tuetur: quod ipsum nos quoq; facere decet, vt ex Dei verbo omnium rationem reddamus, & huius promissionibus nitamur, &c. Atqui hic mirum est, quod quòd apud Ethnicum militem plus æqui tatis inuenit, quàm apud suos, qui pieta- tis & eruditionis titulo superbiebant. A- pertam enim vim prohibuit. Legibus & priuilegijs gaudere passus est. Tandé quia religionis causam sciebat agi, ad eos re- fert, qui huius professione gloriabantur. Prudenter quidé hoc,sed fallitur,vt mul- ti hodie. Docet hoc res ipsa. Sequitur e- nim vt isti cum hypocrisi audaciam & im- pietatem coniunxerint.
units.tr: As Paul was the chosen instrument of Jesus Christ, so Christ wished to teach all his people by Paul's example what awaits them in this world and how they ought to conduct themselves. Acts 9. For first he experienced the bitterest enemies in the Jews, for whose salvation he kept watch day and night, Rom. 10. 9. This same thing happened to all Paul's successors, Matt. 10, etc. Then they stir up arms against him, as the Romans did against Paul. So it happens today. But fearless Paul defends himself by the Word of God, which we too ought to do, so that we give an account of everything from God's Word and rest on its promises, etc. Yet here it is remarkable that he found more fairness in a heathen soldier than among his own people, who prided themselves on the title of piety and learning. For the soldier forbade open violence, and allowed him to enjoy the laws and privileges. Finally, since he knew that the cause of religion was at stake, he referred him to those who boasted of professing it. Prudent indeed, but he was deceived, as many are today. The thing itself teaches this. For it follows that those men joined hypocrisy with audacity and impiety.

units.la: I. Quomodo fe in Concilio Paulus gef- ferit. 1 Oculis intentis ipsos intuetur. Argu- mentum animi fortis & constantis,qui ve ritatis causam decet, ne hostibus animus addatur. NOTA. ¶ Promissionum Christi veritatem. Promisit fe affuturum suis,fi quid tale fiat. Matth. 10. Luc. 21. Ioh. 14. 16. Id hic præstat fidelissimè. Sic Act 4. 5. Consoletur in quauis tentatione,hodie in morbis & mortis articulo, Pf. 107. 91. Io. 5.
units.tr: I. How Paul behaved in the council. 1 He looks at them with fixed eyes. This is the mark of a brave and steadfast spirit, which befits the cause of truth, so that courage is not given to the enemies. NOTE. The truth of Christ's promises. He promised to be present with his own if such things should happen. Matt. 10; Luke 21; John 14, 16. Here he fulfils this most faithfully. So Acts 4, 5. He consoles in every temptation, today in sickness and at the point of death, Ps. 107 [91]; John 5.

units.la: II. Orditur orationem à testimonio in- nocentiç,de qua confidenter pronuntiat. Non autem fe omnis peccati immunè fa- cit,sed ad præfentem causam respicit. Ac- cusabatur enim defectionis ab auita reli- gione,vt hostis populi,templi, legis, item quòd gentes impiè obtruderet populo Dei. Dicit ergo fe bona conscientia versa-
units.tr: II. He begins his speech with a testimony of innocence, about which he speaks confidently. He does not, however, declare himself free of all sin, but looks to the present case. For he was accused of defection from the ancestral religion, as an enemy of the people, the temple and the law, and also of impiously thrusting the Gentiles upon the people of God. He says, therefore, that he has lived in his office with a good conscience, and that he has done nothing rashly in order to heal those who otherwise would not have deigned to listen.

units.la: tum in suo munere, & nihil fecisse temere, vt illis medeatur, qui alioqui non cignati fuissent audire. Alioqui nouerat ie peccatorem esse, i.Tim.1 Rom 7.1.Cor.15. Sic Dauid,Psal.7.26 51.Ezech as.2 Reg 20.
units.tr: Otherwise he knew that he was a sinner: 1 Tim. 1; Rom. 7; 1 Cor. 15. So David, Ps. 7, 26, 51; Ezech. 18; 2 Kings 20.

units.la: Sed Not. ¶ In religionis causa cum primis conscientiae rationem habendam esse. Quia enim illic solius Dei causa agitur, minimè locum habet hypocrisis, cum hunc nihil latere posit, Psal 7.Iere.11.20. Potest autem conscientiae integritas servari, si omnia iuxta Dei verbum instituamus, & vocationem Dei certam habeamus, &c. Ita irreprehensibiles ermus, licet in alijs ex carnis infirmitate labamur. Lapsus alios Deus benignè condonat propter Christum.
units.tr: But note: in a matter of religion, above all, account must be taken of conscience. For since there the cause of God alone is at stake, hypocrisy has no place at all, since nothing can be hidden from him, Ps. 7; Jer. 11. 20. The integrity of conscience can, however, be preserved if we order everything according to God's Word and have a sure calling from God, etc. Thus we are made irreproachable, though in other things we stumble through the weakness of the flesh. God mercifully pardons other lapses for Christ's sake.

units.la: II. Ananias iubet os Pauli percuti: Vel quod titulos insolentes omisisset. (Sunt enim valdè irritabiles sancti illi patres.) Vel quod nondum requisitus coepisset dicere. Vel quod suam innocentiam afferendo, ipsorum iniustitiam suggillare videretur.
units.tr: II. Ananias orders Paul's mouth to be struck: either because he had omitted the insolent titles (for those holy fathers are very irritable), or because he began to speak before being questioned, or because by asserting his innocence he seemed to be branding their injustice.

units.la: Not. ¶ Qualia sint impiorum antistitum Concilia. Calumnijs prius grauatus fuit, vt omnibus exosus fieret. Responden tem clamoribus turbarunt. Nunc vima- pertam adhibent. Sic fere agitur res. Si quis excusationem paret, iam vel clamori bus obstrepunt, vel aperta vi opprimunt. Sic fit Ioh. 18. Sic Stephanus oppressus, Act. 6. 7. &c. Talia iam seculis aliquot fuerunt Concilia. Quid hodie sperandum, In dictiones docent.
units.tr: Note what kind of councils impious high priests are. He was first burdened with calumnies so that he would be hateful to all. When he replied, they drowned him out with shouts, and now they resort to open force. Thus matters usually go. If anyone prepares a defence, they either shout him down or crush him by open violence. So it happened in John 18; so Stephen was oppressed, Acts 6, 7, etc. Such councils already existed some centuries ago. What is to be hoped for today, the trials teach.

units.la: III. Reprehendit Paulus indignissimū facinus. Non imprecatur, nec peccat contra illud Matth 5. Sed ministri officio fungitur, cuius est peccata arguere & poenam denuntiare, Ioh. 16. 2. Tim. 4. Appellat digno titulo, vt Christus Matth. 23. Lucae 11. Rationem reddit, & poenam minatur.
units.tr: III. Paul rebukes the most unworthy deed. He does not curse, nor does he sin against the saying of Matt. 5, but performs the office of a minister, whose task is to rebuke sins and announce punishment, John 16; 2 Tim. 4. He addresses him with a fitting title, as Christ did, Matt. 23; Luke 11. He gives a reason and threatens punishment.

units.la: NOT. Quae sit patientia sanctorum. Non ignauia, quae impiorum audaciam forte ueat. Patienter ferunt in nomine Domini. Interim non blandiuntur, nec Dei iudicium dissimulant. Sic Dauid, Psalm. 7. Christua, Ioh. 18.
units.tr: NOTE. What the patience of the saints is: not idleness, which perhaps encourages the audacity of the impious. They bear patiently in the name of the Lord. Meanwhile they do not flatter, nor do they dissemble God's judgment. So David, Ps. 7; Christ, John 18.

units.la: Interim disce quid exspectent magistratus, qui contra leges opprimunt innocentes, aut opprimi patiuntur. Percutiet illos Dominus, qui medius interest, Ps. 82. Pharao, Exod. 1 2 3. 14. Ananias hic circa belli initium occisus a Manaimo post an. 12. Habes exempla item domestica in Augustriacis praefectis. Caue.
units.tr: Meanwhile learn what magistrates may expect, those who oppress innocent people contrary to the laws, or allow them to be oppressed. The Lord, who stands in the midst, will strike them, Ps. 82. Pharaoh, Exod. 1, 2, 3, 14. Ananias here was killed near the beginning of the war by Manaimo, after twelve years. You have domestic examples too in the Austrian prefects. Beware.

units.la: IV. Astantes Paulum corripiunt, non Ananiam. Ita tyrannis omnia licent per suos adulatores, cum subditis ne mutire quidem liceat. Eadem olim sub papatu ty rannis fuit, vt clerici sacro sancti habiti. At Paulus Ironicè pungit : Nesciebam hunc Pontif. esse, qui adeo nihil Pontificale habet, &c. Si Pont. est cur non audit causas? cur indemnatum percutit? &c. Alioqui non ignoro legem, Deut. 22. Exo. 21. Ro. 13. NOT. Magistratum, si authoritatem suam retinere velit, debitum officium facere debere, vt omnes legitimum magistratum agnoscere queant. Est hoc Dei gloriam prouehere, leges custodire, iniustam vim arcere, populi commodis studere, bono exemplo praeire. Alioqui hoc ipsum illis obijci poterit, quòd hic Ananiae. Vide 1. Sam. 2. Dantur saepe improbi propter populi peccata. Sed ijdem ideo non excusantur, & quoque Dei manum sentiunt tandem. Oremus.
units.tr: IV. The bystanders rebuke Paul, not Ananias. Thus everything is permitted to tyrants through their flatterers, while subjects may not so much as murmur. The same was once the case under the papacy, when tyrants were held to be sacrosanct clerics. But Paul pricks him ironically: I did not know this man to be high priest, who has nothing priestly about him at all, etc. If he is high priest, why does he not hear the causes? Why does he strike the unconvicted? etc. Otherwise I am not ignorant of the law, Deut. 22; Exod. 21; Rom. 13. NOTE. A magistrate, if he wishes to keep his authority, must perform his proper duty, so that all can recognise him as a lawful magistrate. It is to advance God's glory, to guard the laws, to ward off unjust violence, to study the people's welfare, and to go before them with a good example. Otherwise this very charge can be thrown at them: that here is another Ananias. See 1 Sam. 2. Wicked men are sometimes permitted because of the people's sins, but they are not for that reason excused, and in the end they feel God's hand as well. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXVIII.

units.la: 6 Quum vero noffet Paulus vnam quidem partem esse Sadducaeorum, altera vero Pharisaeorum, clamauit in consessu, Viri fratres, ego Pharisaeus sum, filius Pharisaei, de spe & resurrectione mortuorum in iudicium vocor.
units.tr: 6 When Paul knew that one part of the council was Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the assembly: "Men, brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee; I am called in judgment concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead."

units.la: 7 Quum autem haec esset locutus, orta est seditio inter Pharisaeos ac Saddu-cæos: & diuisa est multitudo.
units.tr: 7 When he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the multitude was divided.

units.la: 8 Nam Sadducæi quidem dicunt non esse resurrectionem, neq; angelum neque spiritum: Pharisæi vero vtrunq; confitentur.
units.tr: 8 For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess both.

units.la: VT Deus varie suos exercet: ita va-ria quoque habet liberationis me-dia. Exemplum huius euidentis.præsens Pauli historia exhibet. Petitur ille nouis subinde Iudæorum insidijs, & de vita peri-clitatur. Sed noua etiam subinde Deus au-xilia submini-strat, & quidé insperata. Pri-mo enim per Tribunum & milites illum furentium manibus eripit. Deinde Roma-næ ciuitatis prærogatiua à flagris defen-dit. Nunc vero, cum Tribunus illius cau-sam iniquissimis iudicibus commisisset, ipsos hostes inter se committit, vt olim quoque Madianitas, Iud.7. Imò acerrimi ipsum innocentem pronuntiant. Debent hęc consolari nos, ne metu succumbamus in periculis: quia confirmant promissiones, Psal.34 Mat.10.12 Mar.13.1 Cor.10.
units.tr: Just as God exercises His people in various ways, so He also has various means of deliverance. The present history of Paul is an evident example of this. He is assailed from time to time by new plots of the Jews, and his life is in danger. But God also supplies new aids from time to time, and these unexpected. First, through the tribune and the soldiers He snatches him from the hands of the raging men. Then the privilege of Roman citizenship defends him from the scourge. Now, when the tribune had committed his case to most unjust judges, He sets the enemies against one another, as He once did with the Midianites, Judg. 7. Indeed the fiercest of them declare the innocent man innocent. These things ought to console us, that we not succumb to fear in dangers, because they confirm the promises: Ps. 34; Matt. 10.12; Mar. 13.1; 1 Cor. 10.

units.la: 1. Causa dissensionis ponitur, quòd ad-uersarij essent diuersarum sectarum. At qui Deus vnam religionem præscripserat. Sed post Machab. ante Christum natum
units.tr: 1. The cause of the dissension is given: that the adversaries belonged to different sects. Yet God had prescribed one religion. But after the Maccabees, before the birth of Christ,

units.la: De sectis Iudaorum.
units.tr: On the sects of the Jews.

units.la: anno 130.sub Iohanne Hircano, cum Sacerdotes terrena modo curarent, & verbum Dei cessaret, sectae oriri coeperunt, tres numero, Iosephi lib.13.cap.8.17. Item de bello Iudaico lib.2. cap.7.
units.tr: in the year 130, under John Hyrcanus, when the priests attended only to earthly affairs and the word of God ceased, sects began to arise, three in number: Josephus, Antiquities, book 13, chapters 8 and 17; likewise The Jewish War, book 2, chapter 7.

units.la: A. Pharisaei, qui fatum (vt Stoici) crede bant, & toti pendebant ab astris. Non con tenti Lege. Traditiones item habebant. Operibus considebant, Matt.6.23. Luc.18. Habebantur vulgo sanctissimi. Alexand. potentes fecerat ante Christum 70.
units.tr: A. The Pharisees, who believed in fate (as the Stoics did) and depended wholly on the stars. Not content with the Law, they also had traditions. They relied on works: Matt. 6.23; Luke 18. They were commonly regarded as the most holy. Alexandra made them powerful, 70 years before Christ.

units.la: B. Sadducaei negabant fatum, & credebant liberum arbitrium. Interim spiritus negabant & resurrectionem. Epicuro pro ximi, Psal. 14.
units.tr: B. The Sadducees denied fate and believed in free will. Meanwhile they also denied spirits and the resurrection. They are closest to Epicurus: Ps. 14.

units.la: C. Effeni iustitiam factis expressuri, voluptatibus carebant & feruis, omnia habebant communia, labore suo viuebant, vita bant publica sacra, ne polluerentur. Anabapt. similes, &c.
units.tr: C. The Essenes, wishing to express righteousness in their deeds, abstained from pleasures and from slaves, held all things in common, lived by their own labour, and avoided public sacrifices lest they be polluted. They are similar to the Anabaptists, etc.

units.la: NOTA. 1. Quàm foeda Ecclesiae facies auaritia & discordia sacerdotum in ecta sit. Ita Monachi exorti in Papatu. Vigilandum ergo. Interim agnoscè Dei bonitatem, qui in tanta deformitate feminam quandam seruauit Ecclesiae.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. How foul a face the Church has been given by the avarice and discord of priests. So the monks arose under the Papacy. We must therefore be watchful. Meanwhile acknowledge God's goodness, who in such great deformity preserved a certain remnant for the Church.

units.la: Habes quod Papistis respondeas, rogantibus, an nulla omnino sub Papatu Ecclesia fuerit? Vide 1.Reg.19. If 10.Rom.10.11.
units.tr: You have here an answer for the Papists when they ask whether there was no Church at all under the Papacy. See 1 Kings 19; John 10; Rom. 10.11.

units.la: Et tunc erant Zach. Simeon, Anna, Iosephi &c. Et sub Papatu fuisse pios multos, nemo ignorat.
units.tr: And there were then Zacharias, Simeon, Anna, Joseph, etc. And that many pious people existed under the Papacy, no one is ignorant.

units.la: ¶ 2. Impios licet variè scindantur, convenire tamen aduersus Christum & Veri tatem. Omnes enim eidem principi militant. Vide Lu 22.23. &c. Debebat hoc pios ad vnitatem concordiae studium excitare. Sed hic quod eftGal.5. Nostris dissensio nibus adueísarijs animi & vires crescunt.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Though the impious are divided in various ways, they nevertheless agree against Christ and the truth, for all of them serve the same prince. See Luke 22.23, etc. This ought to have stirred the pious to a zeal for unity and concord. But here what Gal. 5 warns of occurs: our dissensions increase the courage and strength of our adversaries.

units.la: II. Paulus sciens dissidium hoc, ex tem-pore consilium captans, paucis verbis il-los commisit. Videtur dolus malus esse, aut etiam fidei abnegatio. Sed excusatur:
units.tr: II. Paul, knowing of this dissension, seized on a plan on the spur of the moment and set them against one another in a few words. This seems to be a wicked trick, or even a denial of the faith. But it is excused:

units.la: A. Quia no dabatur illi copia dicendi cau sam, & confitendi suam fidem. Cogitur ergo de alia via cogitare, iuxta illud Mat. 10.
units.tr: A. Because he was not given an opportunity to speak in his defence and confess his faith. He was therefore forced to think of another way, according to that saying, Matt. 10.

units.la: B. Non simpliciter totum Pharifaifmum confitetur, sed in solo resurrectionis articulo ipsis coniungitur, in quo recte sentient, &c. De reliquis constat ex epistolis eius. Non ergo patrocinatur exemplum hoc dissimulatoribus & negatoribus.
units.tr: B. He does not simply confess the whole of Pharisaism, but joins himself to them only on the article of the resurrection, in which they judged rightly, etc. About the rest it is clear from his letters. This example therefore does not support dissemblers and deniers.

units.la: NOT. 1. Licere pijs, vt cotra iniquos iudices effugijs vtantur: modo veritas non negetur. Quia ferè sub illorum persona veritas periclitatur, vt et à hic. Ita Dauid. 1. Sa. 21. Pfal. 34. Vide tamen, ne quid cum veritatis aut proximi iactura facias.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. It is lawful for the godly to use escapes against unjust judges, provided the truth is not denied, for truth is often endangered under their persona. So David, 1 Sam. 21; Ps. 34. Yet take care that you do not lose anything of the truth or of your neighbour.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quòd de mortuorum resurrectio ne seiudicari dicit. Atqui aliter sonabant capita accusationis. Sed hanc allegat, quæ totum fidei negotiū comprehendit. Quæ causa est, quod spem quoq; illi coniungit. In hac enim omnis sanctorum spes versatur, 1. Cor. 15. &c. Iob. 19. In mortis articulo hæc maximè consideranda, 1. Thess. 4. Vide quid negent, qui hanc negant. Idem omni impietati fenestras aperiunt; 1. Cor. 15. 2. Pet. 3. Matt. 24. Luc. 17. Oremus.
units.tr: ¶ 2. That he says the matter concerns the resurrection of the dead. Yet otherwise the heads of accusation sounded. But he cites this article, which comprehends the whole business of faith. This is why he also joins hope to it, for in it lies all the hope of the saints: 1 Cor. 15, etc.; Job 19. At the point of death these things are especially to be considered: 1 Thess. 4. See what those deny who deny it. The same opens windows to all impiety: 1 Cor. 15; 2 Pet. 3; Matt. 24; Luke 17. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXIX.

units.la: 9 Ortus est igitur clamor magnus, & quum surrexissent Scribæ ex partibus Pharisæorum depugnabant, dicentes: Nihil mali invenimus in homine isto: quod si spiritus locutus est ei seu angelus, ne repugnemus Deo.
units.tr: 9 And there arose a great cry, and the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and strove, saying: "We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, let us not fight against God."

units.la: 10 Et quum magna seditio esset, Veritus Tribunus, ne Paulus ab ipsis discerperetur, iussit militum manum descendere, & eum rapere de medio eorum, ac ducere in castra.
units.tr: 10 And when there was a great dissension, the tribune, fearing lest Paul be torn in pieces by them, ordered the soldiers to go down, take him from among them by force, and bring him into the barracks.

units.la: DOminus noster IESVS Christus à suis discessurus, eos multis argumentis consolatur aduersus omne genus tentationum. Inter illa præcipuum est propromissio Spititus sancti, qui ipsis aduoca tus futurus & in omnem veritatem indu-&turus fit.Debet hoc non modò de doctri na intelligi, verumetiam quòd in periculis consilia & rationes suggesturus sit, qui bus illa aut declinent,aut vincant,ne quid faciant præter officium. Sic ipse exponit, Luc.21. Præstitit hoc fidelissimè, vt toto hoc libro vidimus Act.3.4.5.&c.Imprimis autem euidens est exemplum, quod hîc proponitur.Paulus iam captus,per Tribu ni impudentiam productus fuit in Conci lium,vt coram iniquissimis iudicibus fidei & doctrinæ suæ rationem redderet. Erat ergo iam res deplorata, quoad homines. Sed in tempore consilium suggerit spiri-tus.Constabat enim cœtus ille ex Phari-sæis & Sadducæis, qui in fide & religione dissentiebant.Hîc ergo Paulus Pharisæum se profitetur quoad resurrectionē, de qua rectè sentiebant, & mox inter se committuntur, qui aduersus illum conspirauerant.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ, about to depart from his own, comforts them with many arguments against every kind of temptation. Among these the chief is the promise of the Holy Spirit, who will be their advocate and will lead them into all truth. This must be understood not only of doctrine but also of the fact that in dangers he will suggest counsels and reasons by which they may either avoid or overcome them, so that they do nothing beyond their duty. He himself explains this in Luke 21. He has faithfully done so, as we have seen throughout this book, Acts 3, 4, 5, etc. But the example set out here is especially clear. Paul, already seized, was brought by the shameless act of the tribune before the Council, so that he might give an account of his faith and teaching before the most unjust judges. So, humanly speaking, the matter was already hopeless. But at the right time the Spirit suggests a counsel. That assembly consisted of Pharisees and Sadducees, who disagreed about faith and religion. Here Paul professes himself a Pharisee concerning the resurrection, on which they held the right view, and straightway those who had conspired against him fall out among themselves.

units.la: ¶ Vsus omnium, vt his exemplis confirmemur in fide promissionis Dei, & in quo vis periculo simus firmi & constantes. Etsi enim aliquando impij conspirent, & omnia in extremum adducta videantur, facilè tamen est Deo suos eripere. 1.Non po-
units.tr: Here is the use of all these examples: that we may be confirmed in faith in God's promise, and be firm and constant in whatever danger we are. For even if the wicked sometimes conspire and everything seems brought to the last extremity, yet it is easy for God to snatch his own from them.

units.la: test diuturnus consensus esse inter eos, qui vtrinque prauis affectbus ducintur. 2. Deus dissipat iusto iudicio (Psal 33. 2.) vt inter se committantur. Typus, Gen. 11. Iud 7. 3. Alijs rationib. hostes in nstrum auxilium excitat, vt 1. Sam. 23 Parth & Iulian. Bella Turcica hodie & similia. Sed praesentem historiam videamus.
units.tr: (1) Agreement cannot long last among those who are driven on both sides by wicked affections. (2) God, by a just judgement, scatters (Psalm 33) and sets them against each other. A type is Genesis 11 and Judges 7. (3) By other means too, he stirs up enemies as our help, as in 1 Samuel 23; Parthians and Julians; the Turkish wars today and the like. But let us look at the history before us.

units.la: I. Qui inter Pharisaeos scribae, id est, Legis periti erant, Paulo patrocinantur, cum illum audiunt recte sentire de resurrectio ne, qui articulus summam fidei & salutis continet. Rem agunt grauiter. 1. Nihil inuenimus in homine isto. Magnum testimonium & insperatum. Sed tanta innocentiae & veritatis vis est, vt ex hostibus quoque testimonium habeat. Exempla sunt in Mose, Num. 16. Samuele, 1. Sam. 12. Dauide, 1. Samuel. 24. 26 Prophetis, Matt. 23. Martyribus, & hodie in multis. Exitet hoc ad studium innocentiae & veritatis, Ps. 34.
units.tr: But note how much better these Pharisees were than the men of our age! As soon as they hear that Paul firmly holds the foundation of faith, the hope of the resurrection, they declare him innocent and raise no further suit against him over the temple and the rites. Today, however, it is agreed that we hold rightly on all the articles of faith, and in the confession of these we agree with our adversaries. Yet we are still judged heretics, worthy of the flames, on account of purgatory, the Mass, candles and similar things, which rest on mere human traditions.

units.la: Sed Notq Quanto meliores fuerint hi Pharifaei hominibus nostri seculi? Vt primum audiunt Paulum fundamentum fidei, spem resurrectionis firmiter tenere, innocentem pronuntiant, neq; vltra ei litem mouent propter templum & ritus. At hodie constat nos de omnibus fidei ac siculis recte sentire, & in horum confessione fione nobis cum aduersarijs conuenit. Ad huc tamen hæretici & flammis digni iudi camur propter purgatorium,Miflam,Ce′ reos & similia, quæ meris hominum tradi tionibus nituntur.
units.tr: But how much better were these Pharisees than the men of our own age? As soon as they hear Paul hold firmly to the foundation of faith, the hope of resurrection, they pronounce him innocent and no longer raise a suit against him over the temple and the rites. Yet today it is agreed that we think rightly about all the articles of faith, and in confessing them we agree with our opponents. Even so we are judged heretics, worthy of the flames, on account of purgatory, the Mass, candles and the like, which rest on mere human traditions.

units.la: II.Si Spiritus,&c.Ergo reliqua fuit in il lis principium pietatis, Non esse reluctan dum Deo: vel saltem tales videri nolunt, fortassis memores Gamal. Act.5. Athodie dum Spiritus S.authoritas ex fciptura al- legatur , multi tamen adhuc sese oppo- nunt.
units.tr: II. If the Spirit, etc. So there remained in them the first principle of piety, not to resist God, or at least they are unwilling to seem to resist him, perhaps mindful of Gamaliel in Acts 5. Yet today, although the authority of the Holy Spirit is alleged from Scripture, many still set themselves against it.

units.la: Sed Nor. ¶ Tales cum Deo bellum su fcipere.Docet hoc Christus,Mat.10. Luc. 10. Quid vero hodie vulgarius? Vide Dei consilium,Pfalm.2. Huic reluctantur Pon tifices & Episcopi,conducunt Iudas & mi lites, qui & crucifigant & sepultum deti- neant. Hos iuuant principes, magistratus, &c.Faciunt idem plerique priuatim. Vult Deus vt omnes Christum amplexi , huic fe consecrent per obedientiam fidei,inno- center viuant,charitati studeant.At pleri- que diuersum faciunt. Fidem simulant & dissimulant,suos sequuntur affectus, &c. Si reprehendantur,in conuitia & blafphe mias erumpût,&c. Quid ergo miru,fi np bifcu etia pugnet Deus peste,fame,bellis? Matt.24. Soletur autem quod omnes isti nihil proficient. Vide Psalm.2.110.&c.
units.tr: But now: to wage war with God is the condition of such people. Christ teaches this in Matthew 10 and Luke 10. Yet what is more commonplace today? Look at God's counsel, Psalm 2. Pontiffs and bishops resist it, they hire Judases and soldiers, who both crucify and keep the buried one entombed. Princes and magistrates help them, and so on. Most people do the same in private. God wills that all who embrace Christ consecrate themselves to him through the obedience of faith, live blamelessly and devote themselves to charity. But most act otherwise. They pretend faith and conceal it, follow their own affections, and so on. If they are rebuked, they break out into insults and blasphemies. What wonder, then, if God also fights against them with plague, famine and wars? Matthew 24. But this is some comfort, that all these people accomplish nothing. See Psalms 2 and 110, etc.

units.la: II. Seditio efferuescit eò vfq;, vt Tribunus milites mittat iterum,&c. Et Paulus rursum prophano auxilio iuuatur.
units.tr: II. The sedition boils up to such a point that the tribune sends the soldiers again, etc. And Paul is again helped by worldly protection.

units.la: NOT. ¶ 1. Laude dignam istius Tribuni industriam. Paulus erat peregrinus, ignotus, alienæ religionis, & de religione his erat,&c. Cauet tamé,ne quid contra leges & æquum fiat de illo. Imo fe fuosq; periculo obijcit. Obseruent magistratus. Finis huius conditionis,tueri bonos,&c. Roman.13. Peccant grauiter qui vel negligunt, vel tradunt, vt Pilatus Ioh. 18.19. Fit hoc frequenter hodie.
units.tr: NOTE. (1) The tribune's diligence deserves praise. Paul was a foreigner, unknown, of a foreign religion, and of the sect concerning which, etc. Yet he takes care that nothing be done against the laws and right in regard to him. Indeed he exposes himself and his own to danger. Let magistrates take note. The purpose of this office is to protect good people, etc. Romans 13. Those who either neglect or hand over the innocent, as Pilate did in John 18 and 19, sin grievously. This happens frequently today.

units.la: Interim non modo de vi aperta, sed adijs quoque casibus hoc debet intelligi. Contra iuuenum seductores. Hic vigilet magistratus, puniat lenones,&c. Non per mittat otium.
units.tr: 2. Fornicators and seducers of virgins. Do not wish to be wiser than God (Exod. 22; Deut. 22). The nations judged these matters more righteously and defended their citizens.

units.la: 2. Scortatores & virginum ftupratores. Ne velis plus sapere quàm Deus, Exod. 22. Deut. 22. Gentes sanctius de hisiudicarunt,& ciues suos defenderunt.
units.tr: 3. Usurers, who are condemned today (Psalm 72).

units.la: 3. Vsurarios,qui hodie damnantur,Psal mo 72.
units.tr: (3) Usurers, who are condemned today; Psalm 72.

units.la: 4. Sycoph. qui sub iuris prætextu alienainuadunt. Sed ò socordiam,&c.
units.tr: (4) Sycophants, who under the pretext of law seize the property of others. But oh, the sloth, etc.

units.la: ¶ 2. Quid fiat ijs,qui veritatis causam & ministros concilij Antichristianis subijcunt. unt. Aut turpiter negligere & deferere, aut maiori periculo liberare coguntur. Exempla vtriufq; generis vidimus nostro seculo.Discant omnes in vnum Deum re/ spicere,& vtut humana cadant,fortes sint in asserenda veritate, quæ & ipsa inuicta est,& Deum habet patronum.Oremus
units.tr: (2) What is to be done with those who hand over the cause of truth and the ministers of the Word to an Antichristian council? They are forced either to desert them shamefully and neglect them, or to free them at greater risk. Examples of both kinds we have seen in our own age. Let all learn to look to the one God, and however human things fall, let them be brave in asserting the truth, which is itself unconquerable and has God as its patron. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXX.

units.la: 11 Sequenti vero nocte adstans ei Dominus, dixit: Confide Paule, vt enim testificatus es de me in Hierusalem, sic te etiam oportet testificari Romæ.
units.tr: 11 But on the following night the Lord stood by him and said: Take courage, Paul. For as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify at Rome.

units.la: 12 Orto autem die quidam ex Iudæis facta concione denouerunt se, dicentes, neque esuros, neque bibituros se, donec occiderent Paulum.
units.tr: 12 When day came, some of the Jews formed a plot and bound themselves by an oath, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

units.la: 13 Erant autem plures quam quadraginta viri qui hanc coniurationem fecerant.
units.tr: 13 There were more than forty men who had made this conspiracy.

units.la: 14 Qui adierunt principes sacerdotum & seniores, & dixerunt: Deuotione denouimus nosmet ipsos nihil esuros vsque quo trucidauerimus Paulum.
units.tr: 14 They went to the chief priests and the elders and said: We have bound ourselves by a solemn vow to taste nothing until we have slain Paul.

units.la: 15 Nunc ergo vos indicate Tribuno ex consessu voluntate, vt eum eras ad vos deducat, veluti exquisitius percognituros de ijs, quæ ad eum spectant: nos verò priusquam appropinquet, parati sumus ipsum interimere.
units.tr: 15 Now therefore you, together with the council, petition the tribune to bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you wished to inquire more carefully into the matters concerning him. But we are ready to kill him before he comes near.

units.la: 16 Quum autem filius sororis Pauli audiisset insidias, venit & ingressus in castra annuntiauit Paulo:
units.tr: 16 But when Paul's sister's son heard of the ambush, he came and entered the barracks and told Paul.

units.la: PAulus Apostolus, 2. Cor. 1. ait: Sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra. Simile est, quod habetur 1. Cor. 10. Merentur hæc fidem eò maiorem, quod ipse Paulus id expertus est, & proindeistud testari potuit. Hucusq; enim grauissime exagitatus fuit Paulus, & multa illum ad desperationem adigere poterant, cum nullibi auxilium apparere ret. Adest ergo pe richtanti Dominus, & dubitantem oraculo consolatur. Imò quod verbis pollicetur, res ipsa præstat, dum illum latronum manibus eripit. Sed præstat singula huius loci ordine considerare.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul, 2 Cor. 1, says: As the afflictions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation abounds. What is found in 1 Cor. 10 is similar. These things deserve all the more faith because Paul himself experienced them, and so could testify to them. For up to this point Paul had been most severely harassed, and many things could have driven him to despair, since no help appeared anywhere. So the Lord stands by the one who is trembling and consoles the doubting man with an oracle. Indeed, what he promises in words, the event itself carries out, while he snatches him from the hands of robbers. But let us consider the individual points of this passage in order.

units.la: I. Consolatio describitur. Nocte varia cogitanti Dominus assistit, nimirum per angelum suum, iuxta promissiones. Matt. 28. Iohannis 14. Iubet bono animo esse, eò quod Romæ etiam de ipso testificaturus sit, &c.
units.tr: I. The consolation is described. The Lord stands by him as he turns over many anxious thoughts, namely through his angel, according to the promises, Matt. 28; John 14. He bids him be of good courage, because he is also going to testify about him at Rome, etc.

units.la: NOT. 1. Deum non negligere res hominum. inum, licet aliquando horum oblitus esse videatur. Videt omnia Psal 14. 113 Admi-nistrat & gubernat, Luc. 12. Patet hoc in praesenti. Quis Paulum hunc Deo curae esse putauisset, &c. Sed iam testatur Domi-nus, nihil se inscio accidere. Sic olim factū, Exo. 1. 3. Meminerint qui innocentes op-primunt. Psal 12. 94.
units.tr: NOTE 1. God does not neglect the affairs of men, although he sometimes seems to have forgotten them. He sees all things, Ps. 14; 113. He administers and governs, Luke 12. This is evident in the present case. Who would have thought that God cared for this Paul, etc.? But now the Lord testifies that nothing happens without his knowledge. So it happened of old, Exod. 1, 3. Let those who oppress the innocent remember this. Ps. 12; 94.

units.la: 2. Qualis haec consolatio fuerit? Si verum habuit relpicias, Deus minari potius & terrere videtur: ut si quis aegroto aut mili, graviores dolores & hostes denuntiet. Solius Romae nomen terrere poterat. Sed duo illum solari potuerunt. Vnum quod se Deo curae esse vidit. Alterum quod audit, se fore organum Christi ad gloriam.
units.tr: 2. What kind of consolation was this? If you look at the truth, God seems rather to threaten and terrify, as if someone were to announce heavier pains and enemies to a sick man or a soldier. The name of Rome alone could terrify. But two things could comfort him. One, that he saw he was a concern to God. The other, that he heard he would be an instrument of Christ for his glory.

units.la: Discimus: A. Vnde nobis consolatio petenda. Non exlaeto rerum successu, sed ex Dei prouidentia, & cum patet nos esse vt sa gloriae. Huc Christus relegat, Matth. 10. Psal. 56. Luc. 12. Obseruandum in morbis, Psal. 39. tu fecisti, &c.
units.tr: We learn: A. Where consolation is to be sought: not from a happy outcome of affairs, but from God's providence, and when it is clear that we exist for his glory. Christ refers us to this, Matt. 10; Ps. 56; Luke 12. To be observed in sicknesses, Ps. 39: "You have done it," etc.

units.la: B. Deum consolando & liberando nos ad maiora certamina praeparare. Sic Act. 4. 5. Intelligunt hoc sancti, & ideo alacri-ter ad opus redeunt. Arguuntur, qui libe-rati sibi immunitatem quandam pollicen-tur, vel etiam carnis libidini improbe in-dulgent.
units.tr: B. That God, by consoling and freeing us, prepares us for greater struggles. So Acts 4, 5. The saints understand this, and therefore return eagerly to the work. Those are rebuked who, once set free, promise themselves some immunity, or even wickedly indulge the lusts of the flesh.

units.la: II. Fidem facit promissioni suæ Domi-nus, dum eximprouiso periculo Apostolum liberat. Circumstantiæ omne excusiendæ.1. Authores & complices. Viri quâ draginta deuouent se non esuros, &c.
units.tr: II. The Lord keeps his promise, while he frees the Apostle from an unforeseen danger. Every circumstance is to be weighed. 1. The authors and accomplices: more than forty men vow that they will not eat, etc.

units.la: Genef.9. Num.35. Deuouent se, non cogitantes, quàm multa possint incidere quæ impediant. Disce deijs iudicare, qui religionem suam armis defendunt. Interim nostra socordia arguitur, qui pro Christi gloria vix mouemus vel digitum.
units.tr: Gen. 9; Num. 35. They vow without considering how many things may happen to hinder them. Learn from this to judge those who defend their religion with arms. Meanwhile our sloth is rebuked, who hardly move a finger for the glory of Christ.

units.la: II. Rem ad sacerdotes referunt, quibus nimirum placuit, &c. Consilio exponunt ipsi, & sceleris socios fieri volunt. Vos petetis vt ad tribunal producatur. Nos euntem intercipiemus, &c.
units.tr: II. They refer the matter to the priests, who of course were pleased, etc. They explain the plan themselves and want to make them partners in the crime: "You ask that he be brought before the tribunal; we will intercept him as he goes," etc.

units.la: Mat.10. Ita olim factum. âtum non semel. Exempla nostri seculi. ¶ Quanta fuerit corruptio totius gentis, quando horrendum hoc facinus Sacerdotes communicare audent. Sic Iudas Iohannes 12. Quare digni fuerunt qui omnes perirent. Hoc ipsum sibi polliceantur, qui hodie contra omne ius Antichristi sacerdotibus seruiunt.
units.tr: Matt. 10. So it happened of old, and not only once. Examples from our own age. ¶ How great was the corruption of the whole nation, when priests dare to share in this horrible crime! So Judas, John 12. Why were those worthy to perish, all of them? Let those who today serve the priests of Antichrist against all right promise themselves the same thing.

units.la: III. Deus turbat nefarium consilium. Re sciscit enim nepos Pauli, iuxta illud, Luc. 12. Per puerum ergo turbatur.
units.tr: III. God disturbs the wicked plan. For the nephew of Paul learns of it, according to that saying, Luke 12. Thus through a boy he is disturbed.

units.la: NOT. ¶ Deo facile esse, vt per ludibrium quoque impiorum consilia turbet, Psalmo 2. 33. Non est enim prudentia neque consilium contra Dominum, Prouerbior. 21. Isaiae octavo. Videt & nouit omnia. Psa. 113. 14. Est item omnipotens. Sic puer expositiuus Moses Ægyptum vexat, Exod. 2. 3. &c. Iahel, Iudic. 4. Iudith, Capite 13. Simile exemplum vrbs nostra habuit. Anno 1350. Fidamus Domino & Oremus.
units.tr: NOTE. It is easy for God to disturb even the plans of the impious, through the very mockery of the wicked, Ps. 2; 33. For there is no wisdom nor counsel against the Lord, Prov. 21; Isa. 8. He sees and knows all things, Ps. 113; 14. He is also almighty. So a child, Moses the expositor, vexes Egypt, Exod. 2, 3, etc. Jael, Judg. 4. Judith, chapter 13. Our own city had a similar example in the year 1350. Let us trust in the Lord, and pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXI.

units.la: 17 Paulus autem aduocato quo-dam ex centurionibus, ait: adolescentem hunc abduc ad tribunum: habet enim quod annuntiet ei.
units.tr: 17 Then Paul called one of the centurions and said: Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him.

units.la: 18 Ille igitur acceptum eum duxit
units.tr: 18 So the centurion took him and brought him

units.la: ad Tribunum, & dixit: Vinctus Paulus aduocatum me rogauit vt hunc adduc̄ adolescentem ducerem ad te, qui aliquid habeat quod tibi loquatur.
units.tr: to the tribune, and said: Paul, the prisoner, called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to say to you.

units.la: 19 Tribunus vero prehensa eius manu, quum secessisset seorsum percontatus est: Quid est quod habes mihi annuntiandum.
units.tr: 19 The tribune took him by the hand, drew him aside, and asked him privately: What is it that you have to report to me?

units.la: 20 Ille autem dixit, Iudaei constituerunt te rogare, vt cras Paulum deducas in concilium, quasi aliquid exquisitius percontaturi sint de eo.
units.tr: 20 He said: The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as if they intended to inquire more closely into something about him.

units.la: 21 Tu vero ne ipsis assentitor: insidiantur enim ei ex illis viri plures quadraginta qui seipsos devoverunt, neque esuros neque bibituros, donec interemerint eum: & nunc parati sunt ex spectantes quid ad te renuntietur.
units.tr: 21 But do not give in to them. More than forty of them are lying in wait for him; they have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink until they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your answer.

units.la: 22 Tribunus igitur dimisit adolescentem, quum ei praecepisset vt nulli effutiret, se haec ipsi indicasse.
units.tr: 22 So the tribune dismissed the young man, after ordering him to tell no one that he had revealed this to him.

units.la: 23 Et aduocatis duobus quibusdam ex Centurionibus, iussit vt parent milites ducentos, qui proficiscerentur Caesaream vsq; ad, & equites septuaginta & stipatores ducentos a tertia hora noctis.
units.tr: 23 Then he called two of the centurions and ordered them to get ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, starting at the third hour of the night.

units.la: 24 Et vt iumenta praeberent, vt impositum Paulum saluum perducerent ad Felicem praesidem. Quam-
units.tr: 24 And they were to provide mounts, so that they might set Paul upon them and bring him safely to Felix the governor. Although

units.la: QVmuis Deus suis iuxta promissio nes semper praesens adsit, ita tamē eosdem consolatur & iuuat, vt aduersis fi-mul illorum successus temperet. Causa est, quòd sic illos in officio retinere, & il-lorum fidem exercere vult, vt ab ipso vno pendere & ad eundem omnia referre di-scant. Exemplum huius in Paulo habemus. Grauissimè tentato apparet Dominus, & ipsam Romæ etiam de se testificaturum dicit, quæ maxima consolatio fuit. Sed ec-ce mox contra illum conspirant xl. viri, sicque rem instituunt, vt vix saluari posse videatur. Id verò planè pugnare videbatur cum promissionibus Dei, &c. Sed a-gnoscit morem Dei Paulus, nec propterea concidit animo, nec etiam promissis suis ille deest. Horum ergo consideratione fi-dem nostram confirmemus, si quando rerum progressus Dei promissionibus minos respondet, & ille cunctatur, Hab. 2. In præsenti personas consideram.
units.tr: Although God is always present with his people, according to his promises, he so comforts and helps them that he tempers their successes with adversities. The reason is that he wishes to keep them in their duty in this way and to exercise their faith, so that they learn to depend on him alone and refer everything to him. We have an example of this in Paul. When he was sorely tested, the Lord appeared to him and said that he would also bear witness concerning him at Rome, which was a very great consolation. But soon afterwards forty men conspire against him and arrange matters so that it seems hardly possible for him to be saved. This indeed seemed plainly to conflict with God's promises, etc. But Paul recognises God's manner, and he does not therefore lose heart, nor does God fail his promises. Let us therefore confirm our faith by considering these things, if at any time the progress of affairs answers less to God's promises and he seems to delay (Hab. 2). Now let us consider the persons in the present case.

units.la: I. Paulum, quid fecerit, vbi periculum audiuit imminere. Non stulte iactat pro-missiones & prouidentiam Dei, &c. Sed (quod vnum restabat in humanis) curat, vt Tribunus rem intelligat, à quo etiam de-sendi cupit, & quidem armata manu. Et ne puer suspectus esset, addit ei Centurionē.
units.tr: I. What Paul did when he heard that danger was impending. He does not foolishly boast of God's promises and providence, etc. But (which was the one thing left among human means) he takes care that the tribune understands the matter, and from him he also wishes to be defended, and indeed with an armed escort. And lest the young man be suspected, he adds a centurion to him.

units.la: NOT. 1. Vt Dei promissionib. & prout dentia vti debeamus. Gubernat is omnia æterno suo consilio, quod non eritirritu. Pf.113.139.33. Mat.10. Idem se pollicetur af- futurum suis, Pf.34. If.65. Zach.2.12 Luc 12. Matt.6 10.28. Credunt his pij firmiter. Interim medijs licitis & diuinitus oblatis vtuntur. Vide Pauli exemplum, &c. Sic Dauid sub Saule, cum Dei promissiones haberet, 1. Sam.16. Psalm.89 132. Ezechias, Isa.36.37. Christus quoq; fugit, &c. Item Matt.4.10.
units.tr: NOTE 1. That we should use God's promises and providence. He governs all things by his eternal counsel, which will not be void (Ps. 113, 139, 33; Matt. 10). He likewise promises to be with his own (Ps. 34; Is. 65; Zech. 2:12; Luke 12; Matt. 6, 10, 28), and the godly firmly believe these things. Meanwhile they use lawful means and those offered by God. See Paul's example, etc. So David under Saul, when he had God's promises (1 Sam. 16; Ps. 89, 132); Hezekiah (Is. 36, 37); Christ also fled, etc. Likewise Matt. 4:10.

units.la: Discimus, non tentandum esse Dominum, vt licita media sub praetextu promissionum Dei negligamus. Eadem ratio observetur, quae in agricultura, 1.Cor 3. Hoc cum primis cauendum, ne ex diffidentia, illicitis vtamur, &c.
units.tr: We learn that the Lord must not be tempted, so that we neglect lawful means under the pretext of God's promises. The same principle should be observed as in agriculture (1 Cor. 3). Above all we must guard against using unlawful means out of distrust, etc.

units.la: 2 Licere pijs, vt magistratus opem & defensione implorent. Licet enim vti bonis Dei ordinationibus. Atqui talis est magistratus, Rom.13. Psal.72.82. Ideo Paulus non modo ad leges recurrit, vt Act.16 22. sed armis quoq; se defendi cupit, & quidem Ethnicis, quaeq; in sanguinis effusione exi re poterant. Nec enim ipse author fuit.
units.tr: 2. It is lawful for the godly to implore the aid and defence of the magistrate. For it is lawful to use God's good ordinances, and such is the magistrate (Rom. 13; Ps. 72, 82). Therefore Paul not only has recourse to the laws (Acts 16:22), but also wishes to be defended by arms, and indeed by pagans, though this could end in bloodshed. For he himself was not the author of it.

units.la: Arguuntur, qui ista simpliciter pijs neg- gant sub patientiae praetextu, & allegant, Matt.5. At si horum exemplum vallet, ne orandum quidem.Sed priuata tantummo do vindicta prohibetur, Deut.22. Interim legitimâ vtendum, vt Deo viuamus diu-tissimè.
units.tr: They are refuted who simply deny these things to the godly under the pretext of patience, and cite Matt. 5. But if their example held, not even prayer should be made. Yet only private vengeance is forbidden (Deut. 22). Meanwhile lawful means are to be used, so that we may live to God as long as possible.

units.la: II. Centurionem,quo internuntio Paulus vtitur.Facilis est,vt captiuo inseruiat. Nota. {a}Deum suis gratiam dare,vt homines illis libenter gratificentur. Sic olim in Ægypto,Exo.12.Ioseph, Gen. 39. Daniel, Cap. 1. Huic ergo nos approbemus vnicè,&c.
units.tr: II. The centurion, through whom Paul makes use of an intermediary. He is readily made to serve the captive. {a}Note that God gives his people grace so that men gladly do them favours. So formerly in Egypt (Exod. 12); Joseph (Gen. 39); Daniel (ch. 1). We should therefore wholly approve this.

units.la: Interim iuxta Centurionis exemplum liberter inseruiamus afflictis. Ita enim Christo seruitur,Mat.25 Hodie ferè pudet nos eorum,qui pro veritate periclitantur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, following the centurion's example, let us gladly serve the afflicted. For thus Christ is served (Matt. 25). Today we are almost ashamed of those who are in peril for the truth.

units.la: III.Tribunum,in quo maximæ virtutes elucent, nimirum Domino has operante. 1.Humanitas.Libenter audit,prehensa manu quasi inuitans.
units.tr: III. The tribune, in whom the greatest virtues shine forth, the Lord working these in him. 1. Humanity: he gladly listens, taking him by the hand as if inviting him.

units.la: Nota. {b}In magistratibus præcipuè requiri,vt facilis ad eos sit aditus,& libenter audiant. Sic Deum imitantur, cuius nomen habent. Et quia multos pudor & metus impediunt, humanitate illis animu ad dant.
units.tr: Note b) In magistrates it is especially required that access to them be easy and that they listen willingly. In this they imitate God, whose name they bear. And because shame and fear hinder many people, they encourage them by kindness.

units.la: II. Non difficulter credit, licet multa possent suspectam reddere narrationem. Sed respicit ad sæpe perspectam Iudæorum malitiam,&c. Nec indignè fert puerum consultorem.
units.tr: II. He does not believe too hard-heartedly, although many things could make the account seem suspect. But he looks to the Jews' malice, which he has often observed, etc. Nor does he take it badly that a youth has come as an adviser.

units.la: No.{q}Magistratus circumspectos esse debere, nec nimium difficiles ad credendum. Vitanda quidem leuitas, sed vbi rationes afferuntur probabiles, non contemnant. Id enim multos bonos, totasque respublicas saepe perdidit, &c. Hodie non licet referre quae noxia sunt. Amyclae.
units.tr: Note q) Magistrates ought to be circumspect and not too difficult to believe. Lightness indeed is to be avoided, but when probable reasons are offered they should not despise them. For this has often ruined many good men and whole commonwealths, etc. Today it is not permitted to report what is harmful. Amyclae.

units.la: III. Inductria summa. Nihil eorum non facit, quae ad casum praesente pertinebant. Silentium praecipit, ne coiuratores nouum consilium capiant. Milites huic negotio destinat, cum iumentis. Obseruat noctem vt sine tumultu res transigatur. Addit literas commendatitias. Facta haec non sine labore & sumptibus. NO T. {q}Magistratus esse, vt in bonis defendendis, nullis vel laboribus vel sumptibus parcant, imo pro illis etiam periclitentur. Nec enim frustra gerunt gladium, Rom. 13. Ita Pilatus, egisse debuit, Ioh. 18. 19.
units.tr: III. Very great diligence. He omits nothing of what pertained to the present crisis. He orders silence, lest the conspirators adopt a new plan. He assigns soldiers and mounts to this business. He schedules the night so that the matter is carried out without tumult. He adds letters of recommendation. These things were done not without labour and expense. NOTE q) Magistrates should be such that, in defending good people, they spare no labour or expense, but even expose themselves to danger for them. For they do not bear the sword in vain (Rom. 13). So Pilate ought to have acted (John 18, 19).

units.la: Arguuntur Ethnici exemplo multi ex Christianis, qui 100. potius ministros tradere vellent hostibus, quàm tot labores & sumptus sustinere &c. Sed ne terreat mun di ingratitudo. Etsi cessent homines, non deerit Deus, qui vbiq; iuuare potest &c.
units.tr: Heathens are put to shame by the example of many Christians, who would rather hand over a hundred ministers to their enemies than undergo so many labours and expenses, etc. But let not the world's ingratitude terrify us. Even if men cease to help, God will not fail, who can help everywhere, etc.

units.la: Oremus.
units.tr: Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXII.

units.la: 25 Scripsit Tribunus literas in hanc summam:
units.tr: 25 The tribune wrote a letter to this effect:

units.la: 26 Claudius Lysias potentissimo præsidi Felici salutem.
units.tr: 26 Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix, greetings.

units.la: 27 Virum hunc comprehensum à Iudæis cum jam esset ab eis interimendus, superveniens cum militum manu, eruì, quum cognovissem Romanum esse:
units.tr: 27 This man was seized by the Jews, and was about to be killed by them. But I came up with a body of soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman.

units.la: 28 Et volens scire causam, cur eum criminarentur, deduxi eum in ipsorum consessum.
units.tr: 28 Wishing to know the charge on which they accused him, I brought him down before their council.

units.la: 29 Quem comperi accusari de quæstionibus Legis ipsorum, nullius criminis reum quod sit dignum morte aut vinculis.
units.tr: 29 I found that he was accused concerning questions of their Law, but that he was charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.

units.la: 30 Quum autem mihi indicatum esset insidias huic viro factum iri à Iudæis, eo ipso momento misi eum ad te: et denuntiavi quoque accusatoribus, ut quæ habent adversus eum, dicant apud te. Vale.
units.tr: 30 When it was reported to me that the Jews were going to lay a plot against this man, I sent him to you at once, and I also told his accusers to state their case against him before you. Farewell.

units.la: 31 Postero autem die relictis equitibus, qui cum eo irent, reversi sunt in castra.
units.tr: 31 So the soldiers, as they had been ordered, took Paul by night to Antipatris.

units.la: 32 Qui quum venissent Cæsaream et reddidissent epistolam præsidi, sisteb bant coram eo etiam Paulum.
units.tr: 32 On the next day they left the horsemen to go on with him and returned to the barracks. When these came to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.

units.la: 33 Quum legisset autem literas Præses, & interrogatus ex qua provincia esset, ac cognovisset e Cilicia.
units.tr: 33 When the governor had read the letter, and had asked from what province he was, and learned that he was from Cilicia,

units.la: 34 Audiam te, inquit, quum accusatores tui adfuerint. Iussitque in prætorio Herodis ipsum custodiri.
units.tr: 34 he said: "I will hear you when your accusers have come." And he ordered him to be kept under guard in Herod's palace.

units.la: SPiritus sanctus summa diligentia com memorat, ut Paulus Romanorum mi-litum opera Iudæorum insidijs subductus sit, ita ut minutissima quæqueferè ad naufragam vsque inculcare videatur. Causa verò huius diligentiæ est, quod ex his Dei fides in promissis suis præstandis, adhæc eiusdem præsentia elucent. Promiserat enim Paulum Romæ etiam de se testificaturum esse. Id quia Iudæi latrones impedire conabantur, illorum conatus mirificè eludit, & quidem illorum opera, qui & ipsi Christianæ fidei hostes, & fortassis ab omni religione alienissimi erant. Quia enim in Dei manu sunt hominum corda (Prou. 21.) pro suo arbitrio illa inclinare, & hostium quoque opera uti potest. Huic ergo hoc omne debet tribui, qui sic egit per milites hosce, ut omnes in Pauli obse-quium & salutem coniurauisse putes. Vsus omnium, ut fidei confirmandæ seruiant. Sed singula ordine videamus.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit recounts this with the greatest care, so that the way Paul was snatched from the plots of the Jews by the work of Roman soldiers is set out, down to almost every smallest detail, right up to the shipwreck. The reason for this care is that by these things the faithfulness of God in fulfilling his promises shines forth, and his presence as well. For he had promised that Paul would also bear witness about himself at Rome. Because the Jews, robbers that they were, tried to hinder this, God wonderfully frustrated their attempts, and indeed through the work of those who were themselves enemies of the Christian faith and perhaps utterly alien to every religion. For the hearts of men are in the hand of God (Prov. 21.), and he can turn them as he pleases, and he can also use the work of enemies. All this, therefore, must be attributed to him, who so acted through these soldiers that you would think they had all conspired for Paul's safety and well-being. He uses all things so that they serve to strengthen faith. But let us look at the individual points in order.

units.la: RHOD. GVAL. HOM. ARCHET. 429
units.tr: RHOD. GVAL. HOM. ARCHET. 429

units.la: I.Ponitur exemplum epistolæ,quo pręter alia docemur,qua breuitate veteres in rebus grauissimis vsi sint.Hodie quia plus simulationis & minùs fidei est,in vsu habe tur verbofitas nimia, &c. Corruptionis magnæ argumentum, quod sub publica authoritate fallere licet.
units.tr: I. The example of the letter is set out, by which we are taught, among other things, with what brevity the ancients handled the weightiest matters. Today, because there is more pretence and less faith, excessive wordiness is in use, etc. It is a great sign of corruption that one may deceive under public authority.

units.la: Partes sunt. 1. Inscriptio,docens à quo Felix quùm & cui mittatur: quisq; tunc temporis lu. Vide Suet. dęs præfuerit,Felix nimirùm,de quo mul ta scribunt historici.Fuit libertus Claudij è vulgo feré principis stoliditate euectus, vt nobilis præriperet honores publicos. Et vt tales feré solent, libidine & crudeli tate infamis fuit. Trium reginarum mari tus, è quibus Drufillam Aziazo Amafo rum Regi eripuit.Cyprij Magi arte & ope ra.Ionathæ Pontif.latrones in templo sub Ios. Antiq. misit.Huiùs iam Paulus committitur. Atta lib.20. c.4. men præter omnem spem sub illo tutus 9. est. Verisimum ergo quod initio dixi mus,& stulti sunt,qui homines metuunt.
units.tr: There are parts. 1. The inscription, which shows from whom Felix, when and to whom it is sent, and who was then governor of the province: namely Felix, about whom the historians write much. He was a freedman of Claudius, raised from the common people by the emperor's stupidity, so that as a noble he might seize public offices. And, as such men usually are, he was infamous for lust and cruelty. He was the husband of three queens, of whom he snatched Drusilla from King Azizus of the Emesenes. By the art and help of a Cyprian magician See Suetonius. ... He sent the robbers of the high priest Jonathan into the temple Josephus, Antiquities. Paul is now committed to him. Yet book 20, chapter 4 contrary to all hope he is safe under him 9. Therefore what we said at the beginning is true, and those are fools who fear men.

units.la: Interim Not.¶Conditionem populi aliquando liberi, qui peccatis Dei iram prouocauit,& libertate exutus est. Tales olim Iudæi, Exod.5.19. Amos 3. Mich.6. Rom.9.Sed non agnouerunt & libertate abusi sunt. Vide Isaiæ 28.Amos 2. 2.Paral. 36.Matt.23.Luc.19.Tandem exteris auxilijs contra se inuicem vsi. Iam ergo tales habent principes. Et tandem omnino reijciuntur, Rom.10.11. Matth.21. Vide quid nobis sperandum hodie, quorum similes mores sunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile, NOTE: the condition of a people once free, who provoked God's anger by their sins and was stripped of liberty. Such were the Jews once: Exod. 5:19; Amos 3; Mic. 6; Rom. 9. But they did not recognise it and abused their liberty. See Isa. 28; Amos 2; 2 Chron. 36; Matt. 23; Luke 19. Finally they used foreign aids against one another. So such people now have princes. And finally they are utterly rejected: Rom. 10, 11; Matt. 21. See what we should expect today, whose manners are similar.

units.la: II. Narrationem instituit, qua Paulum non obscure commendat.
units.tr: II. He begins the narrative, by which he commends Paul not obscurely.

units.la: Primo enim captiuitatis causam in Iudeos reijcit, qui ipsum indicta causa voluerint occidere. Deinde docet Romanum esse. Tertio innocentiae testimonium fert. Hic tamen vt homo prophanus loquitur, & pro communi Romanorum more, qui cum Iudaeorum religionem omnino abolitam cuperent, controuersias de hac obortas facile negligebant. Interim aliter Deus iubet, Deut. 13. Et Christiano magistratui religio cum primis cordi esse debet, cum a Deo ordinatus sit, Deut.1. Rom.13. Psal.72 82. &c.
units.tr: For first he puts the cause of the imprisonment on the Jews, who wanted to kill him without a hearing of the case. Then he shows that he is a Roman. Third, he bears witness to his innocence. Yet here he speaks as a worldly man, and in accordance with the common Roman custom, which, although they wished the Jewish religion utterly abolished, easily ignored the disputes that arose about it. Meanwhile God commands otherwise, Deut. 13. And for a Christian magistrate religion ought above all to be dear to his heart, since he has been ordained by God: Deut. 1; Rom. 13; Ps. 72, 82, etc.

units.la: Interim NOTA. 1. Quam callide diffi mulet errorem suum, quod scilicet ipsum contra Leges vinciuiffet, & flagris examinari iussisset. Solum hoc scribit, quod laudi esse poterat. Proprium filijs seculi hoc, &c.
units.tr: Meanwhile, NOTE 1. How cunningly he dissembles his error, namely that he had bound him contrary to the laws and ordered him to be examined by scourging. He writes only what could bring him praise. This is proper to the children of this age, etc.

units.la: 2. Quam Deo sui curae sint, quando ipsorum innocentiam hostium quoq; testimonio asserit. Ita impletur, Psalm. 34. Ita cum Christo factum, Ioh.18.19. Sic 1.
units.tr: 2. How dear they are to God, when he asserts their innocence even by the testimony of their enemies. Thus it is fulfilled, Ps. 34. Thus it happened with Christ, John 18:19. So 1

units.la: Sam.24.26. Ita hostes Apostolicæ doctri-næ hodie quoq; testimonium ferunt Apo-stolis.
units.tr: Sam. 24:26. Thus enemies of apostolic doctrine even today bear witness to the Apostles.

units.la: III. Præoccupatione exponit causam, quare innocentem non dimiserit, sed tan-tis sumptibus ad Felicem mittat: Propter insidias, quas dimissus non euasisset.
units.tr: III. By anticipation he explains the reason why he did not release the innocent man but sent him with such expense to Felix: because of the plots which, had he been released, he would not have escaped.

units.la: Vbi NOTA. ¶ Magistratibus vnicè cu-randum esse, ne quis vim patiatur. Hoc vnicè requiritur, Pfal.72. Rom.13.
units.tr: Here NOTE: magistrates must take care above all that no one suffers violence. This alone is required: Ps. 72; Rom. 13.

units.la: II. Milites commissum munus fideliffi-mè executuntur, abfq; murmure. Imitan-da humanitas hęc & fides omnibus. Simul verò NOT. ¶ Omne hoc Dei beneficium fuisse, qui horum animos Paulo conciliauit. Ita contra Esauum Iacob defenditur, Ge. 32 33. Huic ergo nos approbemus, nec po-terunt deesse hominum erga nos studia.
units.tr: II. The soldiers carry out the duty entrusted to them most faithfully, without complaint. This humanity and fidelity is to be imitated by all. At the same time NOTE: all this was a benefit of God, who won over the minds of these men to Paul. Thus Jacob is defended against Esau, Gen. 32, 33. Let us therefore commend ourselves to him, and the goodwill of men towards us will not be lacking.

units.la: III. Quid Felix præses? Legit epistolam, & quasi naturam exuerit humaniter quæ-rit cuias fit. Causæ vero cognitionem in aduersariorum aduentum reijcit. Interim in liberali custodia ipsum seruari curat. Ita gentes subinde Iudæis humaniores & æquiores sunt.
units.tr: III. What does Governor Felix do? He reads the letter and, as if he had put off his nature, humanely asks what province he is from. But he defers the hearing of the case until the arrival of his adversaries. Meanwhile he takes care that Paul is kept in liberal custody. Thus Gentiles are at times more humane and fairer than Jews.

units.la: Imitandus Felix Magistratibus & priua-tis. Humaniter agant, in causis alteram quoque partem audiant. Sic locus præclu-ditur calumnijs, Deut.17. Oremus.
units.tr: Felix is to be imitated by magistrates and private persons: let them act humanely and hear the other party too in causes. Thus a place is closed to slanders, Deut. 17. Let us pray.

units.la: CAPVT XXIV. HOMILIA CLXXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24. HOMILY 183.

units.la: POst quinque autem dies descendit Princeps Sacerdotu Ananias cum Senioribus & Tertullo quodam oratore : qui comparuerunt coram praside contra Paulum.
units.tr: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with the elders and a certain orator named Tertullus, and they appeared before the governor against Paul.

units.la: 2 Et citato Paulo coepit accusare Tertullus, dicens:
units.tr: And when Paul was summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying:

units.la: 3 Nos per te tuaeq; prudentiae egregiae in hac gente facmora multam pacem consequutos, & prorsus & ubiq; agnoscimus, praestantissime Felix, cum omni gratiarum actione.
units.tr: Since through you we enjoy great peace, and since your remarkable prudence has brought many reforms to this nation, most excellent Felix, we acknowledge this in every way and everywhere, with all thanksgiving.

units.la: 4 Ne vero te diutius interpellem, rogo te vt audias nos paucis pro tua aequitate.
units.tr: So that I do not detain you longer, I ask you to hear us briefly, in keeping with your fairness.

units.la: 5 Comperimus enim virum hunc esse pestilentem, & qui moueat seditionem omnibus Iudaeis per vniuersum orbem, & principem sectae Nazarenorum.
units.tr: For we have found this man to be a pestilence, one who stirs up sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.

units.la: 6 Qui templum quoque tentauit profanare: quem etiam prehensum voluimus secundum Legem nostram iudicare.
units.tr: He also tried to profane the temple, and we seized him and wanted to judge him according to our Law.

units.la: 7 Sed interueniens Tribunus Lysias, fias, cum magna vi abduxit eum e manibus nostris.
units.tr: But the tribune Lysias came in and with great force took him out of our hands.

units.la: 8 Iussit ipsius accusatoribus adire venire: ex quo poteris ipse, inquisitione habita, de omnibus iis cognoscere, de quibus nos eum accusamus.
units.tr: He ordered his accusers to come to you, so that you yourself, by examining him, may learn of all those things of which we accuse him.

units.la: 9 Consenserunt autem etiam Iudaei dicentes, haec ita se habere.
units.tr: The Jews also joined in the accusation, saying that these things were so.

units.la: DEscribit hoc Cap. Lucas quid Paulo apud Felicem Persidem euenerit, cui illum ab Hierosolymis transmissum fuisse audi-uimus. Et primo quidem actio capitalis proponitur, vbi a quibus & de quibus accusatus sit narratur. Deinde vt sese defendere-t, exponitur. Tandem, vt Felix toto bieni-o captum detinuerit, & discedens in vi-culis reliquerit, quem innocentem esse no-uerat. Describuntur haec, vt inde discamus. A. Quae semper piorum fors in hoc mundo futura sit, & quid aduersum illos mundus facere soleat. Nullis sumptibus aut laboribus parcunt Iudaei. Sic fit nimirum quod Christus praedixit, Matth. 5. 10. Iohan. 15. 16. Mar. 13. 2. Tim. 3. Et hoc Apostolorum exemplis probari oportuit, vt minus offendamur. B. Quomodo pij se gerere debeant, &c. In primis patientiae studendum.Biennio toto,&c. In morbis. In præsenti primam partem videamus.
units.tr: In this chapter Luke describes what happened to Paul before Felix the governor, to whom we heard he had been sent from Jerusalem. First the capital charge is set forth, where it is related by whom and about what he was accused. Then it is explained how he defended himself. Finally, how Felix kept him in custody for two years, and on leaving left him in chains, though he knew him to be innocent. These things are recorded so that we may learn from them: (A) what the lot of the godly is always to be in this world, and what the world is accustomed to do against them. The Jews spare no expense or labour. So, surely, what Christ foretold comes to pass (Matt. 5.10; John 15.16; Mark 13.2; 2 Tim. 3). And this had to be proved by the examples of the apostles, so that we may be less offended. (B) How the godly ought to conduct themselves, and so on. Above all, we must cultivate patience. "For two whole years," and so on: concerning diseases. For now let us look at the first part.

units.la: I. Partes producuntur,quæ coràm Felice comparuerunt. Ab vna parte stete runt Pontifex, Seniores,Tertullus famo- sissimus rhetor. Ab altera Paulus, &c quidem solus atq; vinctus,&c.
units.tr: I. The parties who appeared before Felix are brought forward. On one side stood the high priest, the elders, and Tertullus, a most notorious orator. On the other side stood Paul, alone and in chains.

units.la: Nota. ¶ Qui semper veritatis hostes sint, quibusq; armis pugnent? Nimirum primates huius mundi, &c maxime hi, qui religionem quæstum fecerunt. Tales isti erant,Ioh.2.Matth.15.23. Atq; isti ferè instructissimi sunt,authoritate,præsentia,eloquentia.Econtra pij contempti,&c.Sic olim in Ægypto,Exo.5.6.7.Sub Achab, 1. Reg.18.22.Tempore Ieremiæ. Idem Christus expertus est,& Apostoli.Nec meliora speres hodie.
units.tr: Note: Who are always the enemies of truth, and with what weapons do they fight? Surely the leaders of this world, and especially those who have made a trade of religion. Such men were these (John 2; Matt. 15; 23). And these are usually very well equipped, with authority, presence and eloquence. On the other hand, the godly are despised, and so on. So it was once in Egypt (Exod. 5, 6, 7); under Ahab (1 Kings 18.22); in the time of Jeremiah. Christ himself experienced the same, and the apostles. Nor should you hope for better today.

units.la: Seruiunt hæc: 1.Institutioni,nè ex multi tudine & authoritate sestatorū de religio ne iudicemus.Ita enim Prophetas & Apo stolos damnare oporteret. Pusillus grex Christi fidelium,Luc.12.Matth.7.Alioqui Turca præualeret suffragijs.11.Consolati- oni,ne terreamur,etiamsi nobis quoq; so- lis standum sit.Recurramus ad promissi- ones,Lucæ12.21.Matth.10.Mar.13 &c.
units.tr: These things serve: (1) for instruction, lest we judge about religion by the number and authority of its followers. For in that case we would have to condemn the prophets and apostles. "Little flock" of Christ's faithful (Luke 12; Matt. 7). Otherwise the Turk would prevail by votes. (2) For consolation, lest we be terrified even if we must stand alone. Let us have recourse to the promises (Luke 12.21; Matt. 10; Mark 13, and so on).

units.la: II. Oratio. tribus partibus constans:
units.tr: II. The speech, consisting of three parts:

units.la: 1. Exordio , in quo beneuolentiam captant, tant, partim à Felicis, partim ab ipsorum persona. Sed vtrobiq; mentiuntur. Nam Felix pesfim è prqfuit, vt patet ex Iosepho, Cornelio Tacito, &c. Deinde ipsi quoque subinde tumultuari sunt contra Romanos. Sed ideo laudant tranquillum statum, vt Paulum imitatur reddant, quasi huius tur batorem.
units.tr: (1) The exordium, in which they seek goodwill, partly from the person of Felix and partly from their own. But in both respects they lie. For Felix was a most harmful governor, as is clear from Josephus, Cornelius Tacitus, and others. Moreover, the Jews themselves repeatedly stirred up tumults against the Romans. But they praise the peaceful state of affairs so that they may make Paul look like a disturber of it, as if he were its agitator.

units.la: Nota. Quantum possit Veritatis odium. Impellit vt eum laudent, quem maxime oderant quia mundo nil magis exosum, Ioh. 3. Caesarem Christo praeferunt. Imo Barrabam, Ioh. 19. Luc. 23. Praelusum in deserto, Num. 11. Ita hodie multi Papatum laudant; immemores quarum olim fuerunt. Pacem item publicam, quae tunc nulla fuit. Imo cum hostibus colludere possunt aduersus amicos. Idem patientur quod Iudaei.
units.tr: Note: how much the hatred of truth can do. It drives them to praise the one they most hated, since nothing is more hateful to the world (John 3). They prefer Caesar to Christ; indeed they prefer Barabbas (John 19; Luke 23). A foreshadowing in the wilderness (Num. 11). So today many praise the Papacy, forgetting what it once was, and likewise public peace, which at that time did not exist. Indeed, they can even collude with enemies against friends. They will suffer the same as the Jews did.

units.la: ¶ 2. Officium magistratus adumbratur, quod in duobus maxime consistit: vt pax publica feruetur, & in melius restituantur collapsa & corrupta. Ista fieri non possunt, nisi malis resistatur, Rom. 13. Vsurarij coerceantur. Caueantur foedera insidiosa. Bereinigung &c. Interm arguuntur, qui nihil mutandum putant. Aliter Iosaphat, 2 Paral. 19. 20. Ezechias, 2 Paral. 29, 30, 31. Iosias, 2 Par. 34, 35.
units.tr: (2) The office of the magistrate is sketched, which consists chiefly in two things: that public peace be preserved, and that what has collapsed and been corrupted be restored to better condition. These things cannot be done unless evils are resisted (Rom. 13). Usurers are to be restrained. Treacherous covenants are to be guarded against. Reformation... Meanwhile those are reproved who think nothing should be changed. Jehoshaphat acted otherwise (2 Chron. 19, 20); Hezekiah (2 Chron. 29, 30, 31); Josiah (2 Chron. 34, 35).

units.la: II. Accusant trium capitum. A. Peste vo cant, quia vbiq; terrarum seditiones con-citet. Hic vero improbè illi impinguntquod ab ipsis fiebat, vt vid mus, Act. 13 14. 17.18.19. Sic Christus accusatur, Luc. 23.
units.tr: II. They accuse him under three heads. (A) They call him a pestilence, because he stirs up seditions everywhere on earth. But here they wickedly impute to him what was actually done by themselves, as we see (Acts 13, 14, 17, 18, 19). So Christ was accused (Luke 23).

units.la: A. Authorem sectae Nazaraeorum. Ita per contemptum Christianos vocant. Ita soler Satan. Olim Iulianus. Est vero hoc grauissimum haereseos crimen. C. Prophanati templi.
units.tr: (B) The author of the sect of the Nazarenes. In this contemptuous way they call Christians. Satan is accustomed to do so. Once Julian did. But this is indeed the gravest charge of heresy. (C) The profaning of the temple.

units.la: NOTA ¶ Quibus criminibus grauetur veritas. Sic Exod. 5.1. Reg. 18. Amos 7. Ita hodie seditiosi, haeretici, prophanatores templorum, sacrilegi, &c. dicimur. Non er go offendamur. Nec credamus facilè si-milibus.
units.tr: Note: with what charges the truth is burdened. So (Exod. 5.1; 1 Kings 18; Amos 7). So today we are called seditious, heretics, profaners of temples, sacrilegious, and so on. Therefore let us not be offended, nor readily believe such accusations.

units.la: III. Probant testibus. Primum Tribuni Lysiae, quem tamen obiter etiam accusant. Deinde omnes qui astant, Tertulli verbis assentiuntur.
units.tr: III. They prove their case by witnesses: first the tribune Lysias, whom they nevertheless also accuse in passing. Then all who stand by assent to Tertullus' words.

units.la: NOT. ¶ Impudentiam & audaciam hostium veritatis. Accusant Tribunū & conqueruntur, sibi ereptam fundendi sanguinis occasionem. Partiales sunt, & cum ante accusatores, deinde iudices fuerint, nunc testes quoq; sunt, & tamen quiduis sibi credi volunt. Simile habes, Ioh. 18. Pręterea non timent Dei iudicium, qui falsis testibus grauissimè minatur, Exo. 20. Deut. 19. Prou. 6.
units.tr: Note: the impudence and audacity of the enemies of truth. They accuse the tribune and complain that the opportunity to shed blood was taken from them. They are partisan, and having first been accusers, then judges, they are now witnesses too, and yet they want to be believed in whatever they say. You have a similar case (John 18). Moreover, they do not fear the judgment of God, who most severely threatens false witnesses (Exod. 20; Deut. 19; Prov. 6).

units.la: Debent autem haec simul institutioni seruire, vt horum similes suspectos habeamus. Praeterea non offendamur, si quid tale nobis etiam euenit, &c. Viuit & regnat Christus qui omnia passus est & vicit, &c. Psal. 2. Oremus.
units.tr: These things should at the same time serve for instruction, so that we may regard men like these with suspicion. Moreover, let us not be offended if anything of the kind happens to us. Christ lives and reigns, who suffered all things and overcame, and so on (Ps. 2). Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXXIV.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXXIV.
