units.tr: Let us not therefore be offended today. The harbour of rest is in heaven. Let us therefore imitate the constancy of Paul, and pray without ceasing.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXCVIII.

units.la: 9 Multo autem tempore periclo, & quum iam effet periculosa nauiga-tio,quòd iam etiam ieiunium prate ijs-set,admonebat Paulus:
units.tr: 9 Much time having been lost, and the voyage now being dangerous, since even the fast had already passed, Paul warned them:

units.la: 10 Dicens eis, Viri, video cum mi-nia multoq; damno non solum oneris & navis, sed etiam capitum nostrorum, futuram nauigationem.& c.ad verf.14.
units.tr: 10 Saying to them, Men, I see that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives, &c. to verse 14.

units.la: QVemadmodum Dominus noster Iesus Christus varijs & assiduis tri-bulationibus in hoc mundo tentatus est: Ita quotquot illius discipuli esse voluerint,variè exerceri & affligi solent,2.Tim.3.Ioh.15 16. Et eius rei multa exempla paf-sim proponuntur:partim ne offendamur, quando similia nobis accidunt, Matth.5. partim vero, vt ex ijsdem tum consilium, tum consolationem petamus.In hunc er-go fi. go finem præsentem quoq; historiam referri oportet, in qua hucusque dictum, vt difficili & molesta navigatione in Cretam usque Paulus vinctus peruenerit, qui post graues insidias hostium, nunc maris quoque pericula experitur, &c. Sequitur tamen maioris periculi narratio, quod tandem in naufragium desijt, &c. Sterilis videtur historia, sed multa continet obser-uanda. In præsenti hæc commemorantur.
units.tr: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ was tested in this world by various and constant tribulations, so all who wish to be his disciples are usually tried and afflicted in various ways (2 Tim. 3; John 15:16). Many examples of this are set before us everywhere: partly so that we may not be offended when similar things happen to us (Matt. 5), and partly so that we may seek from them both counsel and consolation. To this end, the history presented here must also be related, in which it has been told so far how Paul, bound, reached Crete by a difficult and troublesome voyage; who, after the grave plots of his enemies, now also experiences the perils of the sea, &c. The account of a greater danger follows, which at last ended in shipwreck, &c. The history seems barren, but it contains many things to be observed. In the present passage the following are recorded.

units.la: 1. In tempore per Paulum illos de periculo Deus admonet. Cùm enim multum temporis propè Lasæam hyemissent, iam prope terito etiam ieiunij tempore, quod partim in Septembrem, partim in Octobrem incidebat (Leu. 16.) hyems instaret, Paulus suadet vt differant, &c. Facit hoc ex spiritus reuelatione, &c.
units.tr: 1. Through Paul, God warns them of the danger at the right time. For when they had spent much time near Lasea, and the time of the fast, which fell partly in September and partly in October (Lev. 16), was almost past, and winter was coming on, Paul advises them to delay, &c. He does this by a revelation of the Spirit, &c.

units.la: NOTA 1. Deum, qui suos nunquam negligit. Quia enim saluos vult homines (1. Tim. 2.) de periculis admonet in tempore vt caueant, & varie quidem. Per prophetas, vt olim, Amos 3. 2. Paral. 36. Zach. 1. Ier. 7. 11. Item Luc. 19. Matth. 24. Per amicos & familiares. Per signa omnis generis vt prædictum Mat. 24. Per occultas fugas, ftiones & Angelos, Pf. 34. Et hæc quidem exiperimur ferè omnes quotidie. Nostrum est non contemnere, ne quid peius accidat.
units.tr: NOTE 1. God, who never neglects his own. For since he wishes all men to be saved (1 Tim. 2), he warns of dangers in time so that they may take heed, and does so in various ways: through the prophets, as formerly (Amos 3; 2 Chron. 36; Zech. 1; Jer. 7, 11); likewise Luke 19 and Matt. 24; through friends and family; through signs of every kind, as foretold in Matt. 24; through hidden flights, quiet warnings and angels (Ps. 34). Almost all of us experience these things daily. It is our part not to despise them, lest something worse befall us.

units.la: ¶ 2. Paulum. Habebat promissionem, se Romam iturū, Act 23. Non tamen ita contemnit omne periculum, vt temere se obijciens periculo Deum tentet. Imo credit diuinæ reuelationi, & alios quoq; monet. Fidei ergo & prouidentiæ doctrina non temerarios reddit & Dei tentatores. Prudentia præcipitur, Mat.10. Vbi etiam legitima media Deus offert, certum est quod nos periclitari nolit. His ergo vtamur piè & religiosè. Vide Christum Mat.4.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Paul. He had a promise that he would go to Rome (Acts 23), yet he did not so despise every danger as to expose himself rashly to peril and tempt God. Rather, he believes the divine revelation and also warns the others. The teaching of faith and providence therefore does not make men reckless or testers of God. Prudence is enjoined (Matt. 10). Where God offers lawful means, it is certain that he does not wish us to be in peril. Let us therefore use these devoutly and religiously. See Christ, Matt. 4.

units.la: II. Non admittitur Pauli consilium, cuius rei causæ etiam proponuntur. ¶ 1. Centurio magis credit gubernatori. Videtur hoc prudenter facere. Sed errat, quòd cō filia non ex ipsis causis, sed personarum respectu æstimat.
units.tr: II. Paul's counsel is not accepted, and the reasons for it are also set out. ¶ 1. The centurion trusts the helmsman more. This seems a prudent thing to do. But he is wrong, because he judges the matter by respect for persons rather than from the causes themselves.

units.la: Not. ¶ In consilijs ipsas rerum causas, non personas respicere debere. Sæpe enim per vices & contemptos optimè consulit Deus. Sic per Micheam 1.Reg.22. Per puellam captiuam, 2.Reg. 5. Per Ieremiā, cui fi Zedechiæ obediuisset, bene habuisset. Sed frequens est error hic hodie, maximè quòd per Pfaffos doceri nolumus. Hinc fit, quòd in bellis barbaros milites obseruamus, & ad fœdera confugimus, If. 30. &c. In morbis solos medicos consuli- mus, vt olim Asa, 2. Paral. 16. In egestate ad malas artes conuertimur. Et eos modò obseruamus, quibus aliquando succesit. Sed tutissimum fuerit Dei verbum obser uare, & in hoc fundata consilia sequi, If.8. Psal.19 & 119.
units.tr: Note. ¶ In counsels one ought to regard the causes of things themselves, not the persons. For God often gives the best counsel through the lowly and the despised. So through Micaiah (1 Kings 22), through the captive girl (2 Kings 5), through Jeremiah, whose advice, had Zedekiah obeyed it, would have gone well for him. But this error is frequent today, above all because we do not want to be taught by the priests. Hence it happens that in wars we rely on barbarian soldiers and flee to alliances (Isa. 30), &c. In illnesses we consult only physicians, as Asa once did (2 Chron. 16). In poverty we turn to wicked arts. And we follow only those by whom we have at some time been successful. But it would be safest to observe God's word and follow counsels founded upon it (Isa. 8; Ps. 19 and 119).

units.la: II. Portus non videtur commodus ad hybernandum. Soluunt ergo, commodio rem quaesituri. Est haec altera causa, quae faniora consilia impedit. Quod non contenti fumus praesenti forte. Hinc fit, quod insatiabiles & caecos affectus secuti, pecca torum laqueis irretimur, tandemq; periclitamur. Ita isti tandem omnium bonorum iacturam faciunt & naufragi vix Melitam attingunt. Similia habes in Israele, Num.11. Item quando postulárunt regé, 1. Sam 8.12. &c. Similiter lere.42.43. &c. Alexander Magnus. Ita maiores nostri Gallias olim petebant. Imitamur ipsi publicè & priuatim.
units.tr: II. The harbour does not seem suitable for wintering. They therefore set sail, seeking the more convenient thing. This is the second cause that hinders sounder counsels: we are not content with what we have at present. Hence, following insatiable and blind desires, we are caught in the snares of sins, and at last we are endangered. So these men at last suffer the loss of all good things and, shipwrecked, barely reach Malta. You have similar things in Israel (Num. 11); likewise when they demanded a king (1 Sam. 8, 12), &c. Similarly Jer. 42, 43, &c. Alexander the Great. So our forefathers once sought Gaul. We ourselves imitate this, both publicly and privately.

units.la: Sed Not. αὐτάρκεια tutissima esse salutis retinendae viam. Haec vna in officio retinere potest, & carnis affectus moderatur. Hinc ita commendatur, 1. Timoth 6.
units.tr: But note that self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] is the safest way of keeping salvation. This alone can keep us in our duty and moderate the desires of the flesh. Hence it is commended in this way (1 Tim. 6).

units.la: III. Succedit initio res, & aspirat aura. Vbi haud dubè Paulus expositus fuit multorum ludibrio. Sed mox inobedientiae poenas luunt.
units.tr: III. Things go well at the start, and a breeze blows. Paul was then without doubt exposed to the mockery of many. But soon they paid the penalty for their disobedience.

units.la: NOTA. ¶Diabolicum hoc stratagema esse, qui peccatorum principia solet feli-cia & facilia facere, vt successus spe pelli-ceat, Psal.36. Vide Gene.3 Ita enim fortu-na ebrij admonitiones sanas spernimus & ridemus, &c. Est hoc videre in militibus mercenarijs, dum diuites fiunt & in pre-tio habentur. In vsurarijs, In adulteris, vt Dauide, 1 Sam.11. Denique omnibus alijs. Sed omnium peccatorum finis mors est, vt de vino immodico sumpto, Solomon dicit, Prou.23. Vide Ge.3. Rom.5.&c. Hæc ergo meditantes, Dei verbum vnicè scðe mur, & Oremus.
units.tr: NOTE. ¶ This is a devilish stratagem, which is wont to make the beginnings of sins happy and easy, so as to entice by the hope of success (Ps. 36). See Gen. 3. For thus, drunk with good fortune, we scorn and laugh at wholesome warnings, &c. This can be seen in mercenary soldiers, while they become rich and are held in esteem; in usurers; in adulterers, like David (1 Sam. 11); and finally in all others. But the end of all sins is death, as Solomon says of immoderate wine (Prov. 23). See Gen. 3; Rom. 5, &c. Therefore, meditating on these things, let us hold fast to God's word alone, and pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCIX.

units.la: 14 Verùm haud multò post impe-git eam ventus Typhonicus (turbu-lentus) qui vocatur Euroclydon.
units.tr: 14 But not long after, a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon (the Typhonic wind), beat down upon the ship.

units.la: 15 Quum abreptum esset nauigium, nec posset obniti vento, dato nauigio flatibus, ferebamur. &c. adver.21.
units.tr: 15 When the ship was caught up and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. &c. adver.21.

units.la: EXposuit D Lucas, vt Deus Pauli co-mites & conductores de imminenti periculo admonuerit: frustra tamen, eò quòd illi salutare consilium non admise-runt. Simul verò huius inobedientiæ cau-sas indicauit. Alteram, quòd gubernatori potiùs potius quàm Paulo credendum esse putà runt. Alteram, quod portu praesenti non fuerunt contenti. Didicimus quid fere ob stet, quo minus admittantur saniora consilia & diuinae admonitiones. Nimirū carnis prudentia, quae personas potius, quàm res ipsas respicit, & quod in praesenti forte non contenti sumus. Illam ergo fidei subijciamus, Num.15. Deut.4.12.2. Cor.10. Deinde αὐτάρκειαν colamus, 1. Timot.6. Porrò, quid istis euenerit, sequitur.
units.tr: Luke sets out that God warned Paul's companions and the ship's crew of the impending danger, but in vain, because they did not accept the wholesome counsel. At the same time he indicated the causes of this disobedience. The first was that they thought they should trust the helmsman rather than Paul. The second was that they were not content with the harbour they had. We have learned what generally stands in the way, so that wholesome counsels and divine warnings are not admitted: namely the wisdom of the flesh, which regards persons rather than the things themselves, and the fact that we are perhaps not content with what is present. Let us therefore subject that to faith, Num. 15, Deut. 4.12, 2 Cor. 10. Then let us cultivate self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν], 1 Tim. 6. Next follows what happened to them.

units.la: 1. Initio successurus videtur conatus. Nam Austro slante aliquo vsq; procedūt. Sic laeta & felicia fere sunt peccatorum principia: quod etiā in primis parentibus cernitur, Psal.36. Gen.3. Et est hoc Diaboli stratagema, qui nos hac arte irretire solet. Ita istis euenit. Quid verò fit? Non multo post insurgit ventus Typhonicus, Euroclydon vel Caecias, prouerbio quoq; nobilitatus, qui nauim totam abripit, &c.
units.tr: 1. At first the attempt seems likely to succeed. For with the south wind blowing, they proceed for a while. So the beginnings of sins are generally happy and prosperous; this is seen even in our first parents, Ps. 36, Gen. 3. This is the stratagem of the Devil, who is wont to ensnare us by this art. So it happened to them. But what then happens? Not long after, a Typhonic wind rises, Euroclydon or Caecias, a name also made famous by proverb, which snatches away the whole ship, etc.

units.la: Nor. Non diuturnos esse illorum suc cessus, qui contra Dei verbum aliquid instituunt. Subito enim aliqua obruuntur calamitate. Exempla sunt in regnis tyrannicis, vt Niniuitico Nah.1.2. &c. Ifraeliti-co, Babylonico, Daniel.5. Romano. In omnibus impletū quod habes Ifa.33. Hab.1.2. Matth.6 Apoc.13. Idem in priuatis perso-
units.tr: Note. The successes of those who undertake anything against the word of God are not long-lasting, for they are suddenly overwhelmed by some calamity. Examples are found in tyrannical kingdoms: the Ninevite (Nah. 1, 2, etc.), the Israelite, the Babylonian (Dan. 5), the Roman. In all of them what you have in Isa. 33, Hab. 1, 2, Matt. 6, Rev. 13 is fulfilled. The same is seen in private persons

units.la: Impietatum successus non diutius nisi sunt.
units.tr: The successes of the impious do not last long.

units.la: nis cernitur,vsurarijs,adulteris, militibus mercenarijs,&c.Huc facit, quod deimpij fortuna dicitur,Pfal.3.
units.tr: ...in usurers, adulterers, mercenary soldiers, etc. To this belongs what is said of the fortune of the impious, Ps. 3.

units.la: Non ergo vel nostris successibus effera mur,vel alienis offendamur,Pfalm.73.37. Quin potius Deo obediamus simpliciter, & verbi regulam sequamur.
units.tr: So let us neither be puffed up by our own successes nor offended by those of others, Ps. 73:37. Rather, let us simply obey God and follow the rule of the word.

units.la: II. Ventus ita nauim rapit, vt resistere non possint.Feruntur ergo incerti omnium. Et quamuis infula Clauda fe offerat, frustra tamen,&c.
units.tr: II. The wind seizes the ship so that they cannot resist it. So they are carried along, uncertain of everything. And although the island Clauda offers itself, it is in vain, etc.

units.la: Nota. ¶ Vanas esse omnium illorum vires,quos diuina vltio persequitur.Quid vanius vento?At inscrutabilis est eius potentia,& vnus sufficit turbandis omnibus Ioh.3 &c.Ita quaeuis alia Deus armare po teft.Vide Exod.5.6 7.
units.tr: Note. All the strength of those whom divine vengeance pursues is vain. What is more vain than the wind? Yet its power is unsearchable, and one wind is enough to disturb everything, John 3, etc. So God can arm any other thing as well. See Exod. 5, 6, 7.

units.la: Discamus partim nihil fidere nostris vi ribus, partim non reluctari Deo,fi quando peccatorum poenas infligit.Vnica salutis via est,vt ad ipsum conuertamur,Zac. 1.Malach.1.Ifa.9. Licet enim interdum spes aliqua appareat,vt istis quoq; dum in Claudam deferuntur,clauda tamen vere est & inanis omnis spes, quae in humanis affulget. Et friuola sunt omnia carnis praesidia, Ieremiae decimofeptimo, Psalmo 146.
units.tr: Let us learn partly to trust nothing in our own strength, and partly not to struggle against God when he inflicts the punishment of sins. The only way of salvation is to turn to him, Zech. 1, Mal. 1, Isa. 9. For although sometimes some hope appears, as it did for these men too while they were being carried towards Clauda, yet every hope that shines forth in human things is truly lame and empty. And all the protections of the flesh are frivolous, Jer. 17, Ps. 146.

units.la: III. Iactum faciunt proprijs manibus, tum mercium, tum armamentorum nauis. Sic omnia sponte abijciunt, vt corpora saluent, qui noluerunt propè Casæam paucis mensibus paulò comodiùs hybernare. In tantum mutati animi,&c.
units.tr: III. With their own hands they throw overboard both the cargo and the ship's tackle. So they willingly cast away everything to save their bodies, men who had not wished to winter a few months near Caesarea, a little more comfortably. So much has their state of mind changed, etc.

units.la: Not. ¶ Sortem illorum, qui vt Deo obediant, nihil omnino ferre, nec quicquam amittere volunt, eorum quoq;, quæ luxui & voluptati modò seruiunt. Tandé ipsi coguntur omnia abijcere. Quod non capit Christus, rapit fiscus. Hostes rapinis & exactionib omnia exhauriunt, quæ nolumus Christo impendere. Ægroti medi cos & pharmacopolas carnifices sontiunt, & eosdem ditant. Et frequenter confcien tijs ita anguntur, vt harum tranquillitatem & pacem, si sieri posset, vniuersis suis opibus redimerent,&c.
units.tr: Note. This is the lot of those who, wanting to obey God, are unwilling to bear anything or lose anything at all, and of those too who serve only luxury and pleasure. In the end they are themselves compelled to throw everything away. What Christ does not take, the treasury seizes. Enemies drain everything with plunder and exactions, which we did not want to spend on Christ. The sick hand over their money to doctors and apothecaries, who are butchers, and those same men grow rich. And often they are so tormented by their consciences that they would, if it were possible, buy back that tranquillity and peace with all their wealth, etc.

units.la: Discamus igitur Christo tum nos, tum bona nostra omnia consecrare, nec graue fit illa propter hunc amittere. Retributio magna promittitur, Mat.19. Mar.10. Quin ipsi abijciamus salutis impedimenta, &c. Matt.18.
units.tr: Let us therefore learn to consecrate to Christ both ourselves and all our goods, and let it not be hard to lose them for his sake. A great reward is promised, Matt. 19, Mark 10. Indeed, let us cast away the hindrances to salvation, etc. Matt. 18.

units.la: IV. Per multos dies nec Sol nec sydera lucent, & tandem omnis salutis spes inter cidit. Perpetuum hoc, vt tenebris malorum inuoluantur, qui in luce verbi Dei nolunt ambulare. Adumbratum in passio
units.tr: IV. For many days neither sun nor stars shine, and at last all hope of salvation perishes. This is a perpetual truth: that those who are unwilling to walk in the light of God's word are wrapped in the darkness of evils. It is foreshadowed in the passion

units.la: Gap.27. he Christi. Hæc enim lucerna est, quam semper tenere oportet, & sydus, quod du cit per mare huius mundi, Psalm.119. Luc. 12 &c.
units.tr: of Christ. For this is the lamp that must always be held, and the star that guides us across the sea of this world, Ps. 119, Luke 12, etc.

units.la: Interim Not. ¶ Quod Paulus quo- que cum alijs periclitatur. Imo ita tenta- tur, vt anxius plane ad preces confugerit, & consolatione opus habuerit. Est hæc piorum fors in mundo. Noe, Gen. 6. 7. 8. Loth, Gen. 14. 19. 2. Pet. 2. Offendit hoc multos, vt olim quoque. Vide Malach. 3. Sed longe alia est piorum ratio. In bonum sibi omnia cedere nouerunt, ad Romanos octauo, priori ad Corinthios vndecimo. Interim bene sibi conscij, orant, & ratas omnino fore sciunt Dei promissiones, 1. Corinth. 10. &c. Econtra impij discrucian tur, pereunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile note: Paul too is endangered along with the others. Indeed he is so tried that he clearly fled to prayer, and needed consolation. This is the lot of the godly in the world: Noah (Gen. 6, 7, 8), Lot (Gen. 14, 19), 2 Pet. 2. This offends many, as it did once too. See Mal. 3. But the reasoning of the godly is quite different. They know how to turn all things to their good, Rom. 8, and 1 Cor. 11 earlier. Meanwhile, conscious of this, they pray, and know that God's promises will certainly be fulfilled, 1 Cor. 10, etc. On the contrary, the impious are tormented and perish.

units.la: Imitemur nos Paulum, & Oremus.
units.tr: Let us imitate Paul, and let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CC.
units.tr: HOMILY 200.

units.la: 21 Et quum multa jam fuisset ine dia, tunc stans Paulus in medio eorum, dixit: Oportebat quidem, o viri, mihi obediendo non prouehi a Creta, & vitae iniuriam hanc & damnum, &c. ad ver. 27.
units.tr: 21 When much time had already passed without food, Paul stood up in the midst of them and said: Sirs, you ought indeed to have obeyed me and not have set sail from Crete, and so have spared yourselves this injury and loss, etc., to verse 27.

units.la: Descripsit Lucas tempestatem gra- uissimam, qua Paulus simul & eius comicomites iaćlati fuerūt, & hanc ita tandem inualuisse dixit,vt de salute omnino defpe rauerint. Hic vero miretur aliquis, qua/lem fe Paulus gesserit, tum erga Deum, cuius promissiones intercidere videban-tur:tum ergafocios, qui inobedientia sua & temeritate periculum hoc fibijpfis conflauerant. Id vero omne ipsius Pauli oratio exprimit,quæ modò describitur.
units.tr: Luke describes a very severe storm, by which Paul and his companions were tossed about, and he says that it finally grew so strong that they utterly despaired of safety. Here someone might wonder what sort of man Paul was, both towards God, whose promises seemed to be failing, and towards his companions, who by their disobedience and rashness had brought this danger upon themselves. Paul's whole speech, which is now described, expresses all of this.

units.la: I. Tempus & omnium conditio nota-tur.Cum inter commemorata pericula fames quoque præuale re inciperet, Paulus ad conciouandum prodit,eò quòd illis ad huc tumultuantibus, non auditus fuisset Nunc vero cum probè defessi sedent, & mortem in figula momenta exspectant, consolationem & consilium profert, sibi à Deo reuelatum. Vnde colligitur,illum inter periculaa non ignauo metu despera-uisse,neque ad aliquem Diuorum,sed per preces ad Deum confugisse,qui illum cor tortauit,vt alijs quoque posset animum facere,&c.
units.tr: I. The time and the condition of everyone are noted. When famine too began to prevail among the dangers already mentioned, Paul comes forward to address them, because he had not been heard while they were still in tumult. But now, when they sit utterly exhausted and expect death every moment, he offers consolation and counsel revealed to him by God. From this it is gathered that he, amid the dangers, did not despair out of cowardly fear, nor did he flee to any of the gods, but took refuge by prayer to God, who had so tested him that he could also put courage into the others, etc.

units.la: NOT.¶ In periculis nom statim defpe-randum esse, sedinsolo Deo habendam spem & fiduciam, qui suos non derelin-quit.Vide Ps.50.Isa.65.Exempla sunt pas-sim.Philo aput Caium.
units.tr: NOTE. In dangers one must not despair at once, but must place hope and trust in God alone, who does not forsake his own. See Ps. 50, Isa. 65. Examples are everywhere. Philo, in his work against Caius.

units.la: Arguuntur hoc loco, qui vt primum in {Cap. 26.} humanis spes nulla superest, vel despe-rant omnino, vel ad Creaturas & Dinos conuertuntur, à quibus opem & auxili-um postulant, &c. Vide Isa. 63. &c.
units.tr: Those are rebuked here who, as soon as no human hope remains, either despair altogether or turn to creatures and false gods, from whom they seek help and aid, etc. {Cap. 26.} See Isa. 63, etc.

units.la: II. Oratio Pauli ponitur, breuis quidem pro temporis ratione, sed quæ res multas & graues complectitur. I. Expro-brat & corripit inobedientiam ipsorum: partim vt in periculo præsenti, ipsius causam, peccatum scilicet suum agnoscant. Partim vt nunc illu animo æquiori audiant. Interim modestissimè agit, ne illis insultare potius, quam consolari aut consulere videatur.
units.tr: II. Paul's speech is set out. It is brief indeed for the circumstances, but embraces many weighty matters. 1. He reproves and rebukes their disobedience, partly so that, while in the present danger, they might acknowledge the cause of it, namely their own sin; partly so that they might now hear him with a calmer mind. Meanwhile he acts most modestly, so that he might seem not to insult them rather than to console or advise them.

units.la: NOT. ¶ Periclitantibus nos non insultare debere, sed potius erroris admonere, & viam salutis monstrare. Peccant contra Pauli exemplum, qui cum rebus adhuc integris nihil potuerint consulendo, in ad uersis aliorum consilia amarulenter exagitant, & illa malè cessisse gaudent. Est hoc calamitosis calamitatem addere, quod à Christiana charitate alienissimum est, Roman 12. &c. Punit Deus. Vide Zach. 1. Isa. 47. &c. Arguuntur item, qui vbi semel non auditi fuerunt, in posterum à consulendo prorsus abstinent.
units.tr: NOTE. We ought not to insult those in peril, but rather to admonish them of their error and show them the way of salvation. Those sin against Paul's example who, when matters were still intact, could advise nothing, and now bitterly harass the counsels of others in adversity and rejoice that they turned out badly. To add calamity to the calamitous is most alien to Christian charity, Rom. 12, etc. God punishes. See Zech. 1, Isa. 47, etc. Also rebuked are those who, once they have not been heard, afterwards refrain altogether from giving advice.

units.la: II. Consolatur magna cum fiducia. Iubet bono animo esse, & simul libere incolumitatem pollicetur.
units.tr: II. He consoles with great confidence. He bids them be of good cheer and at the same time freely promises their safety.

units.la: NOT. ¶Dignitatem Pauli, qua reliquos omnes excelluit. Poterat omnium miserrimus videri. Sed nunc omnibus consola tor & consultor adest. Ita in suis, quando contemptissimi habentur, Christus triumphat, & authoritate illis conciliat, qui prius contemnebantur. Exempla huius generis sunt multa hodie. In Martyribus. Vide Mosem apud Pharaonem & Israelitas, Saulem cum Samuele. In rebus dubiis ad Pharaos concurritur, quos alioqui omnes oderunt.
units.tr: NOTE. Consider Paul's dignity, by which he surpassed all the rest. He could have seemed the most wretched of all men. But now he is present to all as consoler and adviser. So too in his own people, when they are held most contemptible, Christ triumphs and gives authority to those who were previously despised. Examples of this kind are many today, in the martyrs. See Moses before Pharaohs and the Israelites, and Saul with Samuel. In doubtful matters people run to Pharaohs, whom otherwise they all hate.

units.la: III. Oraculum allegat, ne vanus videatur, & quidem maxima authoritate. Ait mihi Angelus Dei. Eius inquam, cujus sum & quem colo. Ille consolatus est, veteres promissiones refricans, Act. 23. Ite omnibus vobis incolumitatem promisit.
units.tr: III. He cites an oracle so that he may not seem vain, and that with the greatest authority: The angel of God said to me. Of that God, I say, whose I am and whom I serve. He consoled him, renewing the old promises. Acts 23. He promised safety to all of you.

units.la: NOT. ¶1. Bonitatem Dei, qui suos nunquam deserit; neque nostri obliuiscitur, quando pro meritis castigat. Non irasci-tur perpetuo, sed ad discip linam castigat, Psal. 103. & 94. Interim consolatur & consulit, 2. Cor. 1. Imo Angelorum quoque ministerium submittit, Psal 34. 91. Sic 2. Reg. 6. Dan 3. 6. Actor. 5. 12. 16. &c. Non ergo despermus. Obseruemus hoc in morbis, egestate, &c.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. The goodness of God, who never deserts his own, nor forgets us when he chastises us according to our merits. He is not angry perpetually, but chastises for our discipline, Ps. 103 and 94. Meanwhile he consoles and counsels, 2 Cor. 1. Indeed he also submits the ministry of angels, Ps. 34, 91. So 2 Kings 6, Dan. 3, 6, Acts 5, 12, 16, etc. Therefore let us not despair. Let us observe this in sicknesses, want, and the like.

units.la: ¶2. Ingenuitatem Pauli circa religio-
units.tr: 2. The frankness of Paul concerning religion.

units.la: nem.Vinctus erat propter hanc.Attamen ingenuè fatetur,se non modò Dei esse,sed inter hunc & Deos gentium distinguens, illum ait absfe coli.Ita ad Rom.1. Ita iube mur Luc.12.Mar.8.Ita Martyres. Vide milites Iuliani.Interim vides, non sufficere vt Dei simus,sicuti aliæ creaturæ,sed à no bis cultum requiri & obsequium, Luc.12. Alioqui respondebitur quod est Mal.1.
units.tr: He was bound on account of this. Nevertheless he freely confesses that he belongs not only to God, but, distinguishing this God from the gods of the nations, he says that the former is to be worshipped. So Rom. 1. So we are commanded, Luke 12, Mark 8. So the martyrs. See the soldiers of Julian. Meanwhile you see that it is not enough to be God's, as other creatures are, but worship and obedience are required of us, Luke 12. Otherwise the answer will be what is written in Mal. 1.

units.la: § 3. Quàm beatum sit bonis cohabitare. Frequenter propter vnum bonum multis malis parcitur,Gen.6.7.14.19. 18.Moses,Rahab,&c.Fit hoc, non vt Diuos inuocemus, sed illorum fidem commendat, & impios quoque sicsuis obstringit Deus.Econtrà vnus impius impunè grassans, multis malum dat. Vide Ioh.1. Iof.7.Iud. 19.20. &c.Vtinam obseruemus.Sed hic a-lucet mundi corruptio,qui pios odit,publicos malorum authores in precio habet.
units.tr: § 3. How blessed it is to live among the good. Often for the sake of one good man many evils are spared: Gen. 6, 7, 14, 19, 18. Moses, Rahab, etc. This happens not so that we should invoke the saints, but because God commends their faith, and in this way binds the impious also to his own. On the contrary, one impious man running about with impunity brings evil upon many. See John 1, Josh. 7, Judg. 19, 20, etc. Would that we observed this. But here the corruption of the world shines forth, which hates the pious and holds in high esteem the public authors of evil.

units.la: IV. Dicit se credere oraculo, & simul modum effugij docet,non carentem periculo. Ita solet iuuare Deus,&c.
units.tr: IV. He says that he believes the oracle, and at the same time he teaches the manner of escape, which is not free from danger. So God is accustomed to help, etc.

units.la: NOT. § Promissiones Dei fide recipi oportere.Ita enim ratæ fiunt. No quod ex nobis dependeat Dei veritas,sed quod sub ista conditione proponuntur. Hinc illa Matth.8.15.Luc.7.Mar.9.16. Actor.15. &c.Quòd si plerique non credant,potest tamen tant en suos ab impijs discernere Deus, ut olim Iosue & Chaleb. Num. 13.14.
units.tr: NOTE. God's promises must be received by faith, for thus they are made valid. This is not because God's truth depends on us, but because they are proposed under this condition. Hence those passages, Matt. 8:15, Luke 7, Mark 9:16, Acts 15, etc. But if many do not believe, God can nevertheless distinguish his own from the impious, as once Joshua and Caleb, Num. 13, 14.

units.la: Hæc nobis hodie obseruanda. Consulit Deus & consolatur. Credamus. Obediamus. Oremus, &c.
units.tr: These things are to be observed by us today. God counsels and consoles. Let us believe. Let us obey. Let us pray, etc.

units.la: HOMILIA CCI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCI.

units.la: 27 Cæterùm quum quarta decima nox aduenisset, & ferremur in Adria, nautæ circa medium noctis suspicati sunt appropinquare sibi aliquam regionem.
units.tr: 27 But when the fourteenth night had come, and we were being driven about in the Adriatic, the sailors suspected about midnight that some region was approaching them.

units.la: 28 Et demissa bolide, inuenerunt passus viginti: & paululum inde progressi, rursum demissa bolide inuenerunt passus quindecim.
units.tr: 28 And having let down a line with a weight, they found twenty fathoms; and having gone a little further, again letting down the line, they found fifteen fathoms.

units.la: 29 Timentesque, ne quo modo in asperà loca inciderent, iactis e puppi anchoris, optabant oriri diem.
units.tr: 29 Fearing lest they should fall upon rough places, they threw out four anchors from the stern and prayed for the day to dawn.

units.la: 30 Nautis verò studentibus fugere e naui, demissa scapha in mare, sub obtentu velut e prora anchoras extendere.
units.tr: 30 But when the sailors were trying to flee from the ship, they let the boat down into the sea, under the pretence of extending anchors from the prow.

units.la: 31 Dixit Paulus Centurioni & militibus, Nisi isti in naui manserint, vos seruari non potestis.
units.tr: 31 Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.

units.la: 32 Tunc abscinderunt milites funes scaphæ, & sinerunt eam excidere.
units.tr: 32 Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it fall away.

units.la: 33 Interim autem dum oriretur dies, hortabatur Paulus omnes, vt caperent cibum, dicens, Dies hic est decimus quartus, ex quo exspectantes jejuni permanetis, nullo cibo sumpto.
units.tr: 33 Meanwhile, while the day was dawning, Paul urged them all to take food, saying, This is the fourteenth day that you have waited and remained fasting, having taken no food.

units.la: 34 Ideo vos hortor, vt sumatis cibum: hoc enim ad salutem vestram spectat. Nullius enim vestrum capillus ex capite cadet.
units.tr: 34 So I urge you to take food, for this concerns your safety. For not a hair of your head will fall.

units.la: 35 Et quum haec dixisset, accepto pane, gratias egit Deo in conspectu omnium, & quum fregisset, coepit edere.
units.tr: 35 And when he had said this, taking bread, he gave thanks to God in the sight of all, and when he had broken it, he began to eat.

units.la: 36 Omnes vero bono animo esse nt, sumpserunt & ipsi cibum.
units.tr: 36 Then all, being of good cheer, also took food themselves.

units.la: QVamuis Deus suos varie tentari patiatur, ijsdem consolatione et consilio adest, ne tentationib. succumbant, 1. Cor. 10. 2. Cor. 1. Psalm. 94. Exemplum eius rei euidens in praesenti historia cernitur. Cum enim eo vsque inuaiuisset tempestas, vt nulla salutis spes reliqua esset, Deus Angelum misit, qui promissionem veterem reuocaret, & sic Pauli ministerio omnes simul consolatus est. Sequitur, vt Deus promissis steterit, & vt partim quidem his crediderit, partim non, &c.
units.tr: Although God allows his people to be tempted in various ways, he is present to them with comfort and counsel, so that they do not succumb to temptations: 1 Cor. 10; 2 Cor. 1; Psalm 94. A clear example of this is seen in the present history. For when the storm had raged so far that no hope of safety remained, God sent an angel, who recalled the old promise, and so comforted them all at once through the ministry of Paul. It follows that God stood by his promises, and that they partly believed them, partly not, etc.

units.la: I. Nautae producuntur. Hi cum putarent rent terram in propinquo esse, omnem diligentia adhibent, vt littus contingant. Videtur hoc fidei opus esse. At vbi bolide se mel & iterum demissa, vident mare decrescere, retiment, & tandem astute fugam moliuntur turpissimam. Vnde patet illos promissioni diuinae non credidisse.
units.tr: I. The sailors come forward. Since they thought land was near, they apply every diligence so that they may reach the shore. This seems to be a work of faith. But when, having let down the line once and again, they see the sea shallowing, they become afraid, and at last they cunningly plan a most shameful flight. From this it is clear that they did not believe the divine promise.

units.la: Not. qu i. Ingenium carnis & omnium, qui huius rationem sequuntur. Primo qui delectantur Dei promissionibus & alacres se illis accommodant, quando nimirum rei euentus his conuenire, & res succeßura videtur. Sed mox nouis periculis obortis, languescunt, & tam contra Deum quam contra homines quiduis faciunt. Vide Israelem, Exod. 4. & 5. Item 12. & 14. Rursus 20. & 32. Exempla huius generis passim hodie extant, & haec fere omnis apostasiae causa est.
units.tr: Note 1: the nature of the flesh, and of all who follow its reasoning. First, those who delight in God's promises and eagerly accommodate themselves to them, when indeed the outcome of the matter seems to agree with them and the thing seems likely to succeed. But soon, when new dangers arise, they grow languid and do whatever they do, both against God and against men. See Israel, Exod. 4 and 5; likewise 12 and 14; again 20 and 32. Examples of this kind are found everywhere today, and this is almost the whole cause of apostasy.

units.la: Discamus carnis rationem a verbo Dei remouere, & in tentationibus ad illud solum, non ad hanc respicere. Haec enim praesentibus modo intenta facile desperat. Fides non item, Rom. 4.
units.tr: Let us learn to remove the reasoning of the flesh from the Word of God, and in temptations to look to that alone, not to this. For the flesh, intent only on present things, easily despairs. Faith does not, Rom. 4.

units.la: ¶ 3. Mores eorum, qui initio nimium confidentes, admonitiones & saniora con filia spernunt. Fecerunt hoc nautae. Nunc vero vbi alios in periculum adduxerunt, ipsi sibi turpissima fuga consulerere insti-
units.tr: ¶ 3. The manners of those who at first are overconfident and scorn admonitions and sounder counsels. The sailors did this. Now, however, when they have brought others into danger, they themselves plan the most shameful flight for their own safety, etc.

units.la: {a} Nautarum incredulitas et perfidia. tuunt,&c. Est hoc fere proprium confi-dentibus & seditiosis. Sic Corah cum su-is,Num.16. Abfolon, 2.Samuel.15.18.Su-specti ergo sint tales,nec illos facile audia-mus.
units.tr: {a} The unbelief and treachery of the sailors. This is almost characteristic of the overconfident and seditious. So Korah with his followers, Num. 16; Absalom, 2 Sam. 15 and 18. Such men are therefore to be suspected, nor should we easily listen to them.

units.la: II. Paulus olfacit nautarum consilium, & per Centurionem & milites obstat, quos iam dicto audientes inuenit,&c.Sed No-TA ¶ 1.Pauli verba: Nisi ispi in nauii manse rint,vos salui non eritis. Atqui saluos fore Deus promiserat.Ergo ne a nautis pende-bat diuinae promissionis veritas? Minimè. Neque hic de Dei potentia aut veritate disputat.Sed ad ordinem naturae respicit & cum nullam haberet de miraculosa libe-ratione promissionem,media,quae ad ma-num erant,non aspernatur, ne Deum ten-tet,&c.
units.tr: II. Paul detects the sailors' plan and, through the centurion and soldiers, opposes it; these he now finds obedient to his word, etc. But NOTE 1: Paul's words, Unless these remain in the ship, you will not be saved. Yet God had promised that they would be saved. Did the truth of the divine promise, then, depend on the sailors? By no means. Nor does he here dispute about God's power or truth. Rather, he looks to the order of nature, and since he had no promise of miraculous deliverance, he does not spurn the means that were at hand, lest he tempt God, etc.

units.la: Docemur,prouidentiam Dei, & fidem quae huic nititur, non pugnare cum legi-timo licitorum mediorum vsu. Vult e-nim abs se institutum ordine seruari Deus.Vide in agricultura,1.Cor.3.In oeconomia,Psal.127.Prov.31. In militia,1.Sam.17. Qui ista negligunt, Deum tentant. Vide Christi exemplum Matt 4. Credebat promissionibus,Psal.91. Sed non admittit con-sequentiam diaboli.
units.tr: We are taught that God's providence, and the faith that rests upon it, do not conflict with the lawful use of permitted means. For God wills that the order he has established be kept. See in agriculture, 1 Cor. 3; in household management, Psalm 127, Prov. 31; in warfare, 1 Sam. 17. Those who neglect these things tempt God. See Christ's example, Matt. 4. He trusted the promises, Psalm 91. But he did not accept the devil's inference.

units.la: Interim non externis medijs, sed vni Deo & eius verbo fides innititur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, faith rests not on external means but on God alone and his Word.

units.la: 2. Centurionem & milites, qui Paulo obtemperant. Magnum fidei argumentum. Ita enim scapham amittunt, cuius in tanto periculo maximus vsus esse poterat. Sed malo suo edocti, obtemperant. Imitemur.
units.tr: 2. The centurion and soldiers obey Paul. This is a great proof of faith. For thus they lose the boat, which in so great a danger could have been of very great use. But taught by their own harm, they obey. Let us imitate them.

units.la: III. Denuo consolatur paulus, & quid faciant consulit. Hortatur ut sumant cibum. Rationes: A. tempore. Dies decimus quartus est, quod nihil sumpsisti. Colligitur hic periculi magnitudo, &c. Deinde saluti vestrae seruiet. Alioqui e mari liberati, fame peribitis. Non cadet capillus. Respicit ad promissiones, & occurrit ijs, quibus nihil profuturus videbatur cibus iam moriturus, Matthaei decimo, Lucae duodecimo. His addit exemplum suum, & ita efficit, ut omnes animum recipiant.
units.tr: III. Paul comforts them again and advises them what to do. He urges them to take food. Reasons: a. from the time: it is the fourteenth day since you have taken anything. Here the magnitude of the danger is gathered, etc. Then, it will serve your safety; otherwise, freed from the sea, you will perish by hunger. Not a hair will fall. He looks to the promises and meets those objections by which food, now about to be of no use to those who are dying, would seem to profit nothing: Matt. 10; Luke 12. To these he adds his own example, and so brings it about that all take heart.

units.la: NOT. 1. Fidei ingenium in Paulo. Quo minus spei superest, eo ille constantior est & fortior. Nouerat enim Deum tunc maxime opus suum facere, quando alienum opus facit, Isa. 28.
units.tr: NOTE 1. The character of faith in Paul. The less hope remains, the more constant and strong he is. For he knew that God then especially works his own work when he does a strange work: Isa. 28.

units.la: 2. Disciplina mensae. Non edit absque gratiarum actione, etiam inter festinandum. Decet haec semper & neffaria est. Quia cibus Dei donum, ut vides Leuit. 26. Micchea 6. Gratiarum actione sanctis. catur,1 Tim. 4. Et licet saturemur, recurrit tamen fames, & semper orandum, Matth. 6. Vide Christi exemplum, Iohan. 6. Matt. 14.16. Arguuntur quos pudet mensae benedicere, &c.
units.tr: 2. Table discipline. He does not eat without giving thanks, even while hurrying. This is always fitting and is necessary, since food is God's gift: see Lev. 26; Micah 6. Thanksgiving sanctifies it: 1 Tim. 4. And even if we are sated, hunger returns, and we must always pray: Matt. 6. See Christ's example, John 6; Matt. 14 and 16. Those are reproved who are ashamed to say grace at table, etc.

units.la: ¶ 3. Omnes recreantur animis. Vide quantum boni ex pijs Dei cultoribus oriatur. Vnus Paulus nunc omnia regit, & solus consilio & consolatione iuuat. Sic Abraham, Gen. 14. Ioseph.
units.tr: ¶ 3. All are refreshed in spirit. See how much good arises from the pious worshippers of God. Paul alone now governs everything, and alone helps by counsel and comfort. So Abraham, Gen. 14; Joseph.

units.la: Discamus tales in precio habere, quando hos contempsisse multis nocuit. Vide Gen. 19. Oremus.
units.tr: Let us learn to hold such men in esteem, since despising them has harmed many: see Gen. 19. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CCII.
units.tr: HOMILIA CCII.

units.la: 37 Erant autem universa capita in navigio ducenta et septuaginta sex.
units.tr: 37 And all the persons in the ship were two hundred and seventy-six.

units.la: 38 Caeterum saciati cibo, alleuabant navim, proijcientes frumentum in mare.
units.tr: 38 When they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship, throwing the wheat into the sea.

units.la: 39 Quum autem dies ortus esset, terram non agnoscebant, sinum vero quendam animadverterunt habentem litus, in quem consilium coeperant, si possent expellere navim,
units.tr: 39 When day came, they did not recognise the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a shore, onto which they resolved, if they could, to run the ship aground.

units.la: 40 Igitur anchoris sublatis, permiserunt eam mari, simul laxatis vinculis gubernaculorum, et sublato arte-mone mone ad auræ flatum, tendebant ad litus.
units.tr: 40 So they cut away the anchors and left them in the sea, and at the same time loosened the ropes of the rudders, and raised the foresail to the breeze, and they made for the shore.

units.la: 41 Sed quum incidissent in locum bimarem, illiserunt nauem: ac prora quidem infixa manebat immobilis: puppis vero soluebatur præ vndarum violentia.
units.tr: 41 But when they had fallen into a place between two seas, they ran the ship aground. The prow stuck fast and remained immovable, but the stern was broken up by the violence of the waves.

units.la: 42 Militum autem consilium erat, vt vinctos trucidarent, ne quis, quum enatasset effugeret:
units.tr: 42 The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim away and escape.

units.la: 43 At Centurio volens seruare Paulum, prohibuit eos ab hoc consilio, iußitq; vt qui possent natare, abijcerent se primos, & in terram euaderent.
units.tr: 43 But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, restrained them from this plan, and ordered that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first and make for land.

units.la: 44 Reliqui vero partim in tabulis, partim quibusdam nauis fragmentis. Et ita factum est, vt omnes salui euaderent in terram.
units.tr: 44 The rest should follow, some on planks, some on pieces of the wreck. And so it came about that all escaped safely to land.

units.la: QVamuis Deus in promissionibus suis veracissimus sit, interea tamen fidem nostram multiuariàm exerceri patitur. Idque in eum finem, vt magis confirmemur, cùm ipsius veritatem per omnia aduersa eniti, & omnia vincere videmus. Et huc quidem præsens historia referri debet, in qua iuxta promissionem suam Paulum cum suis saluat quidem Deus, sed interim nouis subinde insultibus illorum fidem exercet. Sed videamus ordine præsentem hunc locum, qui totius Tragœdiæ finem comprehendit.
units.tr: Although God is most truthful in his promises, he nevertheless allows our faith to be tested in many ways. He does this to the end that we may be strengthened the more, since we see the truth of God striving against all adversities and overcoming them all. And indeed this present history ought to be cited for this purpose, in which God, according to his promise, saves Paul and his companions, yet in the meantime keeps testing their faith with fresh assaults from time to time. But let us look in order at this present passage, which contains the end of the whole tragedy.

units.la: I.Numerus omnium, qui in naui fuerunt, ponitur. Fit hoc partim vt certò nobis constet diuinæ promissionis veritas: partim vt euidentius sit beneficij diuini miraculum. Nam ferè impossibile erat, tam multos simul ex naufragio saluos fieri, vt non ipsi sese mutuo colliderent & impedirent. Dei ergo manus hic sese exeruit.
units.tr: I. The number of all who were in the ship is given. This is done partly so that the truth of the divine promise may be certain to us, and partly so that the miracle of the divine benefit may be more evident. For it was almost impossible for so many to be saved together from a shipwreck without colliding with and hindering one another. Here, therefore, the hand of God shows itself.

units.la: Not. ¶ Deo perinde esse multos atque paucos seruare. Omnia enim in numerato habet, etiam capillos & passercu-los, Luc 12. Matth.10. Ita omnes Israelitas traduxit per mare rubrum incolumes (non minori negotio quàm priùs Mosem seruàrat, Exod.2.) vt nemo periret, Exod.14. Et tot millia in deserto pascere, eidem tam facile fuit, quàm Eliá pascere. Deut.8. Sic etiam in bello multos simul & paucos iuuare potest, 2. Paralip.14. Quapropter his nos fidem in periculis confirmare decet. Item in egestate, liberorum multitudine, &c.
units.tr: Note: For God it is equally easy to save many or few. For he has everything counted, even the hairs of our heads and the sparrows (Luke 12; Matt. 10). So he brought all the Israelites safe through the Red Sea (with no less difficulty than when he earlier preserved Moses, Exod. 2), so that none perished (Exod. 14). And it was just as easy for him to feed so many thousands in the wilderness as to feed them through Elijah (Deut. 8). So also in war he can help many or few at once (2 Chron. 14). Therefore we ought to be confirmed in faith by these examples in dangers. Likewise in poverty, in the multitude of children, and so on.

units.la: II. Cibo sumpto nauem alleuant, & triticum in mare eijciunt. Aliorum etiam iactus ante factus fuerat. Et hoc facere illos coegit necessitas, qui contra Dei voluntatem portum commodiorem & deli
units.tr: II. Having taken food, they lighten the ship and throw the wheat into the sea. Others had also thrown things overboard earlier. Necessity compelled them to do this, since, contrary to the will of God, they sought a more convenient and delicate harbour

units.la: Triticum in mare eijciunt. delicatiorem quæsiuerunt, &c. Ita sæpè gulosis euenit,&c.
units.tr: They throw the wheat into the sea. They sought a more delicate harbour, and so on. So it often happens to gluttons, and so on.

units.la: Interim magnum hoc fidei argumentum est, quod nimirū certò crediderunt, se saluos fore, sicut Deus promiserat. Alioqui nunquam effudisset commeatum, qui vnicus restabat ipsis,&c.
units.tr: Meanwhile this is a great proof of faith, that they firmly believed they would be saved, just as God had promised. Otherwise they would never have poured out the provisions which alone remained to them, and so on.

units.la: Nota. Deo vocante & iubente, ea quo que dimittenda esse, sine quibus vita seruari non posse videtur, Luc.14. Sic Abraham, Gen.12.22. Sic Apostoli, Matth.4.19. 9. Huc pertinet, Rom.8. Heb.11. &c.
units.tr: Note: When God calls and commands, we must also let go of those things without which life seems unable to be preserved (Luke 14). So Abraham (Gen. 12, 22), so the apostles (Matt. 4, 19; 9). To this belongs Rom. 8, Heb. 11, and so on.

units.la: III. Describitur naufragium, vbi multa simul occurrunt, quæ fidem potuerunt labefactare. Non nouerunt littus. Nescsiunt ergo aut in hostes aut in amicos incidant. Periculum frequens naufragij. Ita spes salutis sese eminus ostendens, simul terrorem haud vulgarem admixtum habuit,&c.
units.tr: III. The shipwreck is described, where many things occur together which could have shaken their faith. They did not know the shore. They therefore did not know whether they were running into enemies or friends. Frequent danger in shipwreck. So hope of salvation, showing itself from afar, had mixed with it no little terror, and so on.

units.la: II. Cum omni conatu ad littus tendunt, incidunt in locum bimarem, vbi prora immobili hærente, puppis vi fluctum soluitur. Et hic elucet veritas Dei, qui dixerat nauem perituram, quæ iam euasisse videbatur. Typus eorum, qui contra Dei verbum felices esse in peccatis, & ita perpetuò mansuri videntur. Vide de his Psal. mo 37. 55. 73 &c. Maximum quoque
units.tr: II. With every effort they make for the shore, but they fall into a place between two seas, where the prow sticks fast and the stern is broken up by the force of the waves. And here the truth of God shines forth, who had said that the ship would perish, though it seemed already to have escaped. It is a type of those who seem to prosper in sin against the word of God and to remain so forever. See on these matters Psalms 37, 55, 73, and so on. Also the greatest

units.la: O o o 4 malum ad nautas redit peffimi consilij auc thores.
units.tr: evil returns to the sailors, the authors of the wicked plan.

units.la: III. Milites consultant de captiuis occidendis, ne quis euadat. Mouentur nimirum seueritate legum, quæ tunc fuit, vt vidimus, Actorum duodecimo. Sed iniquitas summa, quod ne Paulum quidem excipiunt, cui vitam non semel debebant. Et hoc quidè periculum ipso naufragio maius fuit. Vides quæ mundi ingratitudo, & quid ab hoc exspectes. Stulti qui huic plac-ere studeant, & non potius Deum obseruant. Interim non deterreamur à beneficiendo, sed remuneratorem Deum obseruemus, qui ex hominibus etiam aliquos mouere potest, vt grati sint, &c.
units.tr: III. The soldiers deliberate about killing the captives, so that none escapes. They are moved, no doubt, by the severity of the laws then in force, as we saw in Acts 12. But their injustice is extreme, since they do not even spare Paul, to whom they owed their lives more than once. And this danger was greater than the shipwreck itself. You see what the ingratitude of the world is, and what you may expect from it. Foolish are those who strive to please it and do not rather observe God. Meanwhile let us not be deterred from doing good, but let us observe God, the rewarder, who can also move some men to be grateful, and so on.

units.la: IV. Centurio saluum volens Paulum, obstat militibus, & iubet vt qui possunt enatent, reliqui tabulis vtantur. Prudens consilium. Itaque omnes salui euadunt, & terram contingunt. Rursum vides quàm prosit cum bonis conuersari.
units.tr: IV. The centurion, wishing Paul to be saved, opposes the soldiers and orders that those who can swim should swim, and the rest use planks. A prudent counsel. So all escape safely and reach the land. Again you see how useful it is to live among good men.

units.la: NOT. Veritatem promissionum Dei, quæ nullis aduersis impediri potest. Vi-dentur omnia in Pauli necem coniurauif-se. Mare. Aer ventis inquietus. Terra nauim detinens. Stellæ negant lucem. Nautæ perfidi. Milites truculentissimi. Sed ne quicquam sunt omnia. Saluantur, vt Deus promisit. Hæc Hęc nos solentur inter huius mundi pericula. Veri samur in mari turbulentissimo. Fiunt quæ prædicta sunt Matt 24. &c. Sed Dei promissiones habemus, Psal. 50. 145. Isaiæ 65. &c. Christum quoque præsentem, Matthæi 28. 18. Iohan. 14. Quis ergo contra nos? Rom. 8. Euademus feliciter in portum salutis, vtut mundus hic tumultuetur & ferociat. Versemur in horum meditatione. Oremus.
units.tr: NOTE: The truth of God's promises, which no adversity can hinder. Everything seems to have conspired against Paul's death. The sea. The air restless with winds. The land holding back the ship. The stars deny light. The sailors faithless. The soldiers most savage. But all these things are nothing. They are saved, as God promised. Let us be comforted by this among the dangers of this world. We are tossed on the most turbulent sea. What was foretold (Matt. 24) comes to pass. But we have God's promises (Psalms 50, 145; Isaiah 65), and Christ present with us (Matt. 28:18; John 14). Who then is against us? (Rom. 8). We shall escape happily into the harbour of salvation, however much this world rages and rampages. Let us dwell in the meditation of these things. Let us pray.

units.la: CAPVT XXVIII. HOMILIA CCIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII. HOMILY CCIII.

units.la: ETcum euasissent, tunc cognoverunt quod Melite insula vocaretur.
units.tr: And when they had escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita.

units.la: 2 Barbari vero præstabant non bu non vulgarem humanitatem: ac censa enim pyra, acceperunt nos omnes propter imbrem, qui vrgebat, & propter frigus.
units.tr: And the barbarians showed us no common kindness; for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the rain that pressed upon us and because of the cold.

units.la: EXposuit hucusq; Lucas, vt Dei Paul nauigantis curam habuerit, & fideliter præstiterit promissiones. Sequitur vt ex naufragio ereptum porrò seruârit, imò vt apud Melitenses illustrem fecerit, & po-
units.tr: Luke has now set out how Paul, while sailing, had God's care, and how faithfully God fulfilled his promises. It follows that God, having rescued him from the shipwreck, further preserved him, and indeed made him famous among the Melitans, and afterwards gave him an occasion for preaching to them at Rome.

units.la: ftca Romæ eidem dederit occasione prædicandi. Vsus totius historiæ est, Dei gratiam non exhauriri, & hunc continuare fauorem suum, ideoq; ex prioribus beneficijs nos noua fidei confirmande argumenta petere debere. Sic Dauid Psal. 22. 1. Sam. 7. Applicent hoc sibi singuli in morbis, in exilio, in fame, &c. In præsenti, vt Melitenses naufragos exceperint, narratur.
units.tr: The use of the whole history is that God's grace is never exhausted, and that he continues his favour; therefore from earlier benefits we ought to draw new arguments for strengthening faith. So David (Ps. 22; 1 Sam. 7). Let each apply this to himself in sickness, in exile, in famine, and so on. In the present passage it is narrated how the Melitans received the shipwrecked men.

units.la: 1. Cum euasissent, agnouerunt insulam Melitam esse. Fuit hæc prima consolatio. Prius enim rerum incerti erant & dubij, ne in hostes inciderent. Sed ducit Deus ad amicos, & in eum locum, vbi Romani regnabant.
units.tr: 1. When they had escaped, they recognised that the island was Melita. This was the first consolation. For before, they had been uncertain and in doubt about their circumstances, lest they fall into enemies' hands. But God leads them to friends, and into a place where the Romans ruled.

units.la: NOTA. Deum subito posse pericula auertere, & præter opinionem nos securos facere. Sunt huius generis exempla passim. Nemo igitur temere desperet, aut facile terreatur.
units.tr: NOTE. That God can suddenly turn away dangers and make us safe beyond expectation. There are examples of this kind everywhere. Let no one therefore despair rashly or be easily terrified.

units.la: II. Quomodo accepti fuerint? Barbari præstiterunt non vulgarem humanitatem. Nec enim hospitio solum excipiunt, sed ignem accendunt, vt rigentes præfrigore & fessos foueant. Vnde colligitur, quod neque reliqua officia hospitalitis omiserint.
units.tr: II. How they were received. The barbarians showed no common kindness. For they received them not only with hospitality but kindled a fire to warm those who were chilled by the cold and weary. From this it is gathered that they also did not omit the other duties of hospitality.

units.la: NOTA. 1. Exemplum hospitalitatis & charitatis. Nesciebant Melitenfes, qui nam isti effent, & ex naufragis nullam remunerationem sperare poterant. Quia tamen miseros & indigos vident, ipso-rum miserti hæc faciunt. Et hanc legem charitatis Christus præscribit, Luc.10. Imi-temur nos erga quosuis, maximè erga pe-regrinos, qui ferè pluribus egent, & ideo nobis palsim commendantur, Exod. 22. Deuteron. 15. 16. &c. Item ad Hebræos 13. Et constat huius studiosissimos fuisse Pa-tres. Vide Abrahamum, Genef. 18. Lo-thum, Genef. 19. &c. Neque id fine fructu fit, quia in his ipse Christus excipitur. Lo-thus multum profuit Sodomæis, Gen. 14. 19. Iofephus Ægyptijs, Genef. 39. &c. Melitenfes quoque habuerunt suam re-tributionem. Obferuârunt hæc Maiores nostri, qui ex hospitalitate summam lau-dem habuerunt.
units.tr: NOTE. 1. An example of hospitality and charity. The Melitans did not know who these men were, and could hope for no reward from the shipwrecked. Yet because they saw them wretched and needy, they did these things out of pity for them. And Christ prescribes this law of charity (Luke 10). Let us imitate this towards all, especially towards strangers, who for the most part lack help, and are therefore commended to us on every side (Exod. 22; Deut. 15, 16, etc.); likewise Hebrews 13. And it is evident that the Fathers were most diligent in this. See Abraham (Gen. 18), Lot (Gen. 19), etc. Nor is this done without fruit, because in these people Christ himself is received. Lot profited the Sodomites greatly (Gen. 14, 19); Joseph the Egyptians (Gen. 39, etc.). The Melitans too had their recompense. Our forefathers observed these things, who gained the highest praise from hospitality.

units.la: ¶ 2. Inprimis verò horum meminerint magistratus. Si enim omnium est ista præ-stare, multò magis eorum fuerit, quos in eum finem Deus ordinauit, vt quosuis tu-antur. Cogitent ergo fe propter populū in hunc gradum constitutos esse, vt Dei iu-dicia exerceant, & affliftis opem ferant, Pfalm. 72. Beneficus erit in attritos & ino-pes, & animas pauperum seruabit.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Above all, magistrates should remember these things. For if it belongs to all to perform such things, it belongs much more to those whom God has appointed to this end, that they should protect everyone. Let them therefore consider that they have been placed in this rank for the sake of the people, so that they may execute God's judgements and bring help to the afflicted (Ps. 72). "He will be merciful to the broken and the needy, and will save the souls of the poor."

units.la: Redimet animas eorum à fœnore & vio‑lentia, & precio‑sus erit sanguis eorum in oculis suis. Vide Pfalm.72. Liberabit pau‑perem clamantem & affli‑ctum, cui deest adiutor, &c. Et ibidem amplissima præ‑mia promittuntur. Longævitas, Imperij propagatio, Gloria, Incolumitas publi‑ca. Hæc vtinam hodie omnes obserua‑rent.
units.tr: "He will redeem their souls from usury and violence, and their blood will be precious in their eyes." See Ps. 72: "He will deliver the poor man crying out and the afflicted one who has no helper," etc. And in the same psalm the most ample rewards are promised: long life, the extension of empire, glory, public safety. Would that all today observed these things.

units.la: ¶ 2. Consolationem hinc petant omnes afflicti, maximè qui propter religionem exulant, &c. Domini est omnis terra, Pfal. 24. ideoque passim feruare potest. Idem manu sua tenet omnium hominum cor‑da. Prouerb.21. Potest ergo vbiuis lo‑corum nobis amicos parare, & oportet promissionem impleri, Mar.19. Experi‑untur hoc multi hodie. Huic ergo nos ap‑probare studeamus, &c.
units.tr: ¶ 2. Let all the afflicted take consolation from this, especially those who are in exile on account of religion, etc. The earth is the Lord's (Ps. 24), and therefore he can preserve us everywhere. The same holds the hearts of all men in his hand (Prov. 21). He can therefore procure friends for us in any place, and the promise must be fulfilled (Mark 19). Many experience this today. Let us therefore strive to be approved to him, etc.

units.la: III. Exemplum Lucæ, qui humanitate hanc tam magnificè describit, & gratiam refert quam potest. Vbi No T. ¶ Quid fie ri debeat à nobis. Gratitudinem lex natu‑ræ commendat, quæ nobis illius exem‑pla in brutis animalibus & in ipsa terra proponit. Hanc ergo singuli præstent om‑nibus. Liberi parentibus. Subditi ma‑gistratibus. Inopes diuitibus. Quòd si gratiam referre non potes, saltem prædi‑ca beca beneficium verbis, & bene precare be-nefactoribus.
units.tr: III. The example of Luke, who describes the kindness so splendidly and records the thanks as far as he can. Here note: what ought to be done by us. The law of nature commends gratitude, and sets before us examples of it in brute animals and in the earth itself. Let each therefore show it to all: children to parents, subjects to magistrates, the poor to the rich. But if you cannot repay the favour, at least proclaim the benefit with words, and bless your benefactors well.

units.la: Peccatur hodie in hoc multiuariàm. Multi beneficia extenuant, & contemptim de illis loquuntur. Multi etiam inuident ijs, à quibus maxima subinde accipiunt. Sunt hi similes Iudæ, Ioh. 12. Maximè hic in magistratum peccatur ab ijs, qui huic imprimis negotia faciunt. Punietingratitudinem hanc Deus,
units.tr: Today this is sinned against in many ways. Many diminish benefits and speak of them with contempt. Many also envy those from whom they receive the greatest things from time to time. These are like Judas (John 12). Most of all this sin is committed against the magistrate by those who especially make a business of it. God will punish this ingratitude.

units.la: Officium ergo singuli faciant, & publicæ salutis studeant. Oremus.
units.tr: Let each therefore perform his duty and strive for the public welfare. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CXCIV.
units.tr: HOMILY CXCIV.

units.la: 1 Quum igitur connoluisset Paulus virgultorum fasces, & imposuisset in pyram, vipera è calore prorepens inuasit eius manum.
units.tr: When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened on his hand.

units.la: 4 Vt verò Barbari viderunt pendentem bestiam exipfius manu, alij alijs dicebant, Omnino homicida est homo ille, quem seruatum è mari vltio non sinit viuere.
units.tr: When the barbarians saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, "Surely this man is a murderer, whom Justice does not allow to live, though he was saved from the sea."

units.la: 5 At ille excussa bestia in ignem nihil malipassus est.
units.tr: But he shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.

units.la: 6 Illi verò exspectabant dum intumescere aut concideret repente mortu-us. Sed quum multum tempus exspeflàssent, & viderent nihil incommodi illi contingere, mutati dicebant eum esse Deum.
units.tr: They expected that he would swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw that nothing unusual happened to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

units.la: Quoniam Deus suos paterno amore prosequitur, non modo in periculis & afflictionibus eos seruat, nec suc-cumbant, verum etiam euentum omnem sic gubernat, vt quae illis exitio fore videbantur, in bonû adiumento sint, & ipsorum tam gloriae quàm saluti seruiant. Exempla passim occurrunt, quorum omnium hic vsus est, vt patienter feramus quaecunque Deus imponit, & illius ope exspectemus cum silentio, certi, quòd cum ratione omnia faciat, & moram tandem auxilij & libe-rationis gloria compensset. Facit huc histo-ria praesens, quae insigne miraculum conti-net, quo Deus Paulum, ante toto biennio captiuum & iam naufragum quoque, apud peregrinam & barbaram gentem ita commendauit, vt non modo ipsum in honore haberent, sed insuper propter ipsum omnibus aliis benefecerint. Quia tamen multa alia quoque hic continentur, pro dérit singulas partes inspicere.
units.tr: Since God cares for his own with a father's love, he not only preserves them in dangers and afflictions, so that they do not perish, but also so governs every outcome that what seemed bound to ruin them turns to their good and serves both their glory and their salvation. Examples occur everywhere, and the lesson of them all is this: that we should bear patiently whatever God lays upon us, and wait for his help in silence, certain that he does all things with reason and will at last repay the delay of help and deliverance with glory. The present history bears on this, for it contains a remarkable miracle by which God so commended Paul, who had been a prisoner for two years and was now also shipwrecked, among a foreign and barbarous people, that they not only held him in honour but, because of him, did good to all the others as well. Since many other things are also contained here, let us look at the individual parts.

units.la: I. Occasio. Paulus colligit sarmenta, im-ponit igni, vipera prosiliens inuadit eius manum, &c. NOTA. ¶ 1. Pauli laboriosam induindustriam. Catenam trahebat, inter nauı gandum præ aliis laborat, modò enatauế‐rat, & dignus erat qui quı sciceret. Sed præ aliis laborat. Commendatur nobis hoc ex‐emplo labor & industria, quæ vt priuatim singulos decet, (quia otium est malefua‐dum,) ita maximē ir publicis necessitati‐bus requiruntur. Tunc enim nemo suo o‐tio consulere debet. Vide Mosem, Heb. ii. Dauidem i. Sam. 17. Arguuntur primò qui charitatis lege abutuntur, vt viuant ex a‐liorum laboribus. Vide 2. Thessal. 3. Item personati Pauli successores, qui Ecclesia‐sticos quoq; labores fugiunt.
units.tr: I. The occasion. Paul gathers sticks, puts them on the fire, a viper leaping out fastens on his hand, and so on. NOTE. ¶ 1. Paul's laborious industry. He was a prisoner dragged in chains, yet during the voyage he laboured more than the others; he had just swum ashore and deserved to rest, yet he works harder than the rest. By this example labour and diligence are commended to us. As they befit each person in private (since idleness is to be avoided), so they are required all the more in public necessities; for then no one should consult his own leisure. See Moses, Heb. ii.; David, 1 Sam. 17. Here are first rebuked those who abuse the law of charity to live off the labours of others. See 2 Thess. 3. Likewise the successors of Paul in name only, who shun even the labours of the Church.

units.la: ¶ 2. Casum mirabilem, qui & vitæ pe‐riculum ferebat, & Melitensibus pessimè de illo suspicandi occasionem præbebat. Homicidij enim insimulant, & quòd illum vltio diuina persequatur. Gentes enim lege naturæ edosti sciebant, Deum pecca‐ta non impunita sinere. Nemesis. Inter peccata autem iam inde ab origine mun‐di homicidium iudicatum esse atrocissi‐mum. Lex vetustissima, Gen. 4 & 9. Hinc exilia, expiationes laboriosæ. Quò magis annitendum Christianis, ne homicidia grassentur. Punit Deus & in hoc seculo, & in futuro, Numerorum 35. Deuter. 27. Psal. 55. Apocal. 21. Obseruemus autem mirabilia Iudicia Dei, qui suorum gloriam per ea maximè illustrat, quæ illis officere videntur. Sic Moses in exilium profugit,sed inde reuocatur, vt populi viridex fiat. Sic Dauid. Non ergo desperemus in eiusmodi casibus. Idem capiti nostro, Christo accidit, Pfalm.110. Si non hic liberamur,sal-tem memoria afferetur, Pfalm.112. Simul discant omnes moderari sua iudicia, ne te merè damnent, quos affligi vident, Pf.73. Luc.13. Peccatur hic hodie multiuariàm, &c.
units.tr: ¶ 2. The wonderful event, which both carried a danger to his life and gave the Melitans a bad reason to suspect the worst of him. They accuse him of murder, and say that divine vengeance pursues him. For the nations, taught by the law of nature, knew that God does not allow sins to go unpunished: this is Nemesis. Among sins, murder has been judged the most atrocious from the very beginning of the world. It is the most ancient law, Gen. 4 and 9. Hence come exiles and laborious expiations. All the more must Christians strive that murders do not run riot. God punishes both in this age and in the future: Num. 35; Deut. 27; Ps. 55; Rev. 21. Let us observe, however, the wonderful judgments of God, who most of all displays the glory of his own through the very things that seem to harm them. So Moses fled into exile, but was recalled from there so that he might become the deliverer of the people. So David. Let us therefore not despair in such cases. The same thing happened to our head, Christ: Ps. 110. If we are not delivered here, at least the memory will be brought to us: Ps. 112. At the same time let everyone learn to moderate their judgments, so that they do not condemn outright those whom they see afflicted: Ps. 73; Luke 13. Sin is committed here today in many ways, etc.

units.la: II. Miraculum. Paulus excutit viperam in ignem, nec quicquam patitur. Impletur promissio, Mar.16. Videmus, vt in media morte Deus possit feruare.
units.tr: II. The miracle. Paul shakes the viper into the fire and suffers nothing. The promise in Mark 16 is fulfilled. We see that God can preserve in the very midst of death.

units.la: Sed Nota. ¶ Veterem serpentem nihil habere iuris in fideles. Momordit omnes in Adamo. Et adhuc inuadit manus & pedes. Sed non nocet lethaliter. Vicit enim hunc Christus, & exarmauit, Iohannis 14. Idem medetur nobis, Isaiæ 53. Typus æneî serpentis, Iohan.3.
units.tr: But note. ¶ The old serpent has no right over the faithful. He bit everyone in Adam, and still attacks hands and feet; but he does not harm them fatally. For Christ has conquered him and disarmed him: John 14. The same Christ heals us: Isa. 53. The type is the bronze serpent, John 3.

units.la: Interim officij nostri est, non locum dare diaboló, sed illum excutere; & procul ablegare, 1.Pet.5. Arguuntur, qui eius contortia quærunt, & sponte fe illi quasi in fauces ingerunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile it is our duty not to give the devil a place, but to shake him off and drive him far away: 1 Pet. 5. Those are rebuked who seek out his snares and of their own accord throw themselves, as it were, into his jaws.

units.la: III. Effectus miraculi apud Melitenses. Vbi hoc vident, mutata mente dicunt Deum esse. Est hic error gentilitius, quo magnorum beneficiorum authores & miraculis illustres in Deorum numerum referebantur. Ita illos decipiebat Satan, vt in proximis causis haerentes, non attollerent animos ad omnis boni authorem, Deum, ad Romanos primo. Ita postea factum, quoad cultum Diuorum. Et facile hoc patitur Satan, modo à Christo abducat, & vt Dei cultum impediat.
units.tr: III. The effect of the miracle among the Melitans. When they see this, they change their minds and say that he is God. This is a heathen error, by which the authors of great benefits and men illustrious for miracles were counted among the gods. Satan deceived them in this way, so that, fixed on secondary causes, they did not raise their minds to God, the author of every good: Romans 1. This happened later too, in the worship of the deified dead. And Satan readily allows this, provided that he draws people away from Christ and hinders the worship of God.

units.la: Imò hodie adhuc durat apud Meliten-ses ortus error, quando sunt, qui Pauli fa-miliam mentiti, serpentes alunt, &c.
units.tr: Indeed, even today the error that arose among the Melitans persists, when there are those who falsely claim to be of Paul's family and keep snakes, etc.

units.la: Sed No T. Vulgi inconstantiam. Pau-lo ante homicidam dixerunt, nunc Deum. Simile quid, sed diuerso ordine, Lystris ac cidit, Actorum decimoquarto. Sic cum Christo factum, Iohan.6. Item Ioh. 7.18. 19. Item Mar.11.15.
units.tr: But note. ¶ The fickleness of the crowd. Shortly before they called him a murderer, now they call him God. Something similar, but in a different order, happened at Lystra: Acts 14. So it happened with Christ: John 6. Likewise John 7:18–19; Mark 11:15.

units.la: Nemo igitur fidat hominibus, sed ab vno Deo omnes pendeant, & huic studeant se approbare, &c. Oremus.
units.tr: Therefore let no one trust in men, but let all depend on the one God, and strive to approve themselves to him, etc. Let us pray.

units.la: HOMILIA CCV.
units.tr: HOMILY CCV.

units.la: 7 Caeterum circa locum illum erant praedia cuidam primario insulae, nomi-
units.tr: 7 Now there were estates near that place belonging to a leading man of the island, named Publius, who received us kindly and entertained us in his lodging for three days.

units.la: mine Publio, qui nos exceptos triduo peramice in hospitio habuit.
units.tr: (Continued from 7) Publius was a man of rank on the island, and he treated us with great friendliness.

units.la: 8 Factum est autem, vt pater Publij febribus ac dysenteria detentus decumberet: ad quem Paulus ingressus, quum precatus esset, impositis ei manibus, sanauit eum.
units.tr: 8 It happened that the father of Publius lay sick, held down by fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.

units.la: 9 Hoc igitur facto, reliqui etiam qui morbis tenebantur in insula, accedebant et sanabuntur.
units.tr: 9 When this had happened, the others on the island who were afflicted with diseases also came and were healed.

units.la: 10 Qui etiam multis honoribus nos honorarunt, et quum proficisceremur, imposuerunt quae vsui nobis erant.
units.tr: 10 They honoured us with many honours, and when we were setting out, they put on board whatever we needed.

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus Marci 10.ait: Nullus est, qui reliquit domum, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut parentes, aut liberos, aut vxorem, aut agros, mea causa & Euangelij, qui non recipiat centupla, &c. Experti sunt hoc Apostoli, quibus cum Christum sequerentur, nihil vnquam defuit, Luc.22. Et postea passim inuenerunt, qui illis fratrum, patrum & filiorum loco fuerunt. Vidimus idem in Paulo huc usque, & in hoc capite hoc ipsum euidentissimè cernitur. Qui enim omnia propter Christum reliquerat, nunc captiuus & naufragus in Melitam venit. Sed mox inuenit fratres, prædia, domus, &c. Imo qui inter Iudaeos contemnebatur, hic tantae authoritatis est, vt propter ipsum reliquis omnibus benefaciant. Et huc facit in primis historia huius loci, quae haec habet.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ says in Mark 10: "There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or parents, or children, or wife, or fields, for my sake and the gospel's, who will not receive a hundredfold," etc. The apostles experienced this, for when they followed Christ, nothing ever failed them (Luke 22). Afterwards, too, they everywhere found people who took the place of brothers, fathers and children for them. We have seen the same in Paul up to this point, and in this chapter it is most plainly seen. He who had left everything for Christ's sake now comes to Malta as a captive and a shipwrecked man, but soon he finds brothers, estates, houses, and so on. Indeed, he who was despised among the Jews is held in such authority that, for his sake, they do good to all the rest. The history of this place, which runs as follows, bears directly on this.

units.la: I. Hospitalitatis exemplum nouum, Publij praesidis. Is in praedijs vicinis exci- pit simul omnes, & toto triduo benignissimè tractat. Eftq; haec beneficentia eó illustrior, quòd homo princeps & diues, ideoque nullius egens, non aspernatur ignotos, imò necaptiuos quidem. Item quòd sine delecta omnes excipit, numero 276. Praestat verè legem de diligendo proximo, Luc. 10.
units.tr: I. A new example of hospitality from Publius, the governor. He receives them all together on his nearby estates and treats them most kindly for the whole three days. This kindness is all the more notable because he is a leading man and wealthy, and so in need of nothing, yet he does not scorn strangers, nor even captives. Again, because he receives them all without distinction (number 276). He truly fulfils the law about loving one's neighbour (Luke 10).

units.la: NOT. Charitatem & beneficentiam omnes decere, & in primis magistratus, Luc. 22. His potissimum commendantur peregrini, viduae, pupilli, pauperes, Psal. 71. &c. Non temerè ergo tales sibi offerri putent. Vide Maiores nostros. Idem ad se trahant alij, qui opibus valent. Meminerint has non sibi solis datas esse, vt suae seruiant libidini, sed se à Deo dispensatores esse constitutos. Lucae 16. Faciant ergo quod habetur posteriore ad Corinthios octauo. Peccant grauiter, qui immi sericordes sibi solis viuunt. Est hoc Sodo mae peccatu, Ezechielis decimo sexto. Et
units.tr: NOTE. Charity and beneficence befit everyone, and especially magistrates (Luke 22). Strangers, widows, orphans and the poor are especially commended to these (Psalm 71, etc.). Therefore let them not think such people are offered to them by chance. Look at our forebears. Let others who are powerful in wealth draw the same to themselves. Let them remember that these things have not been given to them alone, to serve their own lust, but that they have been appointed by God as stewards (Luke 16). Let them therefore do what is written in the later letter to the Corinthians, chapter eight. They sin gravely who live for themselves alone without mercy. This is the sin of Sodom (Ezekiel 16). And
